News.title: Russian soldiers drink urine & eat bark after their own twisted officers abandon them to Ukraine breakthrough offensive
News.content:
Next

DOZENS of Russian soldiers have surrendered after resorting to drinking their own urine to survive – as their high-ranking commanders left them for dead.

Footage shows 94 troops – many of them looking weak and malnourished – lining up in a single file in Donetsk, eastern Ukraine.



The highest-ranking officer among the prisoners of war (PoW), Alexander Manankov, steps upfront to speak on behalf of them, in a video released by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps.

“We surrendered because we did not want to die in vain,” he said.



“Our officers actually ran away… We had no water at our positions. We had to drink water from puddles, we had to drink our own urine.

“We had no food. We had to eat tree bark and grass. We did not have the medicine to help the wounded soldiers.

“Our command simply forgot about us. We were expendable. Therefore, the decision was made to surrender.”

Manankov further appealed to other Russian soldiers used by the Kremlin as “meat assault troops” to not be afraid to surrender.

“The propaganda being spread among us is a pure lie,” he added. “Here you are guaranteed food, water, normal nutrition and living conditions.”

With tears in his eyes, a soldier said one of their comrades had died from dehydration.



“We were starving and sitting there a month and a half ago,” he added. “I ate properly for the first time here, in captivity.

Smoking a cigarette with shaking hands, another said their commanders ordered them to “take up a circular defence” and turned off their radio.

He added three people died due to the lack of medication. Their bodies were never retrieved.



Another Russian servicemember credited Ukrainian troops with removing a piece of shrapnel from his skull and a second from his lower back.

Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, said “Russians surrendered in captivity by entire sub-units, along with officers, pilots, and artillerymen.”

“The enemy’s losses – 2,000 in manpower, over 250 Russians captured as PoWs,” he revealed.



Biletskyi said the success was the third “season” of Vivaldi, an operation to recapture in full the Donetsk region.

Total Russian losses during the three phases amounted to around 5,000 killed and wounded on this section of the front alone.

A special unit was set up within the Corps with the task of bluffing some combat operations that did not correspond to what was happening on the ground.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The latest phase recaptured 31 square miles of territory, bringing the total recovered during Vivaldi to 109 square miles, according to the Third Army Corps.

Among them are Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka as well as Karpivka and Novomikhailivka.

News.title: Brave girl, 6, ‘heard screams in cockpit during hijacking attempt before dad rushed to help stabbed captain’
News.content:
HIJACK HERO Brave girl, 6, ‘heard screams in cockpit during hijacking attempt before dad rushed to help stabbed captain’







Next

ONE of the heroes in the attempted hijack of the Israeli-bound Flydubai jet raced inside the cockpit after hearing the screams of his daughter.

Nina Manes, aged six, was travelling with her parents Tali and Tzika on the hellish flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.



The girl had asked her mother to accompany her to the bathroom at the exact moment when chaos erupted on the flight as the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an alleged attempt to take over the Boeing 737 and crash it.

Her mother heard the suspicious commotion in the cockpit.



As Tali went over to alert cabin crew, the captain fell through the cockpit door with the co-pilot still stabbing him.

“There was blood all over the cockpit and very, very sharp fighting moves,” she told the Israeli Channel 12.



“I screamed, ‘He is stabbing the pilot, he is stabbing the pilot, come help!’ People looked at me and didn’t understand.”

The plane then “entered a tailspin and began to dive,” plummeting 17,400 feet in 90 seconds.

This is when Nina’s father, Tzvika, rushed to grab his daughter from the bathroom.

He said: “The shreaks of my daughters when the plane nosedived [are still with me].



“They said, ‘Dad we don’t want to die.’ [Their cries] were the triggers that caused me to run inside the cockpit.”

He and two other passengers then rushed into the cockpit to neutralise the suspect.

Footage shows them pinning down the alleged attacker and also aiding the injured pilot.



At the same time, one of the additional pilots was already taking control of the aircraft’s controls.

Tzvika told CNN: “We asked if there was a doctor on the plane, there was a dentist actually…

“He saved the life of the Indian captain, gave him oxygen, stopped his bleeding with blankets and all kinds of equipment that was in the area.”



There were 174 passengers, 166 of them Israeli, on board the plane, which eventually landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

So far, the only piece of information released about the assailant is that he is from Oman, but Omani authorities are yet to confirm this.

One of the major twists is indeed his nationality.

As per security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel cannot work on flights to Israel.

Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox: “We have constraints that say you cannot have pilots ⁠from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel.



“So obviously he was able to go through that.”

Multiple investigations are ongoing – in Saudi Arabia, where the suspect is being held, in the UAE and Israel.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

This comes as Donald Trump suggested – but went short of confirming – that Iran was involved in the attack.

When questioned whether the Islamic Republic was behind the attack, he told reporters: “I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now.”

News.title: I’m the last one left on a village street set to be demolished for Universal’s new £5bn theme park – I’m not budging
News.content:
Next

ONE resident is the final man left on a village street set to be demolished to make way for Universal Studio’s £5billion UK theme park.

Ritchie Wood is determined not to be pushed out of his rental home, as all other neighbours on his road in Kempston Hardwick have moved out.



Wood has called the once-countryside village home for 11 years, noting its friendly community and abundance in wildlife.

But over the past few months, residents have slowly been moving out of Manor Road, knowing their homes are set to be demolished.



The street now lies in what will soon be Universal’s new and only Europe-based theme park.

Speaking to the BBC, Wood said: “It’s totally changed to how it used to be – it used to be lovely. We had a nice little community here, lots of wildlife, very quiet.”

The man’s landlord has now sold the home, and Wood knows he will be asked to leave imminently.

He said: “I genuinely have nowhere to go.



“Unfortunately, I wouldn’t be able to afford anywhere in the area for the same sort of rent [I pay now].”

At first Wood was not alone – a number of residents faced the developer and refused to leave their homes.

However, despite protest, all but one packed their bags and demolition work on the homes has now begun.

The road is now closed until November 28 while lorries and diggers tear down the strip.

Wood has called the situation heartbreaking, adding the rubble of once-homes feels surreal.



In a letter sent to residents, Universal said: “We remain committed to being a good neighbour and will continue to update our local

community as our activity progresses.”

Universal United Kingdom Resort, set to open in 2031, will spread across 476 acres and feature the theme park as well as hotels, restaurants, shops and even room for possible future expansion.

While no rides have been confirmed, plans state: “[Guests will] experience blockbuster attractions, adrenaline-pumping coasters, and mind-blowing spectaculars.



“They’ll come face-to-face with incredible creatures, heroes, and villains.

“They’ll discover great food, new laughs, new ways to play, and step into immersive worlds they’ve only ever dreamed of.”

According to analysis by Universal Destinations & Experiences, the theme park could generate almost £50bn of economic value to the UK in its first 20 years.

It is also set to support 20,000 jobs, half of which would be direct employment, and the remainder supplying services to support the site.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A new train station for exclusive park use is also set to open, connecting connect Oxford to Cambridge via Milton Keynes and Bedford.



Universal and Central Bedfordshire Council have been contacted for a response.

News.title: A66 death crash joyrider’s dad, 40, faces jail today for attacking celebrant at his son’s funeral
News.content:
Next

THE dad of one of the A66 yobs who crashed into a police car killing two officers faces jail today for attacking the celebrant at his son’s funeral.

Gye Worthy, 40, flew into a rage when Paul Maull failed to mention him in the eulogy to son Cole Worthy but did reference the teen’s step-dad.



He hurled insults and then attacked him as shocked mourners looked on.

When cops raced to Teesside Crematorium, he also got into a fracas with them.



A source close to the family said that Cole’s mother Natalie McConnell was left “devastated and shocked” by the chaos.

Offshore worker Gye, lives in Acklam, Middlesbrough, where his £200,000 home was rammed on August 22 in an attack directed at his son.

It was part of an escalating gang war which exploded a short time later as Cole, 17, and four pals leapt into a VW Passat and went hunting their rivals.

Cops spotted the car which had cloned plates and gave chase briefly but abandoned it when the motor went the wrong way along the A66.

Moments later it crashed into PC Matthew Blades, 37 and PC Tom Clough, 38, killing both officers and all five occupants of the Passat.

Police said they all had links to organised crime



There is no suggestion that Gye Worthy is linked to organised crime.

He will be sentenced at Teesside JPs court today.

News.title: Burnham’s Man City gaffe is rocket fuel for Farage as he takes every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Burnham’s Man City gaffe is rocket fuel for Farage as he takes every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts







Next

NIGEL Farage vowed to save Brexit as he kick-started Reform’s “general election campaign” in Yorkshire.

At a packed rally in Doncaster, the party leader laid into the PM and fired up activists with his greatest hits.



Reform in power would axe Net Zero, slash migration and cut welfare spending, he told the crowd.

But fundamentally, Mr Farage was there to rally the troops after a bruising 12 months.



Sting operations and rows over donations have dented Reform’s poll lead, while the road to power remains a rocky one.

Recent surveys have put Reform, Labour and the Tories almost neck-and-neck in the race for Number 10.



But Mr Farage reassured activists — some sporting Farage No10 football shirts — that the PM’s hints of reopening the Brexit wars had handed him fresh ammunition.

Leave-voting areas such as Doncaster could prove crucial at the next election, with Labour facing a battle to hold on to its Red Wall seats.

Mr Farage, in full pantomime mode, had the crowd jeering senior Labour figures in Yorkshire, including Yvette Cooper and Ed “Moribund” Miliband.

Mr Burnham, meanwhile, is no stranger to putting his foot in it — most recently with his intervention in the Manchester City case.



A tanned Mr Farage then shot off in his helicopter after the rally, promising to hit the road and get Reform campaign-ready.

Whatever happens, this is rocket fuel for a leader looking for every opportunity to hit the PM where it hurts.

News.title: Angry bird, Trump lookalike croc & bears sharing a joke lead comedy wildlife photo contest – but which is your winner?
News.content:
MAKE IT SNAPPY Angry bird, Trump lookalike croc & bears sharing a joke lead comedy wildlife photo contest – but which is your winner?







Next

THE finalists for the Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards have been revealed – and one lookalike may ruffle some feathers.

Only time will tell whether a sweary orangutan or a grinning croc with a mop of seaweed hair will snap up the prize.



The orange beast was snapped raising his middle finger – while making direct eye contact with the camera.

And one golden ball of feathers was caught with a blazing frown – and dubbed “Angry Bird” by photographer Jan Wittmer.



A total of 40 photos are vying to be top of the pecking order.

Sent in from all over the world, the collection showcases wildlife at its cutest, funniest or most outrageous situations.



The finalists were selected from a vast pool of over 10,000 entries from 112 countries – the highest number in history.

One reptilean beast emerged from a swamp with a mop of black seaweed on its head.

Photographer Paolo Torre said the caiman’s new hairdo looked like Elvis’s rock’n’roll pomapdour – but others have pointed out that the swampy strands more closely resemble Donald Trump’s comb-over.



One owl scowls like a cartoon villain from atop a branch while another appears to karate-kick the air.

Two scheming eagles may yet snatch the prize in scenes that look like a wild seashore heist.

Appearing to have just swooped into the frame, the bird claws a package under the stern beak of a watching eagle.

The photo, by Curt Lundeen, is called “Highway Robbery Get your hands off the merchandise”.

But perhaps a bird in a petal may be worth two splashing in the sea in the eyes of the judges.



The unbelievable shot shows a tiny blue-green bird bathing inside a banana blossom.

Another adorable photo shows a cow called Doris decked in bristling green plants – with the supreme quality of the camera picking up every blade.

In another bizarre showdown a huge white polar bear crouches down to gaze into the eyes of a miniscule gull.



A pic of a strutting eagle – who looked vaguely distressed – was called: “Fashion fades, feather coats are forever”.

Fiendish perspectives make one elephant appear to be poised to kick over a tiny jeep as it stomps across the desert.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The winner will be announced in December 2026.

The top prize is a once-in-a-lifetime safari trip – but various types of Nikon cameras are also up for grabs.

News.title: ‘We could be having a General Election in May’ claims Kemi Badenoch as she rules out ANY pact with Reform
News.content:
Next

KEMI Badenoch claims Britain could head to the polls as soon as next May — but has ruled out any election pact with Reform.

The Tory leader said she believes PM Andy Burnham is “going to call an election sooner than he is saying”.



She added: “All the policies he announced are for after an election.

“We could be having a general election next May.”



But asked about “reuniting the Right”, Mrs Badenoch told the BBC: “There is no deal with Reform.”

Her comments come just days before the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.



The leader will put welfare reform at the heart of their plans.

She wants to stop jobless youngsters going straight from school on to benefits.

Under-25s who have not worked continuously for six months would earn financial support.

Anyone taking part in a new “Get to Work” programme could be required to attend Jobcentres every day.



They would also have to complete work experience or training.

Those who refuse would not receive welfare.

News.title: Now Burnham is PM his words have consequences which is why it was an own goal for him to support Man City’s owners
News.content:
PM’s City ’mare







Next

ANDY Burnham is never shy of an opinion — whether it’s on buses, music or his favourite type of pub snack.

Indeed, there’s seemingly no question to which he won’t offer a folksy answer.



The problem is, he’s Prime Minister now, and his words have consequences.

Which is why it was an own goal for him to support Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owners after they were found guilty of a £1billion cheating scandal that has rocked the football world.



The rules of being in Government are clear: do not interfere with a judicial or independent regulatory process.

Football-lover Burnham has in the past forcefully stated that an independent regulator should oversee the game.

That football regulator is now in existence — having been created by the Labour Government.

The first big decision it will face?

To determine whether, in light of City being found guilty of more than 100 Premier League financial rule breaches, its owners are “fit and proper”.

At the same time, HMRC — also an arm of Government — and the police are coming under pressure to mount their own investigations into the club, who deny any wrongdoing.



By voicing his “concern” about City’s owners quitting Manchester, he risked the perception of political interference.

Indeed, No10 was yesterday forced to try to clear up after the boss, stating that “there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.

Separately, Burnham also appears to have misread the room on this one.

The vast majority of fans want the Premier League to throw the book at the club for not playing fair — not go easy in case the owners walk away.

Make it work

KEMI Badenoch has thrown down the gauntlet to Labour in a high-stakes battle over Britain’s soaring welfare bill.



Andy Burnham is refusing to tackle the huge sums paid to skivers, and is preparing to target pensioner income by scrapping the triple lock.

The Tory leader, by contrast, will force under-25s to work or undergo intensive training rather than instantly signing on.

Britain is desperate for strong action to instil a proper work ethic in a generation that otherwise faces life on benefits.

Kemi’s on the right track.

Debt trap

BRITAIN is stuck in a crippling debt spiral because of Government failure to bring spending under control.



Interest payments on the nation’s £3trillion overdraft have hit a 28-year high, triggering fears of a knock-on effect for mortgage bills.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

We now spend twice as much just servicing the debt as we do on defence.

Things won’t get better until Labour stops maxing out the credit card.

News.title: FlyDubai FZ1073 latest: Netanyahu says hijack pilot 'used axe' in cockpit attack
News.content:
The pilot who allegedly stabbed another pilot and tried to take over FlyDubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday may have used an 'axe' in the attack, Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu claimed

The co-pilot who allegedly stabbed the captain of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 in an apparent attempt to crash the plane may have used an "axe" in the attack, according to Israel's prime minister.

Benjamin Netanyahu told CBS News yesterday: "As they approached Israel, one of the co-pilots stabbed or hit with an axe the other pilot, an Indian pilot. And the pilot that was hit, bleeding profusely, fighting for his life, managed to unlock the pilot's door." Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit for use in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.

The Israeli Prime Minister's comments come as Saudi officials investigating the horror incident said initial findings show the co-pilot "assaulted the captain". Donald Trump has said he believed Iran may be linked to the co-pilot but a senior Israeli official said this had, so far, been ruled out.

The flight issued an emergency hijacking alert yesterday morning, around two and a half hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The injured pilot - identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar - and a number of passengers bravely fought back control and regained control of the plane, which then made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

One of the passengers who helped was Yaniv Hayoun, who Netanyahu described as a "great hero". Mr Hayoun said: "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside."

He then said he helped pull the aircraft's controls. Mr Hayoun claimed he knew how to control the plane after watching the TV show Air Crash Investigation.

News.title: UN human rights chief unleashes scathing attack after Christa Pike's botched execution
News.content:
UN human rights chief unleashes scathing attack after Christa Pike's botched execution

Christa Pike remains unresponsive but not in a coma following her botched execution. The UN human rights chief called on authorities in Tennessee not to pursue any further attempts to execute her

View 3 Images Christa Pike has survived two attempts at lethal injections (Image: J. Miles Cary, Knoxville News Sentinel)

The UN human rights chief and nine independent rights experts on Thursday called on authorities in Tennessee not to pursue any further attempts to execute Christa Pike, saying her case highlights multiple concerns surrounding the death penalty.

‌



‌



Convicted killer Christa Pike remains unresponsive but not in a coma following her botched execution, in which her lawyer claims she was pierced with a needle seven times. Pike, 50, is still alive and in a critical condition, receiving life-saving medical treatment after surviving two full doses of pentobarbital, a lethal drug, during the failed execution attempt on Wednesday evening.

‌



The Tennessee Department of Correction said it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol”, adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an “off-site medical facility” after the horrifying execution attempt.

‌



View 3 Images Christa Gail Pike murdered Colleen Slemmer (pictured) (Image: WVLT 8)

Christa Pike victim's family left furious after death row murderer survives two executions READ MORE :

Pike had been on death row for the brutal murder of Colleen Slemmer in January 1995. Slemmer was killed at age 19, after being lured into an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Pike was convicted alongside her boyfriend in 1996, and the court heard that there was a pentagram carved into Slemmer's chest and Pike kept a bit of her skull as a souvenir.

Pike was set to become the first woman to be executed in the US state in 200 years. In what were meant to be her planned final words, Pike said: “I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life – and that is with love.”

‌



Lawyer Randy Spivey said on Thursday: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment." He added: "But we do know that she is alive right now."

Her lawyers claim that the failed execution amounted to "torture", and they called for her death sentence to be commuted. Spivey said: “I’m haunted by last night. What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”

View 3 Images Christa Pike survives on death row, with a lawyer described her horrifying ordeal (Image: Tennessee Department of Correction/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those watching the execution, told NBC News the botched attempt "was a mess".

The United Nations Human Rights have always been against the death penalty and say Christa Pike's case lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished.

Mr Türk calls on the state authorities not to pursue any further attempt to execute Pike. He said: "The prolonged suffering – physical and mental – arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent and cruel." Adding: “the death penalty has no place in any society.”

News.title: BBC Question Time erupts into laughter as Suella Braverman's conservative jibe backfires: 'you were in the government'
News.content:
BBC Question Time erupts into laughter as Suella Braverman's conservative jibe backfires: 'you were in the government'

Suella Braverman tried to slam the conservative government on tonight's BBC Question Time but her jibe about mass immigration backfired dramatically when two panelists clapped back

View 2 Images Reform UK’s education spokesperson Suella Braverman (Image: BBC)

Suella Braverman made a fool of herself on tonight's BBC Question Time as the crowd erupted into laughter and two panelists clapped back when she slammed the conservative governemnt.

‌



‌



On the panel in Tottenham tonight was; the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh; the Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez; Reform UK’s education spokesperson Suella Braverman; and the journalist and podcaster Oli Dugmore.

‌



The first topic up for debat centered around making immigrants feel welcome, and Suella took the opportunity to explain her family history and subsequently her take on the immigration issue.

‌



View 2 Images Fiona Bruce hosts BBC Question Time each week (Image: BBC)

BBC Question Time panelist Josh Babarinde makes desperate plea after RNLI volunteers abused by far-right thugs READ MORE :

FlyDubai pilot's chilling mayday call as passengers scream amid hijacking fears READ MORE :

Suella confirmed she does not describe herself as of English origin saying: "I think it becomes pretty obvious when people have a lineage, an ancestry, a connection to the heritage to this country which dates back a few generations. I think that that is not unreasonable to expect of people who come to this country."

She added: "Can I deal with the point on border immigration because I think this is a really important question. And actually the question about Englishness has arisen because of the utter failure by the Conservative government on mass immigration."

‌



Miatta Fahnbulleh could be heard saying: "You was in the conservative government Suella." Before Julia Lopez rolled her eyes uttered "Home Secretary". The crowd clapped and laughed as Miatta and Julia reacted.

Suella clapped back saying: "Thank you for raising that, it is the very reason I left the Conservative party because they utterly betrayed the British people on their promises on legal migration. I battled from within for years to cut visas and I was blocked."

Taking to X after the live show podcaster Oli Dugmore wrote: "Tonight on Question Time, I debated Suella Braverman on what it means to be English. I think there’s one word for her position." To which Suella had a lenghty response.

Article continues below

Content cannot be displayed without consent

She wote: "You’ve called me racist this evening- albeit in a contorted way- but in doing so, you’ve lowered the tone of the debate with divisive and inflammatory language. And absurdly, you’re suggesting that I’m being racist against myself. It’s because of irresponsible language like yours that we in Reform need security. The left can keep smearing us as racist for challenging the cosy consensus on mass migration but we will not be bullied into silence."

BBC Question Time returns next week to Peterlee.

News.title: 'Rip-off' airline charges including fees for parents to sit next to children under 14 to be banned
News.content:
'Rip-off' airline charges including fees for parents to sit next to children under 14 to be banned

Holidaymakers will also be given greater flexibility to correct simple name errors including spelling mistakes on bookings for free - rather than facing charges

View 2 Images Airline charges including hidden fees for parents to sit next to children under 14 will be banned (Image: Getty Images)

Rip-off airline charges including hidden fees for parents to sit next to children under 14 will be banned under government plans.

‌



‌



Holidaymakers will also be given greater flexibility to correct simple name errors including spelling mistakes on bookings for free - rather than facing charges.

‌



Under the proposals unveiled today, airlines will be required to seat children under the age of 14 with a parent or adult accompanying them free of charge.

‌



Andy Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about. Giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Earlier this year the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) investigated budget airline Ryanair over such charges costing around £8 each way.

‌



Sure Start-style health services for parents will be rolled out across England READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said: 'Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple' (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Under the airline's old policy parents had to book a "mandatory family seat" to sit with their children aged 2-11 in order to secure a seat when they flew.

But Ryanair - which the CMA said was the only major operator to charge such a fee - changed its policy in June with kids up to the age of 11 seated next to their parents free of charge.

‌



It's website now states: "For safety reasons, children aged between 2 and 11 years must sit next to an accompanying adult, and infants (8 days to 23 months inclusive) must sit on an accompanying adult's lap. Families may choose either to reserve seats or select free random allocation.

"If random allocation is selected, children will be seated next to an accompanying adult on the same reservation free of charge. Other adults and teens on the booking may be allocated seats separately."

The government said that while some airlines already offer protections on fees, the reforms will guarantee the same rights for passengers - despite who they fly with.

‌



British Airways policy already makes clear children up to the age of 12 will be seated for free. It states: "To ensure your family has the best seats when you fly, we recommend choosing yours in advance when you book. There may be an additional fee for this.

"If you don't choose your seats in advance, we always do our best to seat your family together based on flight seat availability. This may mean that you'll be seated in adjacent rows or across the aisle. All children under 12 will be seated with an accompanying adult."

EasyJet's policy adds:"If you leave it to the last minute it's possible that there may not be enough seats left for us to seat your family next to each other.

‌



"We'll still make sure each child under 12 is seated close to an adult on your booking. However we may only be able to arrange this at the airport or on board, which can cause delays for you and other passengers, and not everyone may be seated together."

The government said the move was the latest in the PM's attempts to give people breathing space, including action already unveiled on costly subscription traps and school uniform rip-offs.

Heidi Alexander, Transport Secretary, said: “Parents should not have to feel the pinch just to sit next to their child on a flight, or for amending a simple booking error. That's why we're scrapping these unnecessary charges for all airlines – another everyday fix to help put money back in people's pockets and give households more breathing room.

‌



“And everyone deserves to travel knowing their flight isn’t going to be disrupted by bad behaviour from a small minority. These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”

Rory Boland, Editor of Which? Travel, added: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.

“Which? has successfully pressured many airlines into dropping these fees over the past ten years. So it's welcome to see the government taking firm action on this by outlawing these charges completely and finally putting an end to this rip off.

Article continues below

"It is also positive to see greater flexibility to amend simple mistakes, protecting consumers from unnecessary charges."

News.title: Heartbroken daughter calls for booze ban on apps after dad ordered vodka daily
News.content:
Heartbroken daughter calls for booze ban on apps after dad ordered vodka daily

Brooke Rainbow Adams, 22, lost her father Neil David Adams following his long battle with alcohol addiction — and now she claims her dad was able to have alcohol delivered to his door day after day

View 4 Images Brooke Rainbow Adams is grieving her dad, Neil David Adams (pictured) (Image: Jam Press/@b.rainbow2)

A heartbroken daughter has called for booze to be banned from delivery apps after claiming her alcoholic dad was able to order a bottle of vodka to his home every day.

‌



Brooke Rainbow Adams, 22, lost her dad Neil David Adams following a long battle with alcohol addiction.

Neil, 52, died on August 30 after suffering multiple organ failure, according to Brooke. She claims he had alcohol delivered to his home day after day as his drinking spiralled, including a bottle of vodka every day for around eight months.

Brooke said: "For around two years, he had alcohol delivered directly to his home day in and day out. For eight months, he was able to order a bottle of vodka every single day, and as far as we knew, nothing ever triggered a safeguarding concern or intervention."

View 4 Images Neil passed away aged 52 after suffering multiple organ failure (Image: Jam Press/@b.rainbow2)

Brooke, a clinical support worker, said her family had spent years trying to support Neil with his addiction.

She said she began finding large numbers of vodka bottles in the bin, while her dad repeatedly attended hospital and was warned on several occasions that he could die.

“My dad had struggled with alcohol throughout my life, but his drinking became significantly worse during the last two to three years after he moved out of our family home and his depression spiralled,” Brooke said.

Following Neil's death, Brooke said she discovered receipts showing orders for vodka, beer and other alcoholic drinks through several popular delivery apps. She claims there appeared to be no restriction on how frequently he could order alcohol.

View 4 Images Brooke says her dad had alcohol delivered to his home day after day (Image: Jam Press/@b.rainbow2)

Brooke, who is from from Birkenhead, Merseyside, is now calling for delivery companies to introduce stronger safeguards to identify potentially concerning patterns of alcohol purchases.

She said systems should flag customers who repeatedly order alcohol every day, make multiple orders in a single day or place unusually large orders over a prolonged period.

Brooke added: “I understand that people with alcohol addiction have their own choices and that adults cannot simply have their freedom taken away, but I believe that vulnerable people should still be safeguarded.

“Until these companies understand the reality behind these orders, people can continue receiving multiple deliveries of alcohol every day without anything being done.”

View 4 Images Neil, who was into fishing and was an Everton fan, struggled with addiction (Image: Jam Press/@b.rainbow2)

Brooke has since taken to social media to raise awareness and claims she has received hundreds of messages from people across the UK who have experienced similar situations with loved ones.

She is campaigning for alcohol to be removed from delivery apps, alongside stronger safeguards and earlier intervention for people struggling with addiction.

“My dad's death was one of the most horrific and tragic things I have ever had to experience,” Brooke said.

“I watched my dad lose his life to alcohol through multiple organ failure, and our family has been left completely broken.”

She said her family now has to face life without Neil, with her and her 24-year-old brother unable to share the milestones of their future with their dad.

“My dad was more than an alcohol-dependent person or another order on an app,” Brooke said.

“He was our dad, he was loved, and his loss has broken our family.”

News.title: Tragic baby 'stabbed 15 times' and found dead in outhouse had only just been born
News.content:
Tragic baby 'stabbed 15 times' and found dead in outhouse had only just been born

An inquest has opened into the death of little Maria Skopova who was found at a house in Sheffield with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings

View Image Police rushed to the scene in Wincobank area of Sheffield (Image: MEN Media)

A baby girl found dead in an outhouse had only just been born, an inquest into her death has heard as it opened today (Thursday).

‌



‌



Little Maria Skopova - previously referred to as Baby S in court - suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.

‌



She died on the day of her birth in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield, South Yorkshire, on 30 August, the inquest opening heard.

‌



Senior coroner Tanyka Rawden told Sheffield's Medico-Legal Centre that she was adjourning the inquest until March 25 while there were ongoing criminal proceedings.

Two men and two women are due to stand trial in April over Maria's death.

‌



The baby's mother Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath, 19, Peter Horvath, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, appeared at Sheffield Crown Court last month charged with murder.

A 15-year-old girl also appeared in court charged with perverting the course of justice. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail.

Horvath Jnr, Horvath Snr and Horvathova, all of Holywell Heights, and Skopova, of Robey Street in Grimesthorpe, are also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime. The court was previously told that Maria had been found in an outhouse at the property.

Article continues below

The coroner said today that, on the day of Maria's death, emergency services were called, paramedics attended and they sadly pronounced her deceased.

News.title: 'Childbirth should never depend on whether an ambulance can get you to safety in time'
News.content:
'Childbirth should never depend on whether an ambulance can get you to safety in time'

North Devon’s maternity crisis has left five babies born outside proper maternity care - years of NHS staffing failures have turned childbirth into a postcode lottery

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Five babies have been born in ambulances, A&E departments and a hospital reception because North Devon’s maternity service no longer has enough staff to provide the care women should be able to rely on. That is a shocking failure of one of the NHS's most basic promises: that when a mother goes into labour, safe help will be there. This crisis did not appear overnight. It is the product of years in which successive governments allowed NHS staffing gaps to deepen, services to be hollowed out and maternity care to come under intolerable pressure, particularly in more isolated communities. North Devon is now paying the price. Ministers cannot undo years of neglect overnight, but they can stop accepting a system in which childbirth becomes a postcode lottery, and expectant mothers are left fearing whether they will reach proper care in time. The Government must now guarantee the staff and funding needed to reopen the unit safely, set a firm timetable for doing so, and make clear that no community will again be left without proper maternity provision because years of neglect were allowed to become the norm.

‌



‌



A true hero

There are moments when courage is not measured in words, medals or speeches, but in the instinct to run towards danger when every part of you should run away. That is what Andrew Franks did. Already stabbed and bleeding, he confronted a terrorist, tripped him, warned worshippers to lock the doors and bought precious seconds that helped prevent a massacre inside a Manchester synagogue. He nearly died for it. A year on, Andrew still lives with terrible injuries and trauma, while the families of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby live with unbearable loss. Our Pride of Britain Awards exist to honour people exactly like Andrew: ordinary men and women who, in extraordinary moments, reveal the very best of us. His bravery saved lives. We should never forget it.

Article continues below

Old faithful...

Celebrity Traitors is back, bringing with it the glorious mix of suspicion, scheming and famous faces turning on each other that made it such irresistible television. The cloaks are out, the round table is waiting, and nobody can trust anyone. For viewers, that means one thing: wonderfully wicked telly is back.

News.title: Prisoners walk free early as man with 360 convictions admits 'I’m addicted to stealing'
News.content:
Prisoners walk free early as man with 360 convictions admits 'I’m addicted to stealing'

Around 700 prisoners serving sentences of up to 19 months were released across the country under the early release scheme, which the government said will free up space and tackle overcrowding

View 9 Images Prisoners - though not the man with 360 convictions - leave HMP Brixton (Image: Phil Harris)

Inmates poured out prison gates across the country today as the first groups were released under the early release scheme.

‌



‌



The Mirror was at HMP Brixton, where prisoners' friends and family gathered outside on Thursday morning in wait - alongside TV camera crews, guards and a handful of police officers.

‌



The gates swung open at regular intervals from 7.30am as a steady stream of prisoners emerged throughout the day, with some taken away in cars or vans.

‌



Others covered their faces and walked hurriedly down the quiet perimeter road, hoping to evade the eyes of the public. One shielded his head and most of his torso in a white plastic bag in a bizarre bid to conceal his identity.

View 9 Images David Elliott, 50, said he had an 'addiction to stealing' and needed help (Image: Phil Harris)

'It's help I need - not prison'

David Elliott, 50, spoke of his dire need for support upon his early release. He said: "I’ve been in and out of jail all my life. I’ve got 360 convictions. It’s help I need, I’ve got an addiction to stealing."

‌



Charlene Hefferman, 41, had come to pick up her brother Rikky.

She said he was handed a one-year sentence for an "argument with his partner" - and had served only three months.

View 9 Images Charlene Hefferman had come to pick up her brother Rikky (Image: PHIL HARRIS)

‌



Charlene said: "I’m very excited. He could have served up to a year for it, but he only did three months."

"I don't want my brother around that [prison] anymore.

"There's a lot that goes on in prisons that many people don't understand - a lot of bullying, killings, a lot of damage, 'you pay me this, you pay me that', threats on phones - so now I know he hasn't got to worry about anything.

‌



View 9 Images Two men appeared on a motorbike outside HMP Leeds as prisoners were released (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

"A big thing happened to him before [when he was elsewhere] . He was put in with a lifer, and while he was sleeping he (the lifer) boiled a kettle and poured it over him. He was scarred, lost his hearing, lost his sight, and was stabbed in the eye. My older brother had to stand and watch that."

While she was pleased that would soon get to see her brother, she said of the early release scheme: "I think you need to look closely into the people you are releasing and thoroughly check who you are letting out and who you aren't."

‌



View 9 Images A man was re-arrested outside HMP Wandsworth only seconds after being freed (Image: Jeremy Selwyn)

Three-and-a-half miles away at HMP Wandsworth, a man was arrested by police on Thursday morning only seconds after being freed - and led away in handcuffs.

A British Transport Police spokesperson said: "A 45-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of two counts of Theft of a Pedal Cycle today (October 1) at around 10.40am outside Wandsworth Prison. The man has been taken to custody."

‌



But Labour is sure the move will work, stressing “significant investments” had been made to improve the monitoring of released prisoners. Speaking today, Justice Secretary Alex Norris said: "I've made significant investments to increase staffing, as I say, to give a wide range of tools, with (GPS) tags being the most obvious, but also alcohol tagging, restrictions on the ability to say go to the football or go out in the nighttime economy. So really strong controls on individuals, backed up by our absolutely brilliant probation staff.

“That gives us the confidence to make the changes we're making and to make sure we're managing people strongly in the community.”

View 9 Images Matthew Johnson, 35, said he was 'buzzing' to be freed from HMP Leeds (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire)

‌



'They need to free up some places'

Elsewhere, Matthew Johnson, 35, said he was delighted to be freed from HMP Leeds.

He said of the scheme: "It's a good idea, to be fair. They need to free up some places anyway. "The staff are overwhelmed anyway with what they've got to cope with at the minute. It's hectic. It's crowded. Cells for one person with two people in them."

View 9 Images Jordan Laverack, 26, said he wanted to find a job after being released from HMP Leeds (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire)

‌



Jordan Laverack, 26, said outside the West Yorkshire prison: "The plan for today, it's to go to KFC and after that I'm not sure."

He said: "I think early release is good for myself. I can see why there's a lot of attention behind it, because there might be people doing heinous crime who are getting released early.

View 9 Images People were seen celebrating outside HMP Bristol (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

‌



"But for the average person, who's missed probation like myself, I think it suits somebody like me."

"I just want to get myself some work, some employment, make my family proud, maybe get a girlfriend, get married, you never know.

"They've actually released me with nowhere to stay but I've got a few friends I can stay at. The people who don't will be back doing what they're doing. I've got my life ahead of me."

‌



Prisons remain overcrowded

Measures under the Sentencing Act 2026 came into force on October 1 and led to the first wave of releases from prisons. It means criminals serving fixed-term sentences will serve a third of their time behind bars before being released, rather than half. About 700 prisoners are being freed from jails early across England and Wales on Thursday in the Government’s latest bid to cut overcrowding. This is in addition to about 1,000 who are typically freed each week. About 4,500 prisoners are scheduled to be released in 10 stages over the next year.

As of the end of August, there were 86,843 prisoners behind bars across England and Wales - taking up almost 98% of usable capacity, and leaving fewer than 2,100 places for new arrivals. Nearly one in four prisoners - 23% - is in overcrowded conditions, sharing cells designed to hold fewer people.

Overcrowding can lead to a host of problems, including fewer opportunities for rehabilitation through training, education and employment, more time spent in cells, and an increase in assaults and self-harm.

‌



The Ministry of Justice said: "Failure to act would put victims and the public at untold risk – with courts unable to hold trials, police unable to make arrests and crime going unpunished."

There’s been a spike in the number of offenders being recalled to prison having been released on license.

In the year to March 2026, more than 51,400 prisoners had their license recalled - up 28% from the year before. In comparison, in 2000 the recall population was closer to just 9,000 inmates.

‌



The increase follows a prior early release scheme that was introduced in September 2024 as an emergency measure to try and ease overcrowding, with prisons reaching 99% capacity.

This saw eligible prisoners serve just 40% of their sentence, rather than 50% - and while it was successful in the short term, the sharp rise in recalls limited the overall impact.

View 9 Images Andy Burnham tightened the early release scheme over the summer (Image: CHRIS RATCLIFFE/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Victims’ Commissioner Claire Waxman said she was not convinced by ministers’ claims that robust safeguards are in place. On Wednesday, she said: “As Victims' Commissioner, my concern is that the confidence being projected by government is not yet matched by the reality on the ground.

“Bold assertions in press releases are no substitute for effective planning, robust preparation and consistent delivery. All three have been in short supply.

Andy Burnham tightened the scheme over the summer so that those convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences, grooming and manslaughter are excluded from early release. It came after backlash over the planned early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

Article continues below

PC Harper sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019.

The 28-year-old police officer died after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as the teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary.

News.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford incident, police say
News.content:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 25-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. Two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Police had initially given the dual UK-Iranian national's age as 27 and said a second man had been questioned under caution, but in a later update said that this was not the case.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.

On Thursday, the British ambassador to Iran met the country's foreign ministry at the request of the Iranian government.

News.title: Crypto thieves attack man in home and threaten to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a Â£10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

News.title: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban
News.content:
Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.

The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging for Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies. "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar, he argued.

The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections.

On Thursday, Britain held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately".

"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.

The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.

Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

Britain's Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply.â¯We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

News.title: Chris Mason: Why Andy Burnham's about-turn on Manchester City matters
News.content:
The rows circulating around Manchester City are huge, and they are only going to get bigger.

The Premier League has concluded that City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

This, clearly, matters for the club, but that is just the start of it.

It matters for Manchester, it matters for the Premier League and so, crucially, it matters for the UK's image around the world â because England's top flight is a colossal global brand. In other words, this matters whether you like football or not.

Added to all of this, Andy Burnham pitches himself as Mr Manchester and is a big football fan.

The man who was the mayor of Greater Manchester a matter of months ago is now the prime minister, and so finds himself caught up in it all at a local level, a national level and a diplomatic level.

Diplomatic, because rows will rage over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state. And the state is a big UK ally.

All of this is why I thought it was in the public interest to put a series of questions to Burnham about it when I spoke to him on Wednesday as the Labour Party conference concluded in Liverpool.

His comments, in his interview with me, followed by no fewer than two attempts to backtrack 24 hours later, amount to perhaps his biggest self inflicted tangle since he arrived in Downing Street in July.

He will have expected to be asked about Manchester City, but he didn't expect sustained scrutiny about it.

One particular exchange prompted a lot of interest. I asked if he was worried that Manchester City's owners from the United Arab Emirates might sell up.

It is worth quoting his answer in full.

"Well, I would be really concerned to lose them. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester. Obviously, the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it's ongoing, and because it's still contested by Manchester City, then I think it's right that I don't say much more."

His answer is revealing on several levels, and was leapt on by many in football and then by the Conservatives, who labelled them "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary".

News.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
News.content:
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around â¬1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

News.title: Watch: Celebrity Traitors series two kicks off with a wild curveball
News.content:
Warning spoiler alert.

The new series of Celebrity Traitors has kicked off, with 21 contestants including Bella Ramsey, Maya Jama and Michael Sheen.

But only moments after the game's traitors were selected, a huge curveball was thrown when Richard E Grant did something no one has done on the show before.

BBC culture correspondent Noor Nanji discusses his wild admission, as well as the show's latest twist.

More on this story.

News.title: Chaos, coffins and 'Claudiapatra' steal the show in Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

News.title: Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case
News.content:
Anger and concern about student safety and rape culture on campus was discussed at a public hearing led by the Student Assembly of Cornell University.

The hearing was held in response to an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman, being referred to as Jane Doe, has filed a civil lawsuit against the university alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house on campus.

Cornell has rejected claims that it failed to punish those involved. It has also agreed to have the case examined by an independent investigator.

The BBC's Nada Tawfik spoke to students who attended the public hearing.

News.title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
News.content:
In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m.

The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process" and that it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham replied: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

The Tories have accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

The chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it had "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

News.title: Coroner warns of risk of future deaths at mental health unit where patient was killed
News.content:
On the night of Cahan's death, staff on the ward were found to have been asleep on the job and on their phones for long periods.

East London NHS Foundation Trust (ELFT) says the failings identified were "wholly unacceptable" and that it has undertaken a "significant programme of work" to improve inpatient services.

The coroner's Prevention of Future Deaths report highlights 14 concerns. These include failing to carry out "timely and thorough observations" of patients, then falsifying records "in the safe knowledge that staff on duty would not report or escalate the deception".

The document also says there were delays in starting CPR on Cahan when he was discovered, that staff misled the police as to what the patients had been doing on the night of the incident, and that staff colluded with each other to take two-hour unauthorised breaks.

Torres-Pena was given a hospital order with no time limit after pleading guilty to manslaughter by diminished responsibility in 2023.

The coroner also raised concerns that many of the failings had been brought up at a previous inquest he'd conducted.

"The findings in this inquest are strikingly similar to the findings of an inquest before this court in 2021, remedial measures reported in that case do not appear to have been implemented effectively by the trust", the report says.

"Findings of dishonesty on this scale are extraordinarily rare in a coronial investigation. The public are entitled to expect a clear explanation of how this was allowed to happen and what is being done to ensure it never happens again," says James Cahan, the family solicitor and Hugo's cousin.

News.title: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales before Plaid Cymru conference
News.content:
The first minister and leader of Plaid Cymru has written to the prime minister requesting "a new deal for Wales" ahead of his first party conference speech since taking office.

In his letter to Andy Burnham, sent on Thursday and seen by BBC Wales, Rhun ap Iorwerth calls for more powers to be transferred to Cardiff.

Burnham previously said he would "give a fair hearing" to anything put to him by the Welsh first minister.

Ap Iorwerth will address party members in Llandudno on Friday, five months on from Plaid's historic success at May's Senedd election.

The result saw the party win power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 years in government since devolution began in 1999.

News.title: 'Potential crime' probe into death of Scots wingsuit flyer dropped
News.content:
An investigation into any potential crime after the death of a Scottish wingsuit flyer during a jump in the Swiss Alps has been dropped.

British champion Liam Byrne, 24, was fatally injured on the Gitschen mountain after taking off from 7,874ft (2,400m) in June last year.

An investigation was launched, but documents from the Swiss Federal Prosecutor's Office seen by BBC Scotland News show it was decided to discontinue proceedings.

Byrne, from Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, had featured in a 2024 BBC documentary called The Boy Who Can Fly.

He was described as a very experienced wingsuit flyer - which is a type of skydiving. It involves wearing a special suit with webbing to allow mid-air lift.

Byrne had completed thousands of jumps during his flying career.

News.title: Talks on Drumcree parading dispute end without agreement
News.content:
Regarding the fresh legal bid by GRRC the secretary of state said: "we'll have to see how that plays out".

He added that "the law, in the end, is the law" and he would "urge everybody to cooperate with the police".

The chairman of the GRRC said there had been no "meeting of minds" adding that the current process is "done".

BreÃ¡ndan Mac Cionnaith was speaking after more than two hours of talks hosted by the secretary of state.

Asked if the talks had run their course he replied: "For the time being, yes."

He added: "They may want to re-embark upon another process at some stage, but the current process is done."

When asked if the Garvaghy Road would be blocked if Monday's legal appeal failed, Mac Cionnaith said: "That's not my decision. As we have pointed out, there's 4,000 people in our community signed a petition.

"Those 4,000 people deserve to have their voice heard, and we'll see what goes on that."

Speaking after the talks broke up Portadown District master Nigel Dawson said: "Tonight remains as it has been: That we are in possession of a positive determination issued by the Parades Commission.

"It went through the Court of Appeal and the High Court sat on it and has decided that we have the right to walk down the Garvaghy Road back to Carleton Street Orange Hall, and I would now call on the Secretary of State to apply the law."

Loyalist activist and Portadown district adviser Jamie Byrson said: "There's a court case now taking place on Monday.

"Those who have broken the law are now going back to the Court of Appeal to ask the Court of Appeal to justify their breaking of the law.

"We'll see what happens â that's an interesting argument, but that will take place on Monday."

The Orange Order had been due to parade on Sunday but the march did not take place due to a large protest on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.

Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road, although in much smaller numbers, and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church, about a mile away.

Talks aimed at breaking the deadlock have been talking place since Monday with the secretary of state.

Both parties were given a document during separate meetings at Hillsborough Castle on Wednesday.

Dawson said they were shown a discussion document but stressed it was "not a proposal" while Mac Cionnaith said his group would "agree to it, if the Orange Order did".

News.title: Hundreds of criminals start leaving prison under new early release scheme
News.content:
Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity.

The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday.

The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.

But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community.

Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%.

Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027.

Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves.

News.title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
News.content:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as Â£12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to Â£24m.

News.title: PM warned Rosebank oil field could breach West Bank sanctions
News.content:
The prime minister has been warned that approving a controversial oil field risks contravening his own sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The government will soon have to make a long-awaited decision on whether to go ahead with Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field, which sits off Shetland.

Environmental campaigners and Green Party leader Zack Polanski have both separately written to Andy Burnham and the foreign secretary to raise concerns about Rosebank's links to an Israeli company, Delek Group.

Last year Delek Group was included in a UN database of firms which allegedly provide services or utilities to support settlements in occupied Palestinian territories.

A spokesman for the company told the Daily Telegraph, external it no longer had any involvement in Israeli settlements and was wrongly included in the database.

Delek Group controls Ithaca Energy, which holds a 20% stake in Rosebank.

The campaign group Uplift, whose legal challenge against the Rosebank project in 2023 led to the ongoing delay over a decision on exploration, has helped organise a letter to Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

In a letter seen by BBC News, campaigners from Stop Rosebank and Greenpeace, with assistance from Uplift, have asked the government to clarify whether Delek will fall foul of the sanctions announced last month.

Separately, Polanski has also written to Miliband, asking what steps the government would take to make sure revenue from UK oil and gas production did not finance illegal settlements.

He said: "Rosebank is a test of whether Labour's proposed sanctions regime is fit for purpose.

"Companies blacklisted by the UN for operating in the illegal settlements should not be financed by oil and gas revenues from the North Sea."
