Egyptian authorities on Thursday accused six journalists arrested this week of being members of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, alleging they produced fabricated news for an online outlet in exchange for foreign funding.

The arrests swept up the entire editorial team of Matsadaash (Arabic for “Don't Believe”), one of Egypt’s few independent outlets. Founded eight years ago as a fact-checking platform, it has since expanded into investigative reporting in Egypt and other Arab countries.

“The claims are false,” Matsadaash co-founder Abdelrahman Mansour said from outside Egypt.

Mansour said two of the outlet's editors were arrested in 2023 but were released without charge after State Security investigators found no affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood.

“It's very difficult for us to understand why this is happening,” he said.

Egypt is among the world’s worst jailers of journalists, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights says 26 journalists are now behind bars in Egypt.

The journalists’ whereabouts are unknown

Egypt’s Interior Ministry on Thursday described Matsadaash as an unlicensed page managed from abroad by a “fugitive Brotherhood member” it identified as Mansour.

It said the six people detained were part of a Brotherhood “media committee” that prepared false and fabricated news for Mansour to publish. Only one of the six is a member of the Journalists’ Syndicate— the national press union— the statement said. It said legal measures have been taken but did not specify charges.

The first arrest occurred on Monday night when authorities went to the home of Abdallah Qadry, Mansour said. The other five members of staff were arrested on Tuesday, starting with Mohamed Abu Emaira, who was taken from his home in the early hours. Mansour said Emaira’s library and internet router were destroyed during the arrest.

Omar Helal was arrested in Port Said and Islam Barakat in Gharbia Governorate. Two other members of Matsadaash’s newsroom staff — Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel — were arrested in Cairo.

All had their cellphones and computers confiscated.

The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights said the whereabouts of all six remain unknown. “They have not been allowed to contact their families or legal team,” the advocacy group said. It was the first time an entire newsroom had been arrested in Egypt.

Rights groups call for the journalists' release

Matsadaash, founded in 2018 as an online platform, has gained credibility and a large following in Egypt, where independent media are stifled and government censorship and oversight over newspapers and TV networks are the norm. The Matsadaash website is blocked in Egypt, but its Facebook page has more than one million followers.

Over 80 international and regional rights groups, civil society organizations and independent media called on the Egyptian authorities to release the journalists, condemning what they called an escalating crackdown on independent media.

“Matsadaash has operated openly for years and has built a reputation for credible and accurate reporting on a range of public interest issues across Egypt,” the petition, signed by groups including Human Rights Watch and Reporters Without Borders, said. “Egyptian authorities’ failure to allow free expression to thrive flies in the face of a purported commitment to dialogue, transparency, anti-corruption, and regional leadership.”

Accusing critics of membership in the Brotherhood is common in Egypt, which designated the group as a terrorist organization in 2013, after the military ousted then-President Mohammed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure. Since then, authorities have frequently accused journalists and critics of belonging to the group or spreading false news.

The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in 1928 in Egypt, began as a social and religious movement opposing British colonial rule. It grew into one of the Sunni Muslim world’s most influential Islamist movements, establishing branches in dozens of countries. Egyptian authorities alternated over the decades between tolerating and repressing the group, which was permitted to field candidates in elections for brief periods.

The Muslim Brotherhood is now banned in Jordan, while its branches are designated terrorist organizations by several countries .

Donald Trump has thrown a jab at Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton after the struggling Senate hopeful criticized the Republican midterm convention that the president headlined last month.

Trump went to a truck factory in Denton, Texas, Thursday evening to tout the administration’s work on American manufacturing. But, like in previous speeches, he couldn’t help but insult Paxton in the process.

"He can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I'll be honest,” the president said about the Republican nominee whom he endorsed.

Trump then looked to his left and asked: “Is he here, by the way? Oh, there he is. Good. I didn't even know if he was here! I don't care."

open image in gallery Donald Trump has thrown a jab at Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton after the struggling Senate hopeful criticized the Republican midterm convention that the president headlined last month ( Getty Images )

Trump’s comments come a day after Paxton was reportedly caught slamming the Dallas convention that the president used to drum up support for Republican candidates in tight races.

“To be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton said during a private Washington fundraiser, according to an audio recording obtained by The New York Times.

Paxton and his Democratic opponent James Talarico are neck and neck in the polls.

Talarico was two percentage points ahead of Paxton in a Fox News poll released Thursday, with 51 percent of voter support compared to Paxton’s 49 percent.

The Democrat had an even larger lead over Paxton in a Marist University poll conducted from September 17 to 20. In that poll, 50 percent of Texas voters said they support Talarico and 44 percent said they back Paxton.

open image in gallery "He can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I'll be honest,” the president said about the Republican nominee whom he endorsed during an event in Texas on Thursday ( Getty Images )

Talarico was leading Paxton by three percentage points before the convention.

A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released on August 24 found Talarico with 42 percent of voter support compared to Paxton’s 39 percent.

Paxton’s senior adviser Nick Maddux disputed the reporting on Paxton's private conversation with donors, telling the Times, “This is more manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist.”

“Our latest poll from the last week has Ken Paxton leading by three points, and every serious pollster will tell you that our numbers have improved since early September.”

During both nights of the GOP convention, Trump insulted Paxton over his fashion sense.

open image in gallery Trump’s comments come a day after Paxton reportedly told donors that his polling numbers dropped after the Dallas convention that the president used to drum up support for Republican candidates in tight races ( AFP via Getty Images )

“And I said something yesterday, and I don't know if he'll ever talk to me again…My people said, ‘Please don't say that.’ So I won't say it, but I'll tell you what I was thinking about saying,” Trump said during his closing address on September 10.

“I said, ‘I don't like the way Ken dresses,” the president said. “Although I also said he looked really sharp in that suit yesterday. I thought it was spiffy.”

The night before, Trump told the crowd that Paxton “may not be the best-looking guy I've ever seen, but you know what he is? He's the greatest Attorney General in America, and he deserves to be your next senator.”

After his stop in Texas on Thursday, Trump traveled to Oklahoma and said Paxton would take the Senate seat “whether you love him or not.”

“We're going to send Ken Paxton to the United States Senate because he is whether you love him or don't love him — he's a little controversial, just slightly — but whether you love him or not, he's probably the best or certainly one of the best...attorney generals in the entire United States of America,” Trump told the crowd Thursday night.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order Thursday appointing the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house, stripping the local prosecutor of the case.

Hochul cited a loss of confidence in the Tompkins County district attorney following newly revealed details about the handling of the October 2024 incident.

“Newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University’s campus in October 2024,” Hochul said.

“This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the District Attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time.”

Under the executive order, the attorney general will direct the probe and present evidence to a grand jury if necessary.

open image in gallery New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order Thursday handing control of a Cornell University fraternity sexual assault investigation to Attorney General Letitia James ( Reuters )

“That’s wonderful news … my client and I had zero confidence in this district attorney’s ability to prosecute this case,” Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the alleged victim, told NewsNation’s “CUOMO” following the governor's decision.

Giuffra said he supported the move, questioning how campus police investigated the case and why the district attorney initially declined to file charges.

“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”

The governor’s decision followed a tense evening on campus, where dozens of students and community members gathered for more than two and a half hours at a forum organized by Cornell’s student government. Attendees expressed frustration over the private university’s handling of sexual assault complaints involving fraternity members, with several speakers detailing their own experiences with sexual violence.

open image in gallery Hochul cited a loss of confidence in the Tompkins County district attorney following newly revealed details about the handling of the October 2024 incident ( Getty )

During the forum, the Student Assembly passed resolutions calling for increased transparency in sexual assault cases, a review of orientation programs regarding consent and substance abuse, and the provision of free counseling services for survivors.

“I think what happened here is an American problem,” said Hayden Watkins, an undergraduate and executive vice president of the Student Assembly. “People kind of put Cornell on this pedestal because we are an elite institution. But if it’s happening at places like Cornell, it’s happening on college campuses all across the country.”

Sophomore Jane Wang said in an interview with the Associated Press outside the event that she faced minimal guidance and little follow-up after reporting a sexual assault on campus roughly a year ago. She said the details of the lawsuit felt similar to her own experience.

“My main message for Cornell here is that we can’t be treating these cases only with care and attention after it catches national news,” Wang said.

The case began with a lawsuit filed in September by a student identified in court filings as Jane Doe. The civil suit names seven fraternity members, the university and the Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that one defendant sent a social media message to more than 50 fraternity members inviting them to join the assault.

open image in gallery Jane Doe is suing the Ivy League college and seven male students, alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house during an hours-long assault that university officials failed to prevent or adequately punish ( Reuters )

Lawyers for two of the men named in the suit have denied the allegations, with one stating his client never touched the woman.

In response to public pressure and calls from state officials, Cornell agreed Wednesday to hire external legal counsel to review its handling of the allegations. The university previously confirmed that it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled several students, though it declined to detail specific actions, citing student privacy laws.

The civil filing prompted District Attorney Van Houten to announce earlier in the week that his office would reopen its investigation.

Van Houten defended his original decision against bringing criminal charges, stating that the victim’s initial account to campus police did not indicate she had been forcibly assaulted, drugged or incapacitated beyond giving consent.

After three months with no rain, Sriwati, a shopkeeper and mother of three children living in Penyeladi village on the tropical island of Borneo, can no longer depend on the river for her needs.

Experts say communities like Sriwati’s are facing a severe water crisis as this year’s super El Niño, combined with decades of degradation of the island’s ecologically vital peatlands — ancient wetlands that are critical for carbon storage, water regulation and pollution control — has created the perfect storm exacerbating human-caused climate change.

The Kapuas, Indonesia’s longest river that over 3 million people rely on, has extremely receded in the area near her home. All that’s left is a shallow stream of muddy water that's not safe to drink or wash the rice she cooks to feed her children. She now has to buy water, adding to her monthly expenses.

“The water shortage affects us, especially when it comes to drinking water,” Sriwati, who like many Indonesians uses only one name, told The Associated Press from her small, concrete home.

El Niño and peatland degradation create crisis

El Niño is part of a natural climate cycle of warming ocean temperatures, but this year’s is expected to reach new extremes of drought, heat waves, flooding and other climate-related disruptions across the globe.

Meteorologists forecast it could exceed a record El Niño that began in 1997 and helped trigger billions of dollars in damage from heat waves, floods, droughts, tornadoes and wildfires.

In Borneo, experts say that because vast peatlands have been destroyed by land conversion, the effects of El Niño are already being more acutely felt.

“In Kalimantan, something like 60% of the peatland areas have been drained to make way for palm oil plantations and for pulp and paper concessions,” said Amanda Hurowitz, a senior director at international environmental organization Mighty Earth, using the name for the Indonesia-controlled part of Borneo.

“That means the water is not where it should be. There are all these canals, and because the canals are blocked, the water table goes low,” she continued. “Because it’s so dry, the water has just disappeared.”

In a written statement to the AP, Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry acknowledged the negative impact of drained peatlands, while insisting that specific causes and liabilities must be determined by evidence rather than attributed automatically to El Niño or the presence of businesses.

They added that the government aims to prevent future peatland degradation through ecosystem restoration and strict enforcement of concession holders’ obligations.

“The government’s long-term agenda focuses on preserving and restoring peatland hydrological functions, improving landscape and water management, strengthening fire prevention, and ensuring that all parties managing land fulfill their responsibilities,” they said.

Fires continue to burn across Borneo as water supplies dwindle

Experts say the hot, dry conditions caused by El Niño coupled with peatland degradation have contributed to the enormous fires spreading across Borneo.

Dried peat is highly flammable, allowing fires to easily spread in drained areas. Because the fires often spread underground, they're difficult to extinguish and can easily reoccur, according to the Borneo Nature Foundation.

The dwindling water supply in the area has slowed down firefighting efforts, while Japan has deployed firefighting assistance to the island.

Toxic thick haze blankets the sky. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) away, and breached Malaysia’s emergency-level threshold for air pollution, forcing authorities to declare an emergency last week in a town in Sarawak state on Borneo.

In a written statement to the AP, Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry said the government is shifting its forest and land fire policy toward prevention by strengthening cross-sectoral coordination, enforcing laws against burning-based land clearing, expanding patrols and early detection systems, promoting risk-based monitoring and peatland restoration, and requiring permit holders and communities to take responsibility for fire control.

“Ultimately, controlling forest and land fires is not the task of a single ministry or institution,” they said. “Prevention requires collaborative effort.”

Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry recorded more than 202,000 hectares (499,000 acres) of burned land between January and July, almost three times the size of Singapore.

Communities continue to bear the burden

As the fires continue to burn and water remains scarce, communities continue to suffer.

In Sungai Malaya village in West Kalimantan, fires have burned for over a month, with residents remaining tense around the clock, as fires have sometimes suddenly worsened at night.

Fires have decimated the vacant lots where Rumsiyeh, a 45-year-old mother of five children, and her husband picked ferns to sell at the market.

“Everything’s gone. We can’t make a living anymore,” she said.

Boaters, fishers and others who rely on the river have had their livelihoods impacted, as extremely low water levels mean it’s impossible to fish or travel on the Kapuas. In the areas where there's enough water for boats to operate, the thick haze hampers visibility, making it dangerous to operate, fisherman Abiansah, 39, said.

And the national economic impact remains unmeasured: Large metal barges that usually carry oil palm tree kernels for processing downriver currently lie aground on the sand, as children swing from their untied mooring lines.

Some relief has come from private and government water donations, but residents still fear what the future holds.

“I’m worried about this prolonged dry spell. It’s reached the point where just going about our daily activities — going anywhere at all — has become difficult. We’re facing water shortages, too,” said Sriwati. “I’m at a loss for words to describe it.”

___

Milko reported from Islamabad.

A proposed fee increase to fix a 97-year-old dam on a private Illinois lake has left some residents struggling to afford the new rate, with a few warning the costs could force them out of their homes.

The Master Property Owners Association in Wonder Lake, a private lake community in northern Illinois, is considering raising its yearly assessment from $44 to nearly $1,000 per lot. The association oversees approximately 5,500 properties in the McHenry County village, funding the ongoing maintenance of the local lake and its surrounding infrastructure.

Association leaders say the fee increase is necessary to rebuild depleted reserves and address critical infrastructure needs, including dredging and the eventual replacement of the aging dam.

Estimates to replace the structure run as high as $90 million, but the association currently holds just $60,000 in its reserve fund. Most dams have an expected lifespan of 50 to 100 years.

Ann Freeman, speaking for the association, told CBS News that the increase was long overdue, acknowledging that previous rates failed to adequately fund long-term repairs.

open image in gallery Homeowners on a private Illinois lake say a proposed fee increase to repair a 97-year-old dam is unaffordable, with some warning the higher costs could push them out of their homes ( Getty Images )

“And shame on us, with the MPOA, with charging $44 all these years and not saying, ‘you know, that’s a mistake,’” Freeman said. “We want them to understand that they live on a private lake in a beautiful area of Illinois and they haven’t been paying anything for it.”

Freeman warned that the association was essentially unprepared for a major failure.

“We have rough estimates of $90 million truly to replace the entire thing,” she said.

The proposal faces opposition from residents who live set back from the water and lack direct lake access, as the fee applies per lot rather than per household.

Sue Rose, who lives several blocks from the shoreline and owns two properties, told CBS News the proposal would cost her $2,000 annually.

“And I have two lots, so it’s per lot,” Rose said. “So it would cost me $2,000 for the privilege of being on a lake that I have no access to. I’ll do whatever I can to try and fight this.

“If we have to take it to court, that’s what we are going to do."

Another inland homeowner, Melinda Boyle, told the outlet the fee hike “would cause us probably to move.”

Even some waterfront property owners have expressed hesitation regarding how the costs are distributed across the community. David Crook, who lives directly on the lake, said he could manage the $1,000 fee himself, but expressed concern for neighbors without waterfront views.

“I don’t want to force anything on these people in my subdivision,” Crook said.

The board is scheduled to vote on the fee increase in two weeks.

News.content:

Christa Pike rushed to hospital after surviving two doses of lethal injection

Death row inmate Christa Pike was alive Thursday after Tennessee officials were unable to put her to death a day earlier with two doses of a lethal drug.

Pike, 50, is in critical condition, her lawyer said Thursday. She was due to be the first woman put to death in the state in 206 years, after a court overturned a late stay of execution. Experts say her survival is unprecedented.

Officials administered pentobarbital to Pike twice at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville around 8 p.m. local time, but she was later heard snoring.

Pike was being executed for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a classmate she tortured and killed when she was 18.

The execution had already been delayed for hours after a panel of the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued a stay to allow further review of her legal challenges.

The U.S. Supreme Court later lifted that stay at Tennessee's request in a 6-3 decision, allowing the execution to proceed before Pike's death warrant expired at midnight.

An Arizona man’s 10-year manslaughter sentence has been tossed in a case where a video generated by artificial intelligence portrayed the deceased victim addressing a judge before the punishment was imposed.

In a decision released Wednesday, the Arizona Court of Appeals concluded Gabriel Paul Horcasitas must be resentenced in the 2021 shooting death of Christopher Pelkey because the AI video wasn't reliable.

The court found the video crossed the line, saying it didn’t reflect actual events and presented statements made in the footage as coming directly from the victim.

“Indeed, rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim’s sister,” the three-judge panel wrote.

Jessica Gattuso, an attorney who represented victims in the case, and Kristen Reller, Horcasitas’ lawyer, declined to comment Thursday on the decision.

Reller had argued Superior Court Judge Todd Lang violated due process protections by relying on AI evidence. Gattuso and prosecutors told the appeals court that the lower-court judge didn’t err, saying the footage was an accurate representation of Pelkey’s character.

In what’s believed to be a first in U.S. courts, Pelkey’s family used AI to create a video of his likeness to give him a voice. Pelkey’s sister, Stacey Wales, raised the idea of her brother speaking for himself after struggling to figure out what he would say.

The AI-generated victim impact statement was played during a May 2025 sentencing hearing after nine of Pelkey’s family members and friends stood before the judge describing how emotionally devastated they were by his killing.

Authorities say Horcasitas, 55, fatally shot Pelkey, 37, during a November 2021 road rage encounter at a stoplight in Chandler, a suburb of Phoenix. Pelkey, who was unarmed, was shot after getting out of his truck and walking toward Horcasitas’ vehicle.

Horcasitas was convicted of manslaughter in Pelkey’s death and endangerment for a gunshot that struck another vehicle at the intersection during the encounter.

The AI rendering of Pelkey said he wished he could still be with his friends and family, voiced a belief in forgiveness and said it was a shame Horcasitas had encountered him because “in another life, we probably could have been friends.” The video didn't request a specific prison sentence.

Horcasitas’ appellate lawyer argued her client had no meaningful opportunity to rebut material in the AI-generated video.

It’s not clear if attorneys or the court were aware in advance that an AI-generated video would be used. But attorneys representing Pelkey’s family said in court records that Arizona law does not require victims to disclose statements they plan to make in court to prosecutors, defense attorneys or the judge — and that victims can exercise their rights by speaking before the court or submitting statements that are written or recorded on audio or video.

In a statement Thursday, the Maricopa County Attorney's Office said its prosecutors knew the victim’s family would address the court during sentencing but weren't aware of the nature of it.

While the use of AI within the court system is expanding, it’s typically been reserved for administrative tasks, legal research and case preparation. In Arizona, it’s helped inform the public of rulings in significant cases.

But using AI to generate victim impact statements marks a new tool for sharing information with the court outside the evidentiary phases.

Reller told the appeals court that the video doesn’t disclose who wrote the words used by the AI version of Pelkey and wasn’t backed up with evidence establishing that its contents accurately reflected Pelkey’s views. It also had an “undue emotional weight” and conveyed an authenticity that wouldn’t have been there had a family member read the same words aloud, Reller said.

Horcasitas’ lawyer contended the judge weighed the statements made in the AI-generated video when deciding on a sentence, but prosecutors argued Lang didn’t consider the footage when issuing the punishment.

Shortly before delivering the sentence, the judge commented that he “loved that AI” but didn’t say from the bench whether the video factored into his decision. Lang said he felt Pelkey’s “obvious forgiveness of Mr. Horcasitas reflects the character I heard about today.”

The family’s lawyers say the judge was already inundated with relevant information from Pelkey’s family and friends before the AI video was played — and that nothing in the video was inflammatory. They also said Pelkey’s previous attorney didn’t object to the AI video.

News.title: FTSE 100 tumbles amid bond market sell-off
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. House prices fell unexpectedly last month as mortgage borrowers prepare for a jump in interest rates.

Typical property values declined by 0.2pc during September, reversing 0.2pc growth in August, according to the Nationwide house price index.

The figure was much worse than analysts had forecasts, with most expecting prices to remain steady.

Over the course of the year to September, the rate of house price growth halved from 1.6pc to 0.8pc, which was the weakest rate since December 2025.

The value of the average home has fallen to £274,251 over concerns the Bank of England is on the cusp of raising interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for mortgage holders.

Money markets indicate there is an 84pc chance policymakers will raise rates from 3.75pc to 4pc in November in an effort to bring down inflation caused by the Iran war energy shock.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:“Market activity and house prices have remained subdued in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop.

“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns.

“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank Rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Polanski urges Miliband to block Rosebank oil field over Israel links | Green leader claims North Sea project is a test of Foreign Secretary’s proposed sanctions regime

2) Netherlands ditches wealth tax over exodus fears | Dutch PM scraps plan to target paper profits, instead introducing a more convention capital gains levy

3) Diesel crisis deepens as UK’s biggest refinery shuts for 10 weeks | Fears of squeeze on supplies after fuel costs rise higher than £2 per litre

4) Debt-ridden France branded ‘the new sick man of Europe’ | Investors hope the European Central Bank sees the struggling country as ‘too big to fail’

5) Britain blocks foreign lawyers after surge in south Asian applicants | Bar Standards Board halts scheme unless candidates have already secured a position

What happened overnight

The cost of government borrowing edged higher in Asia as soaring energy costs sparked inflation fears.

Bond yields, a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money, surged in September as investors brace for a period where interest rates stay higher for ​longer.

The yield on benchmark US 10-year Treasury notes hit 5.31pc, the ‌highest level since mid-June 2007. The 10-year yield gained 87 basis points in the July-September quarter, the biggest quarterly rise since 1994.

Market focus has been on how long US Treasury yields stay above the psychologically important 5pc level, while some investors even contemplate the possibility of yields breaching 6pc.

Yields in Japan have climbed to multi-decade highs too, while those in Germany, France and Britain have all hit 17 to 19 year peaks.

On Thursday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government ​bond yield was at 3.11pc, not far from the 30-year high it hit last week.

Asian technology stocks rose after a boost from AI chipmaker Micron, ​although US bonds struggled ‌after their sharpest quarterly sell-off in more than three decades as inflation risks from elevated energy prices linger.

Stalling peace talks between the US and Iran to end the seven-month-long war in the Middle East have kept crude prices aloft.Brent futures surged 42pc in the July-September quarter.

The high-stakes earnings from Micron, a key supplier to AI bellwether Nvidia, signalled strong demand for AI memory chips, with financial commitments under long-term supply agreements at $32 billion, up from $22 billion in June.

That helped push tech-heavy stock markets in Asia higher. Japan’s Nikkei jumped over 3pc, and South Korea’s Kospi reversed earlier losses to gain 1.7pc. Taiwan’s stock benchmark was 0.8pc higher.

News.title: Chewing tobacco killed 250,000 people in one year, study shows
News.content:
Chewing tobacco killed around a quarter of a million people in 2023, with use of the product remaining stubbornly high, according to research.

The smokeless tobacco is particularly popular in south Asia that is placed between the cheek and lower gum. It is flavoured and sometimes sweetened, and users often spit out unwanted juices while chewing. It is often viewed as safer than smoking but it is a major cause of stroke, as well as head and neck cancer.

Chewing tobacco is different to white snus or nicotine pouches, which contain no tobacco. These white pouches are also made up of flavourings and sometimes sweeteners, and deliver a hit of nicotine through the lining of the mouth.

Despite a successful fight against smoking over the last few decades, rates of chewing tobacco use have fallen little and it has often been overlooked in tobacco control efforts, researchers point out. In a study published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in the US estimate that 241 million people aged 15 years and older used chewing tobacco in 2023.

Researchers looked at data on use in 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 and found that there was no significant decrease in the number of users of chewing tobacco over that period. And in 24 countries there was a significant uptick in the number of people using the product. Researchers estimate that about one in five men and one in 10 women in south Asia chewed tobacco in 2023.

Bangladesh has seen the biggest increase in the number of people using the product with 15 million new users between 1990 and 2023. Nepal, Madagascar and Yemen also saw increases in the number of users.

In India 105 million people chew tobacco regularly, accounting for just over two thirds of users globally. Historically, Indians would chew paan, tobacco in its raw form which was mixed with betel leaf and areca nut, a mild stimulant. But the use of chewing tobacco exploded in the 1980s when manufacturers began grinding these into a powder and selling them in packets known as gutkha. This was banned in 2012 but is still widely available. Chewing tobacco is also popular in Pakistan, China and Vietnam.

News.title: Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
News.content:
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.

When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.

In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.

Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.

Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.

In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.

She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”

News.title: Laptop running slowly? These tips will improve performance (and save your sanity)
News.content:
MacBooks and Windows laptops both have modes intended to maximise battery life. Low Power Mode (Mac) and Power Saver (Windows) should be avoided if you want peak performance.

On a Mac, you’ll find the Low Power Mode switch in Settings > Battery. For the best experience, set this to Never, but remember to change it back if you need your MacBook to last longer.

On a Windows laptop, there are two controls you need to consider. Both are found in Settings > System > Power & Battery.

Energy Saver mode uses multiple tactics to reduce battery consumption, including lowering maximum power. Switch this off, and you have access to Power Mode controls.

Your options are Best Power Efficiency, Balanced and Best Performance. While Balanced is the default, I was able to unlock up to 33 per cent more power by playing around with these settings using my own laptop.

To make matters more complicated, some laptops have their own performance modes. Many Asus laptops have MyAsus or Armory Crate, for example. Lenovo has the Vantage app, Dell has MyDell, and MSI laptops have MSI Center.

3. Stop applications from opening on start-up

If your laptop is slow when it first starts up, it may be because a whole bunch of apps have been given the green light to wake up with it.

Some applications such as antivirus software are critical, but most can be toggled off. As an example, I make sure apps such as Spotify, Steam and WhatsApp don’t open on startup; I only launch them when I need them.

On a MacBook, you can see which apps have this permission in Settings > General, under Open at Login. Select an app entry and click the “minus” button to remove it.

On a Windows laptop, you’ll find the list of start-up apps in Settings > Apps > Startup. Each entry has a little on/off slider.

News.title: Why the UK medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks
News.content:
The UK’s medicine supply chain is dangerously exposed to global shocks, experts have warned, with the NHS dependent on a system where much of the world relies on a handful of countries for its drug supplies.

India and China are the backbone of the global medicines market, manufacturing around two-thirds of the world’s active pharmaceutical ingredients. This leaves countries exposed to factory shutdowns, natural disasters, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruption and sudden changes in the price or availability of raw materials, experts told The Telegraph.

“We rely now more than ever on other countries to make sure we can get access to the medicines that the vast majority of people take,” said Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England.

Nearly all the active ingredients in the UK’s most widely used medicines are made overseas, around 80 per cent of them in China and India, leaving the NHS exposed to shocks thousands of miles beyond its control.

The resilience of Britain’s medicine supply has eroded gradually in recent years, as global instability has placed growing strain on the supply chains it depends on.

“We’ve seen more global turbulence in general,” said Dr Davies. “It’s not unique to the UK, but it’s affecting countries across Europe, across the Western world, with the Iran war, with difficulties flying things over Ukraine and Russia, and challenges with shipping in the Red Sea.”

In the UK, shortages have been reported across a wide range of products, including antibiotics, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder medicines, epilepsy treatments, hormone replacement therapy, and some diabetes medicines.

The drugs most at risk are the cheapest and most widely used – statins, blood pressure pills and antibiotics – taken by millions of people and manufactured in China and India at huge scale and minimal cost.

“Some antibiotics are almost exclusively made in China,” said Dr Davies. “For some of the blood pressure medicines, they’re more likely to be made in India. But across the board, those two are where most of the raw ingredients for those active pharmaceutical ingredients come from.”

News.title: Fraudster jailed for 41 years over Pakistani nurse scam in Saudi
News.content:
A fraudster who sent 92 Pakistani nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake documents in an elaborate scam to provide workers for short-staffed Gulf hospitals has been jailed for 41 years.

Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali used forged experience certificates, created fake verification QR codes and phoney employment platform IDs.

Ali was being paid by the Saudi authorities to find staff, but also charged genuine Pakistani nurses who wanted a job overseas, in a racket that has caused major embarrassment to the Pakistan’s authorities.

Gulf nations including Saudi Arabia are experiencing a severe shortage of nurses, compounded by rapid population growth, a rising burden of chronic diseases, and heavy dependence on nurses from abroad.

The World Health Organization (WHO) forecasts a global shortfall of 4.5 million nurses by 2030, and recruiting nurses for developed countries is a lucrative trade.

The 91 women were all genuine nurses, but did not meet the criteria for the “Nurse Highly Qualified” visa category under which they were sent.

When the Saudi authorities realised the fraud they deported all the nurses.

Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bukhari, director of Pakistan’s Federal Investigation Agency, told the Telegraph: “They lost both their money and their employment, and the incident caused serious embarrassment to Pakistan internationally.”

Investigators found that between October 2022 and September 2023, a Pakistani employment firm called M/S Sahou Manpower obtained permissions for the recruitment of 108 nurses for a Saudi-based manpower company, to work in hospitals under the visa category “Nurse Highly Qualified”.

The investigation found the Saudi employer bore all recruitment costs, including visa processing fees and air tickets.

It paid the Pakistani recruiting firm between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,100 (GBP 830) per candidate. However, Ali was also demanding between $800 (GBP 600) and $1,000 (GBP 750) from each nurse.

Investigators found the candidates were genuine nurses, but did not meet experience requirements and were given fake certificates.

Meanwhile Ali had not uploaded their details to Saudi systems designed to verify and check qualifications and give each applicant a QR code. Instead he provided them with faked QR codes and verification platform IDs.

Ali was convicted of cheating, two counts of forgery and emigration offences.

He was given 41 years imprisonment by the special court in Rawalpindi. He was also fined £1,904 and ordered to pay £25,031 compensation – £272 to each of the 92 nurses.

His accomplice, Ghulam Fareed, was given three years’ imprisonment and a £544 penalty.

Nasreen Begum, one of nurses, told the Telegraph: “We are thankful to FIA for compensation. Most of us have genuine qualifications as nurse-midwives, licenced practical nurses, clinical nursing assistants and a lady health visitor but our documents weren’t verified and that landed us in a difficult situation.”

Zeenat Khan, another victim of the fraud, said she had opted to take a job in Saudi Arabia because she was jobless despite having nursing qualifications.

She said: “I have three kids and wanted to give them a good education. Now, I hope to get back my money,” she said.

Swera Ali said she had been working in a private hospital in her native Lahore, Punjab province, but received only £50 a month and performed 16 hours duty.

She said: “My parents took a loan from relatives to facilitate me, but my hope of making money from an overseas job was short-lived when they deported us after less than a month.”

Mr Bukhari added: “The investigation established that their nursing diplomas were genuine. The fake QR codes and fake [employment platform] IDs were created by the accused, and the experience certificates were forged by the visa agent without the knowledge of the nurses.”

News.content:
Yes, for sure [this is as good as I’ve felt in an England shirt. My football IQ, I’m getting better and better, smarter and smarter. I need time to really feel at home, to feel comfortable and once I have that I don’t look back.

I knew exactly where I wanted to go, where I needed to go but I needed some guidance. I think the same way as him [Jude]. We don’t think there’s any limit on what we can achieve, wanting to win, wanting to win in a good way by going for the throat. Fearlessness.

It ate me up for a good couple of weeks after [losing the semi-final]. I’d scored… on the same pitch as Messi, the man I idolised as a kid. It was the highest possible moment of my entire life. And within 20 minutes it had come completely crashing down. There’s been a lot of controversy, a lot of talk about that. Going forward, if we are going to lose a game, it’s going to be like how we lost to Spain. We went for their throats, we missed a penalty and lost the game. But the way we went for them, no regrets. I want to stay as far away from that [regret] as possible.

[Did you ever think you would sign for Barcelona?] Yes. No one ever achieves anything in life by playing it safe. My personality is based on being bold, taking risks and going for whatever you want.

At this level we’re all as talented as each other but only the most mentally competitive and driven people can maintain success for a long time.

I always thought in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never respected my quality and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick. In Barcelona if you’re not technical, if you’re not smart, you’d stand out like a sore thumb.

News.title: How vaccines and antibiotics can beat some cancers
News.content:
At least one in eight cancers worldwide are caused by viruses and bacteria, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 – out of a total of 20 million recorded worldwide – were caused by common infections, almost all of which could have been prevented with treatments such as antibiotics or vaccines.

Almost half of infection-linked cancers, around 760,000 cases, were caused by H. pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach, researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer found.

The pathogen, which is typically ingested through contaminated food and water and is carried by around 60 per cent of the world’s population at any given time, can remain relatively undetected in the gut for between 20 and 40 years without causing any symptoms.

If left untreated, it can trigger chronic inflammation in the stomach and cellular mutations that, in some cases, lead to gastric cancer.

Cases of stomach cancer linked to H. pylori are particularly common in East Asia, where roughly 80 per cent of the population carries the bacterium. This is due in part to the prevalence of a more aggressive strain of the pathogen, known as CagA, which is endemic to the region.

East Asian diets – which typically include salty, pickled or smoked foods – can also damage the stomach’s protective lining and accelerate the inflammatory processes that can contribute to stomach cancer, researchers have found.

While H. pylori infection is treatable with a course of antibiotics, its symptoms often mimic those of other digestive problems and can be difficult to distinguish without testing.

This means the infection can remain undetected for years, allowing inflammation and damage to progress.

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Andy Burnham's new statement and 'evidence' to appeal guilty verdict
Sports.content:
The latest news on Manchester City after the club were found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules, as the deadline to appeal the decision moves ever closer

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football's Manchester City charges live blog for Thursday, October 1.

The Premier League announced earlier this week that City had been found guilty of 114 charges brought against them for financial breaches.

City responded by maintaining their innocence and have until Friday to launch an appeal, with the club expected to do so before the deadline.

It now remains to be seen what punishment is given to City, with reports claiming that chiefs at other football clubs want a sanction to be imposed before the end of the season.

Etihad, the main shirt sponsor for City, meanwhile, have also issued a statement in response saying they are "deeply concerned" by the Premier League's announcement. There are also concerns that City's Abu Dhabi owners could be stripped from the club, something Prime Minister Andy Burnham doesn't want to happen.

City are now set to argue that the government of Abu Dhabi - not the club's owners - part-funded the "sham" sponsorship deals that contributed to them breaching Premier League financial rules.

Stay tuned for the latest news and updates in our live blog below as the saga continues to unfold...

Sports.title: Ireland vs Austria match suddenly halted as furious supporters stage Israel protest
Sports.content:
Ireland vs Austria match suddenly halted as furious supporters stage Israel protest

Ireland's Nations League clash with Austria at the Aviva Stadium was disrupted twice by protest, with tennis balls bearing the Palestine flag thrown onto the pitch in the 20th minute

View 3 Images Security staff tackle a protestor wearing a Palestine flag (Image: Charles McQuillan, Getty Images)

Ireland's match with Austria was twice halted by protestors as demonstrators voiced their opposition to Israel, ahead of the nation's second Nations League match with the side this week. Supporters hurled tennis balls onto the pitch forcing tonight's to stop for a couple of minutes.

‌



‌



The incident took place in the 20th minute, when numerous balls bearing the Palestine flag were lobbed onto the playing surface. It is the second time in succession that a protest has utilised tennis balls at the Aviva Stadium following a friendly against Qatar in June.

‌



A second interruption occurred in the 36th minute when a supporter attempted to invade the pitch but was quickly intercepted by security. They also carried the Palestinian flag.

‌



Before kick-off, protestors gathered with the Stop the Game campaign outside the Aviva Stadium. The movement has been demanding that Ireland boycott the Nations League fixtures with Israel during this international break.

Lionel Messi officially completes takeover as icon splashes out on second football club

Inter Miami star Lionel Messi has completed the takeover of a second team in Spain as the Argentina international continues to build a portfolio of clubs

Lionel Messi has officially completed his takeover of Club Deportivo Eldense to continue growing his football empire. The Inter Miami star already has Spanish side UE Cornella under his ownership and has now added second-division side Eldense to his collection.

‌



‌

‌

Sports.title: Premier League to avoid £4.5bn 'refunds' over Man City verdict after discount talks
Sports.content:
Premier League to avoid £4.5bn 'refunds' over Man City verdict after discount talks

Manchester City were found guilty of 114 of their 115 Premier League financial breaches, leading to concerns that the Premier League's broadcast partners could take action

View 2 Images Premier League are facing calls to significantly sanction Man City but they will not be forced to refund broadcasters after lucrative deal (Image: Getty Images)

The Premier League will reportedly avoid paying billions in refunds after Manchester City's guilty verdict in their legal battle with the top-flight. The Manchester club are left reeling after the independent commission found them guilty of 114 out of 115 charges, a verdict they are expected to appeal after steadfastly maintaining their innocence.

‌



‌



In 2018, the Premier League agreed a domestic TV rights deal worth £4.5billion, which fell in the last year of the investigation into City's alleged financial breaches starting in 2009/10. Broadcasters boast showing thousands of football matches with Sky Sports and TNT Sports/HBO Max holding the rights to the top-flight, with the offering of Premier League matches making up a significant portion of their investment.

‌



It has been suggested that organisations could seek compensation from the Premier League, having paid to show one of the most lucrative periods in the competition's history, due to question marks over the integrity in light of the findings surrounding City.

‌



Man City appeal could force case to drag on until 2027 as Premier League feud intensifies READ MORE :

However, the Daily Mail have rubbished the claim with the prospect of calls for refunds deemed 'highly unlikely', it was also noted that subscription figures could diminish dependent on City's punishment result but it was also described as unlikely.

This week, the Premier League confirmed that an independent commission had found City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the financial rules over a nine-season period.

It was alleged that the club "arranged sham contracts" and relied "on sham agreements with others to artificially inflate" the true state of finances.

‌



City have been found guilty of concealing the true state of finances from auditors and football regulators, as well as significantly breaching top-flight and UEFA spending rules.

View 2 Images Manchester City are facing serious questions and face significant sanctions (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

‌



In a statement, the Premier League's current leaders said: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

"The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums. The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted.

Article continues below

"Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence. The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: Man City appeal could force case to drag on until 2027 as Premier League feud intensifies
Sports.content:
Man City appeal could force case to drag on until 2027 as Premier League feud intensifies

Manchester City have until Friday to submit their appeal after an independent commission found the club guilty of 114 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules

View 2 Images Manchester City are fighting to overturn the guilty verdict (Image: Chelsea Football Club/Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

Manchester City will launch an appeal based on evidence which has already been branded “untrue” by the Premier League. And now the appeal is set to become even more bloody and bitter - and the feud between City and the Premier League could drag on beyond the end of the season.

‌



‌



City’s lawyers will argue that an Abu Dhabi government body - rather than Sheikh Mansour - provided the funding at the heart of the bitter financial dispute. City were found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules and used “sham” arrangements to inflate figures and sponsorship deals to the tune of £900m.

‌



But City will lodge an appeal by Friday’s deadline arguing that the financial top-ups were provided by the Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Court (CPC). City chief executive Ferran Soriano said in an address to staff after the Premier League verdict was published: “The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation – that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true.

‌



“Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows that it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner.”

FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



The Premier League’s 40-page core decision published on Tuesday shows the independent commission rejected the CPC explanation as “untrue” in its findings, adding: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme.”

City immediately indicated their intention to appeal on Tuesday evening, saying the commission’s decision contained “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.” City plan to challenge the Premier League’s assertion but it would seem unlikely there will be a complete U-turn.

The appeal board - appointed by the Chair of the Judicial Panel will have three members - will hear City’s defence but the appeal is already in danger of turning into a farce. Rival clubs are also queueing up to take legal action against City to sue for damages in the wake of the Premier League’s guilty verdict.

‌



Can Manchester City win their appeal? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano have pleaded their innocence (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

Former England defender Gary Neville has said the Premier League has “been dragged through the mud” by the whole case. Neville said on the Stick to Football podcast: “To listen to this, it is chilling.

Article continues below

“We always think that we’ve got an enormous integrity, the Premier League, that we are the sort of league that sets the standard, and that it’s other leagues that have got corruption, fraud, doping scandals, match-fixing, referee scandals.

“This is now coming to our country. This is now coming to our league. This is the greatest export that we have in our country. At the moment we’re being dragged through the mud.”

Sports.title: Humphries dazzles on the doubles to reach Grand Prix quarter-finals
Sports.content:
Luke Humphries put in a much-improved display as his doubling prowess and a 10-dart finish secured a 3-0 rout of Jermaine Wattimena and a spot in the World Grand Prix quarter-finals.

There were also 3-1 victories for James Wade and Niels Zonneveld over Stephen Bunting and Gary Anderson respectively, while Gian Van Veen came through a deciding-set cracker with Ryan Searle to triumph 3-2.

Humphries - the title favourite after defending champion Luke Littler's shock defeat to Luke Woodhouse on the opening night - had averaged only 80 and gone at 26 per cent on his closing doubles in a scruffy 2-0 win over Dave Chisnall on Tuesday evening.

Two nights later, the 2023 champion and 2024 and 2025 runner-up averaged 94.11 and secured a finishing-double percentage of 64, although his starting-double percentage of 74 was the most eye-catching stat as he peppered double 16 early in legs.

Image: Humphries will take on Niels Zonneveld in Friday's quarter-finals

'Cool Hand' - who will face Wattimena's fellow Dutchman Zonneveld in the last eight on Friday - hit his 10-darter at the start of the third set, while Wattimena twice hit the wrong double in the opening set.

Humphries said afterwards: "I've got a good chance of winning this. At the moment I'm a bit up and down, but if I can put that right I'm going to be tough to beat.

"It wasn't the best performance, but it was a good performance. It was a lot better than it was on Tuesday.

"I think I got in every time with my first three darts. When you're doing stuff like that, it's going to take a top performance to beat you."

Wade: Double start is 'hellish'

Wade, meanwhile, delivered a starting masterclass to reach his eighth World Grand Prix quarter-final, hitting an opening shot of 160 five times during his win over Bunting.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player James Wade regularly started legs with 160s against Stephen Bunting

The sixth seed dropped his standards in the third set but was electric in the other three as he set up a meeting with Van Veen.

Wade said: "I am so grateful as it is so hard to win with a double start. We can all play it cool and pretend to be relaxed but it is awful, it is hellish, really hard work.

"I don't feel anywhere near my best but I am having to play better against better players. I have loads more gears to go - but talk is cheap.

"And I am full of cheap talk!"

Van Veen wins thriller to secure Wade showdown

Elsewhere, Searle - who landed a 167 checkout, the highest of the week - threw for the match against Van Veen after breaking the Dutchman with a finish of 100 in the fourth set, only to be broken straightaway in the deciding leg.

Van Veen, who had led 2-0 in the penultimate set before being pegged back to 2-2 by Searle, then blitzed the final set 3-0.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ryan Searle pinned a brilliant 167 finish on the bull during his defeat to Gian van Veen at Mattioli Arena

The third seed said: "When I was 2-1 down in sets, I was like, 'oh no, this is not how I want to go out'.

"As good as double 16 went for me in the first round, it kind of bothered me today. But at the end it really came good.

"I was quite happy with my scoring, but just missed a couple of darts at a crucial time. Luckily I got the job done."

Anderson tumbles out as Zonneveld's run continues

Van Veen's compatriot Zonneveld followed his opening-round win over Josh Rock by dumping out Anderson, starting by winning a first set in which every leg went against the throw.

Anderson made a terrible start to the match, hitting single one and then suffering two bounce-outs, while he was the victim of another bounce-out in the fourth set as he aimed for a leg-winning bullseye.

Zonneveld subsequently broke before closing out victory in the next leg.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Anderson sees the humorous side as he misses a double, followed by two bounce-outs, on his first three darts

The 28-year-old said: "Especially in this tournament, it is one of the biggest things in my whole career.

"I have achieved many things Pro Tour-wise and Euro Tour-wise but not on the main stage, just once at the World Series Finals.

"I have become a dad so less sleep and all that but I feel in rhythm again."

Sports.title: 'Awful' and 'hellish' - Wade's brutal verdict on unique World Grand Prix format
Sports.content:
Veteran James Wade admits playing the World Grand Prix is "awful" and "hellish" despite reaching the quarter-finals on Thursday.

The 43-year-old, who last lifted a major trophy at the UK Open in 2021, continued his bid for a third World Grand Prix after producing a superb display to defeat Stephen Bunting 3-1 in the unique double-start format in Leicester.

Wade averaged 93.20 and fired in 15 140s, defying a 96 average from Bunting to book his place in the last eight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Polly James and Paul Nicholson discuss Wade's chances at the World Grand Prix

"I just felt like it was timing at the right place and the right time. It wasn't the right place for Stephen," Wade, nicknamed 'The Machine ', told Sky Sports' Polly James.

"I was better than average, I think. I am just grateful to win. It's so hard to win a double start.

"We can all play it cool and pretend to be relaxed and enjoying the game. But it's awful, it's hellish.

"It's not very nice. It's graft and just really hard work. We're not all cool, we are working very hard."

Wade, who took in a local art gallery in Leicester as part of his preparations, was asked whether he is currently playing some of the best darts of his career.

"Nowhere near really," he replied. "But I am having to play better against better players. I've got loads more gears to go.

"But talk is cheap and I am full of cheap talk."

Speaking at his press conference, Wade said: "I get nervous, I make myself feel ill, I don't want to get involved in it.

"I just want it to be over and done with quick.

"So am I well equipped or do I just deal with the c***** end of the stick better than others? It's so nerve-wracking; it's awful."

Sports.title: Shaw earns Man City draw with late Real goal dramatically disallowed
Sports.content:
Bunny Shaw and a dramatic last-gasp decision from the referee ensured Manchester City took a point off Real Madrid with a 1-1 draw in the Women's Champions League.

Standout Linda Caicedo had given Real the lead in the first half but City improved after the interval and Shaw levelled with an equally expert finish across the goalkeeper to put the league-phase clash in the balance.

Shaw headed over and Yui Hasegawa volleyed wide for the hosts before Ayaka Yamashita had to pull off an excellent stop to deny Irune Dorado as both sides pushed for a winner.

Silvia Cristobal thought she had clinched it in the 89th minute for Real Madrid with a wonderful finish into the top corner - but referee Silvia Gasperotti had whistled to stop play after inadvertently blocking Beth Mead from reaching the ball.

Real Madrid's players and coaching staff were furious and appealed for the goal to stand but ultimately this closely fought contest ended in a draw - the same result City achieved in their opening game away to Bayern Munich last week.

They will now turn their attention to this weekend's Women's Super League clash with Arsenal, live on Sky Sports, while Real prepare to face Barcelona.

Jeglertz: A lot of noise but players are very calm

Man City boss Andree Jeglertz:

"Of course there is a lot of noise outside but the players are very calm. There are no discussions, no thoughts from us [about the Premier League investigation].

"I haven't seen or noticed anything which would take any percentage out of the players' performance."

Real Madrid protest disallowed goal

Image: Real Madrid's Silvia Cristobal (left) reacts after referee Silvia Gasperotti rules out her goal

Image: Real Madrid head coach Pau Quesada protested against the ruled-out goal after the final whistle to referee Silvia Gasperotti

As it happened…

10: OFF THE BAR! Alex Greenwood clips an excellent free-kick from out wide into the Real Madrid six-yard box where Mary Fowler meets it - but sends her header against the bar!

21: BIG SAVE! Ayaka Yamashita rushes out to close down Felicia Schroder as she spins and shoots close to goal.

29: GOAL! Linda Caicedo runs around the outside of Laura Blindkilde Brown down the right and then is allowed too much space in the box by Greenwood before clipping her shot inside the far post.

40: CHANCE! Shaw shows good hold-up play in the box before laying off for Yui Hasegawa to shoot - and Maelle Lakrar bravely heads the powerfully hit effort away.

51: GOAL! Bunny Shaw hauls City level with a sharp finish across the keeper after Hasegawa does really well to turn the ball over in midfield.

62: OVER! It looks like a great chance for Shaw to add a second from Lauren Hemp's cross - but her header sends the ball over the bar.

75: OFF TARGET! A Greenwood corner comes out to Hasegawa just inside the area... but for the second time in the game she sends a volley wastefully wide!

77: SAVE! Another excellent stop from Yamashita, who gets a hand to Irune Dorado's shot.

89: BALL IN THE BACK OF THE NET...BUT NO GOAL! Real Madrid are fuming! Silvia Cristobal picked out the top corner and thought she had scored, but the whistle had already gone because referee Silvia Gasperotti had inadvertently blocked Mead, preventing her from getting to the ball.

Shaw pleased with second-half improvement from City

Man City's Bunny Shaw to Disney+:

"We started the second half much better than how we started the first half and that's something we're going to look on as a team.

"We're disappointed we didn't win the game but definitely [showed] fight at the end and that's good as well."

Analysis: City stay focused for hard-fought draw

Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom at City Football Academy:

"A hard-fought draw for City in their first home game back in this competition. There were a lot of distractions for everyone connected to the club in the build-up but it didn't show in their performance.

"An excellent strike from either side with moments of quality and it gives both teams something to build on from here.

"Big games await for both this weekend - City hosting Arsenal at the Etihad while Real Madrid go to Barcelona."

Sports.title: Bellamy gets perfect response as Wales beat 10-man Norway
Sports.content:
Wales responded to their disappointing defeat to Denmark with a spirited victory over Erling Haaland and 10-man Norway in Cardiff.

Craig Bellamy had admitted he was hurt by the performance against the Danes as his side continued their winless start to their Nations League campaign.

However, after a slow start, the Dragons showed their heart by producing an unerring display in front of their home fans to turn around an early deficit to secure three points.

The big news pre-match was that Erling Haaland started for the visitors in his first game since Manchester City were found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission.

Image: Oscar Bobb opened the scoring for Norway

Haaland was largely anonymous though, and it was another former City man in Oscar Bobb who opened the scoring in the worst possible start for Bellamy's men. However, the setback appeared to galvanise the hosts, who responded brilliantly.

Sorba Thomas looked unstoppable down the left-hand side, and after a number of dangerous crosses came to nothing, he found his mark shortly before the half with Daniel James sliding home an equaliser.

Image: Dan James equalised for Wales before half-time

James was at the heart of a chaotic opening few minutes of the second half. Torbjorn Heggem fell asleep at the restart, and was forced to pull down James as he looked to nip in and bear down on goal just 15 seconds into the half.

The defender was shown his marching orders, and Neco Williams smashed home the resulting free-kick low to the goalkeeper's right to turn the game on its head.

Wales had numerous chances to extend their lead and failure to do so made for a nervy ending. However, they held on to secure their maiden Nations League A victory.

Key moments from Cardiff

11: GOAL! Bobb gives Norway early lead after silky Odegaard assist.

17: INJURY! Ryerson forced off early on, with Sorba Thomas toying with replacement Holmgren Pedersen for remainder of the half.

28: CHANCE! Wicked Thomas cross nearly put into own net by Ajer.

38: GOAL! Thomas finally gets his reward as he sets up James for equaliser.

46: RED CARD! Heggem dismissed 15 seconds into second half for dragging down James.

48: GOAL! Williams completes comeback with resulting free-kick.

59: CHANCE! Haaland heads over from close range.

71: WIDE! Thomas misses target in search of deserved goal.

81: HAALAND CHANCE! Striker heads straight at Ward.

Williams: The first two games wasn't us - we put it right today

Wales defender Neco Williams speaking with BBC Sport:

"We knew the first two games wasn't us. The principles, the standards. We knew we had to put it right today.

"We analysed, we were looking at what went wrong in the first two games. We worked in training and we had to put that right. Obviously that worked.

"Going 1-0 down early, it is easy for heads to drop. How we felt in the last two games, it was easy to do that again. But we never did. We kept going and we deserved to win in the end."

Image: Neco Williams says Wales showed their true selves after disappointing performances against Portugal and Denmark

On his goal:

"I think it was more instinct. Looking at the goalkeeper's position and where the wall is. You just decide what's best. Going across the goalkeeper was the best tonight."

On beating a team the level of Norway:

"It's massive for us. Everyone saw how well they played at the World Cup and how good they are as a nation. They've got world-class players. We can do it against these top nations. We have to look forward now until the next game."

Sports.title: Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier League
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister.

Government officials are ­understood to be unhappy they were not given notice that the ­independent commission’s damning judgment of £900m of financial manipulation and “sham contracts” would be published shortly after Burnham’s address at the Labour party ­conference on Tuesday, and his response has not gone down well with several ­Premier League clubs concerned by his ­relationship with City’s owners.

In a series of interviews on Wednesday Burnham said he would be “really concerned” if City’s owners were forced to sell after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.

Such was the reaction that ­Downing Street felt compelled to ­clarify ­Burnham’s position on ­Thursday, with a No 10 ­spokesperson saying the prime minister had made clear that “the initial judgment is ­serious” and “there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.

With City appealing against the verdict, the spokesperson noted the process had to be allowed to run its course but said: “If wrongdoing is established those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” That phrase raised eyebrows given City have been found guilty by an independent commission after a 42-day hearing that produced 7,000 pages of witness evidence, eight years after the Premier League began investigating the club.

Burnham’s apparent sympathy for City, with a warning about ­jumping to conclusions and praise for the ­owners’ investment in ­Manchester, has alarmed some clubs but the ­Premier League declined to respond.

HMRC is facing calls to get involved, with Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury committee, asking for its response to the commission’s judgment. In a letter to John-Paul Marks, the permanent secretary of HMRC, Hillier sought assurances that the tax authority was “seized of the importance” of the case and asked whether it had requested an unredacted copy of the commission’s verdict.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

The Times and Daily Mail have reported that City’s appeal will be based on evidence the club claim proves their sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club. The commission rejected that argument as “untrue”.

Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and ­conceal the realities of the Disguised ­Funding Scheme.”

Burnham has history with the ­Premier League, which he ­mentioned in Wednesday’s ­interviews by ­referencing his criticisms of its ­prosecution of his club, Everton, for financial rule breaches after they were docked 10 points – reduced to six on appeal – by an independent commission three years ago.

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham with the Manchester City chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at Vincent Kompany’s testimonial in 2019. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live News

In November 2023, Burnham, when mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Premier League chair, Alison Brittain, accusing the league of an “abuse of process” and claimed Everton were being used as a pawn in efforts to show an independent ­regulator was not required in football.
