World.title: Trump launches midterms campaign blitz amid record low approval ratings
World.content:
In a series of campaign-style rallies, Trump seeks to boost Republican odds despite opposition to the Iran war and rising fuel costs.

United States President Donald Trump has kicked off a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections that could see his Republican Party hurt by his handling of the war on Iran and the economy.

On Thursday, Trump travelled from Washington, DC, for back-to-back rallies in Texas and Oklahoma.

At his first stop in Denton, Texas, Trump sought to shift the narrative around his drooping approval ratings, offering a personal assessment of his administration’s performance.

“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything,” Trump told a crowd of supporters at the Peterbilt Motors Company, a truck manufacturer.

The president also blamed unfair media coverage for his growing unpopularity, arguing that his pre-election rally blitz was necessary to set the record straight.

“We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion and an extremely great job of running the country,” Trump said.

But Trump’s poll numbers have raised concerns about Republican prospects ahead of the November 3 midterm election.

Trump himself is not on the ballot, but Republican candidates across the country are seeking to defend the right-wing party’s majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

The economy and Trump’s war on Iran are expected to weigh heavily on the election outcome.

On Thursday, The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research released new poll results showing that 71 percent of Americans disapprove of the war, which has driven up the price of fuel.



About half of survey respondents also said they were worried they would not be able to afford food and petrol. Only 26 percent approved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

Taking centre stage

Still, despite record low approval ratings, Trump has positioned himself as key to the Republican midterm strategy.

At a first-of-its-kind Republican midterm convention in September, Trump encouraged voters to consider his record while at the ballot box. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said.

During Thursday’s tour, he touted the impact of his tariff campaign, which he credited with creating thousands of manufacturing jobs.

“For decades, you were heartlessly betrayed by politicians, lousy politicians, who let foreign trade cheaters plunder your wages, loot your factories, close up your jobs,” Trump told Peterbilt workers. “They’d still be doing it if I wasn’t here, believe me.”

Trump’s tariffs, however, have been highly controversial, prompting a series of court challenges. Critics have argued that the sweeping import taxes surpass the president’s constitutional powers.

Trump also used his stump speech to ease concerns about the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28. Both sides have declared victory, though a ceasefire remains elusive.

“Just as I promised, I’m ensuring that Iran will be very quickly ended. I will tell you the energy prices are going to be rapidly, rapidly coming down,” Trump said.

“We’ll win very easily right now,” he added. “I believe right after the election we’ll win, but maybe before the election.”

The war, however, resulted in Iran stopping commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global fuel trade.

The price of diesel — the fuel the trucks built at the plant use — soared to record highs of more than $6 per gallon (3.8 litres) last week. Petrol prices have similarly skyrocketed.

Hurting or helping his fellow Republicans?

Trump, however, has acknowledged that the stakes are high for his presidency in the upcoming midterms.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, as are 35 seats in the 100-member Senate.

Losing Republican control of either chamber could create roadblocks for Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.

But Trump has also expressed concern that he could be impeached for a third time, after two prior impeachments during his first presidency.

At Thursday’s second stop, in Durant, Oklahoma, the Republican leader repeated that fear. “Pretend I’m running, please,” he told the crowd. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.”



Many of the places Trump is scheduled to visit this month are perceived as reliably Republican voting districts. Following his stops in Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump will be heading to Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska in the coming days.

Still, some elections that ordinarily would be considered shoo-ins for Republicans have grown more competitive in recent months.

In Texas, for instance, no Democrat has won a statewide race since the 1990s. But this year, Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is struggling to win a Senate contest against Democrat James Talarico.

During both of Thursday’s stops, Trump sought to bolster Paxton’s prospects. At the Peterbilt factory, for instance, he called Paxton “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”.

“We gotta get this guy elected,” Trump said, before pivoting to criticisms of Talarico, whom Republicans have sought to paint as out of touch with Texas’s large beef industry.

“He’s a vegan,” Trump said of Talarico, repeating an unsubstantiated rumour. “And vegans don’t do well in Texas.”

But leaked audio appeared to show Paxton lamenting the negative impact Trump had by holding the Republican midterm convention in Texas last month.

“It dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped,” Paxton reportedly said.

Trump touts social conservatism

Trump has nevertheless used his pre-election tour to highlight social issues he feels will help rally voters to the Republican cause.

On Thursday, he returned to familiar subjects like immigration and transgender rights, which he depicted as a part of the Democrats’ “radical” agenda.

“They want women in men’s sports. They want open borders. They want transgender mutilation for your children,” Trump said. “What the hell are you thinking about, you liberals?”

The president also used his Texas appearance to push back against critics of data centres, despite bipartisan concern.

Critics worry that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has fuelled the proliferation of data centres, which require large amounts of electricity and water to process mass data quantities.

While Trump has dismissed fears about AI as largely unfounded, a poll last month found 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the technology’s environmental impacts.

Even fellow Republicans in Texas are responding to public pressure about the growing number of data centres, more than 300 of which are operational, with hundreds more in progress.

In August, Governor Greg Abbott called for an audit of all data centres to map their water and electricity usage, and the following month, Paxton in his role as state attorney general launched an investigation into whether they were complying with water reporting requirements.

Trump nevertheless used his Texas rally to tout the expansion of such enterprises.

“It’s a huge thing. It’s bigger than the industrial revolution,” he said, dismissing the concerns as part of a “scam”. He then explained he had urged AI companies to “take care of the people”.



“They’re making a fortune for the communities,” he added.

World.title: Trump says US may ask Europe to release diesel reserves
World.content:
EU trade chief said a US ban on diesel would be “unexpected” but would have detrimental effects on Europe’s economy.

Share Trump says US may ask Europe to release diesel reserves on social media

President Donald Trump has said that the US could ask European countries to release diesel reserves, as Washington tries to rein in rising diesel prices due to the war on Iran.

The US president told reporters on Thursday that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.

“Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” Bessent said in a social media post.

Earlier, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that he believes France, Germany and Italy “would love to have a ⁠⁠⁠⁠cooperative path forward with the ⁠⁠⁠⁠United States on ⁠⁠⁠⁠how we get more diesel to market”.

European capitals have spent Thursday coordinating diesel measures, while US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global prices by releasing emergency diesel inventories. ⁠⁠

US diesel prices have surged, hitting a record of $6.53 ⁠⁠⁠⁠per gallon a week ago, as data published by the European Commission showed 12 EU member states had recorded new all-time highs, including Italy, Belgium, Romania and Poland.

The spike in US diesel prices prompted the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers to consider restricting US diesel exports ahead of upcoming midterm elections.

France and Germany hold more than a third of the EU’s strategic diesel reserves, according to the Reuters news agency. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said a US ban on diesel would be “unexpected” but would have detrimental effects on Europe’s economy.

World.title: UK-Mauritius Chagos sovereignty deal stalls amid fears of further delays
World.content:
Renewed talks over the stalled agreement have revived hope of resettlement, but ageing Chagossians fear time is running.

Pointe aux Sables, Mauritius – “At one funeral, we scattered sand from Chagos into an elder’s tomb to honour his unfulfilled wish to breathe his last in his homeland,” says Olivier Bancoult of the Chagos Refugees Group.

For elderly Chagossians displaced from their Indian Ocean homeland decades ago, delays to a treaty allowing their return are raising fears that they may never see the islands again.

The agreement, signed by Britain and Mauritius in May 2025, would allow resettlement on islands other than Diego Garcia, which would remain a military base. But it has yet to enter into force amid opposition from US President Donald Trump.

“We remain unshaken by Trump’s interference in the Chagos deal,” Bancoult says.

“The 2019 ICJ advisory opinion in favour of the archipelago’s return to Mauritius has restored our dignity and faith in our rights as native Chagossians.”

The Chagos archipelago, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, was separated from Mauritius by Britain in 1965, three years before Mauritius gained independence. Britain later established a military base with the US on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the group.

Between 1968 and 1973, Britain removed an estimated 1,400 to 1,700 Chagossians from the islands. Many were resettled in Mauritius and the Seychelles, with others later moving to the United Kingdom. British authorities also made it illegal to remain on or return to the islands without permission.

“If Trump wants to meddle in this matter, well, let him,” Bancoult says. “We’ve had the 2019 ICJ [International Court of Justice] advisory opinion, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea’s 2021 judgement, and the 2025 UK-Mauritius treaty providing for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the archipelago. International law is squarely on our side.”



Signed on May 22, 2025, the treaty provides for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, while allowing the UK to exercise rights over the Diego Garcia military base for an initial 99-year period. It also allows Mauritius to arrange for the resettlement of Chagossians on islands other than Diego Garcia. The treaty has not yet entered into force.

In April, the UK government told Parliament that the legislation needed to implement the agreement could not complete its passage during the 2024–26 parliamentary session. The session ended on April 29, meaning the bill made no further progress.

In January, Trump criticised the agreement, calling it an “act of great stupidity ” and questioning whether it adequately protected the Diego Garcia military base.

The issue returned to the diplomatic agenda in September. On September 21, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK would work with Mauritius and the US on a way forward that secures the operation of Diego Garcia and protects UK national security.

On September 26, Mauritian Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam travelled to the UK for talks with British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell and other officials on the Chagos issue. He remains in London, with the Mauritian government saying the discussions would cover recent developments concerning the archipelago.

For Bancoult, the central question is whether elderly Chagossians will live long enough to see the treaty’s promises fulfilled.

“Chagossians born on the archipelago are now aged between 58 and 100. We are growing old, and we have lost several Chagossian elders this year alone,” he says.

For younger Chagossians, the consequences are also cultural.

Chrisyl Wong-Hang-Sun, a PhD researcher in anthropology at the University of Edinburgh, says years of displacement and migration are making it harder to preserve Chagossian culture.

“During my fieldwork, many diaspora members expressed concerns over cultural loss, such as words in Chagossian Creole and recipes that are difficult to recreate abroad,” she says. “Descendants of Chagossians, myself included, long to know the islands of their relatives and ancestors.”

The dispute has also exposed political differences among Chagossians.

“The actions of both the British and Mauritian governments have resulted in very nuanced and differing political opinions among Chagossians across the UK, Mauritius and the Seychelles,” Wong-Hang-Sun says.



The Chagos Refugees Group is at odds with UK-based second-generation Chagossian Misley Mandarin and his supporters, who favour resettlement under British rather than Mauritian sovereignty and have received backing from Reform UK.

Wong-Hang-Sun says those differences should be recognised as negotiations continue.

Both governments, she says, need to “find ways to prioritise and engage with the Chagossian diaspora as a whole”.

Mauritius keeps talks largely private

Mauritius has disclosed little publicly about the substance of the latest talks on Chagos.

At the United Nations General Assembly in September, Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful reiterated Mauritius’ position that its sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago was “non-negotiable”. He also described the 2025 agreement as a vindication of international law and said Mauritius was committed to diplomacy and dialogue over the issue.

Beyond official statements and communiques, the Mauritian government has provided few details about the substance of the current discussions.

International relations consultant Bruno Donat, who has previously worked at the UN, says Mauritius should focus on sustained engagement with diplomatic partners, including the African Union, small island states, the Commonwealth Secretariat and sympathetic voices in the US Congress.

“Being in New York corridors for a photo” is not the priority, Donat says. Sustained engagement, he argues, can build pressure on Washington and prevent the issue from remaining unresolved indefinitely.

The Chagos Refugees Group has pursued a similar approach. In June, two months after the treaty stalled, its members travelled to the UK to lobby representatives of British political parties, with the exception of Reform UK.

The unresolved question of Diego Garcia

But Diego Garcia remains the most contentious part of the agreement.

Lalit, a Mauritian political organisation that has campaigned for decades for the closure of the base, opposes its continued military use. Lindsey Collen of Lalit says the treaty, as it stood in April, would have kept the base open and brought Mauritius into a closer relationship with the US military presence on the island.

“In addition to the moral responsibility, we have the knowledge that we might become a target for self-defence if our land is used this way,” she says.

Collen is also concerned about a new partnership between the Mauritius Police Force and the New Mexico National Guard, as well as what she describes as the “enormous military-looking buildings” of the new US embassy in Mauritius.

Donat argues that the treaty could instead give Mauritius greater leverage over how Diego Garcia is used.

“Mauritius has publicly stated that the strikes launched from Diego Garcia against Iran breached international law,” he says. “That is not the position of a government staying silent to protect a lease payment.”



For Bancoult, those wider strategic questions are secondary to the need to ensure that elderly Chagossians have the chance to return to their homeland during their lifetimes.

“We are opposed to war, ethically, but we are also running out of time.”

The Chagos Refugees Group hopes to soon celebrate the 101st birthday of one of its members.

“God willing, he’ll stay with us for more years,” Bancoult says.

World.title: Israeli drone kills Palestinian in Gaza, settlers kill another in West Bank
World.content:
Gaza’s health toll mounts, with 1,439 dead and 5,052 injured since the ceasefire began in October 2025.

Share Israeli drone kills Palestinian in Gaza, settlers kill another in West Bank on social media

An Israeli drone strike has killed a Palestinian man and wounded several others in southern Gaza while settlers shot dead another Palestinian man near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

The body of Tamer al-Hamayda, 42, and three wounded people were brought to Nasser Medical Complex on Thursday after the strike hit a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis on the southern coast of the Gaza Strip.

Another Palestinian succumbed to wounds sustained in an earlier Israeli drone strike on Tuesday that targeted a gathering of Palestinians in Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, according to medical personnel in Nasser Medical Complex.

Israeli forces also carried out a large-scale demolition operation targeting buildings east of Gaza City’s al-Tuffah neighbourhood.

The Gaza Health Ministry reported eight new deaths and 26 wounded over the past 24 hours, putting the toll since the “ceasefire” took effect in October 2025 at 1,439 killed and 5,052 wounded, with 834 bodies recovered from the rubble.

Israel’s war on Gaza has killed at least 74,040 Palestinians and wounded 175,168 since October 2023, the ministry said.

Occupied West Bank pogroms

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers shot dead a Palestinian man and wounded another during a raid on the village of Yasuf, north of Ramallah, on Thursday.

51-year-old Mashhour Yassin was shot dead by settler gunfire, the Palestinian Health Ministry said.

Describing the attack, the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Israeli forces had detained an ambulance, seizing its key and throwing it aside, “in a crime that reflects clear coordination between the settlers and occupation forces.”



It said the killing “falls within the framework of a serious and continuous escalation in organised settler crimes,” saying Israel gives free rein to settler “terrorism against our people in the service of settlement, annexation, forced displacement and ethnic cleansing plans.”

Yasuf Mayor Jumaa Abdel Fattah told the AFP news agency that dozens of Israeli settlers armed with sticks and firearms had attacked the village, which lies between four Israeli settlements.

“Yassin was at his doorstep when the settlers attacked the village homes. He went out to defend his house,” Abdel Fattah said, adding that Yassin’s nephew was also wounded in the attack.

Abdel Fattah said the settlers had come from Havat Anton, an illegal Israeli settlement established in July that has previously attacked the village’s residents.

Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have reported a surge in settler pogrom attacks in recent months.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements considered illegal under international law.

According to the UN, at least 1,112 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since October 2023, including at least 37 killed by settlers.

World.title: Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections, lawyer says
World.content:
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.

Her attempted execution on Wednesday was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.

Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".

On Thursday afternoon, Pike's lawyers offered more details about what happened during the attempted execution, describing a harrowing scene shrouded in secrecy.

"Last night, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line for an hour," Spivey said. "I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt."

Spivey said that observers were kept in a dark room behind a closed curtain, after the second lethal dose had been administered and "it was clear that Miss Pike was still breathing" minutes later.

"No-one knew what was going on behind that curtain," Spivey said. "I had no idea when and if medical professionals began to assist."

Spivey said the state's governor must commute Christa's sentence now, a request that was denied previously.

Stephen Ferrell, another of Pike's lawyers, said they were also looking at other legal options.

"We want to think this through and we want to make sure that Christa recovers and has some input in what she wants," he said.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review and said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".

"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."

Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.

His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.

The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.

It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."

Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, in accordance with state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings by her lawyers.

"This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.

The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."

US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".

"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.

Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".

"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.

This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.

In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a year's reprieve.

With additional reporting by Stephanie Hegarty, World Service correspondent

World.title: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
World.content:
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.

On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC in an email: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she [Pike] will have a brain injury."

Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.

In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.

A Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to send Willie Francis, a teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old, back to the electric chair.

The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Francis was executed aged 18.

"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.

World.title: Netanyahu says Flydubai attacker had 'Islamist radical indoctrination'
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.

UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

World.title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
World.content:
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.

"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.

He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.

"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."

He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.

Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.

Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".

Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.

He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.

He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.

"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

World.title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
World.content:
The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.

Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep in January. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest.

One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said.

A White House spokeswoman in a statement called the lawsuits "baseless".

The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good.

Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed."

"We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children.

In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death", according to the family's lawyer.

It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.

The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border tsar Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents and private actors".

"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci told Thursday's news conference.

World.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
World.content:
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.

Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.

Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.

Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.

"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."

Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.

The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.

He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.

World.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
World.content:
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (Â£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

Correction 1 October: An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men.com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men.com, is a legitimate business activity.

World.title: Japan raises permanent residency fee by 20 times
World.content:
Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; Â£955).

Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.

Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.

The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.

In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners â its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".

Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.

Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.

Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.

In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.

"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.

Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.

From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought â from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.

Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.

Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.

Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.

The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.

"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.

"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."

From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.

Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

World.title: Tinubu, Akpabio, Sanwo-Olu, others attend MKO documentary premiere
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu, Senate President Godswill Akpabio, Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu and Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, attended the national premiere of MKO, a documentary on the life and political legacy of the late businessman and politician, Moshood (MKO) Abiola.

The premiere was held on Thursday at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts in Iganmu, Lagos, as part of activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary.

Mr Tinubu, who served as Chief Host of the premiere, attended the event alongside First Lady Oluremi Tinubu.

Dignitaries

Also present were Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun, Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, Deputy Senate President Jibrin Barau, Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives Benjamin Kalu, Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy Hannatu Musawa, and former Ogun State Governor Segun Osoba.

The documentary’s director and producer, Nigerian-American filmmaker Ose Oyamendan, was also present.

The president’s arrival was captured in a video shared by presidential aide Dada Olusegun, showing Mr Tinubu and the First Lady entering the venue as a band played the national anthem.

Tinubu’s role in June 12 struggle

Speaking on the significance of the premiere, Mr Oyamendan paid tribute to Mr Tinubu and recalled his involvement in the struggle against military rule following the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Oyamendan said it was an honour for the film team that Mr Tinubu agreed to serve as Chief Host, adding that the significance of his role went beyond his attendance at the premiere.

The filmmaker said Mr Tinubu was among those who stood with the demand for the recognition of the June 12 mandate during the period of military rule.

According to Mr Oyamendan, the documentary examines the choices political actors made during the crisis and the consequences of those choices for Nigeria.

He said Mr Tinubu “risked his life, livelihood and his family’s safety by standing with the people’s mandate.”

Mr Oyamendan said the documentary was not simply about Mr Abiola but also about the struggle that shaped Nigeria’s democratic journey.

He added that 33 years after June 12, the documentary provides an opportunity for Nigerians to revisit what happened, understand its significance and reflect on its implications for the country’s democratic development.

Documentary revisits June 12

MKO chronicles the life, political career and legacy of Mr Abiola, with particular focus on the June 12 1993 presidential election, its annulment by the military government and the pro-democracy struggle that followed.

The documentary also examines Mr Abiola’s detention and the circumstances surrounding his death in custody in 1998.

It combines archival footage with first-hand accounts from people connected to the events.

Among those featured are former military leaders Ibrahim Babangida and Abdulsalami Abubakar, former President Olusegun Obasanjo, Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka and Mr Abiola’s running mate in the 1993 election, Baba Gana Kingibe.

Other contributors include former United States Ambassador to Nigeria Walter Carrington, former US Deputy Secretary of State Thomas Pickering, former Canadian High Commissioner Gerald Ohlsen, members of the Abiola family, foreign journalists and Theodore Zadok, who served as Mr Abiola’s security guard during his detention.

President Tinubu is also featured in the documentary, reflecting his involvement in the pro-democracy movement during the period.

Personal connection

The documentary also draws from Mr Oyamendan’s own experience of the June 12 period.

The filmmaker worked as a young journalist with Weekend Concord during the crisis and has used archival material and interviews with key personalities to reconstruct Mr Abiola’s political journey and the events surrounding the annulment.

Mr Oyamendan said the film’s extensive archive and testimonies provide an intimate account of one of the most significant periods in Nigeria’s political history.

The 108-minute documentary had its international premiere at the Sheffield International Documentary Festival in the United Kingdom on 12 June, before its Nigerian premiere in Lagos.

Cinema opening

Following Thursday’s national premiere, MKO is scheduled to open in cinemas across Nigeria from Friday, 2 October.

Nile Entertainment is handling the film’s Nigerian theatrical distribution.

The distributor’s Managing Director, Moses Babatope, said the project was particularly significant to him because his father worked at Concord Newspapers, one of the media organisations founded by Abiola.

Mr Babatope said the documentary would help preserve an important chapter of Nigeria’s political history and make it accessible to younger Nigerians who did not experience the June 12 crisis.

The choice of 1 October for the national premiere links the story of Abiola and the June 12 struggle with Nigeria’s Independence Day celebrations.

The event therefore brings together the country’s independence history, the June 12 political crisis and the subsequent struggle for democracy in a single national screening.

World.title: Wike’s Rainbow: Governor Dauda Lawal’s red line, By Emmanuel Ado
World.content:
Did Chinua Achebe, the foremost African writer, have Nyesom Wike, the former governor of oil-rich Rivers State and now the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), specifically in mind—or was he writing about politicians generally—when he wrote his famous book, A Man of the People? The question arises not because of Achebe’s devastating portrayal of corruption among the political elite, but from his portrayal of Josiah, the petty thief whose unbridled greed ultimately became his greatest undoing.

Wike is not a petty thief; the connection between him and Josiah would soon be made.

Josiah had spent many years getting away with his shenanigans. He stole, deceived and exploited others with remarkable impunity. But then he crossed the red line, stealing a blind man’s walking stick, an outrageous act that finally provoked the community into action. Josiah had not suddenly become a thief; he had simply overreached himself. And in doing so, he learnt, sadly too late, a timeless political lesson that there is often a point at which audacity ceases to be tolerated and becomes the very thing that will provoke outrage and resistance.

The connection between Josiah and Wike is not that the Minister is a petty thief. Far from it. It is the pattern of conduct: the belief that political power can be exercised without caution, and that every boundary can be tested and overcome with greater force. Josiah’s undoing, like Wike’s, is not that he had suddenly become more audacious; it is that his accumulated excesses eventually crossed a threshold that made continued tolerance impossible.

Clearly Wike’s political audacity has reached a breaking point where it has united the All Progressives Congress (APC) governors, who had hitherto tolerated his excesses, against him.

Since he was thrust into the national limelight, Wike has spent years taking on virtually everyone who crossed his path, including his benefactors. He also played a significant role in the crisis that destroyed the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), allegedly following his failure to secure its presidential ticket and Atiku Abubakar’s decision not to choose him as his running mate. It is an open secret that part of his mandate as minister was to weaken the opposition parties, a task that he accomplished with missionary zeal and with great success.

In return, he was rewarded with enormous power over the political direction of Rivers State and strategically emboldened in his efforts to politically annihilate Governor Siminalayi Fubara, his successor with whom he was locked in a prolonged power struggle. But, like nzia —the little bird that, after a heavy feast, became so emboldened that it challenged its chi (personal god) to a fight—Wike decided to venture beyond his political territory, meddling in the affairs of other states in ways he would never have tolerated.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

While the APC governors had for long tolerated Wike and his trademark brashness, the emergence of his “Rainbow Coalition” appears to have ended what was always an uneasy political relationship.

What might previously have been dismissed as Wike’s familiar political swagger has become, in their view, a direct challenge to their own authority and control of the political structures in their respective states. The coalition is a cross-party platform through which Wike says he is mobilising support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election while backing candidates of other parties in governorship and legislative elections.

For the APC governors, however, that arrangement is totally unacceptable: they see support for the President at the presidential level while backing candidates outside the APC at other levels as a threat to the party and its candidates. Their position, as expressed through the Progressive Governors Forum, led by Hope Uzodimma is that Wike’s support for President Tinubu must extend to APC candidates at the governorship and legislative levels.

It’s Governor Dauda Lawal of Zamfara State that has put the governors’ position very bluntly. “Be on one side. You can’t be on two sides,” he bluntly told Wike, insisting that if the minister was genuinely committed to supporting President Tinubu, he should join the APC and campaign for its candidates. Lawal went further: “It’s either he is in APC or he is out.” He also promised to raise Wike’s political position with President Tinubu, making it clear that, from the perspective of the APC governors, Wike’s era of political ambiguity had reached its limit.

This is where the Wike matter is becoming particularly interesting. From every indication, his political usefulness that once gave him the considerable leverage appears to have largely diminished. His influence was closely tied to the dirty role he played in the internal crisis that destroyed the PDP, but the political landscape has since changed. The PDP is no longer the threat that the APC feared; the party is now confronted with challenges from Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, whose political movements are the real threat to the party. Consequently, the political value of keeping Wike within that old equation may no longer be what it once was.

Considering all of these, it is politically unwise for the all-knowing Wike to put President Bola Tinubu in a position where he has to choose between him and the 32 APC governors. He ought to have backed down. As Governor Lawal has indicated, the matter will inevitably get to the President, and when it does, Wike may find himself asking Tinubu to choose between a political alliance built around him and the governors who control the political structures of their respective states.

That is a difficult position to put any President in, particularly when the dispute concerns the interests of his own party. Wike may therefore discover that the political leverage he once enjoyed has limits when it comes up against the collective interests of the governors.

As a former governor, Wike ought to know the power that governors wield in Nigeria. Since the return to democratic rule in 1999, governors have gradually emerged as the most formidable political forces in the country. The transformation of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, particularly from 2003 onward, strengthened their capacity to act collectively and have their way.

There is ample evidence of the influence they have exercised. In 2010, for instance, the Governors’ Forum flexed its political muscle over the choice of a running mate for President Goodluck Jonathan, who eventually picked Namadi Sambo, then governor of Kaduna State. Even the powerful President Olusegun Obasanjo was not immune to the collective power of governors. During his administration, governors organised themselves around issues of fiscal federalism and challenged the Presidency in court over the distribution of federal revenues. In one notable confrontation, they successfully challenged Obasanjo’s position on the implementation of constitutional revenue-sharing provisions.

This history is important because Wike is not an outsider when it comes to the powers of the governors. He has been on that same side of the table. He knows what it means for 32 governors to speak with one voice, and he knows that they control political structures, influence delegates, shape party machinery and command substantial grassroots networks across their states that the president would not want to toy with.

It is the consequence of arrogating too much political sagacity to himself and forgetting that he is now playing on a national stage, and not in Rivers State, where the political tradition has often been for an incumbent governor to run his predecessor out of town.

Wike appears to have carried that political style beyond Rivers, assuming that the same political brashness would continue to give him the upper hand. But the circumstances are different. He is no longer dealing with a single political opponent; he is confronting 32 governors who have both a direct stake in the outcome and the institutional and political structures to defend it.

If Fubara had succeeded in running Wike out of Rivers State, Nigeria might have been spared the Wike problem. But politics, as it often does, has apparently convinced Wike that he can continue to ride roughshod over everyone and dictate the terms of every political contest, even when he has clearly lost ground. What Fubara failed to accomplish, the APC governors now appear determined to do. The difference, however, is that Wike is dealing with a determined group of governors who have a common political interest in stopping his influence from extending into their states.

And when that political battle is finally over, Wike may discover, perhaps too late, that he had an exaggerated opinion of his importance.

The APC governors are clearly not in the mood to further indulge him. He poses not just an immediate danger, but a future danger in 2031 with his Rainbow Coalition, which threatens the governors’ control of their political structures and their interests in the 2031 elections.

Like Josiah, the question is not merely whether Wike crossed a line, but whether, in pushing his political influence beyond acceptable boundaries, he has finally crossed a red line that forced Governor Dauda Lawal to tell him: enough is enough. The question, whether Wike has realized that he is engaged in one battle that he stands no chance. Like Josiah, he has definitely reached the point where the accumulation of confrontations has begun to create a broader resistance to him.

Governor Dauda Lawal’s decision to draw a red line against Wike’s so-called Rainbow Coalition—with the apparent support of his fellow APC governors—shows that Wike may finally have encountered the political resistance his accumulated confrontations have been building towards. Like Josiah, the issue is no longer simply how far he can push the boundaries, but whether he has pushed them far enough to unite those who have the political capacity to resist him.

*Emmanuel Ado, a public affairs analyst, writes from Abuja.

World.title: Independence Day: Wike urges FCT residents to elect leaders who can sustain infrastructure projects
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has urged residents to use the 2027 general elections to elect leaders with the vision and capacity to sustain and expand ongoing infrastructure development in the territory.

Mr Wike made the call in his Independence Day message to FCT residents on Thursday, as Nigeria marked its 66th anniversary.

The minister said the election would give residents a chance to choose leaders capable of consolidating the development projects underway across the territory.

“My dear residents, as the nation prepares for the forthcoming general elections in January 2027, I enjoin you all to see it as an opportunity to vote in progressive, visionary leaders that will sustain and expand the infrastructural revolution that has commenced in the FCT, leaders who have vision and capacity to bring more development and prosperity to the people,” he said.

Mr Wike said the FCT Administration had invested heavily in roads, public transportation, healthcare and education as part of its efforts to transform Abuja into a modern and functional capital.

He said the administration has expanded the road network from the city centre to communities across the territory, with drainage systems and solar streetlights incorporated into some projects.

The minister added that the projects were intended to improve access to communities while also addressing security concerns in areas farther from the city centre.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Wike also disclosed that an ultramodern bus terminal had been constructed in the Abuja Municipal Area Council, with plans to extend similar facilities to Kuje, Bwari and Gwagwalada.

He said the administration was also improving healthcare and education across the six area councils by rehabilitating primary healthcare centres and schools.

“Healthy and educated populations are the foundation of sustainable development,” Mr Wike said.

On security, the minister said the FCT Administration was working with security agencies to protect lives and property across the territory.

He said surveillance had been intensified, while community policing and modern technology were being deployed to combat crime.

Mr Wike urged residents to support the government’s development efforts by obeying the law and protecting public infrastructure from vandalism.

He also called on residents to maintain cleanliness and orderliness in the capital and promote peaceful coexistence among people from different ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds.

Describing Abuja as a symbol of national unity, the minister said the FCT remained a place where Nigerians from different parts of the country lived and worked together.

“The Federal Capital Territory stands as the ultimate symbol of our national unity, a place where Nigerians from every tribe, tongue, and faith come together to live, work, and thrive in peace,” he said.

Mr Wike said the administration’s primary mission was to transform Abuja into a world-class capital city where public services work for residents across the territory.

He said the development agenda was being extended beyond the city centre to ensure that residents in satellite towns and rural communities also benefited from government projects and services.

The minister also expressed optimism about Nigeria’s future and commended President Bola Tinubu’s administration for its reform efforts.

He said the FCT would continue to align with the federal government’s Renewed Hope agenda while extending development to communities across the territory.

“We acknowledge the challenges that have faced our nation in the past 66 years, but also see a great opportunity for renewal and sustainable growth. We are very optimistic that the future is brighter,” Mr Wike said.

World.title: Igbo-Eze South chairman speaks on reelection, vision for second term
World.content:
The Chairman of Igbo-Eze South Local Government Council, Enugu State, Ugo Ferdinand Ukwueze, thanked the people of the area for re-electing him for a second term.

“The mandate entrusted to us is both an honour and a covenant with the people of Igbo-Eze South,” he said in a Facebook post on Wednesday, 31 September, after his inauguration.

Mr Ukwueze was among the 17 local council chairmen sworn in on Wednesday in Enugu by Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State after the ruling APC won the 17 chairmanship and 260 councillorship seats in the election conducted on Saturday, 26 September.

At the swearing-in ceremony, Mr Mbah told the officials that they had just sealed a social contract with the people and advised them to hit the ground running.

“I would, therefore, imagine that you are going to hit the ground running because there is really no honeymoon when we have quite a whole number of tasks ahead of us at this point,” the governor said.

‘Resilient people’

Mr Ukwueze, in the Facebook post, described the Igbo-Eze South people as resilient, and said he was addressing them with “a heart overflowing with gratitude, humility and a profound sense of responsibility”.

He started by thanking God for his victory at the election and then let out his heart on how much he appreciated the people for their trust and support.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“To the good people of Igbo-Eze South, I offer my most sincere appreciation. Your confidence and support have been invaluable, and your decision to entrust this responsibility to us once again is a testament to the faith you have placed in our collective journey.

“I recognise that this mandate does not belong to me; it belongs to the people, and we remain conscious that every mandate carries with it an obligation to serve. Your renewed confidence in us is therefore a renewed charge to deepen our commitment to the welfare of our people, to broaden the reach of development and to ensure that government remains responsive to the realities of the communities we are privileged to lead.”

Mbah, ‘a modern wonder in the realms of governance’

The chairman thanked Governor Mbah for his trust and support, and the commitment to transform Enugu State. He described the governor as “a modern wonder in the realms of governance”.

“The vision of his (Mbah) administration, particularly its emphasis on infrastructure, human capital development, innovation, economic growth, education and improved public health delivery, has continued to provide a broader framework for meaningful development across the state.

“As a Local Government, we recognise that our progress is intrinsically connected to the progress of Enugu State. We shall therefore continue to align our efforts with the development direction of the state government while remaining attentive to the peculiar needs, circumstances and aspirations of the people of Igbo-Eze South.”

Vision for second term

Mr Ukwueze promised to build on the foundation his administration laid in his first term and to “accommodate more of the aspirations of Ndi Igbo-Eze South”.

“Our young people will remain at the centre of this vision.

“We live in an era in which technology, digital enterprise, artificial intelligence and new forms of economic activity are rapidly transforming the world of work.

“We must therefore prepare our youths not merely to seek employment, but to acquire the skills, knowledge and entrepreneurial capacity to create opportunities for themselves and others. We shall continue to pursue skills development, entrepreneurship and digital empowerment, while supporting initiatives that can equip our young people to participate meaningfully in the economy of the future.

“Education will equally remain a fundamental pillar of our development efforts, because every meaningful conversation about the future of a society ultimately returns to the quality of education available to its children. We shall continue to complement the broader interventions of the state government in education, ensuring that the child who should be in a classroom must not be condemned to the streets during school hours.”

Mr Ukwueze renewed his administration’s commitment to the security and well-being of the people and to continue to pursue the maintenance and improvement of rural roads, the rehabilitation of existing water facilities and the provision of additional infrastructure where necessary.

He also spoke on his vision for sports, environment, healthcare, and agriculture.

“I must, however, emphasise that the transformation of Igbo-Eze South cannot be achieved by government alone.

“Government can provide leadership and formulate policies, but enduring development is a collective enterprise.

“There are still communities that require great attention, young people who need opportunities, roads that require intervention, and farmers who need improved access to infrastructure and markets. We are neither oblivious to these realities nor complacent about the journey so far.

“The road ahead may present its own challenges, but we are confident in what we can achieve when leadership and the people work together with a shared sense of purpose.

The mandate entrusted to us is both an honour and a covenant with the people of Igbo-Eze South. We shall therefore approach the years ahead with renewed vigour, greater experience and an unwavering commitment to the common good of our people.

“Together, let us continue the journey of building an Igbo-Eze South that is more prosperous, more secure, more united and better prepared for the future.”

World.title: Akwa Ibom moves closer to having local supply hub for CNG
World.content:
Akwa Ibom State is moving closer to having a local supply hub for Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) as Nsik Oil & Gas Company Limited takes delivery of critical equipment for its planned 10 million standard cubic feet per day (10 MMSCF/D) CNG mother station in Esit Eket Local Government Area of the state.

The equipment which arrived on Wednesday night and Thursday morning is expected to strengthen the availability and distribution of CNG in the state at a time the federal government is expanding infrastructure and incentives targeted at moving Nigerians, particularly transport operators, away from petrol towards cheaper alternative fuels.

The facility at Uquo Isi Edoho is designed beyond compressing gas but also to serve as the supply point for a network of stations planned across Akwa Ibom.

This means the project could provide an important supply connection between the state’s growing demand for CNG-powered vehicles and the gas required to keep them operating.

The project consultant, Mkposong Asuquo, disclosed the development on Thursday while speaking at the project site during the delivery of the first consignment of equipment manufactured by China-based Original Equipment Manufacturer, CIMC.

The consignment includes four reciprocating compressors, dehydration and filtration systems, heat exchangers and four generating sets.

Mr Asuquo said the equipment followed the successful completion of a Factory Acceptance Test in China involving the project team and regulators from the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

.“We have our first set of equipment from CIMC China, all the way from Jiangsu Province in China. We actually went there, we did the Factory Acceptance Test with the regulators from NMDPRA,” he said.

He said the equipment had been cleared and transported directly to the project site, where it would serve as the core of the facility’s compression and processing system.

Bridging CNG supply gap

The development is noteworthy because increasing the number of CNG-powered vehicles without a corresponding expansion of refuelling and gas distribution infrastructure could constrain the federal government’s effort to make CNG a viable alternative to petrol.

The Nsik facility is designed to address part of that supply challenge in Akwa Ibom.

Mr Asuquo said the promoters had already ordered two trailers for transporting compressed gas from the mother station to planned stations.

The daughter-station model, he said, would allow the company to distribute CNG beyond the immediate host community to motorists, industries and other consumers.

“Our intention is also to feed most of the vehicles that are already CNG-powered,” he said.

The facility is strategically located near existing gas infrastructure. Mr Asuquo said it is about 500 metres from Frontier Energy and three kilometres from Savannah Energy’s Accugas facility, from which the project is expected to obtain its gas feedstock.

The project is an equity partnership between Nsik Oil & Gas Company Limited and the Midstream and Downstream Gas Infrastructure Fund, supervised by the Ministry of Petroleum Resources (Gas).

Supporting Tinubu’s CNG ambition

The project aligns with the federal government’s post-subsidy strategy of increasing the use of natural gas in transportation and other sectors.

President Bola Tinubu’s administration has promoted CNG as an alternative to petrol, particularly because of the sharp increase in transport costs following the removal of the petrol subsidy.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that the federal government had expanded its CNG infrastructure target, with President Tinubu ordering the rollout of an additional 500 CNG refuelling stations, bringing the planned nationwide total to 1,000.

The federal initiative has also included subsidised vehicle conversions, CNG buses and financing arrangements intended to encourage motorists and transport operators to switch from petrol and diesel.

However, the availability of CNG infrastructure remains central to whether increased vehicle conversion translates into sustained use.

The planned Nsik mother station adds another dimension to the federal programme by increasing the potential supply of compressed gas at the state level.

Akwa Ibom’s plan

For the Akwa Ibom State Government and other stakeholders promoting CNG adoption in the state, the facility could provide the infrastructure needed to support an expanding network rather than relying solely on CNG supplied from outside the state.

The Special Adviser to the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas) on Political Affairs, Kufre Sam said the project was expected to serve as a mother station for daughter stations across the state’s 10 federal constituencies.

He said the expansion would bring CNG closer to communities, businesses and industries.

The planned network, he added, could reduce transportation costs and subsequently affect the cost of goods and services.

“That alone will transform to reducing the cost of transportation, reducing the cost of goods, reducing the cost of services,” Mr Sam said.

He also said the network could generate direct and indirect employment through transportation, logistics, contracting and other businesses that would emerge around the daughter stations.

READ ALSO: Tinubu urges CNG rollout as petrol prices surge

The state already has a significant gas resource base, but the project seeks to convert proximity to gas infrastructure into a more accessible energy source for transport and industrial users.

From gas resources to consumers

Mr Asuquo said the project had already crossed several stages, including land acquisition, site clearing, geotechnical investigations, Environmental Impact Assessment, Front-End Engineering Design, Detailed Engineering Design, regulatory approvals and gas supply arrangements.

The remaining stages will involve installation and commissioning of the equipment. He expressed confidence that the facility would be commissioned soon.

If completed as planned, the 10 MMSCF/D station would give Akwa Ibom an additional CNG supply and distribution platform at a time the federal government is seeking to expand the fuel’s use nationwide.

The planned stations would then determine how far that supply reaches, particularly whether CNG becomes readily available to motorists and businesses beyond the immediate location of the mother station.

World.title: Imo police confirm abduction of prospective corps members travelling from Ibadan
World.content:
The Imo State Police Command has confirmed the abduction of prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members and other passengers after gunmen attacked two buses travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to orientation camps in the South-east and South-south.

The command in a statement signed by its Police Public Relations Officer, Okoye Henry, said the attack occurred at about 6:30 a.m. on Thursday along the Owerri-Onitsha Road near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State.

According to the police, the two buses were carrying prospective corps members and other passengers travelling to Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, and Bende, Abia State, respectively.

The command said 10 victims were rescued at the scene following the intervention of the police and other security agencies, while the exact number of people still in captivity was being verified.

“The rescued victims are in safe hands and are being attended to. The exact number of persons abducted is being verified and will be made public once confirmed,” the statement read.

Mr Henry said the police would sustain the operation until all victims were safely recovered and the suspected abductors arrested.

The command also said it was working with the NYSC authorities to contact the families of affected corps members and keep them informed as the rescue operation progresses.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Operatives are conducting coordinated search and rescue operations, backed by intelligence-led tracking of the suspects.

“The Commissioner of Police, alongside other Service Commanders, visited the scene for an on-the-spot assessment and to give operational direction. He assured the public that the Command will sustain the operation until all victims are safely recovered and the suspects are brought to justice.”

The development came amid frantic efforts by families of prospective corps members to establish the whereabouts of their loved ones.

Parents cry for help

The abduction has triggered panic among families of the affected prospective corps members, with some relatives appealing to security agencies and the federal government to intensify efforts to rescue their loved ones.

One parent, whose daughter was among those travelling to an orientation camp in Abia State, said in video that she received a distress message from her daughter early Thursday morning.

According to the parent, the daughter had been sharing her live location with the family through a WhatsApp group as she travelled from Ibadan.

The parent said the daughter suddenly sent the word “kidnapper” to the family group shortly after 6:00 a.m. prompting relatives to immediately call her phone.

The calls initially went through, but she did not answer before the phone eventually became unreachable, the parent said.

“She quickly typed ‘kidnapper’, and we tried to call immediately to see what happened. Since then, she has been offline,” the parent said in an appeal for help.

The parent said family members later learnt that passengers and the driver of the bus had been taken away, while some passengers travelling in another bus managed to escape.

READ ALSO: NYSC punishes 27 corps members in Osun

Fresh concern over safety of corps members

The Imo incident has renewed concerns about the safety of prospective corps members travelling long distances to their orientation camps.

The development comes weeks after another highway attack in which corps members were among people abducted by gunmen in Kogi State.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the attack occurred on 26 August around Ogene Zaria, near the Ogene Zaria-Onicha-Igo junction, along the Aloma-Egane Expressway.

The police later said 11 people, including corps members, were rescued following a joint security operation.

World.title: Lagos governorship candidates speak on education, housing, healthcare, Yoruba cultural preservation, business protection plans
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate, Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, has said Lagos is Yoruba land and promised to deepen efforts to preserve the language, culture and history of the Yoruba people in the state.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour made the remarks during a town hall meeting with millennials and Gen Z voters in Lagos on Thursday.

The meeting, organised by The Platform Nigeria, brought together governorship candidates from different political parties to respond to questions from young Lagos residents.

Other candidates at the event were the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate, Obafemi Hamzat; the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate, Funso Doherty; and the National Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate, Deji Doherty.

An attendee asked Mr Rhodes-Vivour what he would do to ensure that the Yoruba language and culture are preserved and protected in Lagos.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour was initially responding in English when members of the audience interrupted him and asked him to answer the question in Yoruba.

He said he was at the event to discuss politics, but stressed that Lagos is Yoruba land, and criticised the treatment of the Yoruba language in schools.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Today, we have about twenty-something years of the APC government, but till now, if you speak Yoruba in primary school and secondary school, they say it’s vernacular, and they beat and punish you,” he said.

He said the issue should also be directed at representatives of the Lagos State government who were present at the meeting.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour then linked cultural preservation to broader concerns about education, healthcare and the cost of living, saying families would be less concerned about such questions if they had access to quality public services.

“The fact of the matter is this: we must ensure that our culture is preserved,” he said.

He promised to create a ministry responsible for culture in his administration and said his government would examine Lagos’ culture and history more deeply.

“We have an entire ministry that’s going to be in charge of that, and we’re going to look at our culture and our history, even deeper than the surface level at which we are doing it,” he said.

During the 2023 Lagos governorship election, Mr Rhodes-Vivour faced criticism over his Yoruba identity and ability to speak the language, with his mixed Yoruba and Igbo heritage becoming a subject of political debate.

His comment during a Channels Television interview that he did not “think in Yoruba” drew criticism during the campaign, with the issue becoming part of the wider debate over his Yoruba identity and his suitability to govern Lagos.

Hamzat promises to scrap untraceable levies, support SMEs

Mr Hamzat promised to remove unauthorised and untraceable levies imposed on businesses, saying operators should know exactly what they are required to pay.

He said the state would work with the federal and local governments to harmonise taxes and charges imposed on businesses and prevent multiple collections.

“The role of government is to ensure that businesses start, survive and are able to grow. So what we will do is to make sure that any levy that is unauthorized, that is not known, that even we can’t track will go.
