World.title: Liberia: With Boakai’s Name now in the Record, Mary Broh Hands Rice Defendants a Story, But Not the Numbers
World.content:
Monrovia – Mary T. Broh walked into Criminal Court “C” on Tuesday and gave the defense something it had been missing in the Saudi rice trial: a story jurors can follow.

By Rodney D Sieh

In her telling, nobody stole anything. The rice was rescued, stored in the government’s own warehouse, logged in and out with gate passes, and some of it went to feed hungry young people cleaning up Monrovia ahead of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s inauguration.



It was a confident performance. It also put the President’s name into the court record, which is sure to keep this trial on the front page for a while.

But jurors will have to decide more than whether Broh sounded believable. They’ll have to decide whether her account explains the rice the government says it can’t find. Her testimony does less on that point.

She Has Skin in the Game

Broh came to court as a subpoenaed witness for former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and his co-defendants. She is also named in the same indictment she called “character assassination.”

That doesn’t mean she’s lying. It does mean prosecutors will remind the jury, probably more than once, that in defending the others she is also defending herself.

She had a ready answer. She said she turned over documents to investigators that could trace the rice, and asked why anyone planning a theft would do that.

Jurors may find that convincing. But it also sets a test. If those records are complete, they should match the numbers. If they don’t, the defense will have handed prosecutors their best evidence.

Why Was Foreign Affairs Involved?

The government’s case leans heavily on the claim that Kemayah and others took over a job the law gave to the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA).

Broh said the Foreign Ministry was involved because the rice came from Saudi Arabia, and relations with other countries are its business. She described a meeting at the GSA with Foreign Affairs, Internal Affairs, NDMA and GSA, where minutes were taken and the agencies agreed to work together.

If the defense can produce those minutes, they could matter a great deal. It is hard to call something a secret takeover when NDMA was in the room.

Still, Broh can’t settle whether the Foreign Ministry had legal authority to direct disaster relief. That is for the court, and prosecutors will argue that working together is not the same as having the power to act. GSA as the Right Place Broh’s simplest point may be her strongest. GSA, she said, is the government’s custodian of property and runs warehouses for donor supplies, emergency goods and mosquito nets. NDMA, she said, didn’t have room for that much rice. If jurors buy that, the transfer of 13,895 bags from NDMA to GSA looks less like the start of a diversion and more like ordinary storage. The trouble is that storage is not what the case is about. The government’s complaint is what happened after the rice reached GSA. Putting rice in a warehouse doesn’t explain rice that later disappears. The Cleanup Rice The most politically charged part of her testimony concerned about 1,050 bags. Broh said John-Charuk Siafa, now Monrovia City Mayor, showed her a letter from then-President-elect Boakai appointing him to coordinate the inaugural cleanup. The letter, she said, told him to contact her for help. When cleanup workers complained they hadn’t eaten, she said, she told Siafa to write the Internal Affairs Ministry, and rice was released. Nothing in that account suggests President Boakai ordered the Saudi rice handed out. What it does is tie a Boakai transition activity to the start of a chain of requests that ended with donated rice going to cleanup crews. That helps the defense on theft. Rice released by a ministry at an official’s request is not rice carried home.

It may help less on another charge. The donation was meant for disaster victims and vulnerable communities. Even if no one kept a single bag, feeding inauguration cleanup workers could still be treated as misapplication of entrusted property.

Jurors will also notice who hasn’t testified. Unless Mayor Siafa or former Internal Affairs Minister Varney Sirleaf takes the stand, or the letters are put in evidence, they have only Broh’s word for how it happened.

The Numbers

This case is increasingly a fight over arithmetic, and Broh didn’t end it.

The donation was 29,412 bags. Prosecutors say 11,200 bags were already at GSA and 13,895 more came from NDMA, for a total of 25,095. The indictment says 25,054 bags were diverted or unaccounted for.

Those figures are only 41 bags apart, which suggests the government is treating nearly everything that passed through GSA as missing. Yet former Deputy Internal Affairs Minister Momolu Johnson testified that 2,281 bags were still sitting at GSA, and questioned how another 720 bags were counted.

If Johnson is right, the government’s total is too high. But if the defense’s own gate passes can’t account for the rest, a smaller number may still be enough.

Where It Leaves the Defense

Broh gave the defense a legal basis for GSA holding the rice, a reason for Kemayah’s role, and a humanitarian explanation for at least some of the disputed bags.

What she didn’t offer, at least so far, is a full account of where the rest of the rice went. Her gate-pass system is only as good as the paper behind it, and the jury hasn’t seen that paper yet.

Cross-examination, and whatever documents make it into evidence, will decide how much her testimony is worth.

The defendants have pleaded not guilty and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. The trial continues.

World.title: Liberia: Court Rejects Acquittal Bid, but Key Questions Remain
World.content:
Monrovia – Peter Bon Jallah’s lawyers asked Criminal Court “E” on Wednesday to end his trial before he ever had to answer the charges. Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr. said no.

By Willie N. Tokpah

But the ruling, handed down on Wednesday, September 30, decided less than it might appear. Judge Wesseh made clear he was not declaring Jallah guilty or innocent. He was saying only that the prosecution had produced enough evidence for the defense to answer before he makes up his mind.



The 63-year-old is on trial over allegations of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy. He has denied the charges and chose to be tried by the judge alone, without a jury. That means one man will weigh every inconsistency, every piece of medical evidence and every word Jallah says when he takes the stand.

The Bar Was Low

To win Wednesday’s motion, the defense had to show that the prosecution’s evidence was “wholly insufficient,” the standard set by the Supreme Court in Republic of Liberia v. Robert A. Smith in 1976. That is a steep hill for any defense lawyer to climb.

The prosecution did not have to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt to survive. It only had to show evidence on each element of the charges. After calling 12 witnesses, including the alleged victim, police investigators, medical staff and a forensic expert from Rwanda, the judge ruled it had done that much.

He also refused to settle questions of who was telling the truth at this stage. Those questions remain open.

Where Was the Crime Scene?

The defense’s strongest point may be the one it made about Camp Johnson Road.

The alleged victim told the court he was taken to a place there and sexually abused. But according to the defense, Police Officer Lindsey Gould testified that investigators could not find or identify the location. A woman the boy said he encountered there was never produced in court.

The defense wanted that part of his testimony thrown out entirely. The judge declined to do so for now, but the problem has not gone away. Prosecutors will have to explain why police could not locate a place central to their own case, and why a potential witness never appeared.

Still, the Camp Johnson Road allegation is not the whole case. There are separate allegations tied to Jallah’s home in Airfield, which the defense itself acknowledged in its arguments. And courts have not always expected a traumatized teenager to give investigators precise directions.

Dates That Don’t Match

The defense also pointed to differences between what the boy told the court and what police wrote on the charge sheet about the dates and places of alleged encounters at the Airfield residence. How much that matters will depend on the judge. Small gaps between a witness’s memory and a police officer’s paperwork are common. Gaps that go to the core of what happened, and when, are harder to explain away. What the Medical Evidence Shows, and Doesn’t A nurse testified that she observed lacerations and bruises on the alleged victim. The defense did not dispute the injuries. Its argument was that she never said, in so many words, that rape caused them. That is often how medical testimony works. Nurses and doctors describe what they see and whether it is consistent with an allegation. They rarely swear to the cause. The DNA evidence raises a similar question. The defense argued that the Rwandan expert’s analysis could not prove penetration, and could not on its own show that the offenses amounted to statutory rape or gang rape.

What the defense did not appear to argue, at least as described in the ruling, is that the DNA found no link at all. Its complaint was about the limits of what the science can prove. Exactly what the analysis matched, and to whom, has not been fully laid out in the public record, and it may end up carrying more weight than anything else in the case.

Who Else?

A charge of gang rape suggests more than one attacker. Yet the ruling says nothing about who else is alleged to have been involved, or whether anyone else has been identified or charged. Expect the defense to press hard on that question.

A Door the Defense Left Closed

Jallah’s lawyers also argued that the indictment itself was flawed. Judge Wesseh said that argument came too late. Citing Potter v. Republic and Logan v. Republic (1985), he ruled that such objections belonged in a motion to dismiss filed before the trial began.

Jallah’s Turn

Now the defense opens its case, and Jallah is expected to be its first witness.

It is a gamble. On the stand, he can give the court his own account and offer the explanation his lawyers need. He will also face cross-examination from prosecutors looking for any slip that undercuts the doubts his team has spent weeks raising.

Whatever he says may not be the last word. The prosecution has said it could call rebuttal witnesses after the defense rests.

One of Jallah’s lawyers excepted to Wednesday’s ruling and said the defense would take advantage of the statute governing exceptions, keeping the issue alive for possible appeal. The judge noted the exception.

Citing Allen Yancy v. Republic (1935), Judge Wesseh said all the circumstances of a case should be before the court before it reaches a decision. He ordered the trial to proceed “unhindered.”

World.title: Liberia: Tarpeh Under Fire After Calling CDC Supporters ‘Mentally Deranged’ Over Lone Star Defeat
World.content:
MONROVIA – The final whistle had barely faded on Tuesday when the debate moved from the pitch to the timeline. Liberia had lost at home to Mali in the ongoing Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers, and the man chosen to bring the country together around the Lone Star had something to say.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Rev. Dr. J. Luther Tarpeh is Chairman of the ruling Unity Party and Chair of the National Mobilization Committee for the national team. Within hours, his post had done what few losses manage: it united a large part of the public, though against him rather than behind the team.



Two Posts in One

The message read like two documents stitched together. The first was a conventional thank-you. Tarpeh praised the “amazing” turnout, told Liberians not to lose heart, and reminded them that “Rome was not built in one day.” He asked the public to keep backing the team until Liberia has a competitive side able to hold its own in Africa.

The second was a political rebuttal. Tarpeh wrote that he was struck by supporters of the opposition Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) who were blaming his government for bringing the Lone Star’s troubles to the national level.

He asked whether they were still bitter that he, Amos Tweh and others had led the campaign that removed the CDC from power, and whether that loss had left them “mentally deranged” and unable to separate politics from patriotic service. He then added a personal note: “No leave. No transfer.”

The Case for the Defense

To be fair to Tarpeh, his argument has substance. He said the CDC government, whose political leader used football to build a national and international profile, did little for the national team while in office. He also pointed out that, under that administration, McGill and others had been named to lead a mobilization effort for the Lone Star. If that was acceptable then, he asked, why is it wrong now?

He also described how his current role took shape. During a trip to Casablanca to watch the Lone Star face Libya in a friendly, he said he spoke candidly with the players about the obstacles they face. Back home, he said, he took those concerns to the National Assembly and the Executive Branch.

The President and the Minister of Youth and Sports agreed to act, and he said the players are now happy to give their best. “I am proud to mobilize my government to show vested interest in the National Team,” he wrote, promising to do more. That would have been a defensible message on its own terms. What followed made it hard to hear.

The Line That Crossed It

Tarpeh said that if he did not count “very good few friends” in the CDC, he would launch a campaign to “donate” CDC supporters “somewhere else” so they could leave the country alone. He described their reasoning as “detestable” and their outlook as toxic, labeled them “crab mentality CDcians,” and told them to “get use to it.”

For critics, the wording did more damage than the argument. A call to relocate political opponents, even meant rhetorically, sat badly with a role built around inclusion.

A Rebuke from Inside the Tent

The most consequential response came from within the government Tarpeh was defending. Youth and Sports Minister Cornelia Kruah, the official he credited with taking up the team’s cause, made clear she did not share his message.

“As Minister of Youth and Sports, I do not agree with this post,” she wrote, adding that she would speak with Tarpeh but wanted her disagreement on the record first, since his position was already public. The mobilization chair’s role, she said, is not meant to be divisive but to serve as a bridge between politicians and the citizens who love the team. Her closing line was blunt: “This cannot be another CDC vs UP moment.”

What Ordinary Liberians Said

The public response, much of it from people who said they wanted to cheer for the team, followed a few recurring themes. Moriah Yeakula argued that the post proved why Tarpeh should not have been given the position, since the role is “not to just mobilize govt, it’s to mobilize the country.” She asked whether he thought the Lone Star was “UP FC.” Elijah Sumo went further, telling him to “step aside” and leave politics at party headquarters.

Several commenters pointed to Tarpeh’s standing as a reverend and doctorate holder. Samuel Bondoe said the title should have meant language of “reconciliation and healing,” and noted that the post named no current problems and offered no solutions. Moriah Yeakula told him the post did not reflect him as a reverend, a scholar or a party leader.

Theophilus Quaye said the communication should have been a simple thank-you and a call to keep trying together, adding that nothing said about the team now is new. Joseph Peabody praised the opening lines as “the kind of message our national team needs right now,” but said Tarpeh should have stopped there, since bringing in old elections “changes the message completely.”

Emmanuel Toe urged him, respectfully, to be more open and to recognize that not every critic is a CDCian working against the team. Elijah Reeves asked for an apology and a message of hope. Francis Peters warned that continued division could have “catastrophic” consequences.

Ishmael Jones put it plainly: “Liberia is not UP or CDC and our national team should never be politicized.” Eric Sulunteh went further, saying the team belongs to every Liberian, and warned that a government preoccupied with politics could repeat earlier administrations’ mistakes, “where politics overshadowed meaningful development in sports.”

The Question Underneath

Strip away the insults and a real policy debate remains. Few Liberians dispute that the Lone Star needs stronger government backing, and Tarpeh’s account of pressing that case with the President and the sports ministry is, on its face, the kind of advocacy supporters want.

The disagreement is about tone, timing and purpose. A mobilization chair is a unifying figure by design, someone who can bring the whole country into the stands regardless of how it voted. Critics say Tarpeh used a moment of national disappointment to settle scores, and that in doing so he narrowed the very audience he is meant to expand. Many also noted what the post left out: any account of what went wrong against Mali, or how the team will fix it.

The immediate test is the conversation the Sports Minister says she will have with Tarpeh. It could produce a clarification, an apology, or nothing visible at all. Some commenters want him replaced, but there is no sign the government is weighing that.

The Lone Star still has fixtures to play, and Tarpeh himself wrote that hope is “not totally dashed.” Whether that hope translates into results may depend on what the country does around the team. As Eric Sulunteh put it, when the Lone Star take the field there should be no political identity on the pitch, “just Liberia.”

World.title: Liberia’s ‘Falling’ Inflation Hides Rising Prices, Economist Argues
World.content:
New paper says converting dollar prices at a stronger Liberian dollar rate makes inflation look lower than it is; suggests true rate could be above 9 percent

Monrovia – An independent Liberian economist is challenging the official view that inflation in Liberia is cooling. He argues that the way the country measures prices hides a cost of living that households feel rising every time they go to the market.

By Rodney D Sieh



In a policy research paper dated September 30, 2026, Dr. Paul Columbus Collins, a chartered accountant and independent economic policy researcher based in Monrovia, says the steady fall in headline inflation reported by the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) “is not an economic anomaly but a measurement artifact.”

Using what he describes as illustrative calculations, Dr. Collins estimates that inflation in September would stand at about 9.5 percent under his proposed method – more than double the roughly 4.3 percent he says the current method produces.

Prices up, inflation down

The paper sets out what it calls “the inflation paradox.” According to the figures it compiles, reported headline inflation eased from about 6.2 percent in January to about 4.3 percent in September. The September figure is provisional; the Liberia Institute for Statistics and Geo-Information Services (LISGIS) normally publishes it in mid-October.

Over the same period, the Liberian dollar strengthened from about L$187 to between L$172 and L$175 to the US dollar, an appreciation of about 7 to 8 percent.

Yet the prices of everyday essentials kept climbing in US dollars. The paper cites a 25kg bag of rice rising from US$16.75 in January to US$18.50 in September, an increase of 10.4 percent. By the author’s estimates, gasoline rose about 16 percent, diesel about 18.5 percent, cement 11.5 percent and cooking oil 9.4 percent. Prices paid in Liberian dollars also went up: the paper estimates Monrovia transport fares rose from L$150 to L$165, and the fare from Monrovia to Gbarnga from L$800 to L$950.

“For the ordinary Liberian household – whose budget is split between LRD cash earnings and USD-priced essentials – the cost of living is unambiguously rising,” Dr. Collins writes.

How the numbers shrink

The problem, the paper argues, lies in how the Consumer Price Index (CPI) is put together. Many items in the basket – imported food, fuel, rent, school fees – are priced and paid for in US dollars. According to the paper, those dollar prices are converted into Liberian dollars at the going exchange rate before inflation is calculated.

When the Liberian dollar gets stronger, each US dollar converts into fewer Liberian dollars. That pulls the converted price down, even when the dollar price has gone up.

The bag of rice shows how it works. At January’s rate of about L$187.2, the US$16.75 bag was worth about L$3,136. At September’s rate of about L$172.5, the US$18.50 bag is worth about L$3,191. A 10.4 percent price increase in dollars becomes a 1.8 percent increase on paper.

The paper gives a second example: an item whose dollar price rises 5 percent between January and September would appear to have fallen 3.3 percent in price once converted.

“The statistic has ceased to measure the cost of living and instead measures the exchange rate with a price signal buried inside it,” the paper says.

Across 12 dollar-priced items in the paper’s extended table, prices rose by an average of about 12 percent in US dollars. Converted into Liberian dollars, the same items rose by only about 3 percent.

A dollar economy

Dr. Collins says the distortion matters more in Liberia than almost anywhere else. The IMF has described Liberia as one of the most highly dollarized economies in the world. Citing IMF studies, the paper notes that between 2007 and 2020 about 84 percent of bank deposits and 91 percent of bank lending were in US dollars, with overall dollarization estimated at 82 to 95 percent.

In such an economy, the paper argues, “the choice of measurement currency is not a technical detail – it determines what the index actually measures.”

Risk to policy

The paper warns that the stronger the Liberian dollar becomes, the lower measured inflation will fall, regardless of what happens to real prices. That, it says, could push policymakers to ease monetary policy when they should not.

It points to the CBL’s decision in July to cut its monetary policy rate to 16 percent, which the paper says may have been based on “a possibly distorted price signal.”

The CBL’s own statement on that cut, as reported in the local press, put headline inflation at an estimated 5.4 percent in the second quarter, up from earlier in the year, and projected it would ease to 4.4 percent, plus or minus two percentage points, in the third quarter.

Two numbers instead of one

Dr. Collins proposes that Liberia measure inflation separately in each currency. Price collectors, who already visit markets and shops, would record whether each price was quoted in US or Liberian dollars. LISGIS would then calculate one inflation rate for US-dollar prices and another for Liberian-dollar prices, without converting between them.

The official headline rate would be a weighted average of the two, based on how much of the economy runs in each currency. The paper suggests starting with 85 percent for the US dollar and 15 percent for the Liberian dollar, reviewed every year.

Applying this method to his September estimates, Dr. Collins arrives at 9.1 percent inflation for US-dollar prices and 11.8 percent for Liberian-dollar prices, giving a weighted headline of about 9.5 percent.

“No official exchange rate enters the computation at any point, so exchange-rate movements can no longer masquerade as price movements,” the paper says.

Recommendations

The paper calls on LISGIS and the CBL to pilot the two-currency index using existing price surveys, and to publish both currency rates alongside the headline figure. It urges the IMF to review Liberia’s CPI method under its Extended Credit Facility program with the country. Until any change is made, it says, the authorities should at least publish a US-dollar price index so that users can see the effect of the exchange rate.

The paper also argues that an accurate index matters for Liberia’s standing in ECOWAS, which sets a regional inflation target of 5 percent or less.

Estimates, not official data

The paper is careful to say that many of its numbers are estimates. Its price table is described as the author’s own compilation, anchored to reported market prices, and should be read as “indicative magnitudes rather than official statistics.” Where official monthly data for 2026 were not available, the paper fills gaps with interpolations. The 9.5 percent figure is described as an illustrative calculation meant to show how the method would work, not a full recalculation of the CPI.

The IMF’s own projection, cited in the paper, puts Liberia’s inflation at 6.7 percent by the end of 2026.

World.title: Diplomatic funfair backs grow Zambia agenda
World.content:
Dean of the Diplomatic Corps in Zambia Hawa Hassan Mohamed says the foreign mission is supporting the Grow Zambia Agenda through the 2026 Diplomatic Fun Fair to be held on October 3rd, 2026.

Ambassador Mohamed disclosed that the fun fair which will see over 30 missions represented is a tourism platform that will showcase different cultural heritage from Zambia and other countries.

The Foreign Envoy, who is also Somali’s Ambassador to Zambia described the upcoming event as a cultural diplomacy that will connect people of different nations at all levels of interaction, in an informal way.

Speaking during a Special Interview with the media, Ambassador Mohamed indicated that it’s a window for Zambia to the world and vice versa.

She added that it is a platform for foreign companies to connect with Zambia through investment, trade and commerce.

The Diplomatic Corps is interpreting the growing Zambia agenda through the fun fair by interesting more people to support the government in enhancing tourism and development.

We are selling our different cultural heritage, traditions to everyone living in Zambia, thereby enhancing cultural diplomacy,” she said.

And she assured of exciting experiences where the public will be treated to the various culture, food, tradition among other activities within Zambia, adding that it will be like a global village

The Dean of the Diplomatic Corps in Zambia expressed optimism of different outcomes to be achieved from the government, Diplomatic Corps and also from people.

Ambassador Mohamed also hopes to make stronger relationships at all levels, including the general public.

The event is scheduled to take place this Saturday, on October 3rd at the Showgrounds and entrance is free.

It will be held under the theme, Zambia moves you: connecting cultures, and inspiring the future.

World.title: President Hichilema returns home, secures over us$2.1bn investment commitments
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has arrived back home following a working visit to the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

Speaking to the media shortly after his arrival at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport, the President highlighted the investment commitments and policy measures arising from the Zambia–UAE Business and Investment Forum, and how they are expected to create jobs and promote growth for all Zambians.

Mr Hichilema cited investment agreements worth over US$2.1 billion, noting that the figure could increase as further investments are to be finalised by tomorrow.

He called on the private sector to collaborate with the Government, and work together to deliver the agenda, saying it remains central to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President said the working visit was deliberately aligned with the Grow Zambia Agenda and that the Government is continually improving the business environment to support the private sector.

He urged businesses of all sizes to help advance the agenda, while the Government continues to create an enabling environment through infrastructure development, tax laws and other initiatives.

The Head of State said these efforts are intended to encourage reinvestment, create jobs and improve people’s wellbeing.

He added that, in turn, they would grow government revenue and increase reserves for future generations.

World.title: Start preparing for 2028 Olympics now – Matete
World.content:
Athletics icon Samuel Matete says Zambia must start preparing for the next Olympic Games and Commonwealth Games now after a poor showing at the recent Games in Glasgow.

The 2028 Summer Olympics will be hosted by Los Angeles in the United States, while India will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.

Matete has rated Team Zambia’s performance at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland as below expectations.

Team Zambia minted two bronze medals through boxing, as sprinter Muzala Samukonga failed to defend his 400 meters title won at Birmingham 2022 after clocking 45.61 seconds.

There was a yawning gap between Team Zambia and Africa’s best performing nation Nigeria, who minted seven gold, seven silver and seven bronze medals at the Glasgow Games.

In an interview with Icengelo Magazine from Kitwe, the former World Athletics Champion said Team Zambia has a lot of work to do to start winning more medals at international events.

The 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games Silver Medallist said having qualified youth coaches and participating in more junior championships would be key to enhancing Team Zambia’s display at major global competitions.

“All of us are not very pleased with the performance of our sports men and women that represented us at the Commonwealth Games. Coming back with two bronze is short of what we anticipated and it just shows all of us that our performance has gone down,” Matete said.

He said the quality of athletes Zambia sends to international events has a huge impact on the team’s performance.

“It all goes back to the kind of preparations we had put in before the games. It is important that we shift gear and start preparing upcoming athletes for the next Commonwealth Games,” he said.

“Good performance at such games does not depend on entering in all the events. It is not about the quantity of athletes but the quality of the sports men and women.”

Matete said preparations for the next Commonwealth Games and the Olympics must start now.

“As we speak now there is a world championships in athletics in Uruguay but at the moment we don’t have any representative as Zambia at these games. These are the games that determine the future athletes but we are not there.”

“We have athletes that have potential but what are we doing to support them? Are we putting them in camp? Are we attaching coaches that know how to groom them? We are not doing it. We should not wait for last minute preparations and if we continue with that trend it will be difficult for us to reap the medals we want,” Matete said.

At his peak, Matete won a gold medal at the 1991 World Championships and was twice silver medallist at the 1994 Commonwealth Games.

World.title: State House Challenges Catholic Bishops’ Statement
World.content:
State House has challenged concerns raised by the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops over fear, ethnic manipulation and the shrinking democratic space, saying such claims should be supported by evidence.

In a statement issued in Lusaka, State House Chief Communications Specialist CLAYSON HAMASAKA said Government respects the Church’s role in national life but disagrees with suggestions that the country is facing a national crisis.

Mr. HAMASAKA said concerns about fear and anxiety should not be presented as representing the experience of the entire country without evidence.

He also defended the electoral process, saying concerns over elections should identify specific failures and demonstrate how they affected the outcome before questioning the decision made by voters.

On arrests involving opposition figures, State House said lawful accountability should be distinguished from political persecution.

Mr. HAMASAKA said an arrest does not amount to proof of guilt or persecution, adding that allegations of unlawful detention should be examined on an individual basis.

He also rejected suggestions of widespread insecurity or military control, following concerns raised by the Bishops regarding military personnel, violence and insecurity.

The Catholic Bishops had expressed concern over political polarisation, the manipulation of ethnic identities and tribal sentiments, freedom of expression, electoral credibility and reports of arrests and political violence.

State House welcomed the Bishops’ call for dialogue, civic education, accountability and reconciliation, but said such efforts should be based on verified facts and respect institutional independence.

Government also raised concern about the timing of the pastoral statement in relation to ongoing court proceedings involving a senior member of the clergy.

Mr. HAMASAKA said the timing of the statement alone does not establish an intention to influence the proceedings, but cautioned that messages portraying widespread fear and institutional failure could affect public sentiment around a matter requiring independent determination.

He stressed that the accused person’s dignity, presumption of innocence and right to a fair hearing must be protected, while investigators, prosecutors and the courts should perform their duties without interference.

State House has called for measured public communication, saying national dialogue should promote peace, cooperation and respect for lawful processes.

World.title: MUKANDILA Faces Forgery and False Document Charges
World.content:
Tonse Pamodzi Secretary General CELESTINE MUKANDILA has pleaded not guilty to charges of forgery and uttering false documents.

Mr. MUKANDILA, aged 36, entered the plea yesterday before Lusaka Resident Magistrate ANNA HOLLAND.

The prosecution alleges that between July 14, 2022 and July 25, 2024, Mr. MUKANDILA forged the signature of YAEES SALIM SHETH on a letter purporting to surrender shares in ZRIMS Farm Limited.

It is alleged that the letter falsely indicated that Mr. SHETH had surrendered his shares in the company.

Mr. MUKANDILA is also accused of fraudulently uttering a notice of forfeiture or surrender of shares, which is a document issued by the Patent and Companies Registration Agency -PACRA-.

Meanwhile, Mr. MUKANDILA has been granted 20,000 Kwacha cash bail pending trial.

He has also been ordered to provide two working sureties, each bound in the sum of 15,000 Kwacha in their own recognisance.

World.title: HELSB Seeks Private Investment in Student Loans
World.content:
The Higher Education Loans and Scholarships Board -HELSB- is calling for increased private sector investment in student financing to help bridge the funding gap in higher education.

HELSB says 45.3 percent of student financing needs remained unfunded in 2025, highlighting the need for additional sources of funding beyond government support.

HELSB Chief Executive Officer JOHN MACHAYI says banks, pension funds, insurance companies and asset managers can play a greater role in financing higher education.

Dr. MACHAYI says expanding the financing base will help increase access to higher education and provide Zambia with the skilled workforce needed for economic growth.

Speaking at the Zambia Capital Market Conference and Awards in Livingstone, Dr. MACHAYI, who is also President of the Association of African Higher Education Financing Agencies, said investment in student financing allows young people to acquire qualifications and enter the labour market.

He said HELSB’s annual disbursements increased from about 558 million Kwacha in 2021 to 1.8 billion Kwacha in 2025, while its loan portfolio grew to more than 10 billion Kwacha by June 2026.

Dr. MACHAYI has called on commercial banks to develop education-financing products tailored to the needs of working families.

He proposed financing options such as salary-linked repayments, staged payments based on verified university costs, and loans covering tuition, accommodation and learning materials.

Dr. MACHAYI said having a salary does not necessarily mean parents can meet university expenses when payments fall due.

He has also encouraged pension funds, insurers and asset managers to consider investing in structured education-financing arrangements.

Dr. MACHAYI said possible financing models could include bonds, social bonds and other investment instruments, but clarified that no bond issuance or investment commitment has been announced.

He said improved loan recovery will be important in building investor confidence.

HELSB recovered about 233.8 million Kwacha in 2025 and 129.9 million Kwacha during the first half of 2026, while the number of beneficiaries repaying their loans increased to more than 22,000 by June 2026.

Dr. MACHAYI has urged employers and beneficiaries to make timely repayments, saying recovered funds are used to support other students.

He said financial barriers could prevent young people from acquiring the skills needed for Zambia’s future development.

Dr. MACHAYI said he will prepare a concept proposal for consideration by the HELSB Board and engage relevant government authorities on possible financing options.

This is according to a statement issued to the media by HELSB Manager Corporate Affairs CHISELWA KAWANDA.

World.title: DEC Unearths Suspected Counterfeit Fertiliser Plant
World.content:
The Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) has uncovered a plant allegedly involved in the manufacture of counterfeit fertiliser in 9 Miles and Meanwood Vorna Valley.

DEC Public Relations Officer Allan Tamba says the operation spans Chibombo and Chongwe districts in Central and Lusaka Provinces.

Mr. Tamba says four people have been arrested in connection with the alleged operation.

They are 40-year-old agricultural consultant Iwa Siame and businessmen John Ngulube, 34, Fortune Kalima, 49, and Stan Penti, 45.

Mr. Tamba says the four have been charged with producing farming requisites at an unregistered plant, possession of property suspected to be proceeds of crime, conspiracy to commit a felony and money laundering.

He said in a statement that the suspects allegedly manufactured and processed farming requisites at unregistered premises between January 1, 2025 and September 19, 2026.

Mr. Tamba said the DEC has seized 739 bags of suspected counterfeit fertiliser, as well as raw materials and equipment allegedly used in the operation.

He said the suspects are also accused of setting up an unauthorised operation involving the deceptive packaging and distribution of the fertiliser.

Mr. Tamba further alleged that proceeds from the sale of the suspected counterfeit fertiliser were used to acquire property for the suspects’ benefit.

He said the four suspects are in custody and are expected to appear in court soon.

Mr. Tamba has urged farmers and members of the public to exercise caution when buying fertiliser and other farming inputs and to source them only from legitimate suppliers and distributors.

He has also called on the public to report suspected criminal activities to the authorities.

World.title: Business community tipped on ZRA voluntary disclosure
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary Milner Mwanakampwe has urged the business community to take advantage of the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme by the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA).

Dr Mwanakampwe says the scheme allows businesses and individuals to disclose previously declared liabilities and settle principal tax obligations with relief from qualifying penalties and interests.

Speaking when he officiated at the stakeholder engagement meeting on the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme organized by ZRA in Kabwe, Dr Mwanakampwe said the voluntary exposure scheme seeks to regularise tax affairs on favourable terms to avoid penalties.

He emphasized that sustainable national development relies heavily on a robust revenue collection and voluntary tax compliance.

He said the government’s goal is to build a prosperous country powered by fair, transparent and collaborative tax administration.

And ZRA Assistant Director Sylvia Mukwiza says the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme has been introduced to address tax-related challenges facing the business community.

Ms Mukwiza says ZRA wants to ensure that every eligible taxpayer in Central Province accesses this opportunity and operates with greater tax certainty and peace of mind moving forward.

Under this programme, taxpayers who disclose undeclared liabilities and settle their principal tax obligation receive a proportionate waiver of qualifying penalties and interest of up to 100 percent.

World.title: Nigeria: Govt Skips Independence Day Parade for Second Year Running
World.content:
For the second consecutive year, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's administration has dropped the traditional Independence Day military parade.

The development has left unanswered questions over why the ceremony has not returned.

This is despite the government's confirmation that officers accused of plotting a coup have been identified and are facing military trial.

Unlike previous years when October 1 celebrations culminated in a ceremonial military parade, guard of honour, military drills and other displays of national pageantry, the Federal Government's official programme for Nigeria's 66th Independence anniversary contained no parade.



Instead, the government announced a low-key celebration comprising religious services, a public lecture and a nationwide presidential broadcast.

The decision is significant.

The military parade was held at the Presidential Villa in Abuja as recently as October 1, 2024, when Tinubu, Vice President Kashim Shettima and other dignitaries watched military drills, a colourful parade and the presidential change of guards.

It was, however, absent from the 2025 programme after the Federal Government announced on September 29 that the parade scheduled for the 65th anniversary had been cancelled.

At the time, the government did not give a detailed reason beyond saying that the cancellation did not diminish the significance of the anniversary and that other programmes would continue as scheduled.

The cancellation came against the backdrop of the arrest of military officers over allegations that later became a confirmed coup investigation.

But the connection between the two developments was disputed by the military at the time.

In October 2025, the Defence Headquarters rejected reports that the parade had been cancelled because of an alleged coup attempt.

It said the decision was to enable Tinubu to attend a strategic bilateral meeting outside the country and allow members of the Armed Forces to sustain operations against terrorism, insurgency and banditry.

The DHQ also said the officers initially arrested were being investigated for professional misconduct and that the process was a routine internal disciplinary matter.

Months later, however, the military position changed.

In January 2026, the DHQ confirmed that investigations had identified some officers as having allegations of plotting to overthrow the government.

It further noted that those with cases to answer would be arraigned before appropriate military judicial panels.

By July, reports on the prosecution of alleged coup suspects provided further details about the investigation.

This includes evidence concerning some of the officers arrested in 2025.

Yet, with the coup investigation now publicly acknowledged and the suspects facing due process, the military parade has not returned.

Instead, the Federal Government formally announced another low-key Independence Day celebration this year.

The Inter-Ministerial Committee inaugurated by the government said the 66th anniversary would comprise a World Press Conference, Juma'at service, church service, an Independence Day public lecture and the President's nationwide broadcast.

There was no military parade listed among the approved activities.

The government has not publicly said that the absence of the parade this year is connected to security concerns, the alleged coup plot or the ongoing prosecution of the suspects.

It has also not announced that the parade was cancelled this year, as it did in 2025.

Rather, the parade simply does not feature in the official programme released for the anniversary.

That has created a striking contrast with 2024, when the government staged a full military ceremony at the State House to mark the 64th anniversary.

Tinubu attended that event in person, arriving at the venue with his wife, Oluremi Tinubu, before being ushered onto the saluting dais for the national salute and anthem.

He subsequently inspected the guard of honour and watched military drills and the ceremonial change of guards.

The President's physical presence has also not been an obstacle this year.

Tinubu returned to Lagos on Tuesday, September 29, after spending about four weeks in Europe described as a working vacation by the Presidency.

The State House said he deliberately returned through Lagos to honour the memory of late Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola.

It said he would attend the premiere of a movie honouring Abiola at the Wole Soyinka National Theatre, Iganmu, on Independence Day.

The Presidency also said he would hold strategic meetings with political leaders and associates in Lagos before returning to Abuja after his engagements there.

On the anniversary itself, his principal national engagement was the traditional broadcast to Nigerians.

Tinubu addressed the country from Lagos this morning, using his 66th Independence Day message to declare that Nigeria had moved from the difficult phase of economic reforms into an "age of prosperity."

The government's decision to keep this year's anniversary low-key was announced well before October 1.

Speaking at the inauguration of the Inter-Ministerial Committee on September 17, Secretary to the Government of the Federation, George Akume, said the celebration would be low-key.

He cited the need to reflect on Nigeria's journey and the contributions of the country's founding fathers.

The programme subsequently released by the committee did not include the military parade raising questions about whether it can simply be described as a continuation of the 2025 security response.

There is no official statement saying the 2026 decision was taken because of the alleged coup plot.

Indeed, the government has not publicly linked this year's low-key celebration to the military investigation.

Close 

The development is unfolding against a different security backdrop from the one officially presented last year.

Last year, Tinubu spent the anniversary period in Lagos and delivered his Independence Day broadcast from Dodan Barracks.

The State House later said he had spent ten days in Lagos, where he also commissioned the renovated National Theatre.

This year, his return to Lagos similarly coincides with the anniversary, but the official programme is considerably more restrained.

Rather than the spectacle of troops, military formations and ceremonial drills, the Federal Government's listed events have focused on religious observances, reflection, a public lecture and the President's address.

The absence of the parade therefore marks a clear departure from the format witnessed in the past, even as the government insists that the anniversary itself remains significant.

For now, neither the Presidency nor the Federal Government has publicly provided a specific explanation for why the military parade has not been restored in 2026.

The unanswered question is whether that explanation represents a broader shift in the government's approach to national celebrations or whether security considerations surrounding the military establishment continue to influence the format of the anniversary.

What is clear is that the traditional military spectacle that featured prominently in the 64th Independence anniversary is missing again this year, making 2025 and 2026 the first two consecutive Independence anniversaries under Tinubu in which the parade has not been held.

World.title: Kenya: Politrack Poll - Ruto 45.1 Percent, Sifuna 19.6 Percent, Kalonzo 10.3 Percent If Elections Held Today
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto leads the presidential preference survey by Politrack Africa, with 45.1 per cent of respondents saying they would vote for him if elections were held today.

The survey, released at a press conference in Nairobi on Thursday, places Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna second at 19.6 per cent, followed by Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka at 10.3 per cent. Undecided respondents account for 8.4 per cent, while former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang'i has 7.2 per cent and former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua 6.0 per cent.

In its assessment, Politrack says Ruto "leads the national presidential preference tally at 45.1%", while Sifuna has emerged as a significant challenger with 19.6 per cent support.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Other candidates recorded lower levels of preference, with Prof George Wajackoyah at 1.1 per cent, Martha Karua and David Maraga at 0.8 per cent each, James Orengo at 0.4 per cent and Jimmy Wanjigi at 0.3 per cent.

At party level, Ruto's United Democratic Alliance leads with 32 per cent, followed by the Democracy for the Citizens Party at 11.7 per cent and ODM at 10.6 per cent. Jubilee has 6.9 per cent, Wiper 5.6 per cent, Kenya Kwanza 3.5 per cent and Azimio 3.2 per cent.

The survey also found a near-even split over the direction of the country, with 45.2 per cent saying Kenya is moving in the right direction and 44.6 per cent saying it is moving in the wrong direction. Another 10.2 per cent were unsure.

On government performance, respondents identified roads and housing, both at 16.3 per cent, as the areas where the government is performing best, followed by health services, SHIF and SHA at 13 per cent and agriculture at 10 per cent.

However, health services, SHIF and SHA also featured prominently among areas respondents viewed as performing poorly, at 19.2 per cent, followed by the fight against corruption at 18.4 per cent and the economy and cost of living at 12 per cent. Jobs and youth opportunities followed at 10.4 per cent.

The survey also examined attitudes towards a woman becoming Kenya's first female deputy president. Politrack reports that 53 per cent of respondents were ready for a woman deputy president, comprising 16 per cent who were "very ready" and 37 per cent who were "somewhat ready". Among those open to the prospect, Anne Waiguru had 36 per cent support, followed by Martha Karua at 27 per cent and Gladys Wanga at 15 per cent.

Politrack says the survey was conducted between September 15 and 25 among 20,419 respondents across the country. The national estimates were weighted according to each county's share of registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points and a 95 per cent confidence level.

World.title: Kenya: Nairobi Tests Flood Response As Agencies Set Up Emergency Command Centre
World.content:
Heavy rains left more than 23 people dead in Nairobi in March 2026.

Nairobi — Nairobi has begun testing its emergency response system ahead of the October-December rains, with national and county agencies setting up a joint command centre at Charter Hall.

The exercise, dubbed Operation Okoa Maisha, is intended to test how authorities would respond to flooding and other emergencies, including the flow of information, deployment of rescue teams and evacuation of residents from high-risk areas.

The exercise brings together the Nairobi County Government, National Disaster Operations Centre, Kenya Red Cross, Kenya Defence Forces, Kenya Coast Guard and other emergency agencies.

Charter Hall will serve as the central coordination point during the exercise, with participating agencies expected to relay reports from the field to a single command post.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Governor Johnson Sakaja said the arrangement was intended to avoid different agencies working with separate information during an emergency.

"We need one report and one communication," Sakaja said.

The preparations come amid renewed attention to Nairobi's vulnerability to flooding, particularly in areas around the Mathare, Ngong and Nairobi rivers.

County teams have been clearing drains, desilting waterways and deploying earth-moving equipment in areas identified as flood hotspots.

The county has also identified evacuation centres and established emergency numbers 1508 and 1190 for residents requiring assistance.

Sakaja said authorities would also seek to move people living in areas considered dangerous, including sections of riparian land.

"Occupying riparian land is non-negotiable. You must move. We do not want you to die," he said.

The simulation is expected to expose weaknesses in the response system before an actual emergency occurs.

Among the issues being tested are how quickly an alert reaches response teams, how agencies coordinate rescue operations and whether residents in affected areas can be moved to safety.

The exercise also provides an opportunity to establish which agency takes responsibility for particular operations when several government and humanitarian organisations are responding to the same incident.

Nairobi has in previous rainy seasons experienced flooding in several parts of the city, disrupting transport and displacing residents.

The county is now using the simulation to test whether its current arrangements can cope with a major flood emergency when the rains intensify.

World.title: Nigeria: Tinubu Compares His Tough Policies to Painful Cancer Treatment
World.content:
"Nigeria was like a sick patient who receives the terrible news that he has cancer."

President Bola Tinubu on Thursday compared his tough policies to the essential cancer treatment a patient needs.

The Nigerian leader, in a televised address marking the country's 66th Independence Anniversary, said the situation inherited in 2023 warranted tough decisions that economists argue have caused Nigeria's worst cost of living crisis in a generation.

"Nigeria was like a sick patient who receives the terrible news that he has cancer. His doctor explains that the treatment will be difficult and painful, but that it offers a strong prospect of recovery. The patient has a choice. He can begin treatment, endure its discomfort and fight the disease. Or he can ask only for morphine, dull the pain and leave the cancer to spread.



"For too long, Nigeria's leaders chose morphine while praying for a miracle that never came," he said.

Mr Tinubu said previous administrations had focused on the symptoms of the country's economic problems while allowing the underlying issues to worsen.

"When this administration assumed office, we resolved to do things differently. We chose to excise the cancer. The reforms that followed were difficult. The side effects were real. Yet, we must never confuse the medicine with the disease," he said.

The President's comparison comes at a time when cancer remains a major health burden in Nigeria, with many patients diagnosed late and facing difficult treatment.

Cancer burden

The latest estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) show that Nigeria recorded an estimated 152,261 new cancer cases and 90,795 cancer deaths in 2024.

Breast cancer accounted for the highest number of new cases, followed by prostate and cervical cancers.

The figures highlight the scale of a disease that continues to claim thousands of lives in Nigeria each year, particularly where patients present late or are unable to access timely treatment.

Nigeria's 2025 Cancer Control Capacity and Needs Assessment also found that more than 70 per cent of cancer patients in the country present with advanced disease.

The National Institute for Cancer Research and Treatment (NICRAT) conducted the assessment with support from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the World Health Organisation (WHO).

The report identified late presentation as one of the major challenges affecting cancer outcomes in the country.

A 2025 study involving 264 cancer patients in Kano and Ibadan also found significant delays in diagnosis.

Close 

Researchers reported a median period of 12 months between patients first noticing symptoms and receiving a cancer diagnosis, with patients visiting a median of three health facilities before receiving a formal diagnosis.

Chemotherapy, other treatments can be difficult

Chemotherapy, one of the major treatments used for cancer, can cause side effects including severe tiredness, nausea and vomiting, hair loss, mouth sores and reduced blood-cell counts, depending on the drugs used and the individual patient.

Other treatments, including surgery and radiotherapy, can also be physically demanding and may require repeated hospital visits over weeks or months.

In Nigeria, access to these treatments remains a challenge. The 2025 national cancer-control assessment estimated that more than 120 radiation machines would be needed to adequately treat the country's cancer patients, but only 13 functional radiation machines were available at the time of the assessment.

It also found that patients often have to travel long distances to access radiotherapy.

The report further identified shortages of oncology specialists. It estimated that Nigeria had about 0.03 oncologists per 100,000 people and noted that skilled oncology staff were inadequate for the country's population.

World.title: Ethiopia: 'We Are Completely Isolated - Humanitarian Access Is Urgently Needed'
World.content:
Adigrat — "It is extremely urgent to facilitate humanitarian access, dialogue for peace and every form of dialogue. We are completely isolated, communications are blocked, and we have no contact with anyone." This is the message sent to Fides by the Eparch of Adigrat, Tesfaselassie Medhin, in a brief message sent with the support of UNICEF, which continues to assist the Church and, where possible, to maintain a minimum connection with the outside world.

"All communications are blocked; our Church, our missions, religious, the local clergy, we are in our places, as usual," the Eparch said. "We will accompany and help the people with our presence, through which we carry out the Church's mission of incarnation."

Medhin describes a situation of mounting difficulty: "Banks are also closed. We do not know for sure how our seminaries and schools will continue operating, but it is our intention to continue. We have no idea how we will manage provisions. Only God knows; we rely on Divine Providence."

Meanwhile, the situation in Ethiopia's northern region continues to deteriorate (see Fides, 30/9/2026). At the end of yesterday's General Audience, Wednesday, September 30, Pope Leo XIV expressed his "deep concern" over the renewed outbreak of hostilities in Tigray and appealed to all parties.

"I extend my heartfelt plea to all parties to choose the path of dialogue," the Pope said. "Armed conflict never solves problems but only worsens them, leaving in its wake a trail of death, destruction, and resentment. Only honest engagement can lay the foundations for lasting peace." Leo XIV also expressed the hope "that the international community will offer its generous and timely contribution, to ensuring that all humanitarian aid be provided to those in need."

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 1, 2026
World.content:
press review

Ethiopia Fighting Kills 52 Civilians in Tigray

At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Government troops appeared to have taken control of the town and may be advancing towards Mekelle. Clashes have also spread to neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions. More than 700 wounded people have reportedly been admitted to hospitals supported by Médecins Sans Frontières. The fighting follows months of tension between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, which accuse each other of violating the 2022 peace agreement. Communications and banking services have been disrupted in Tigray, worsening the humanitarian situation. Dozens of foreign tourists remain stranded in Lalibela after the airport closed. There are also concerns that Eritrea could become involved in the conflict.

Botswana Criticised for Killing 23 Elephants for Independence Celebrations

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Botswana has authorised the killing of 23 elephants and other wildlife for meat as part of celebrations marking the country's 60th anniversary of independence, drawing criticism from animal rights and conservation groups. The Elephant Protection Society warned that using elephants for celebratory feasts could undermine conservation efforts and encourage poaching. The decision has also sparked concerns over hygiene and disease amid a foot-and-mouth outbreak. Local officials are calling for the meat to be processed and distributed more safely. Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and defends regulated hunting as a way to manage human-wildlife conflict and generate funds for communities and conservation. The government's hunting policy remains controversial, with conservation groups questioning its sustainability while supporters point to the damage elephants do to crops, property and communities.

Somali Families Face Renewed Violence as Hunger Crisis Worsens

Children have been killed and injured in renewed fighting in Baidoa, Somalia, with a health facility also damaged, according to UNICEF and other humanitarian agencies. Clashes between government forces and fighters loyal to the former South West State president have intensified in recent weeks, adding to an already severe humanitarian crisis. About two million children across Somalia are acutely or severely malnourished, while 26,000 people in Baidoa face catastrophic food insecurity. Families are also struggling with displacement, droughts, floods and conflict. Humanitarian funding cuts have sharply reduced food assistance. The World Food Programme now reaches just over 670,000 people, compared with more than four million during previous crises.

Morocco Whistleblower Reveals Surveillance of Journalists and Activists

Amnesty International has accused Moroccan authorities of operating an extensive surveillance system targeting journalists, human rights defenders and other critical voices. In a new report, the organisation says authorities have used spyware, phone interception, tracking devices, hidden recording equipment and other technologies to monitor and intimidate critics. Evidence linked the Direction Générale de la Surveillance du Territoire to the use of Pegasus spyware. Amnesty said its investigation identified 103 Moroccan phone numbers entered into the country's Pegasus system in 2017, including those belonging to journalists, human rights defenders, lawyers and academics. Morocco has previously denied using spyware against its citizens. Amnesty is calling for an end to unlawful surveillance and for independent investigations into alleged abuses.

Malawi MPs Demand Answers Over Chilima Wreckage Discovery

Malawi's parliamentary committee investigating the 2024 plane crash that killed former Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others has raised concerns over conflicting records showing when the wreckage was discovered. The Malawi Defence Force logged the discovery at 10:58 am while police reportedly logged it at 9:30 am, raising questions about the search operation, possible survival opportunities and the handling of evidence. The committee plans to travel to the Northern Region to verify evidence and question police, firefighters and other witnesses involved in the search. Former MDF commander Major General Richard Chagonapanja also told the inquiry that the military continued searching overnight despite fog, poor visibility and concerns over night operations. He said the aircraft's emergency locator transmitter was not functioning because its battery had expired, making the search more difficult. The inquiry is also examining conflicting witness accounts as it works to establish a definitive timeline of the crash and recovery operation.

World.title: Mozambique: Government Denies Reports of Fuel Shortage
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambique's the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy (MIREME) denies that the country is facing another fuel shortage despite long queues of vehicles at filling stations in Maputo and other cities.

On Monday and Tuesday, long queues were seen in filling stations, which raised concerns of a return to the fuel supply shortage experienced in the country last April and May.

A week ago, hundreds of motorcycle taxi drivers protested against fuel shortage in the northern province of Nampula. The protesters blockaded the city's key routes, including sections along the country's main north-south highway, National Road Number One (EN1). The disruption severely affected the movement of people and cargo across the city during the morning rush hour.

MIREME, in a statement, claims that fuel supply continues normally across the country, given that there has been no disruption of stocks. However, it admitted that these difficulties were related to logistical constraints during the weekend, which coincided with the celebration of a national holiday, which marked the 60th anniversary of the National Liberation Struggle and the 51st anniversary of the Armed Forces for the Defense of Mozambique (FADM) Day.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The constraints affected the regular loading and distribution cycle, preventing some petrol stations from receiving fuel on time. Several stations in central Maputo were closed, while others with fuel available faced long queues", reads the note.

According to the document, operational teams were mobilized at the Matola Terminal, allowing 1.176 million litres of petrol to be loaded, close to the daily average of about 1.2 million litres.

The ministry has revealed that 8,000 tonnes of petrol are expected to arrive in Mozambique by Thursday, adding that the fuel currently available is sufficient to meet demand in Maputo.

To prevent similar situations, MIREME said it will strengthen coordination among operators in the fuel supply chain, extend loading hours at terminals when necessary and allow loading operations on Saturdays.

"The measures are intended to ensure greater continuity in fuel distribution during extended weekends and periods of increased demand", reads the note.

The previous fuel shortage caused long queues of vehicles at filling stations in Maputo and other cities. According to the authorities, the crisis was influenced by the US-Israel aggression war against Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which is responsible for the daily flow of almost 20 percent of the world's oil sales.

Close 

About 80 per cent of Mozambique's fuel imports pass through routes connected to the Strait of Hormuz, which means that the impact of the war in the Middle East is potentially disastrous for the country's economy.

This situation forced the government to increase, at the beginning of this May, the prices of the main liquid fuels by up to 45, 5 percent.

The authorities also pointed out the bankruptcy of fuel distributors and the shortage of foreign currency (particularly US dollars) as the main cause of the crisis.

World.title: Botswana: Chapo Reaffirms the Need for Stronger Cooperation With Botswana
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambican President Daniel Chapo has described his state visit to Botswana as positive, highlighting stronger bilateral cooperation, new investment prospects and plans to establish air links between the two countries.

Speaking on Wednesday in Gaborone, at a meeting with Mozambican citizens living in Botswana, Chapo called on the diaspora to strengthen its organization and participation in the "Inclusive National Dialogue", stressing dialogue as a means of addressing differences and finding solutions for the country.

"If I think differently from my brother there, I do not need to use force, violence, hatred, disinformation, manipulation or any other inappropriate means to impose my ideas, but I have to provide arguments", he said.

On the economic front, Chapo highlighted the potential for deeper cooperation between Mozambique and Botswana, particularly in tourism, and announced that the two countries are working to establish air links to Mozambican tourist destinations, including Vilankulo, Inhambane and Maputo.



The initiative is expected to facilitate the creation of integrated tourism packages, taking advantage of the geographical proximity between the two countries and the connections of their tourist destinations.

Chapo also identified the gas sector as a potential source of revenue to finance economic diversification. He said gas projects under development or preparation could attract investments of between 50 and 60 billion US dollars over the next five to 10 years.

He added that his government intends to use gas revenues, including taxes and royalties, to boost sectors such as agriculture, tourism, infrastructure, logistics, industrialization, trade and digitalization.

World.title: AOC's dramatic retelling of Cornell rape allegations collides with complaint details

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., painted a far more sweeping picture of a Cornell University sexual assault case than what's alleged in the underlying civil complaint, while also making claims the university disputes.

Speaking during a town hall hosted by More Perfect University on Sunday in Ithaca, New York, Ocasio-Cortez addressed allegations outlined in a civil complaint filed last month by a former Cornell student identified as Jane Doe, who alleges she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in October 2024.

"Seven men drugged and gang raped a 20-year-old woman," Ocasio-Cortez said.

"They lured her in to a fraternity house," she continued. "They drugged her with ketamine. They then posted to a group chat that she was incapacitated, and seven men took turns gang raping her for seven hours."

CONVICTED RAPIST WHO PREYED ON WOMEN AT AMERICA'S TOP PARTY SCHOOL FACES RECKONING AFTER COURTHOUSE DASH

"Their fraternity knew. This was reported to Cornell University. And after looking into this matter, they expelled two of them and made the rest write essays as their form of punishment," Ocasio-Cortez said. "I want to be clear that the culture of rape, sexual assault, and pedophilia is protected in elite institutions across the United States and including Cornell University in this instance. It has got to stop."

Cornell has disputed Ocasio-Cortez's characterization of the disciplinary action, saying expulsions and suspensions were issued and that no respondent was required to write an essay as the sole consequence. The civil complaint alleges that several students who received temporary suspensions were given an opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to the university.

Ocasio-Cortez's comments come as a civil lawsuit filed by Doe contains graphic allegations about what happened inside the Chi Phi fraternity house nearly two years ago.

YALE STUDENT CHARGED AFTER ALLEGED SEX ASSAULT ON PACKED MANHATTAN SUBWAY TRAIN, ATTORNEY PUSHES BACK

The 101-page civil complaint names Cornell, fraternity-related entities, seven individual defendants and other defendants. It alleges that Doe was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after being plied with alcohol and drugs.

According to the complaint, Doe arrived at the fraternity house intoxicated, was pressured into taking ketamine and was subjected to sexual acts without her consent.

It further alleges that one fraternity member posted a sexually explicit message about her in a fraternity Snapchat group.

The incident ended at around 5:45 a.m., according to the complaint.

EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office reviewed Doe's sworn statement in November 2024 and initially determined that the facts contained in that statement did not support criminal charges under New York law.

Van Houten said Doe's November 2024 sworn statement "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped." He also said the statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

Van Houten said his office has reopened an investigation into the allegations and will revisit the decision about whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members. He said a senior prosecutor experienced in sex-crime cases is preparing the matter for presentation to a Tompkins County grand jury, which could consider Doe's testimony and new evidence raised by the civil complaint.

LSU FRAT PLEDGES ALLEGEDLY WATERBOARDED, FORCED TO CHUG MILK IN HAZING RITUALS: REPORT

Scott Kretzschmar, an attorney for one of the accused students, said his client welcomes the renewed investigation. He strongly denied the allegations against his client, who he said had no sexual contact with Doe.

Attorneys representing several other accused fraternity members have also denied wrongdoing. No criminal charges have been announced in connection with the allegations.

Cornell said it supports the reopened investigation and said its own months-long investigation resulted in a range of sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions. The Chi Phi chapter was also closed and barred from campus.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday that she has appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case.

World.title: Hasan Piker vows he will pressure James Talarico to govern as a leftist, not a moderate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker vowed Wednesday that he would push Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico to govern as a leftist rather than a moderate Democrat if Talarico was elected.

"Hopefully, after James Talarico wins, we’ve got to hold him to account," Piker said during a campus event at the University of Texas at Austin. "We've got to make sure that he doesn’t become another, ‘do nothing Democrat’ ‘business as usual,’ and we've got to keep up that pressure.

"We have to remind him that we are the force that backed him both early on," he continued. "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power and if he wants to maintain it, he’s got to play ball. Right?

"And that’s good to build a resilient movement anyway, so job’s not done even after he wins," Piker added. "So, just remember that, and, you know, remember that we do hold a lot of power in mass organizing."

UNIVERSITY EVENT WITH HASAN PIKER IN TEXAS DRAWS BACKLASH FROM BOTH SIDES OF THE AISLE

Fox News Digital reached out to Talarico's campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Talarico has moderated his rhetoric during his run for Senate, disavowing some of his past statements.

Piker, an internet personality popular on the Twitch platform, has become a major player in left-wing politics in recent years and has a long history of controversial comments, ranging from saying "America deserved 9/11" to praising an official in New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration after a clip showed her saying she wanted to "impoverish the White middle class."

Proximity to Piker has been a lightning rod for Democrats. Since the left-wing streamer appeared with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on the campaign trail, the candidate repeatedly tried to shrug off Piker’s controversial remarks.

TALARICO’S ‘PROUD CAPITALIST’ ABOUT-FACE COLLIDES WITH RESURFACED CALL TO ‘DISMANTLE’ CAPITALISM

Jesse Arm, a Manhattan Institute vice president and pollster from Michigan, wondered whether Talarico’s avowed moderation will stick.

"Talarico is wise to acknowledge, in effect, that many of his past comments on key policy questions were absurd, but Texans have reason to wonder whether his convictions have changed or merely his political incentives," he told Fox News Digital.

"If he is as wise a lawmaker as he is a crafty politician, he will govern as the more moderate liberal he currently purports to be.

"Hasan Piker’s faction can certainly exert pressure," he added. "And I would expect it to push Talarico back toward his earlier, more radical positions on policing, gender, race, immigration and energy."

A better indicator, he argued, was the fact that genuinely moderate Democrats have been driven out of office.

"We cannot know how Talarico would govern, but the broader Democratic Party gives us plenty of reason for skepticism: Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema were driven out, and John Fetterman faces endless hostility for breaking with its activist orthodoxy," he said.

"Governing as a genuine moderate would give Talarico a better chance of keeping a Texas Senate seat beyond an unusually favorable Democratic election cycle, but Piker is already openly demanding that he ‘play ball’ with the far left."

Arm suggested Piker might actually be making a tactical mistake by suggesting Democrats are only campaigning as moderates but will govern like leftists.

"Above perhaps all else, this episode exposes Piker’s political stupidity: publicly suggesting that a candidate’s moderation is temporary and that radicals will call the shots threatens the very victory he claims to want," Arm said.

"In truth, I suspect Piker would prefer an election cycle in which Talarico comes up short, but El-Sayed gets across the finish line. That would help advance Piker’s position that radicalism is the only viable path forward for the Democratic Party."
