World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: British foreign secretary reiterates support for the Falklands in meeting with Cheryl Roberts
World.content:
British foreign secretary reiterates support for the Falklands in meeting with Cheryl Roberts

1st Thursday, October 2026 - 23:07 UTC Full article

Roberts holds the Trade, Industry and Mineral Resources portfolio in the archipelago's government and announced on September 21 the five-year extension of offshore hydrocarbon licences.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband hosted Cheryl Roberts, a member of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, in London on Thursday, and reiterated to her that the United Kingdom “stands shoulder to shoulder” with the archipelago's residents and “remains steadfast” in supporting their right “to determine their own future and develop their own resources”.

Miliband posted the message on X after the meeting, held at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. The Legislative Assembly said the foreign secretary had expressed London's “unwavering” support for the archipelago. Neither side gave details of the topics discussed.

Roberts holds the Trade, Industry and Mineral Resources portfolio in the archipelago's government and announced on September 21 the five-year extension of offshore hydrocarbon licences.

It is the foreign secretary's first meeting with an assembly member since Argentina announced arbitration against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project on September 28, giving London two weeks to halt exploitation. The “shoulder to shoulder” wording echoes the response issued on September 30 by Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago and maintains that licences granted by the local government are invalid. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: British-Iranian man arrested over the RAF Fairford incident
World.content:
British-Iranian man arrested over the RAF Fairford incident

1st Thursday, October 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran “played a part” in what happened, though he said he could not give details and that the investigation was ongoing

British counter-terrorism police on Thursday arrested a 25-year-old man with dual British and Iranian nationality in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, in connection with Sunday's incident near RAF Fairford, an airbase in western England used by the United States Air Force.

The arrest took place in Westminster, where two properties were searched. Police had initially said the detained man was 27 and that a second man had been questioned, but corrected both points in a later update. The five men arrested near the base on Sunday — British nationals aged 23 to 25 who live in London — remain on police bail. None has been charged.

The five were detained in the early hours after reports of three suspicious vehicles heading towards the base, first on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in vans near the site. According to the BBC, one of them had himself dialled the emergency number an hour before a local resident reported a group of masked men.

“The investigation is hugely complex,” said Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, adding that “all possible angles, including foreign state involvement” are being examined.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were “strong indications” that Iran “played a part” in what happened, though he said he could not give details and that the investigation was ongoing. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi replied that Burnham was “barking up the wrong tree”, and Tehran denied any involvement. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken on Monday of “the hands of a foreign actor”, without providing evidence. Washington criticised the release on bail; Burnham defended it, citing the strict conditions imposed.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force for decades. In recent months, bombers have taken off from there for the Middle East after the British government approved its use for what it called defensive strikes on Iran.

World.title: Christa Pike survives a failed execution in Tennessee and remains in critical condition
World.content:
Christa Pike survives a failed execution in Tennessee and remains in critical condition

1st Thursday, October 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

Pike, 50, was given both doses of pentobarbital set out in the state protocol — two 50-millilitre syringes — at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville

Christa Pike, the only woman on death row in the US state of Tennessee, survived a lethal injection execution attempt on Wednesday and remains in critical condition in hospital, her lawyers said. Her defence has asked Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence.

Pike, 50, was given both doses of pentobarbital set out in the state protocol — two 50-millilitre syringes — at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Witnesses said she was still breathing and could be heard snoring nearly an hour later, when they were escorted out of the room. She was taken by ambulance to a nearby hospital. “Christa is alive right now. We don't have a sense of her prognosis, but we do know that she is alive and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey of the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender said on Thursday.

The Department of Correction said “every step of the state's lawful and established execution protocol” approved by the Attorney General's office had been followed, but did not explain why the procedure was not completed or give details of her condition. The defence alleged difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital and a lack of emergency medical care, and criticised the secrecy of the protocol. Joel Zivot, a professor at Emory University's School of Medicine and an adviser to Pike's legal team, told the BBC the drug probably never reached a sufficient level in her blood and that she was likely to suffer brain injury.

Pike was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville in January 1995, when she was 18. The victim's family has demanded answers following the failed procedure. Had it been completed, it would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in more than two centuries.

The state adopted its single-drug protocol after a three-year pause: Governor Lee halted executions in 2022 when an investigation found prison officials had not followed their own drug-testing rules, and they resumed in 2025. In January of that year, then US Attorney General Merrick Garland withdrew the federal pentobarbital-based protocol, citing the risk of unnecessary pain and suffering. In January 2026, Pike sued the state, arguing that a blood disorder made the method unconstitutionally cruel in her case; a judge declined in August to block the execution.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, seven of the twenty execution attempts carried out in the United States in 2022 had visible problems.

World.title: Punta Arenas and Falklands businesses hold more than 800 meetings
World.content:
Punta Arenas and Falklands businesses hold more than 800 meetings

1st Thursday, October 2026 - 21:33 UTC Full article

The event precedes a direct sea link using a Chilean-flagged vessel operated by Easter Island Naviera, which the company plans to launch between mid-November and the end of the year

Business people from Punta Arenas, in southern Chile, and from the Falklands held 822 business meetings over two days, at an event the organisers described as a success and which serves as a prelude to the reopening of a direct sea route between the Chilean city and Stanley, planned for the coming months.

The “Punta Arenas – The Islands Business Meeting” took place on Monday 28 and Tuesday 29 September at the Hotel Cabo de Hornos. It was organised by the Municipality of Punta Arenas and Chilean shipping company Easter Island Naviera, and brought together some 60 Magallanes companies and a delegation of 42 representatives from 32 companies and organisations in the archipelago, led by Louise Ellis, deputy managing director of the Falkland Islands Development Corporation. Sectors invited included food, cleaning products, cement, timber and spare parts. According to the organisers, several business people closed contracts, though no number was given.

“It has been a good couple of days; we are on a journey to connect the past with the future. We have worked with Punta Arenas and Magallanes for many decades. It was interrupted recently, but we hope to work again with old and new friends,” said Mike Summers, director of the Falkland Islands Chamber of Commerce and a former member of the Legislative Assembly. Ellis said there was interest on both sides in doing business.

The event precedes a direct sea link using a Chilean-flagged vessel operated by Easter Island Naviera, which the company plans to launch between mid-November and the end of the year. Its general manager, Pablo Pacheco, described it as a supply route “between private parties”. The mayor of Punta Arenas, Claudio Radonich, said the city aims to become the islands' “big supermarket”.

The Chilean government has called the initiative “a business between private parties”. Defence Minister Fernando Barros had said days earlier that Chile's support for Argentina's sovereignty claim does not imply restrictions on trade with the archipelago. According to the Chilean press, Argentina's foreign ministry followed the event closely; there was no official Argentine statement on it.

The new route would compete with supplies that currently reach the islands from Montevideo.

World.title: Uruguay's foreign minister separates the "invaded island" from the money extracted from the Falklands
World.content:
Uruguay's foreign minister separates the “invaded island” from the money extracted from the Falklands

1st Thursday, October 2026 - 09:32 UTC Full article

The minister said this was the main subject of his conversation with his Argentine counterpart, Pablo Quirno, and denied discussing with him Uruguay's interest in acquiring British ships

Uruguay's Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin argued that the Falklands dispute has changed in nature with oil exploration: one thing, he said, is “the invaded island” and “the fight against colonialism”, and another is “when a lot of money is taken from there”. His remarks come as Yamandú Orsi's government considers buying two patrol vessels from the Royal Navy, a deal that has already prompted a resolution from twenty deputies of Argentine President Javier Milei's party.

“When the process of oil prospecting by the United Kingdom began in the islands, the whole logic of the Malvinas issue changed,” he said on Wednesday on Canal 10's Arriba Gente programme, referring to the economic use of a territory he described as “taken colonially”. “That means that behind it comes military articulation, because you will try to defend those funds,” he said, calling for a move to “another phase” that includes reflection by the political system. He also said Argentina “is defending its rights and its heritage”.

The minister said this was the main subject of his conversation with his Argentine counterpart, Pablo Quirno, and denied discussing with him Uruguay's interest in acquiring British ships.

The United Kingdom has offered Uruguay three first-generation River-class offshore patrol vessels — HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn — of which the defence ministry hopes to acquire up to two. A navy mission visited the Mersey in London in May, and a transfer could take place in 2028, when the Royal Navy retires them. No final decision has been taken. The search follows the cancellation in October 2025 of a contract with Spanish shipyard Cardama for two patrol vessels, which the government rescinded after finding “strong indications” of fraud.

The Uruguayan navy has raised technical objections, including the lack of a helicopter hangar. Opposition senator Javier García, a former defence minister, called the deal “more political than technical” and warned of the signal it would send to Buenos Aires in the current context.

In Argentina, deputy Damián Arabia and 19 other La Libertad Avanza lawmakers filed a draft resolution expressing “bewilderment and concern” over the possible purchase. “Our fraternal ties and Uruguay's historic, supportive and generous backing for the Malvinas Cause warrant avoiding this acquisition,” he wrote. The resolution is non-binding and the Argentine government has not lodged an official protest.

The remarks come amid an escalation. On Monday Argentina announced arbitration against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project; British Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran replied on Wednesday that such conduct “raises questions” about Argentina's reliability as a partner. The United Kingdom maintains that the activity is governed by the archipelago's legislation in accordance with international law. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: The Spectator likens Milei's Falklands push to Galtieri's
World.content:
The Spectator likens Milei's Falklands push to Galtieri's

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 23:01 UTC Full article

An opinion column published on Wednesday in the British weekly The Spectator likens Argentine President Javier Milei's campaign over the Falklands to that of dictator Leopoldo Galtieri in 1982, with the difference, its author argues, that the current government is using legal rather than military means. The piece, by law professor Andrew Tettenborn, is an argument of opinion rather than a report of new facts.

The columnist calls “lawfare” — the use of legal instruments for political ends — the arbitration Argentina announced on Monday over the Sea Lion oil project. He argues that the real aim is to reopen the sovereignty question, that Milei sees the United Kingdom as weak and divided, and that he is seeking a distraction from domestic difficulties. These are the author's assessments; he also directs personal characterisations at British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and at Milei himself.

The legal core of the column is its most concrete part: the author argues that Argentina's claim is in substance a territorial sovereignty dispute and that the international law of the sea tribunal has made clear it does not see that as its role. In previous cases, tribunals constituted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea have declined to rule on sovereignty disputes, as in the 2015 arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands. The procedure Buenos Aires has announced is an Annex VII arbitration; from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, Argentina would only seek provisional measures while the arbitral tribunal is constituted.

The column contains inaccuracies. It places the environmental lawsuit against the project in Buenos Aires and suggests it was filed with Milei's tacit approval; it was filed on September 1, before the presidential address that launched the campaign, by the Falklands War Veterans Centre of La Plata and an association of environmental lawyers before the federal court in Río Grande, Tierra del Fuego. Nor is it confirmed that the criminal complaints cover Rockhopper executives, as the text states.

Tettenborn advises the British government to reject the claim and “hold our nerve”, and argues that international courts have lost impartiality. The British statement issued the same Wednesday, however, expressly invokes the Law of the Sea Convention as the legal framework for oil activity in the archipelago.

Argentina argues that unilateral exploitation contravenes UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49 and that the residents' wishes do not settle the dispute. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: London rejects Argentina's arbitration and questions its "reliability" as a partner
World.content:
London rejects Argentina's arbitration and questions its “reliability” as a partner

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 22:59 UTC Full article

MLA Roberts this morning working the Labour Party Conference with Minister of Overseas Territories and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting

The British government has rejected Argentina's decision to initiate international arbitration over the Sea Lion oil project and said Buenos Aires' campaign over the Falklands “raises questions about Argentina's reliability as a partner for the United Kingdom”. It is the first time London has extended the dispute to the bilateral relationship as a whole.

The statement, signed by Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Overseas Territories Uma Kumaran and released on Wednesday, describes the recourse to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as “the latest attempt to undermine the rights and livelihoods” of the archipelago's residents. It says they “have freely and democratically chosen their future” and have the right to develop their natural resources “without intimidation, coercion or interference from others”, and that hydrocarbon activity is regulated under local law “in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS”. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

According to the text, London told Argentina's ambassador to the United Kingdom this week that efforts to obstruct economic activity “are not acts of responsible international engagement” but “deliberate attempts to undermine the prosperity and economic security of a self-governing people”. The statement concludes that the United Kingdom will continue to stand “shoulder-to-shoulder” with the archipelago's government and will “robustly defend” its wishes, its economy and its right to self-determination. On X, Kumaran wrote: “The Falkland Islands are British.” Rockhopper Exploration, the project's British partner, said it would press ahead with Sea Lion and called Argentina's claim “illegitimate”, according to the Buenos Aires Herald.

President Javier Milei on Monday ordered the start of arbitration proceedings under Annex VII of the Convention and gave London two weeks to prevent exploitation in the basin north of the archipelago; if it does not, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. Buenos Aires argues that unilateral exploitation contravenes General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49 and causes “irreversible and irreparable” harm to its rights. In previous cases, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on territorial sovereignty disputes.

Argentina also has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints against ten companies. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Trump and six tech companies sign a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord
World.content:
Trump and six tech companies sign a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 19:10 UTC Full article

The document, titled “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities”, was posted by the president after a lunch with industry executives

US President Donald Trump and the heads of six technology companies signed a voluntary accord at the White House on Tuesday under which the companies commit to ensuring the safety of their own artificial intelligence systems. Trump called it “morally binding” and said it was “almost like a constitution”.

The document, titled “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities”, was posted by the president on his Truth Social network after a lunch with industry executives. It was signed by Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Elon Musk.

According to the text, the companies are responsible for the safety of their own technology, will implement safeguards so models operate as intended, will quickly detect and fix problems and will work with independent auditors to verify their systems do not access other technical systems in unintended ways. The accord sets no consequences for breaches. Trump also announced a board to oversee the area, without naming its members, and the appointment of a government official to lead on the issue in the coming days.

Zuckerberg described it as “a start”; Pichai as “historic and consequential”; and Amodei as a way “to win safely”. Specialists consulted by the BBC were critical. Kimberlee Weatherall, a law professor at the University of Sydney, said the accord lets companies “define what counts as safety” and called it “deeply unimpressive”. Jeannie Paterson of the University of Melbourne warned that self-regulation could mean “only minimal safeguards”.

The accord comes amid calls from parts of the industry and from experts for tighter oversight of the technology. According to the BBC, OpenAI cancelled the release of one of its models on Monday over safety concerns.

The same day, Trump signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” or “SI” in official correspondence, websites and reports, and tasking his science and technology adviser with proposing a legal definition within 60 days. In his address to the UN General Assembly last week, the president said the word “artificial” made the technology “sound fake”.

Trump reiterated his support for the expansion of data centres, whose construction has become a sensitive issue ahead of November's midterm elections: a Marist poll for NPR and PBS found 65% of registered voters oppose having them built in their area.

The accord puts into practice the position Washington set out in New York against calls for common rules. There, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for “a single set of global principles and standards”, while Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei rejected any pre-emptive regulation.

World.title: Vice principal killed, 3 injured in attack by former students at Torreón school
World.content:
A vice principal was killed at a secondary school in Torreón, Coahuila, on Thursday, in an attack allegedly committed by two former students.

Three other people, including students, were injured in the attack at the Number 13 Secondary School in Ejido La Unión, located north of downtown Torreón.

The alleged aggressors, 18-year-old twin brothers, were armed with machetes and explosives, according to witnesses cited in media reports. School prefect Héctor Rodríguez said that “explosions began in the bathroom” and that students ran to take shelter in classrooms. He also said that the alleged attackers entered the school behind a teacher between the second and third lessons of the day.

The two men were detained after the attack on Thursday morning. Video footage indicates that students helped to restrain the suspects.

Police, emergency services and Civil Protection authorities all responded to the attack in Torréon, located about 250 kilometers west of state capital of Saltillo, near Coahuila’s border with Durango.

The deceased vice principal was identified as Nery Edith Narváez González, who was aged in her mid-fifties. The cause of her death has not been confirmed, but it appears likely that she was stabbed.

Coahuila Attorney General Federico Fernández told reporters that two 18-year-old brothers were identified as the “probable” perpetrators of what he called a “brutal attack.” He noted that they were detained and turned over to the Coahuila Attorney General’s Office.

“What we’re told is that they are ex-students of this school,” Fernández said.

“… These two former students arrived and attacked the institution’s administrative authorities as well as some students,” he said, noting that the vice principal was killed.

Fernández acknowledged reports that the aggressors were carrying explosives, but said that authorities hadn’t confirmed that to be the case.

“They’re talking to us about bladed weapons … and a kind of firecrackers,” he said.

Regarding the possible motive for the attack, Fernández said that preliminary investigations indicated that the alleged aggressors had “feelings” against staff at the school.

He said that one of two students injured in the attack had been reported in “serious” condition.

Asked whether there was gunfire at the school, Fernández said that could be “ruled out for now.”

He said that he and state Security Secretary Hugo Gutiérrez were heading to Torreón to conduct investigative work and determine what weapons were used in the attack.

Federal authorities are assisting the investigation

The federal Security Cabinet said on social media that it is collaborating with Coahuila authorities to “shed light on “the events at the school in Torreón and “contribute to the development of the investigations.”

“We regret the death of a member of the educational staff and express our condolences to her family, as well as our solidarity with the entire educational community. Three people injured in these events are receiving medical care, and two individuals identified as responsible for the attack have already been detained,” the Security Cabinet said.

The federal Ministry of Public Education (SEP) described the attack as “reprehensible” and expressed its condolences to the family and friends of the deceased woman as well as to the “educational community.”

Fatal attacks are fairly rare at schools in Mexico, but there have been a number of previous cases.

In March, a teenage boy allegedly shot and killed two female teachers at a high school in the Pacific coast port city of Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán. At a Torreón primary school in January 2020, an 11-year-old boy shot and killed his teacher and wounded six others before turning his guns on himself.

With reports from Milenio, El Financiero, Reforma and El País

World.title: Hurricane Rachel and the season’s first cold front bring heavy rain to central and northern Mexico
World.content:
Rachel, hard on the heels of Polo, has become the latest major hurricane in the Pacific. Poised to increase to Category 4 as early as Friday, it is fueling dangerous flood threats along coastal areas.

Rachel — a Category 3 hurricane as of early afternoon Thursday, with maximum sustained winds of 195 km/h (121 mph) and gusts reaching 240 km/h (149 mph) — was about 415 km east-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco.

⚠️ ¡Alerta por tiempo severo! Un #FrenteFrío y un #Huracán detonarán lluvias torrenciales del 28 de septiembre al 4 de octubre 🌧️🌀. José Martín Cortés con el panorama completo en 🔗https://t.co/MtmR1SPTWb pic.twitter.com/YsjTDgj1P8 — Meteored México (@meteoredmx) September 28, 2026

The center of the storm system was 390 kilometers south of Cabo San Lucas, Baja California Sur, and was moving west at 6 km/h. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 40 km from Rachel’s center, with tropical-storm-force winds extending outward up to 260 km.

While expected to increase to Category 4 and remain a major hurricane through Saturday, Rachel’s projected northwestern course suggests it will not make landfall in Mexico.

However, the National Meteorological Service (SMN) is forecasting very heavy rainfall for Nayarit, Sinaloa and southern Baja California Sur (up to 75 mm) through Friday, increasing the risk of landslides, cresting rivers and flooding.

The National Civil Protection Coordination is urging local authorities and residents of potentially affected areas to follow updates on Rachel’s development.

State and federal authorities are also on alert in the states of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. The Jalisco state government ordered schools closed on Wednesday, but they had reopened on Thursday.

The season’s first cold front has arrived

At the same time, the first cold front of the 2026-2027 season arrived and was poised to cause heavy rains, strong gusts of wind and a drop in temperature in several northern and central states.

According to the SMN, the cold front will move from the northern border towards the northern Gulf of Mexico, its mass of cold air lowering temperatures and stirring up conditions of atmospheric instability.

The SMN forecasts that the most significant effects of the cold front will last three to four days, impacting the following states: Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, Durango, Chihuahua, Sonora and Aguascalientes.

In addition to the colder temperatures, Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, Durango, Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí could see from 75 to 150 mm of rainfall.

Additionally, these northern and central states could see winds gusting up to 60-70 km/h (37-44 mph) with possible whirlwind formations in northern Coahuila.

With reports from El Informador, The Associated Press and La Crónica

World.title: Mexican writer Juan Villoro honored with the Carlos Fuentes international literature prize
World.content:
Mexican writer and journalist Juan Villoro, whose work moves from novels and essays to soccer writing and children’s books, has won the 2026 Carlos Fuentes International Prize for Literary Creation — an honor that he said should propel him toward his next book.

The National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) and Mexico’s Culture Ministry announced the unanimous decision Wednesday. The prize recognizes writers whose bodies of work, written wholly or substantially in Spanish, have enriched humanity’s literary heritage.

Villoro, who turned 70 on Sept. 24, was cited for “the breadth and scope of his work, which encompasses different genres with mastery and rigor,” according to Gaceta UNAM, the university’s official news publication.

The jury also praised Villoro as “a shaper of new readers” whose thought has had “a transcendent presence in essays and journalism in Latin America.” It said his work promotes a dialogue between the present and tradition “from a humanist perspective full of humor and irony.”

The prize includes a sum in pesos equivalent to US $125,000, a diploma and a reproduction of a sculpture by Vicente Rojo.

Villoro is the 11th recipient and the fourth Mexican to win the prize, after poet Eduardo Lizalde in 2016, writer and critic Margo Glantz in 2022 and writer Elena Poniatowska in 2023.

The prize’s other winners include Peruvian Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa, who received the inaugural award in 2012, and Sergio Ramírez, the novelist, essayist and former vice president of Nicaragua, honored in 2014.

Villoro’s career has spanned fiction, nonfiction, theater, screenwriting, journalism and literature for younger readers. His work also explores the pleasures and demands of reading.

His 2004 novel “El testigo” (“The Witness”) won Spain’s Herralde Prize, while “El libro salvaje” (“The Wild Book”), published in 2008, has sold more than 1 million copies and been translated into numerous languages.

His subjects extend to violence and everyday apprehension in Mexico, such as this English translation of a 2015 newspaper column in which he recounts a drive to Ayotzinapa, Guerrero, that turns into a reflection on mutual fear amid cartel control.

Additional books include “Dios es redondo” (“God is Round”), about soccer, and “Vértigo horizontal: una ciudad llamada México” (“Horizontal Vertigo: A City Called Mexico”), an essayistic portrait of the capital.

Villoro called the prize “a great surprise, a great honor, but also a commitment,” adding that he regarded awards not as a completed achievement “but as an incentive to keep doing it.”

Established in 2012, the year Carlos Fuentes died, the prize honors the Mexican novelist whose best-known works include “La muerte de Artemio Cruz” (“The Death of Artemio Cruz”), “La región más transparente” (“Where the Air Is Clear”) and the Mexico News Daily-recommended “Aura.”

This year’s jury comprised playwright Flavio González Mello, poet Myriam Moscona, writer and editor Mónica Nepote, novelist David Toscana and Nicaraguan writer Gioconda Belli, the 2025 recipient.

The prize, which became an annual award in 2019, will be presented in November on a date to be announced.

With reports from El Heraldo de México, EFE and Gaceta UNAM

World.title: Report: AMLO government’s targeting of journalists and activists could be crimes against humanity
World.content:
Researchers at the University of California-Berkeley Human Rights Center (HRC) say that legal grounds exist to try former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador for crimes against humanity, after a new report established a pattern of persecution including hostile rhetoric and digital espionage.

The HRC report assesses whether the former president’s constant disparaging rhetoric toward journalists and activists, as well as the alleged espionage carried out by his administration, amounts to a pattern of persecution that could fall under the Rome Statute.

The investigation also examined what role state institutions played in carrying out or enabling targeted killings, enforced disappearances, surveillance, stigmatization and other forms of harassment.

It then considered whether, taken together, these actions constitute crimes against humanity under the Rome Statute, the founding international treaty that established the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity from its base in The Hague.

The Berkeley report, entitled “Under Attack: Targeting of Journalists and Human Rights Defenders in Mexico,” makes the claim that Mexico was the most dangerous country in the world for journalists during López Obrador’s six-year term and the second most dangerous for human rights defenders.

The HRC documented 337 killings — 78 journalists and 259 human rights defenders — while also compiling 75 cases involving killings and enforced disappearances.

🧵1/6: After a multi-year investigation, we’ve launched the platform “Under Attack: Targeting of Journalists and Human Rights Defenders in Mexico,” which documents attacks on civic watchdogs during the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador. pic.twitter.com/5kU3trgWfx — Human Rights Center (@hrcberkeley) September 29, 2026

Researchers identified 2,827 instances of rhetoric they characterized as “explicitly disparaging and aimed at undermining the credibility and safety of independent journalists and civil society organizations.”

The report argues that the volume of vitriol “contributed to an increasingly hostile environment for journalists and human rights defenders in Mexico.”

In addition to the confrontational rhetoric, the Defense Ministry allegedly operated unlawful surveillance tools, including Pegasus spyware, to spy on the targeted groups.

In a separate publication, one of the lead authors asserted that although the numbers are indeed staggering, they are not the basis for the central finding.

Instead, Lindsay Freeman points to the “systematicity and the context in which they occurred,” describing the killings as “the visible edge of a broader attack … one the state openly encouraged and rarely punished.”

“The president used his daily press conferences to discredit and attack the press … and networks of fake accounts linked to state media amplified that rhetoric into threats and harassment online,” she said.

Freeman said that the unlawful surveillance, harassment, stigmatization and physical violence could be sufficient for the ICC prosecutor’s office to consider opening a preliminary examination under Article 7 of the Rome Statute.

With reports from UPI, LópezDóriga.com, Proceso and The Daily Californian

World.title: Volaris will end Tulum flights as airline exodus from the Caribbean coast resort continues
World.content:
Low-cost Mexican airline Volaris has announced it will end service to Tulum, Quintana Roo, after the end of this year, joining the exodus of national and international airlines from the troubled beach resort and cultural destination

Just this week, Mexico’s legacy airline Aeroméxico announced it would suspend flights to Tulum as of today, Thursday, describing the move as a “temporary suspension.”

Both carriers cited “market conditions”— meaning a lack of profitability — as the reason for their suspension of service

“We have had to review the profitability of our routes and temporarily suspend certain flights with lower load factors — including our operations to and from Tulum — starting January 7, 2027,” the airline told the newspaper El Financiero.

Ticket sales to and from the destination will stop this weekend.

The airlines’ “lower load factors” (i.e. fewer passengers) can be directly linked to the shrinking visitor base to the once-thriving tourist destination, known for its enticing combination of sunny beaches and archaeological sites.

Data by the Tulum Hotel Association cited by the newspaper El Economista revealed that occupancy levels by mid-September were 10% lower compared to the same period last year. Beachfront hotels saw occupancy below 20% and all-inclusive resorts below 30%, prompting some to consider operating only during peak season.

Figures from the Tulum airport (TQO) also reflect this downturn.

El Economista reported that according to the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC), TQO handled 471,500 travelers between January and June — a 33.2% drop from the 705,400 recorded during the same period in 2025.

Volaris said reasons for the drop in international arrivals include increased fees and other charges related to foreign tourist travel, such as the recent announcement of an increase in the Non-Resident Fee (DNR), which will rise by 35% starting next year.

The DNR fee paid by foreign visitors entering Mexico would rise from 983 pesos (US $54) to 1,334.80 pesos (US $74) if Congress approves the Economic Package proposal for 2027. This fee is included in the ticket price and directly increases the cost of international itineraries.

A price hike in the Airport Use Fee (TUA) was also cited as a cause, which now stands at 300 pesos (US $16) per passenger, as well as costs related to fuel and air navigation services.

Tulum’s airport was one of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s flagship projects. It began operations in December 2023, nearly eight months before President Claudia Sheinbaum started her term in office.

With reports from Expansión

World.title: Sheinbaum praise and social media gripes: 5 takeaways from the unveiling of AMLO’s book ‘Pueblo’
World.content:
Two years after completing his six-year term as president, Andrés Manuel López Obrador returned to the spotlight on Wednesday with an 80-minute video message to promote his new book, a political history of Mexico called “Pueblo” (People).

AMLO’s message, filmed at his home in Palenque, Chiapas, and posted to YouTube and Facebook, was reminiscent of the many lengthy, meandering addresses he delivered at his morning press conferences while president between 2018 and 2024.

🟢 AMLO reaparece y presenta su nuevo libro “Pueblo” El expresidente Andrés Manuel López Obrador (@lopezobrador_) reapareció públicamente este miércoles mediante un videomensaje desde Palenque, Chiapas, para anunciar la publicación de su nuevo libro, “Pueblo”. López Obrador… pic.twitter.com/uDKvjoL454 — Rosa Lilia Torres- Noticias (@rosaliliatorrs) October 1, 2026

Beyond his new book — a follow-up to his 2025 book “Grandeza” (Greatness) — López Obrador touched on a range of topics, including his own health and happiness, the state of social media today, and the performance of Claudia Sheinbaum as president.

Here is a broad overview of AMLO’s message.

AMLO reports he’s happy and doing well

At the start of his message, López Obrador — who has had a range of health issues over the years — said that he has been doing well.

“Thanks to the Creator, to science, to luck, thanks to life, I’m content, I’m happy, here at La Chingada,” he said, referring to his property in Palenque whose name can be translated as “Hell.”

(AMLO, 72, used to joke that he would “go to La Chingada” once he finished his presidency.)

López Obrador said that he, and “many millions” of other Mexicans, are “very happy” with what has been “achieved: a transformation, the fourth transformation of public life in Mexico.”

AMLO founded the ruling Morena party and the broader “fourth transformation” (4T) political movement now led by Sheinbaum.

While he now lives in Palenque and has largely withdrawn from public life, López Obrador said that he occasionally goes to Mexico City to see his wife, Beatriz Gutiérrez Müller, and his sons.

“They come here as well,” he added.

AMLO didn’t make any mention of the scrutiny his son Andrés Manuel López Beltrán is facing over allegations he has ties to organized crime and fuel smuggling. López Beltrán, who revealed last month that his U.S. visa had been revoked, is a former secretary of organization for Morena and is now aiming to be elected as a federal deputy at elections next June. He denies any wrongdoing.

Social media platforms are no longer ‘free,’ AMLO says

López Obrador acknowledged that he used to refer to social media — of which he was formerly an avid user — as “blessed.”

“When Twitter and Facebook first emerged, I used to say, ‘Blessed social media’ because we were surrounded by the mainstream media: radio, newspapers, and television,” he said.

AMLO said that Televisa and TV Azteca, as well as “almost all” the newspapers and “almost all” the radio stations, carried out “campaigns” against him and his political allies.

“Then social media emerged, and we finally had a way to communicate. The information blockade was broken. But what happened? How long did social media remain free? Ten years. Now all [the social media sites] are taken over, controlled,” said López Obrador, who in early 2021 criticized social media companies for blocking the accounts of U.S. President Donald Trump after a violent mob of his supporters broke into the Capitol Building in Washington, D.C.

Earlier in his message, AMLO railed against political “publicists” and their use of social media.

“Now there are a lot [of publicists] and they’re very modern now. They manage the platforms, social media, the internet and bot farms — computers to spread lies,” he said.

Is AMLO still in charge behind the scenes?

Early in his message, López Obrador said that he is “retired from politics after nearly 50 years of fighting intensely for justice, freedom, democracy and to transform our country.”

AMLO — who many Mexicans believe continues to wield power behind the scenes — said he decided to abruptly cut off his involvement in politics because he didn’t want to be a “cacique, caudillo, supreme leader or power behind the throne.”

“We shouldn’t be too attached to power or money. Money isn’t happiness, nor is power. Happiness is being at peace with oneself, being at peace with our conscience, and being at peace with others,” he said.

Referring to the end of his six-year term, AMLO said that “the time came” for him to end his life in politics.

“In the two years … since I left the presidency, I’ve spent my time writing here,” he said.

“It wasn’t easy — [I went through] years of intense struggles,” said López Obrador, who unsuccessfully contested the 2006 and 2012 presidential elections before winning a landslide victory in 2018.

Sheinbaum said last month that, “This idea that, behind the president, López Obrador is governing is a very sexist idea.”

“… It has to do with an idea that women can’t govern,” she said.

AMLO describes Sheinbaum as ‘the best president in the world’

Near the end of his message, López Obrador noted that he had dedicated his new book to Sheinbaum, who served as his environment minister when he was mayor of Mexico City between 2000 and 2005.

“I dedicate it to Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, our president and great pride, example of hard work, honesty, rectitude and loyalty to the people,” he said, reading from a page at the start of “Pueblo.”

AMLO said he was “very happy” that the person to whom he handed over the “baton of command” has turned out to be “extraordinary, the best president in the world, including men and women.”

“I’m not one to flatter … [but] the president is exceptional,” he said.

At her Thursday morning press conference, Sheinbaum said she appreciated AMLO’s words.

Mexican history, with a twist

Of course, López Obrador also spoke about “Pueblo,” one of 21 books he has written.

He said that the book has 10 chapters and covers “more than 200 years of political history” in Mexico, starting with Mexico’s independence from Spain and concluding with the ongoing “fourth transformation,” of which Sheinbaum is said to be building a “second story.”

AMLO noted that the book is published by Planeta, which he described as a “very good publisher.”

In addition to Mexico’s independence and the 4T, Lopez Obrador said that Pueblo includes chapters on “the U.S. invasion” — i.e. the 1846-48 Mexican-American War — the “Porfiriato” (the lengthy rule of Porfirio Díaz) and the Mexican Revolution, among other periods of Mexican history.

With a smile on his face, AMLO said that chapter 9 is called “The neoporfirismo prianista,” focusing on the period between 1982 and 2018 when four Institutional Revolutionary Party presidents (Miguel de la Madrid, Carlos Salinas, Ernesto Zedillo and Enrique Peña Nieto) and two National Action Party presidents (Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón) governed Mexico.

López Obrador is an outspoken critic of governance in Mexico in the so-called “neoliberal” period between 1982 and 2018, saying in his video message that it was a time of “oligarchy” with a “facade of democracy” and the “handing over the assets of the nation” to private interests.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: From Robbie Williams to trash fishing
World.content:
October paints an exciting events picture for residents and visitors of Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, one of Mexico’s tourist hotspots and premier expat destinations.

Included on the upcoming events calendar are highlights such as a museum exhibition showcasing Mexico’s maritime history, a PGA golf tournament, a performance from an internationally known pop star, and a one-of-a-kind eco-friendly competition at sea.

Our list covers everything from last-minute plans this weekend to big events that will require you to plan ahead before tickets run out.

Here’s a curated list of exciting upcoming events in Puerto Vallarta.

Discover Mexico’s navy history at Museum Night

No plans for the weekend? Don’t panic — we’ve got you covered.

Saturday, Oct. 4, will see the Mexican Naval Museum in Puerto Vallarta host the ninth edition of its “Museum Night” cultural program, a free event dedicated to the 205th anniversary of the founding of the Mexican Navy.

The event will take place from 6 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. at the museum, located at Zaragoza Street No. 4 in the city center, near the Malecón.

The program is designed for adults and kids alike and will combine historical outreach, recreational activities and exhibits showcasing the Navy’s current operations.

Visitors can expect a Marine Corps booth, information from the Search and Rescue Station (ENSAR), a K-9 unit demonstration, workshops — such as nautical knot-tying, drawing and choreography — and a musical performance by Dan Gutiérrez.

The Naval History Museum opened in 2006 in a colonial-style building that previously served as the Port Authority office. It is adjacent to Los Arcos del Malecón in Puerto Vallarta’s Historic Center.

On your marks, get set — trash collection time!

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Limpia tu Mar Puerto Vallarta A.C. (@limpiatumarpv)

If you’re looking for an eco-friendly activity that makes a difference in the environment, look no further than the International Trash-Fishing Competition, an event that seeks to catch floating waste instead of fish.

The competition will take place Oct. 18, starting from Los Muertos Pier in Puerto Vallarta, with activities scheduled between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m.

Organized by nonprofit Limpia Tu Mar (Clean Your Ocean), this initiative is back for its third edition with a capacity of up to 40 vessels.

Participation is open to visitors and residents alike, who will have to form teams consisting of five participants each. Children over 8 years of age are welcome as long as they’re accompanied by a parent or legal guardian.

The activity focuses exclusively on floating waste classified into three categories: plastic items made from polyethylene terephthalate (PET), glass and expanded polystyrene (Styrofoam). This year’s goal is to collect at least 1.5 tons of waste.

Team registration costs 5,000 pesos (about US $271) and includes a boat, equipment, caps and a collection kit. The call for participants also seeks volunteers for both onshore and on-board roles.

The registration deadline is Oct. 6. You can register here.

Get your tickets to see Robbie Williams )

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Vallarta es Música (@vallartaesmusica)

Puerto Vallarta is rarely a stop for international pop stars’ world tours. That will change Oct. 27, when British pop star Robbie Williams performs live at the VidantaWorld Vallarta–Nuevo Nayarit esplanade as part of the VidantaWorld Concert Series.

The show, which is set to start at 8 p.m., is part of Williams’ Britpop Latin American tour, which sees the 52-year-old singer visiting cities such as Bogotá, Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires, Mexico City, Querétaro and São Paulo.

The concert will be part of a weeklong lineup of entertainment, sports and themed activities at Vidanta, running from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1.

In addition to Williams’ performance, the schedule includes the partial opening of BON Luxury Theme Park, performances of LUDÕ by Cirque du Soleil, Day of the Dead activities, and the VidantaWorld Mexico Open (more on this ahead).

Williams’ performance will headline one of the main event nights during the week leading up to the tournament.

Concert tickets are still available at the VidantaWorld Concert Series website. But hurry, because they’re selling fast.

The Mexico Open at Vidanta returns for its fifth edition

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Where To Go Vallarta (@wheretogovallarta)

The 2026 VidantaWorld Mexico Open will bring together the elite of professional golf from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1 at the VidantaWorld Vallarta course, located within the VidantaWorld Vallarta–Nuevo Nayarit complex.

This marks the fifth consecutive year the destination has hosted this official PGA Tour tournament, considered one of the premier professional golf events in Mexico.

Designed by Greg Norman, the course is set in the area between the Ameca River, the Sierra Madre mountains and the Pacific Ocean, offering stunning natural views.

The competition will feature 120 players, a US $6 million purse and 500 FedExCup points, attracting PGA Tour stars as well as top golfers from Mexico and Latin America.

Visitors can choose between general admission and several hospitality packages. General admission includes access to the course, Fan Zone, Fan Shop and food area, while hospitality options are available at holes 1, 4, 9, 10, 17 and 18.

Tickets can be purchased at the official VidantaWorld Mexico Open website.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Health and healthcare
World.content:
Last week we published Part 1 of the MND Mexico Well-being Series, which focused on eight health and healthcare indicators, including life expectancy, health expenditure per capita and hospital beds per 1,000 people.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article is a condensed version of that report — a concise presentation of the key data, complemented by visual features.

As we noted last week, the MND Mexico Well-being Series — a collection of articles on a range of topics related to well-being — will draw on the most recent internationally comparable data, as well as data from the past decade, to assess what has changed in Mexico during the eight years that the ruling Morena party has been in office.

A “Mexico in Numbers” companion piece will complement each article in the series.

Without further ado, let’s take a look at the key data from Part 1 of the series.

* The data in Part 1 of the MND Mexico Well-being Series, and hence the data in this article, comes from the OECD’s Health at a Glance 2025 report. The OECD report includes health and healthcare data for the 38 OECD countries, as well as OECD partner and accession countries in some cases.

Life expectancy at birth

Mexico’s life expectancy rose only marginally, from 75 years in 2015 to 75.5 years in 2024, leaving it 5.6 years below the OECD average of 81.1 years. In 2024, Mexico ranked 46th of 49 countries on this measure.

Avoidable mortality

Mexico recorded 418 avoidable deaths per 100,000 people in 2023 — almost twice the OECD average of 222 — to rank 40th of 44 countries, or fifth worst. Its preventable mortality rate rose about 10% between 2013 and 2023 to 243 deaths per 100,000 people, while the treatable mortality rate increased about 15% to 175.

Obesity

Some 36% of Mexicans aged 15 and over are obese, 10 percentage points above the OECD average of 26% and the second-highest rate among the 14 countries with measured data, behind only the United States (41%). Mexico’s obesity rate has risen from 33.3% in 2015, although its combined overweight-and-obesity rate has remained broadly stable at above 70% over the past decade.

Healthcare coverage

Mexico provided coverage for a core set of health services to 78% of its population in 2023, 20 percentage points below the OECD average of 98% and the lowest rate among 40 countries assessed. Coverage has deteriorated over the past decade, falling from 92.3% in 2015.

Health expenditure as a % of GDP

Mexico spent 5.9% of GDP on health care in 2024, 3.4 percentage points below the OECD average of 9.3%, ranking 42nd of 49 countries. Spending rose only marginally from 5.8% of GDP in 2016.

Health expenditure per capita

Mexico spent US$1,588 per person on health care in 2024, compared with an OECD average of US$5,967, which is 275% higher. Mexico ranked 43rd of 49 countries on this measure. Although real per-capita spending grew at an annual average of 2.1% between 2019 and 2024, Mexico’s spending gap with the OECD average widened slightly from 2016.

Hospital beds

Mexico had just 1 hospital bed per 1,000 people in 2023, compared with an OECD average of 4.2, ranking last among 44 countries assessed. The ratio was unchanged from a decade earlier.

Satisfaction with healthcare availability

In 2023, 56% of Mexicans said they were satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live, eight percentage points below the OECD average of 64%. Mexico ranked 27th among 38 countries. Satisfaction increased only marginally from 55% in 2014.

Nigeria · Labour

Latest — 2 October 2026. The strike is now formally under way. In a circular issued on 1 October, the Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council directed federal, state and local government workers to begin the three-day warning strike from midnight on Thursday, 2 October, ordering “total compliance” through Sunday, 4 October. Background: what the unions are demanding and why.

Nigeria’s public sector unions have called a three-day warning strike starting Friday, 2 October 2026, after the government let a 30 September deadline lapse without meeting their demands. —Who called it. The Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council (JNPSNC), which groups eight public sector unions including the civil service, health workers, senior civil servants and nurses. —The demands. Cut petrol to ₦500 a litre, approve a wage award for workers, and start negotiating a new national minimum wage of at least ₦500,000 from 2027. —Why now. Pump prices range from ₦1,450 to ₦2,500 a litre across the country, and the current ₦70,000 minimum wage has been eroded by the worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation. —Backing. The Nigeria Labour Congress, the country’s biggest union federation, has thrown its weight behind the demands.

Nigeria’s public sector workers say they will down tools for three days from Friday, after President Bola Tinubu’s government failed to answer demands for cheaper petrol, a wage award and talks on a new minimum wage — on the very day the country marked 66 years of independence.

Unions want the government to sell crude to the Dangote refinery and modular refineries on terms that bring pump prices down.

The Strike Call

The Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council (JNPSNC) said its 30 September deadline for the Federal Government to act “remains in effect”, and that workers had been mobilised for a three-day warning strike with effect from Friday, 2 October 2026, if the demands were not addressed. The council had written to President Bola Tinubu on 21 September; its national secretary, Gbenga Olowoyo, said no visible action had followed.

The JNPSNC brings together eight public sector unions, among them the Nigeria Civil Service Union, the Medical and Health Workers Union, the Association of Senior Civil Servants of Nigeria and the National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives. A warning strike of three days is a step short of an indefinite shutdown — but it is the strongest escalation since the pay campaign began, and it lands the day after Nigeria’s 66th Independence Day, an occasion the unions said the president’s address should have used to answer their demands.

The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), the country’s largest union federation under president Joe Ajaero, has backed the demands, coupling them with its own call for an immediate petrol price cut, a nationwide wage award and urgent negotiation of a new national minimum wage. Whether the NLC’s wider structures formally join the Friday action was not confirmed by Wednesday evening.

The Three Demands

First, fuel. The council wants the price of Premium Motor Spirit — petrol — cut to ₦500 a litre. Pump prices currently range from about ₦1,450 to ₦2,500 a litre depending on the state, a spread the unions call unsustainable. To get there, they propose an intervention fund to cover landing costs, support for oil and gas operators, and the sale of crude to the Dangote refinery and modular refineries “at appropriate terms” to lift domestic refining and pull prices down.

Second, a wage award — an immediate, across-the-board payment to cushion what the council calls the harsh economic conditions facing workers, their dependants and vulnerable Nigerians. Third, the urgent constitution of a tripartite committee to negotiate a new national minimum wage of at least ₦500,000 a month, to take effect from 2027. The unions say the committee must be set up now to avoid administrative delays once a figure is agreed and passed into law by the National Assembly.

The current minimum wage of ₦70,000 a month was agreed in July 2024, up from ₦30,000, after the NLC and the Trade Union Congress argued that President Tinubu’s reforms — above all the 2023 fuel subsidy removal — were eroding pay. Since then the naira and prices have moved further against workers: on May Day 2026 the NLC was already demanding ₦154,000, and Ajaero has since added a national minimum pension to the movement’s platform, calling today’s arrangements “poverty wages”.

Why Abuja Has a Problem

Africa’s most populous nation is in what unions and critics alike describe as its worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation. The government has argued that subsidy removal and exchange-rate liberalisation were unavoidable and are beginning to stabilise the economy; the unions answer that stabilisation has not reached the payslip. A three-day strike by the public sector’s largest council would disrupt ministries, hospitals and agencies across the federation — and test the government’s room for manoeuvre ahead of the 2027 budget and wage round.

The council has left the door open: the strike triggers only if the government fails to act. Overnight concessions — a committee announcement, a wage award framework, or movement on the petrol interventions — could still avert it. For now, the unions say members are mobilised and the deadline has passed.

What We Could Not Confirm

Whether the strike will actually begin on Friday depends on last-minute talks we cannot verify. The government had not publicly responded to the 21 September letter at the time of publication. We could not confirm how many state-level workers will join, whether the NLC and TUC federations will formally extend the action beyond their backing, or the government’s estimate of the fiscal cost of the demands. Petrol price ranges cited by the unions vary by state and were not independently verified.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Nigeria’s public sector warning strike start?

The JNPSNC has called a three-day warning strike with effect from Friday, 2 October 2026, after the Federal Government let a 30 September deadline pass without addressing the unions’ demands. The action can still be averted if the government moves on the demands.

What are Nigerian unions demanding?

Three things: a cut in the petrol price to ₦500 a litre (from roughly ₦1,450–2,500 today), approval of a wage award for workers, and the immediate creation of a tripartite committee to negotiate a new national minimum wage of at least ₦500,000 a month from 2027.

Which unions are taking part in the warning strike?

The call comes from the Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council, which groups eight public sector unions including the Nigeria Civil Service Union, Medical and Health Workers Union, Association of Senior Civil Servants and the nurses’ and midwives’ association. The Nigeria Labour Congress has backed the demands.

ECONOMY · MEXICO

Key Facts — The country Mexico, Latin America’s second-largest economy and a major factory exporter to the United States.

— What happened The IMEF Manufacturing Indicator rose to 50.0 points in September 2026 from 49.9 in August, the neutral line, IMEF reported on 1 October.

— The numbers The non-manufacturing (services) gauge rose to 49.2 from 49.0, still below 50. The size-adjusted factory index slipped 0.6 points to 51.9 (IMEF, 1 Oct 2026).

— What it means for you Factory activity has stopped shrinking but is not yet growing. Firms selling into Mexico face flat demand rather than a new slump.

— Still open Whether public investment holds up after a 13% monthly drop in public construction spending in July, and how the USMCA trade review plays out.

Mexico PMI data from IMEF for September show the factory sector reaching the neutral line of 50.0 points, up from 49.9 in August. The figure comes from the IMEF Manufacturing Indicator, published on Thursday 1 October 2026.

IMEF, the Mexican Institute of Finance Executives, compiles its own PMI-style survey of purchasing managers. It is separate from S&P Global’s Mexico Manufacturing PMI.

The IMEF index runs from 0 to 100 points. A reading above 50 signals expansion, below 50 signals contraction.
