The institute called the picture “mixed signals”. Activity has stopped deteriorating as fast, but IMEF said there is not enough evidence to confirm a broad recovery.

Mexico PMI Reaches the Neutral Line

The headline factory index gained 0.1 points to 50.0 in September. IMEF said this came after a prolonged period in contraction territory.

The trend-cycle series, which strips out monthly noise, rose 0.3 points to 49.9. That suggests the contraction is losing intensity rather than reversing.

IMEF manufacturing and non-manufacturing indicators, August and September 2026 (50 = no change). Source: IMEF, 1 Oct 2026.

One measure moved the other way. The index adjusted for company size fell 0.6 points to 51.9, though it stays in expansion territory.

Services Stay Below 50

The IMEF Non-Manufacturing Indicator, which tracks services and commerce, rose 0.2 points to 49.2. It remains under the 50 threshold.

Its trend-cycle series fell 0.1 points to 49.0. The size-adjusted index dropped 1.2 points to 48.5, which IMEF read as wider weakness across firms.

What Is Driving the Mexico PMI

IMEF linked the slight improvement to two forces. Public investment in physical works rose between April and June, very probably because of the football World Cup.

The second force is exports of computer equipment. IMEF said these grew 200% through July, but most inputs come from Asia and local value added is low.

That makes the export boom an opportunity and a risk at once. The institute flagged the review of the USMCA, the North American trade agreement, as the main exposure.

Washington’s stance on that pact already shifted in September, as covered in USMCA Review Ends Without Renewal as Washington Starts 2036 Expiry Countdown.

Risks and Stabilisers

Public construction spending fell 13% from June to July, according to IMEF. If that marks a new squeeze on public works, growth could slow for the rest of the year.

Public finances are also under pressure from rigid spending, IMEF said. It warned that rising pension costs raise the chance of a sovereign credit rating cut.

On the stabilising side, IMEF said the Bank of Mexico is expected to hold its interest rate for the rest of the year. Inflation still carries upside risk, mainly from services.

The job market offers little extra support so far, as shown in Unemployment in Mexico Edges Up to 3%, With 55% of Workers Off the Books.

What Is Not Yet Known

One month at 50.0 does not establish a trend. The October Mexico PMI reading from IMEF, due in early November, will show whether factories move into expansion.

It is also unclear whether public investment recovers after July’s drop. IMEF noted the peso has weakened on expectations of tighter US monetary policy, which could narrow the carry trade.

Official industrial production data from INEGI, the national statistics institute, will test the survey signal over the coming weeks.

Sources: IMEF (Mexican Institute of Finance Executives), “Señales mixtas: Indicador IMEF”, IMEF News, 1 October 2026; El Economista, “La economía de México muestra señales mixtas: Indicadores IMEF”, 1 October 2026.

Africa Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 1 October 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

Ethiopia — Addis Ababa expels ten Eritrean diplomats, and Asmara answers by cutting every tie. Ethiopia — Blasts rattle the capital hours after a drone ban, and the army reports it is near Mekelle. Nigeria — Tinubu tells the nation the age of reform is over, with no inflation or reserves figure to show for it. Zimbabwe — A helicopter crash near Marondera kills six, among them the businessman Wicknell Chivayo. Mali — More than 2,400 schools cannot open as the new school year starts.

Africa’s temper this Thursday is a region holding its breath and finding it can no longer hold it. Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, explosions were heard in Addis Ababa, and hospital sources counted at least 52 civilians dead around Alamata, while Abuja declared an age of prosperity and Mali began a school year with more than 2,400 schools still closed.

The register is institutions failing at the edges while ceremonies continue at the centre. Embassies close, classrooms stay locked, a tycoon’s helicopter falls out of the evening sky near Marondera, and a jubilee in Botswana is overshadowed by what was served at it.

What steadies the continent is thinner than usual. Nigeria’s currency has held near 1,327 to the dollar, according to EODHD, Zambia’s IMF talks run to 10 October, and Ghana is preparing a cedi redesign for 3 November. These are the quiet routines of states that still plan ahead.

The through-line is a continent measuring distance: how close the war is to the capital, how far a promise is from a pay packet, how wide a gap sits between a slogan and a classroom. Africa this evening is a map being redrawn by the people who live on it.

Key Facts —The severed tie. Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said on 1 October it would close its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats out within 48 hours; Eritrea’s foreign ministry replied that it would sever all diplomatic ties, Reuters reported on 1 October. —The Addis blasts. Three diplomatic sources told Reuters on 1 October they heard explosions in Addis Ababa overnight; a source linked to the opposition alliance claimed several drone strikes, which Reuters could not verify, and an intelligence official told AP three blasts occurred in three places. —The drone ban. Ethiopia’s National Intelligence and Security Service banned all drone flights over Addis Ababa and its surroundings indefinitely from Wednesday 30 September, Reuters and AP reported on 1 October. —Alamata’s toll. Hospital sources told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed in three days of fighting around Alamata in Tigray, reported on 1 October; Médecins Sans Frontières said more than 700 wounded had reached hospitals it supports. —The front line. Africanews reported on 1 October that government troops were advancing north from Alamata toward Korem, about 100 kilometres south of Mekelle, with communications disrupted across Tigray. —Abuja’s verdict. President Bola Tinubu said in his 66th Independence Day broadcast on 1 October that Nigeria’s economy had grown by more than 4 per cent this year and that non-oil exports topped US$6 billion in 2025, Channels Television reported. —Marondera’s crash. Six people died when a helicopter carrying the businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife, Lucy Muteke, crashed near Marondera, east of Harare, on the evening of Wednesday 30 September; the Civil Aviation Authority said the cause was yet to be ascertained, Nehanda Radio and News24 reported on 1 October. —Mali’s empty classrooms. Africanews reported on 1 October that more than 2,400 Malian schools remain closed as the new school year begins; Education Cluster data to the end of April put it at 2,444 of 11,860 schools, affecting 733,200 children.

Addis And Asmara Cut The Last Thread

Ethiopia and Eritrea ended diplomatic relations on Thursday, 1 October. Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said it would close its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave within 48 hours, citing “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”, Reuters reported on 1 October.

Eritrea’s foreign ministry said it had “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties”, and accused Addis Ababa of three years of “incessant hostility” aimed at winning sovereign access to the sea, Reuters reported. Eritrea denies backing the opposition alliance that has fought federal forces since last week. Ethiopia’s embassy in Asmara had reopened in 2018 during the thaw that earned Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed the Nobel Peace Prize.

The register in the Horn is a door closing on the people who held the key. Embassies are where wars get negotiated before they get fought, and both capitals have now removed the room.

Blasts Reach Addis Ababa

Three diplomatic sources told Reuters on 1 October that they heard explosions overnight in the capital. A source linked to the opposition alliance said it had carried out several drone strikes, including some aimed at military headquarters. Reuters could not verify the claim, and witnesses saw no damage near the military base.

An intelligence service official told AP that three blasts occurred in three different locations, without giving details, and it remained unclear whether they were an attack or part of training exercises at the defence headquarters. The National Intelligence and Security Service had banned all drone flights over Addis Ababa and its surroundings, indefinitely, on Wednesday 30 September. The federal government and the military had not commented when Reuters filed.

The register in the capital is a city listening to the sky. If the drone claim is ever confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on Addis Ababa. Until then the unknown does the work, and the African Union, which sits in the same city, must plan around a risk nobody has proved.

Alamata Counts Its Dead

Hospital sources told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed in three days of heavy fighting around Alamata, in Tigray. A doctor at Alamata General Hospital said the dead included children and herders, and that 12 people died in one strike on the market. Government troops appear to have taken the town, the BBC reported on 1 October.

Médecins Sans Frontières said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted over recent days to hospitals it supports in Tigray. Communications are disrupted across Tigray, so every figure here comes with the warning that nobody outside can easily check it. Africanews reported that government troops were advancing north toward Korem, about 100 kilometres south of Mekelle.

The register in Alamata is arithmetic done in a hospital corridor. The toll is rising faster than the diplomacy. What could still stabilise the north is access: whoever lets aid convoys and cameras in first changes the story.

Abuja Declares An Age Of Prosperity

President Bola Tinubu told Nigerians on Thursday, 1 October, in his 66th Independence Day broadcast, that “the emergency treatment is over” and that “the age of reform has done its work”, as Channels Television and The Guardian Nigeria reported. He said the economy had grown by more than 4 per cent this year, oil theft was down and the foreign exchange market had stabilised. Non-oil exports exceeded US$6 billion in 2025, a record, he said.

The speech gave no figure for inflation, reserves or the naira, Channels reported. EODHD data show the naira at about 1,327 to the US dollar on 1 October, almost unchanged from 1,329 the day before. Tinubu also warned against “regressive voices” who want fuel subsidies back.

The register in Abuja is a government declaring the cure finished while patients still feel the treatment. The test of the phrase “age of prosperity” will be the price of food, not the price of oil. A steadier currency supports the claim; a household that stops believing it would undo it.

Marondera Mourns A Tycoon

A helicopter crashed on the evening of Wednesday 30 September at Kudenga Farm near Marondera, east of Harare, killing all six people aboard. They included the businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife, Lucy Muteke, family spokesman Herbert Chivayo confirmed, according to News24 and Nehanda Radio on 1 October.

Government spokesman Nick Mangwana said there were no survivors. George Mashababe, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe, said the cause was yet to be ascertained and that preliminary findings showed fuel spilled on impact and a fire followed, which does not explain why the aircraft came down, Nehanda Radio reported. No official cause has been given.

The register in Harare is a country that knew this man’s name and now waits for the facts.

Mali’s School Year Starts Without Classrooms

Mali’s school year began on Thursday, 1 October, with more than 2,400 schools still closed, Africanews reported. French-language coverage put the figure at 2,444 of the country’s 11,860 schools, more than one in five, directly affecting 733,200 children, citing the Education Cluster’s report of 24 June, which reflects data to the end of April 2026.

President Assimi Goïta has named the 2026-2027 academic year the “Year of Education and Culture”, the same coverage noted. About 1,300 schools were closed at the 2020 start of term and about 1,800 in 2024, so the number keeps climbing.

The register in Bamako is a slogan next to a locked door. What could steady it is a negotiated reopening in districts where armed groups allow it, though none has been announced.

Botswana’s Jubilee Feast Draws Fire

Botswana marked 60 years of independence on Wednesday 30 September amid criticism of a licence to kill 23 elephants and other wild animals for meat. The Ministry of Environment and Tourism licence, seen by local media, allocated the animals across eight districts, according to allAfrica and the BBC on 1 October. The government has not confirmed how many elephants were killed.

The Elephant Protection Society warned that celebratory killings could undermine conservation, its chairman Oaitse Nawa said. Botswana’s government defends regulated hunting as a way to manage conflict between people and wildlife in a country with more than 130,000 elephants; hunting resumed in 2019 after a five-year ban.

The register in Gaborone is pride and optics pulling in opposite directions, with a real argument on each side.

What This Means From Latin America

Ethiopia’s escalation is a question of sea lanes before it is a question of Africa. The dispute behind the severed tie is Addis Ababa’s demand for sovereign access to the sea, and a country of that size that is landlocked and at odds with its coastal neighbour makes Red Sea risk a permanent line in the insurance and freight models. Latin American importers of Asian goods and exporters of grain, soya and coffee to the Middle East pay part of that premium, even when no ship of theirs goes near Eritrea.

Brazil and Ethiopia sit in the same BRICS grouping. The quieter link is coffee: Ethiopia is one of the world’s great coffee origins, and in the desk’s reading a war that interrupts roads and ports in the Horn tends to lift the price that Brazilian growers can ask.

Tinubu’s “age of prosperity” speech rhymes with a Latin American habit: governments that finish a stabilisation declare victory long before households agree. The useful comparison is the lag between a steadier currency and recovering wages, and Nigeria is now in that gap.

The comparison is set out at greater length elsewhere. The dossier carries the leader, the country health check and the outcome table with its Latin America column — open the Africa Intelligence Dossier.

What We Are Watching

Next 48 hours: the diplomats’ departure — Ethiopia ordered the 10 Eritrean diplomats out within 48 hours. Whether the exits are orderly, and whether Asmara answers in kind on the ground, shows how far both sides want to escalate.

— Ethiopia ordered the 10 Eritrean diplomats out within 48 hours. Whether the exits are orderly, and whether Asmara answers in kind on the ground, shows how far both sides want to escalate. The coming days: Addis Ababa’s explanation — Neither the federal government nor the military had commented on the blasts when Reuters filed. An official account would settle whether this was an attack, an exercise or an accident.

— Neither the federal government nor the military had commented on the blasts when Reuters filed. An official account would settle whether this was an attack, an exercise or an accident. This week: the road to Korem and Mekelle — Africanews reported federal troops advancing north from Alamata toward Korem, about 100 kilometres south of the Tigrayan capital. How far they get will show whether a negotiated pause remains possible.

— Africanews reported federal troops advancing north from Alamata toward Korem, about 100 kilometres south of the Tigrayan capital. How far they get will show whether a negotiated pause remains possible. Through Saturday 10 October: Zambia’s IMF mission — The mission led by Edward Gemayel is in Lusaka to discuss a successor to the US$1.7 billion arrangement that expired in January. A staff statement usually follows the mission.

— The mission led by Edward Gemayel is in Lusaka to discuss a successor to the US$1.7 billion arrangement that expired in January. A staff statement usually follows the mission. Wednesday 14 October: the Malindi hearing — The Environment and Land Court in Malindi is due to hear the dispute over the Lamu refinery site, where a status-quo order is in force, IntelliNews reported on 29 September.

— The Environment and Land Court in Malindi is due to hear the dispute over the Lamu refinery site, where a status-quo order is in force, IntelliNews reported on 29 September. Tuesday 3 November: Ghana’s Heritage Series cedi — The Bank of Ghana will launch new Heritage Series notes from GH¢1 to GH¢200 (about US$17 at the EODHD rate of 11.70 cedis to the dollar) at Bank Square in Accra; current notes stay legal tender.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties?

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said on 1 October it was closing its embassy in Asmara and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats for activities it said threatened national security, citing “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”, Reuters reported. Eritrea replied that it would sever all diplomatic ties and denied backing the opposition alliance fighting federal forces.

What happened in Addis Ababa overnight?

Three diplomatic sources told Reuters on 1 October they heard explosions in the capital, hours after the intelligence service banned drone flights. A source linked to the opposition alliance claimed drone strikes, which Reuters could not verify. An official told AP there were three blasts but gave no cause.

How many civilians died in the fighting around Alamata?

Hospital sources told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed in three days of fighting around Alamata. Médecins Sans Frontières said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports. Communications are cut in Tigray, so the figures could not be independently checked.

What did Tinubu say in Nigeria’s Independence Day speech?

President Bola Tinubu said on 1 October that “the age of reform has done its work” and that economic growth had passed 4 per cent this year. He said non-oil exports exceeded US$6 billion in 2025. The speech gave no figures for inflation, reserves or the naira, Channels Television reported.

Asia Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 1 October 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

South Korea — The best export month on record, and a stock market far below its peak. Japan — Business mood at an eight-year high; the prime minister speaks on Monday. Taiwan — A navy vice admiral takes a coast guard post as Chinese patrols continue. India — Eight losing weeks in a row, the longest run in 25 years. Pakistan — A capital lined with containers waits for a march that starts on Sunday.

Asia’s temper this Thursday is a boom that does not quite trust itself. South Korea reported the biggest export month in its history, Japanese manufacturers reported their best mood since 2018, and India’s stock market still closed an eighth straight losing week.

The register is prosperity with a bill attached. The bill is oil near US$98 a barrel, a Korean border incident that Pyongyang refuses to own, and floods that closed Toyota plants in Thailand.

What steadies the region is the thing it makes. Chips and AI hardware lifted factory surveys in South Korea (53.9) and Taiwan (56.7), and President Lee Jae Myung used Armed Forces Day to offer the North talks rather than threats.

The through-line is concentration. Asia’s good news now rests on one global appetite for computing, and its bad news arrives from everywhere else: energy, weather, border mines and capital outflows.

Key Facts —Record month. South Korea’s exports rose 83.5% in September from a year earlier to a record US$120.9 billion, the trade ministry said on 1 October; imports of US$71.09 billion left a surplus of US$49.85 billion. —The chip engine. Semiconductor exports rose about 263% to US$60.3 billion, the first month above US$60 billion, according to the same ministry data reported by the Korea JoongAng Daily on 1 October. —The paradox. The Kospi closed at 6,971.35 on 1 October, up 1.95%, yet it sits 23.5% below its closing high of 9,114.55 on 22 June, according to EODHD data. —Factory surveys. S&P Global’s September PMIs read 53.9 in South Korea, 56.7 in Taiwan and 54.1 in Japan, where growth was the weakest in six months; Reuters reported on 1 October. —Tokyo’s mood. The Bank of Japan’s Tankan index for large manufacturers rose to +24 from +22 in June, the highest since March 2018; large non-manufacturers slipped to +35 from +37, on 1 October. —Seoul’s offer. President Lee Jae Myung said on 1 October that South Korea would pursue practical steps to reduce military tension with the North and build nuclear-powered submarines by the mid-2030s, Reuters and the Korea Herald reported. —India’s streak. The Nifty 50 and Sensex fell for an eighth straight week to 1 October, the longest losing run in 25 years, The Week reported; the rupee closed at 96.31 per US dollar, EODHD data show. —Thailand’s floods. The interior ministry counted at least 24 deaths and flooding in 44 of 77 provinces, Reuters reported on 1 October; the government spokesman cited 40 deaths from health ministry figures.

Seoul Posts Its Biggest Export Month Ever

South Korea’s exports reached US$120.9 billion in September, up 83.5% from a year earlier, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said on 1 October. The ministry’s data show semiconductors at US$60.3 billion, up about 263% and the first monthly figure above US$60 billion.

Shipments to China were US$26 billion, up 123%, and shipments to the United States US$24.33 billion, up 137%, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Imports rose 26% to US$71.09 billion, so the trade surplus came to a record US$49.85 billion.

The register in Seoul is triumph with an asterisk. The Kospi rose 1.95% to 6,971.35 on the day, its biggest gain since 18 September. Even so, it closed 23.5% below its 22 June peak, according to EODHD data. Record exports and a falling stock market can coexist when one product category dominates both the trade data and investors’ fears.

For readers outside Korea, the lesson is concentration. A single product category now explains most of September’s export growth, and the same demand cycle can end as quickly as it began.

Asia’s Factories Run On AI And Pay For Oil

Factory activity expanded across much of Asia in September, Reuters reported on 1 October, helped by global demand for AI hardware. S&P Global’s manufacturing index reached 53.9 in South Korea, its highest in four months, and 56.7 in Taiwan, up from 54.7 in August.

Japan’s reading slipped to 54.1 from 54.9, the weakest expansion in six months, while firms there raised selling prices at one of the sharpest rates since late 2022. India’s manufacturers posted their fastest growth in seven months. The Philippines and Malaysia contracted, while Indonesia and Vietnam grew.

The register is optimism that keeps one eye on the pump. Brent rose about 14% in September, Reuters reported, and the front-month December contract traded near US$98.15 a barrel in early Asian trade on 1 October as talks between Washington and Tehran stalled. Japanese firms and Indian manufacturers reported rising input costs.

This is a story of two Asias. The economies that sell chips are expanding, and the economies that mostly buy energy are paying for it.

Lee Offers Dialogue And Orders Submarines

President Lee Jae Myung used Armed Forces Day on 1 October to ask North Korea to return to “the path of restoring trust and resuming dialogue”, the Korea Herald reported. He said his government would pursue practical measures to reduce military tension between the two Koreas.

In the same speech, Lee said South Korea would build nuclear-powered submarines by the mid-2030s, upgrade missile defence with AI-based command systems and high-energy laser interceptors, and complete the transfer of wartime operational control from the United States during his term, Reuters reported.

The backdrop is the blast of 21 September, when mines in the demilitarised zone wounded three South Korean soldiers, the Korea Herald reported. The United Nations Command found an armistice violation. On 30 September Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader’s sister, rejected Seoul’s findings. No new North Korean statement had appeared in the reports reviewed by the desk by the evening of 1 October.

The register is firmness spoken softly. Seoul pairs an open door with a long procurement list, and, the Korea Herald reported, leaves its formal response to the incident open; Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said corresponding measures would follow if a full investigation confirmed responsibility.

Tokyo Reads The Tankan Between The Lines

The Bank of Japan’s quarterly Tankan survey on 1 October put the large-manufacturer index at +24, up from +22 in June but below the +25 economists expected. It is the highest reading since March 2018. Large non-manufacturers slipped to +35, their first fall in five quarters.

Companies expect inflation of 2.6% in three years and 2.5% in five, still above the bank’s 2% goal. The bank raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, the highest since 1995, with two board members dissenting. Its next meeting is on 29 and 30 October.

Markets liked the day more than the data. The Nikkei 225 rose 3.3% to 68,956.72, its highest close since 17 August, according to EODHD data. The yen stood near 158 per US dollar.

On Monday 5 October, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi opens an extraordinary Diet session with a policy speech. The Nikkei newspaper reported that she will promise a nimble response to unexpected market moves and set debt issuance with interest rates in mind. The register is a government that wants to sound calm about money.

Taipei Puts A Vice Admiral In Charge Of The Coast

On 1 October President Lai Ching-te promoted Vice Admiral Yuan Sheng-hua from deputy chief of staff of the navy to deputy director-general of the Coast Guard Administration, Focus Taiwan reported. He is the first active-duty navy officer in that post.

Lai said the navy and the coast guard must share maritime intelligence and keep command stable in every circumstance, Reuters reported. The Chinese coast guard has patrolled off Taiwan’s east coast since June and announced another patrol this week. Beijing calls it law enforcement in its “jurisdictional waters”, a claim Taipei rejects.

The wider quarrel runs on two tracks. On 29 September Beijing accused Taipei of “desecrating the martyrs” for questioning China’s account of the second world war, Reuters reported. Taipei’s reply is that the government that fought in that war was the Republic of China. Taiwan’s stock benchmark closed at 48,353.49 on 1 October, up 0.9%.

The register is quiet administration under pressure. In effect, Taipei answers grey-zone patrols with personnel decisions rather than slogans.

Mumbai Counts Eight Losing Weeks

India’s equity benchmarks fell for an eighth straight week to 1 October, the longest losing run in 25 years, according to The Week. The Nifty 50 closed at 22,421.95 on Thursday, down 0.88%, with markets shut on Friday 2 October for Gandhi Jayanti.

Foreign funds sold more than 360 billion rupees (about US$3.7 billion at 96.31 rupees per dollar, EODHD) of Indian shares in September, according to those reports. The rupee has slid past 96 to the dollar, which raises the cost of imported fuel.

The contrast with the factory floor is sharp. India’s manufacturing survey reached its fastest growth in seven months on 1 October, Reuters reported. The register in Mumbai is an economy that works while its market worries about how the world sees its currency.

Bangkok Dries Out, One Forecast Ahead

Thailand’s floods have killed at least 24 people, according to the interior ministry, and affected 44 of 77 provinces, Reuters reported on 1 October. The government spokesman put the toll at 40, citing the health ministry. Bangkok was declared a disaster zone after 320 millimetres of rain in three days.

Toyota suspended operations at four Thai facilities because parts could not be delivered. Thai Airways stopped taking cargo from 30 September until 6 October. Authorities hope to return the capital to normal in two or three days, though the weather agency forecasts more heavy rain from 5 to 8 October.

The register is recovery with a forecast hanging over it. Thailand’s car and cargo industries have shown how one storm can interrupt supply chains that reach customers on other continents.

Islamabad Lines Its Roads Before The March

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi confirmed that the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) long march will leave Peshawar on Sunday 4 October, a week later than first planned, Tribune reported. The party wants jailed former prime minister Imran Khan released. Khan’s birthday on 5 October will be marked in Swabi.

On 1 October PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan said the party accepted the government’s offer of talks before the march, Geo News reported. The federal government has placed shipping containers along main roads in Islamabad, Tribune reported, and Gohar warned against imposing governor’s rule in the province.

The register is negotiation with a deadline. Each side talks while preparing for the day it may not need to.

What This Means From Latin America

Korea’s chip boom is likely a demand signal for the hemisphere’s industrial metals and for electronics assembly in Mexico. Presidents Lee Jae Myung and Claudia Sheinbaum signed 17 cooperation documents in Mexico City on Thursday 24 September, including a supply-chain dialogue, but no tariff deal, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported (Mexico South Korea Summit Ends With 17 Agreements but No Tariff Deal). The AI cycle that fills Korean order books is the same one that decides how much Latin America can sell upstream.

Oil near US$98 is a split verdict. It lifts fuel import bills in energy-poor Central America and the Caribbean and helps oil exporters such as Brazil, Colombia and Guyana. Asian factories report rising input costs, which will reach Latin American buyers of Asian goods with a delay.

India’s rupee at 96 per dollar and eight weeks of foreign selling are a reminder that emerging markets share one funding environment. Latin American finance ministries watch the same US yields and the same oil price, and capital that leaves Mumbai can as easily leave São Paulo.

The comparison is set out at greater length elsewhere. The dossier carries the leader, the country health check and the outcome table with its Latin America column. Open the Asia Intelligence Dossier.

What We Are Watching

2 to 4 October: PTI talks and the march — The government and PTI were due to talk before the march leaves Peshawar on Sunday 4 October; a failed round raises the chance of emergency rule in the province.

— The government and PTI were due to talk before the march leaves Peshawar on Sunday 4 October; a failed round raises the chance of emergency rule in the province. The coming days: Seoul’s answer to Kim Yo Jong — Lee has offered talks, but Pyongyang has rejected the mine findings; any new border activity tests both positions.

— Lee has offered talks, but Pyongyang has rejected the mine findings; any new border activity tests both positions. 5 October: Takaichi’s policy speech — The Diet session opens in Tokyo; question time in both chambers follows from 7 to 9 October.

— The Diet session opens in Tokyo; question time in both chambers follows from 7 to 9 October. 5 to 8 October: more rain for Thailand — The weather agency forecasts further heavy rain just as Bangkok drains its floodwater.

— The weather agency forecasts further heavy rain just as Bangkok drains its floodwater. Week to 9 October: India’s ninth week — Markets reopen on Monday 5 October after Gandhi Jayanti; a rebound would end the longest losing streak in 25 years.

— Markets reopen on Monday 5 October after Gandhi Jayanti; a rebound would end the longest losing streak in 25 years. 29 and 30 October: the Bank of Japan — The Tankan and the September meeting summary keep both an October and a December rate rise open.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big were South Korea’s exports in September 2026?

The trade ministry said on 1 October that exports rose 83.5% from a year earlier to a record US$120.9 billion. Semiconductor exports reached about US$60.3 billion, and the trade surplus was US$49.85 billion.

What did Lee Jae Myung say to North Korea on Armed Forces Day?

On 1 October he urged the North to join Seoul on the path of restoring trust and resuming dialogue, and said his government would pursue practical measures to reduce military tension. He also said South Korea would build nuclear-powered submarines by the mid-2030s.

Why did the Bank of Japan’s Tankan matter on 1 October?

The index for large manufacturers rose to +24, the highest since March 2018, though below the +25 forecast. Firms expect inflation of 2.6% in three years, which keeps the case for further rate rises open before the bank meets on 29 and 30 October.

Why are India’s stocks falling while its factories grow?

Indian markets fell for an eighth straight week, the longest run in 25 years, as foreign investors sold shares, oil stayed high and the rupee passed 96 per US dollar. Reuters reported on 1 October that manufacturing grew at its fastest pace in seven months.

Europe Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 1 October 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

Ukraine — Two drones hit a Kyiv bridge for the first time, and the war reaches a nuclear institute’s grounds. United Kingdom — Gilts touch 6 per cent, and the prime minister raises rejoining the EU. France — A budget of savings arrives with the highest borrowing cost since 2002. Germany — Inflation climbs to 3.3 per cent, the highest since December 2023. Poland — Looser air-defence rules start today, and the border checks stay until March.

Europe’s temper this Thursday is a balance sheet read aloud. Bond yields, a French budget, a German price print and a British prime minister’s sentence about 2016 all arrived within hours of each other, while Russian drones reached a Kyiv bridge at midday.

The register is the rising price of time. Governments pay more to borrow it, with the UK 30-year gilt yield touching 6 per cent and France’s 10-year yield at its highest since 2002. They also give themselves less of it to decide, as Poland lets pilots engage a target without seeing it.

What steadies the continent is calendar discipline. Serbia votes on 25 October, the European Central Bank meets on 29 October, and the European Council gathers on 15 and 16 October. Eurozone factories, by the HCOB final survey, kept expanding in September.

The through-line is that Europe is paying more for the future and being given less notice about it. Every file today, from the Kyiv bridge to the French deficit, is a decision about who carries a cost and how soon.

Key Facts —The bridge. Two Russian drones hit near a support of Kyiv’s Southern Bridge at about 11:30 local time on 1 October as a metro train crossed, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, and the Kyiv Independent reported it as the first strike on a bridge in the capital. —The reactor site. A drone struck the grounds of Kyiv’s Institute for Nuclear Research at about 6:18 pm on 30 September, starting a fire without injuries, Ukraine’s nuclear regulator said on 1 October; its research reactor has been shut down since February 2022. —Poland’s air rules. New rules took effect on 1 October that let pilots engage on radar data, entry into a no-fly zone or Ukrainian information instead of visual identification, according to Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk, who announced them on 28 September. —Poland’s gates. The Interior Ministry extended controls on the German and Lithuanian borders to 30 March 2027, Reuters reported on 1 October, citing nearly 1,300 entries denied at the Lithuanian border and nearly 1,200 at the German one since July 2025. —Germany’s print. Destatis’s flash estimate on 30 September put September inflation at 3.3 per cent, up from 2.9 in August and the highest since December 2023, with energy prices 14.9 per cent above a year earlier and core inflation at 2.4 per cent. —The yield rout. The UK 30-year gilt yield touched 6 per cent on 1 October for the first time since 1998, Reuters reported; France’s 10-year yield reached 4.94 per cent, its highest since 2002, Euronews reported the same day. —Paris’s budget. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s 2027 budget targets a deficit of 5 per cent of GDP, down from 5.4 per cent expected this year, through a €54 billion (about US$61 billion) effort, Euronews reported on 1 October. —Britain’s sentence. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC’s Today programme on 30 September that he wants Britain to rejoin the EU “in my lifetime”, while stressing that it is not necessarily the next step, Yeni Şafak reported.

Kyiv’s Bridge Joins The Target List

Two Russian drones hit near a support structure of the Southern Bridge in Kyiv at about 11:30 local time on Thursday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. Cars and a metro train were crossing, and public transport over the bridge was halted. The Kyiv Independent reported it as the first time Russian drones had targeted one of the capital’s bridges.

The night before, at about 6:18 pm on 30 September, a drone hit the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv, Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said. A fire was put out quickly and nobody was hurt. The research reactor has been shut down since February 2022, its core unloaded, and radiation stayed at 0.16 to 0.20 microsieverts per hour, within the normal background range.

The register in Kyiv is a city counting what it still relies on. A bridge, a school hit earlier the same day, according to Ukrinform, and a nuclear campus show targets moving from the grid to the fabric of daily life. Odesa had its own morning: Russia hit a business centre and one person was injured, regional officials said, while the head of the city’s military administration, Serhiy Lysak, said infrastructure was damaged.

What steadies Kyiv is that the metro kept running on its underground sections and the reactor was inert. What could tip it is repetition: a bridge is a repair job once, and a pattern the second time.

Warsaw Loosens Its Trigger And Keeps Its Gates

Poland’s new air-defence rules took effect on 1 October. Pilots and commanders may now act on “positive verification”, such as a radar reading, an object entering a no-fly zone or information from Ukraine, rather than first seeing the target. Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced the change on 28 September, and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the army had the procedures ready; no new law was needed.

On the ground, the Interior Ministry extended controls on the German and Lithuanian borders from 2 October to 30 March 2027, Reuters reported on 1 October. The checks began on 7 July 2025. The ministry said they have denied entry to nearly 1,300 people at the Lithuanian border and nearly 1,200 at the German one.

The register in Warsaw is a frontline state tightening both of its edges. One decision shortens the time to shoot, the other keeps the Schengen gates half closed. Neither is an escalation in itself, but together they say Poland expects the next incident to arrive faster than a committee can meet.

London Watches Gilts Touch Six Per Cent

The UK 30-year gilt yield touched 6 per cent on Thursday for the first time since 1998, peaking at 6.029 per cent, Reuters reported, and the 10-year yield reached 5.51 per cent, the highest since July 2007. The FTSE 100 fell 1.7 per cent to 10,428, and sterling stood at about US$1.33 (EODHD). The new finance minister, John Healey, delivers his first Budget later this month.

The Bank of England held its rate at 3.75 per cent on 17 September on a 6–3 vote, and Reuters said markets price close to an 80 per cent chance of a rise to 4 per cent on 5 November. Reuters pointed to the Iran war, higher US yields and Britain’s borrowing needs, though no single cause is confirmed.

The register in London is the arithmetic of a long-dated promise. When a government pays 6 per cent for 30 years, every pledge in the next Budget is priced against it. Britain holds about 42 days of diesel in reserve, according to a UK press report, and took part in Thursday’s fuel call.

London Opens The Door It Closed In 2016

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC’s Today programme on 30 September that he wants Britain to rejoin the EU “in my lifetime”, Yeni Şafak reported. He listed options from the status quo to a customs union, the single market or full membership.

In Madrid the same day, Emmanuel Macron called it “excellent news” and Pedro Sánchez said “we would open our arms”, Reuters reported. Both also asked Brussels for flexibility on the EU budget before October’s negotiations, with Sánchez asking for “a little more empathy” for governments facing voters.

The register is cautious welcome. Burnham did not announce an application, and a rejoin vote is not on the calendar. What could tip it is the market: a government paying 6 per cent will find it hard to promise anything expensive to Brussels.

Paris Presents A Budget Of Savings

The government presented the 2027 budget on Thursday with a deficit target of 5 per cent of GDP, against 5.4 per cent expected this year. The effort totals €54 billion (about US$61 billion), of which €43 billion (about US$48 billion) comes from new measures, Euronews reported. It includes a public-sector pay freeze, limits on pension indexation and changes to state-funded sick leave. The conversion uses EUR/USD of 1.124 (EODHD, 1 October).

France’s public debt is forecast at 119.3 per cent of GDP in 2026 and 121.7 per cent in 2027, and its 10-year yield reached 4.94 per cent on Thursday, the highest since 2002. Public-sector unions struck on Tuesday 29 September against the pay freeze. The finance bill must go to the National Assembly by 6 October.

The register in Paris is austerity in a fragmented house. Without a clear majority, Lecornu faces a 70-day constitutional window for debate, and the Socialists have already called the plan a “bitter austerity potion”. Background: How France Lost the Ability to Pass a Budget.

Berlin Posts Its Highest Inflation Since December 2023

Destatis reported on 30 September that inflation rose to 3.3 per cent in September from 2.9 in August, the highest since December 2023, when it stood at 3.7. Energy prices were 14.9 per cent higher than a year earlier, against 10.5 per cent in August. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, held at 2.4 per cent.

The first read is that this is an energy story and not yet a wage story, because core did not move. The second is that Europe’s largest economy has crossed 3 per cent just as the euro area flash estimate is due on Friday 2 October, with economists polled by market-data services looking for 3.6 per cent.

The register in Berlin is a factory floor with a price tag. The HCOB final manufacturing survey for the euro area came in at 52.9 for September, above the 52.7 flash reading, with output and new orders growing at their fastest since early 2022. Orders are strong, and so are costs. The European Central Bank raised rates by 25 basis points on 11 June and again on 10 September, and meets next on 29 October.

Brussels Phones About Diesel

The European Commission, Britain, France, Italy and Ireland held a call on Thursday about whether emergency diesel stocks should be released, Reuters reported, citing an EU official. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said European countries “are sitting on reserves of diesel” and that European prices are higher than American ones.

Reuters also reported that the Trump administration told France and Germany to release stocks or risk a US diesel export ban. Greer did not confirm that. An Élysée official said Macron plans to call a G7 video summit on fuel costs, according to market reports.

The register in Brussels is a dilemma managed by telephone. Releasing stocks eases prices now and leaves less in the tank if the Iran talks fail. No decision had been announced when this brief was compiled on Thursday, and the volumes under discussion were not confirmed.

Belgrade Campaigns Without A President

Aleksandar Vučić resigned as Serbia’s president on Sunday 27 September to lead the Progressive Party’s list in the snap parliamentary election on 25 October. Parliament speaker Ana Brnabić is acting president, and a presidential election must follow within three months.

The main challenger is the Student List, led by the Novi Sad cardiologist Ilija Srdanović and backed by several opposition parties. The movement grew out of protests after the 1 November 2024 collapse of the Novi Sad station canopy, which killed 16 people. N1 hosted a televised debate between party representatives on Thursday.

The register in Belgrade is a ruler testing whether he can win a mandate he no longer needs by office. Vučić told CNN he would congratulate an opposition winner on election night. What could tip the contest is turnout, because the polls disagree on who leads.

What This Means From Latin America

In the desk’s view, Europe’s bond rout reaches Latin America through the borrowing calendar. When UK and French long yields rise together, the benchmark that Latin American Eurobond issuers price against can move too, and the 29 October ECB decision is the next date to watch.

The diesel call is the closest link to the hemisphere. In the desk’s view, Latin America competes with Europe for refined fuel, and a coordinated stock release would lower global diesel prices at the margin. A refusal would leave the competition for cargoes intact, a point worth watching for the region’s fuel importers.

Britain’s rejoin debate and the Madrid summit matter to Latin American diplomacy in a quieter way. In the desk’s view, Spain and France are among the region’s main EU voices, and both are asking Brussels for budget flexibility, which affects how much room remains for trade and development finance.

The comparison is set out at greater length elsewhere. The dossier carries the leader, the country health check and the outcome table with its Latin America column — open the Europe Intelligence Dossier.

What We Are Watching

Friday 2 October: euro area inflation flash — Eurostat’s first September reading follows Germany’s 3.3 per cent; polled economists look for 3.6.

— Eurostat’s first September reading follows Germany’s 3.3 per cent; polled economists look for 3.6. Tuesday 6 October: France’s finance bill deadline — Lecornu must lodge the 2027 budget with the National Assembly.

— Lecornu must lodge the 2027 budget with the National Assembly. 15 and 16 October: the European Council — Leaders meet with the EU budget talks on the agenda.

— Leaders meet with the EU budget talks on the agenda. Sunday 25 October: Serbia’s parliamentary election — The first verdict on the post-protest order, with a presidential vote to follow.

— The first verdict on the post-protest order, with a presidential vote to follow. Thursday 29 October: the ECB decision — The next rate decision, after hikes in June and September.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did UK gilt yields hit 6 per cent?

The 30-year gilt yield touched 6 per cent on 1 October for the first time since 1998, Reuters reported, citing the Iran war, higher US yields and Britain’s borrowing needs. The Bank of England held its rate at 3.75 per cent on 17 September, and markets price a likely rise on 5 November.

What changed in Poland’s air-defence rules?

From 1 October, Polish pilots and commanders can engage an unidentified air target on “positive verification”, such as radar data, entry into a no-fly zone or information from Ukraine, instead of visual identification, according to Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk. The change is made at army level and needs no new law.

How high is German inflation?

Destatis’s flash estimate put German inflation at 3.3 per cent in September, up from 2.9 per cent in August and the highest since December 2023. Energy prices were 14.9 per cent above a year earlier, and core inflation was 2.4 per cent.

What is France’s 2027 budget aiming for?

The government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu targets a deficit of 5 per cent of GDP in 2027, down from 5.4 per cent expected in 2026, through a €54 billion (about US$61 billion) effort, Euronews reported on 1 October. The finance bill is due at the National Assembly by 6 October.

USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 1 October 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

Washington — Yields at a 24-year high, seven states in court, a carrier heading east. The bond market — The 10-year Treasury touched 5.34 per cent, a level not seen since 2002. Ottawa — Pacific Link becomes the first national-interest project, with talks with Washington still suspended. Quebec — Four days out, with the sovereigntist Parti Québécois in front. Alberta — Eighteen days from a ballot question about holding a referendum.

North America’s temper this Thursday is long-term commitment under short-term strain. Ottawa named its first national-interest project, the Treasury market priced the highest borrowing costs since 2002, and seven states went to court over money Congress had already voted.

The register in Washington is confrontation by instrument: a lawsuit, a carrier group. In Ottawa it is construction as policy, with a pipeline to tidewater, a trade minister in Milwaukee and formal talks with Washington still suspended.

What steadies the continent is institutions that keep their calendars. The courts will hear the states, the Federal Reserve meets on 27 and 28 October, and Quebec votes on Monday 5 October as scheduled.

The through-line is the price of the long term. A pipeline, a Treasury bond and a constitutional spending rule all promise decades of stability, and each was repriced, litigated or contested within the same twenty-four hours.

Key Facts —The 24-year high. The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.342 per cent on Thursday 1 October, its highest since 2002 and above its 2007 peak, Reuters reported; EODHD records a close of 5.34 per cent. —The long end. The 30-year yield stood at about 5.67 per cent on 1 October, its highest since 2002, CNN reported. —The PCE print. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on 30 September that August PCE prices rose 3.4 per cent from a year earlier and core PCE 3.0 per cent, in line with the revised July rate, with core flat on the revised series. —Williams’ line. New York Fed President John Williams said on 29 September that after the September increase there was no need for urgency, Reuters reported; the Fed’s range is 3.75 to 4.00 per cent. —The lawsuit. California and six other states sued in the Northern District of California on 1 October over about US$810 million in funds the White House moved to cancel, Reuters reported. —Pacific Link. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Danielle Smith announced in Fort McMurray on 1 October that the pipeline is the first project of national interest under the Building Canada Act, CBC reported. —Quebec’s lead. The Parti Québécois leads with 30 per cent to the Liberals’ 26 in the latest Léger poll, and Qc125 projects 67 seats against the 64 needed for a majority; the vote is Monday 5 October. —The oil jump. Brent settled at US$102.31 a barrel on 1 October, up 4.4 per cent, and WTI at US$92.87, CNBC reported after the Wall Street Journal reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt is heading to the Middle East.

Washington Borrows At A 24-Year Peak

The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.342 per cent on Thursday, its highest since 2002 and above the 2007 peak, Reuters reported. The yield is the interest rate the US government pays to borrow for ten years, and it anchors mortgages, corporate loans and emerging-market borrowing costs. EODHD records the close at 5.34 per cent, and the 30-year yield stood at about 5.67 per cent.

Reuters added that the benchmark posted its biggest quarterly rise this century in the third quarter. Equities looked past it: EODHD shows the S&P 500 closing up 0.30 per cent at 7,674.27 and the Dow up 0.04 per cent at 50,928.61.

The register is a market that has stopped waiting for permission. Stocks are steady, but a bond that pays more than at any point in 24 years is a verdict on debt, inflation and a war that has lifted fuel prices.

The Fed Lowers Its Voice, The Curve Does Not

John Williams, president of the New York Fed, said on 29 September at the University at Buffalo that there was no need for urgency after the September increase, Reuters reported. The Fed raised its range by a quarter point to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent on 16 September. Traders trimmed their bets on a hike at the 27 and 28 October meeting, according to Reuters.

The inflation data met the revised July rate. The BEA reported on 30 September that August PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, was 3.4 per cent a year and core PCE 3.0 per cent, in line with the revised July rate, below the 3.7 per cent forecast and flat on the revised series for core. CNN reported that the BEA changed how it measures some prices, so the softer reading is partly arithmetic.

Friday’s September jobs report is the next test. The register at the Fed is patience with an audit attached: officials can pause, but the bond market is not obliged to follow.

Fort McMurray Names A Pipeline To Tidewater

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced on Thursday in Fort McMurray that the West Coast oil pipeline is a project of national interest, CBC reported. It is the first project designated under the Building Canada Act. The project is called Pacific Link and would carry about one million barrels a day from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia, according to Global News.

Trans Mountain Corporation, the federal Crown company that already runs a pipeline to the coast, and the Alberta government would hold equal ownership, and Pembina Pipeline Corporation has expressed interest as a private investor, reports said. The aim is to complete consultations, safeguards, financing and Indigenous partnerships by 1 September 2027, according to the Boe Report.

Politically, the pipeline is Ottawa’s answer to a trade dispute in which Canada suspended talks with Washington: it widens routes to Asia.

The same logic runs through Milwaukee, where G20 trade ministers met for two days. Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a pull-aside conversation on Wednesday, and the Globe and Mail reported no visible effect on the stalled talks. Sidhu also met France, Australia and Türkiye on Wednesday, with India, the EU and Brazil scheduled for Thursday. Canada suspended formal talks with Washington on 21 August, and the US import bans took effect on 29 September.

Seven States Take A Pocket Rescission To Court

California and six other states sued the Trump administration on Thursday in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, Reuters reported. They say the White House unlawfully withheld about US$810 million that Congress had appropriated for immigration, race and education programmes. The other plaintiffs are Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico and Oregon.

A pocket rescission is a request to cancel funding sent so close to the end of the fiscal year, 30 September, that the money expires before Congress can vote. The states argue that this breaches the separation of powers and the Constitution’s appropriations and presentment clauses. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said, “Just because the President doesn’t like a program doesn’t mean he can defund it.”

The register is a constitutional argument dressed as a budget line: who holds the purse, and what a vote by Congress is worth once the fiscal year ends. No hearing date has been published in the reports we have seen.

Quebec Votes Monday With The Sovereigntists In Front

Quebec votes on Monday 5 October, and the Parti Québécois, which wants a third sovereignty referendum, leads. Léger put the party at 30 per cent against 26 per cent for the Liberals, and the Qc125 projection gives it 67 seats against the 64 needed for a majority, Global News reported. The governing Coalition Avenir Québec, with 79 seats at dissolution, is in steep decline.

Party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised a referendum in a first term. The trade war is the campaign’s unspoken subject.

Alberta pulls the other way. Its 19 October ballot asks voters whether to remain a province or start the legal process toward a binding separation referendum. The register in Canada is a federation being asked, in two provinces within a fortnight, how much it still wants to hold together.

Oil Jumps As A Carrier Heads East

Brent crude settled at US$102.31 a barrel on Thursday, up 4.4 per cent, and US benchmark WTI at US$92.87, CNBC and Bloomberg reported. The move followed a Wall Street Journal report that the USS Theodore Roosevelt will reach the region by the end of November, with Marine ships carrying up to 10,000 more troops. CNBC reported that the Roosevelt is expected to relieve a carrier already there.

Donald Trump told TIME that US military action against Iran could resume after the 3 November midterms if no agreement is reached, and that Iran’s latest offer, to reopen only “some aspects” of the Strait of Hormuz, was not good enough.

The register is bargaining under a deadline the president himself has named. For Canada, higher oil prices raise the value of Pacific Link on the same day it was approved; for Washington, they feed the inflation that Fed officials are trying to talk down.

What This Means From Latin America

The yield is Latin America’s financing weather. A 10-year Treasury at 5.34 per cent raises the benchmark against which Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and every dollar bond issuer from Chile to the Caribbean is priced. If the Fed pauses while the curve rises, governments get no relief from policy and a full penalty from the market.

Oil is the region’s split screen. With Brent above US$100, exporters such as Brazil, Colombia and Guyana gain revenue, while importers across Central America and the Caribbean pay more for fuel. Pacific Link would add about a million barrels a day of Canadian crude aimed at Asia, a competitor for the same buyers, though no in-service date has been published and the project is years from steel.

Canada’s search for new markets reaches the hemisphere. Sidhu’s priorities include talks with the Mercosur bloc, according to Canadian Press, and every Canadian dollar diverted from the United States is a negotiating opportunity for Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. The states’ lawsuit matters to Mexico and Central America because the disputed funds include immigration programmes.

The comparison is set out at greater length elsewhere. The dossier carries the leader, the country health check and the outcome table with its Latin America column: open the USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier.

What We Are Watching

Friday, 2 October: the September jobs report — The next hard data on whether the economy can carry a 5.3 per cent ten-year yield.

— The next hard data on whether the economy can carry a 5.3 per cent ten-year yield. Monday, 5 October: Quebec votes — A Parti Québécois majority would put a sovereignty referendum on the national agenda.

— A Parti Québécois majority would put a sovereignty referendum on the national agenda. Monday, 19 October: Alberta votes — The question asks whether to start a legal process toward a binding separation referendum.

— The question asks whether to start a legal process toward a binding separation referendum. 27 and 28 October: the Fed meets — Williams has said there is no need for urgency; the curve has not agreed.

— Williams has said there is no need for urgency; the curve has not agreed. Tuesday, 3 November: US midterms — The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump expects bombing to resume in November.

— The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump expects bombing to resume in November. Coming weeks: the states’ case — The first hearing date in the Northern District of California is not yet published.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.34 per cent mean?

It is the annual interest the US government pays to borrow for ten years, and it reached 5.342 per cent on 1 October, the highest since 2002, Reuters reported. It sets the baseline for mortgages and corporate loans and raises borrowing costs for emerging markets.

What is Pacific Link?

It is the name of the West Coast oil pipeline that Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Danielle Smith named a project of national interest on 1 October, CBC reported. It would run from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deepwater port near Delta, British Columbia, carrying about one million barrels a day, according to Global News.

What is a pocket rescission?

It is a request to cancel funding made so late in the fiscal year that the money expires before Congress can vote. California and six other states sued on 1 October over about US$810 million that they say was withheld this way, Reuters reported.

When does Quebec vote and who is leading?

Quebec votes on Monday 5 October. The Parti Québécois led with 30 per cent to the Liberals’ 26 per cent in the latest Léger poll, Global News reported.

World.content:

Africa feels strained and short-tempered today, as leaders promise order and repair while citizens count what fuel, pay and conflict are costing them.

Source: RT live market data (RT), Thursday 1 October 2026; currency pairs are late-session quotes, and a rise means a weaker local currency. MASI official Casablanca Stock Exchange close; NASI official Nairobi Securities Exchange statistics. NGX All-Share shows the Wednesday 30 September close; the exchange was shut for Independence Day.

The Continent’s Mood Today

The pulse of Africa on the first day of October is strained. Ethiopia and Eritrea broke off diplomatic relations, Nigerian unions answered an upbeat Independence Day speech with a strike call, and Zambians woke up to fuel about 24% dearer.

Governments spoke the language of order and repair. Abuja promised prosperity, Algiers voted to bring back executions and Rabat is still building a coalition around Morocco’s first woman head of government.

The mood is not panic, but impatience. Across the continent people are adding up what the day costs them, while their leaders ask for more time.

North Africa – Order First

Algeria chose the hard line. On Thursday the National People’s Assembly, the lower house, adopted a Penal Code reform that allows death sentences to be carried out again for deliberate arson, for sabotage linked to treason or organised crime, and for child abduction.

The reform follows deadly forest fires at the end of August. The Council of the Nation, the upper house, must still approve it. Algeria has not carried out an execution since 1993, although the death penalty stayed in the code.

Morocco is in a different mood: cautious hope. King Mohammed VI named Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) head of government on Tuesday, the first woman in the post. Her party won 97 of 395 seats, so she needs partners to reach the 198 required for a majority.

In practice, a foreigner doing business in North Africa should expect governments to put security and political control first in the weeks ahead.

West Africa – Sixty-Six and Impatient

Nigeria marked 66 years of independence with a public holiday. In his broadcast, President Bola Tinubu argued that the hardest phase of his reforms is behind the country. “The emergency treatment is over,” he said, and named the cost of living as his next priority.

Labour had already set out a darker reading. In a statement on Wednesday, the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) warned of “a full-scale survival crisis”, with petrol at ₦1,430 a litre or more in major cities, about US$1.08 at Thursday’s rate.

Hours later the Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council (JNPSNC), which groups eight public-sector unions, called a three-day nationwide warning strike from Friday 2 to Sunday 4 October. Its secretary, Olowoyo Gbenga, said the speech ignored their demands on petrol prices, a wage award and new minimum-wage talks.

In practice, anyone who needs a Nigerian government office, permit or hospital service should expect disruption from Friday, and markets reopen the same day.

East Africa – A Border Turns Cold

The Horn of Africa had the darkest day. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it would close its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, giving them 48 hours to leave.

Eritrea replied within hours. Its foreign ministry said it had “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing the armed opposition fighting in northern Ethiopia since last week, which Eritrea denies.

Fear has reached the capital. Blasts were heard in Addis Ababa on Wednesday night, hours after the security services banned drone flights over the city. The cause was not clear.

Elsewhere the region is busy with rules and prices. In Kenya, annual inflation rose to 6.8% in September, the highest since January 2024, the statistics bureau said on Wednesday.

In practice, travellers to northern Ethiopia or the Eritrean border should follow their embassy’s advice closely, and expect consular services between the two countries to stop.

Central Africa – An Anniversary With Old Wounds

Cameroon marked the 65th anniversary of reunification on Thursday. On 1 October 1961 the British-administered Southern Cameroons joined the French-speaking republic.

The date is sensitive. Separatist fighting in the two English-speaking regions, the Northwest and Southwest, has not ended. The mood is sombre and inward-looking rather than festive.

In practice, a foreigner planning road travel in Cameroon’s Northwest and Southwest regions should still check local security advice first.

Southern Africa – Grief at the Top, Pain at the Pump

Zimbabwe is in shock. Businessman Wicknell Chivayo, a contractor close to the ruling elite, died with his wife when their helicopter crashed near Marondera on Wednesday afternoon. President Emmerson Mnangagwa said the nation was left “numbed and in deep shock and grief”.

Zambia feels the cost. The Energy Regulation Board raised petrol from K25.29 to K31.46 a litre and diesel from K26.86 to K33.27 after a six-month tax relief ended. That is a rise of about 24%, taking a litre of petrol to about US$1.60 at Thursday’s rate of 19.62 kwacha per dollar.

South Africa has reasons to smile. Bafana Bafana beat Eritrea 5–0 in Cairo on Wednesday in a qualifier for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations. Factories also returned to growth, with the Absa purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rising to 50.7 in September; any reading above 50 signals expansion.

In practice, a visitor driving in Zambia this month should budget for fuel about a quarter dearer than in September, with value-added tax due back on fuel on 1 December.

Thursday’s Data, One by One

Markets, briefly: Egypt’s EGX30 rose 2.24% to 53,055.03 after nine losing sessions; Johannesburg’s Satrix 40 Top 40 tracker fell 0.98% as the rand weakened 1.5% to about 16.67 per US dollar; Nairobi’s NASI rose 0.50%; Casablanca’s MASI fell 0.87%. The Nigerian Exchange was closed. Our evening Africa market wraps for Egypt, South Africa, Kenya and Morocco carry the detail.

South Africa, Absa PMI (September): 50.7, up from 45.8 in August (Absa). New vehicle sales (September): 61,645 units, up 12.7% year on year; exports down 18.8% (naamsa).

Zambia, fuel prices (October): petrol K31.46, diesel K33.27 a litre (Energy Regulation Board). Kenya, inflation (September): 6.8% year on year (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics).

Friday: the Nigerian Exchange reopens and the JNPSNC warning strike begins.

The Shared Mood

The shared mood is impatience under official optimism. From Abuja to Lusaka, governments ask citizens to trust reforms whose bills arrive first, while Algiers and Addis Ababa answer pressure with a harder line.

The through-line is the gap between the promise of stability and the cost of getting there. What steadies the picture is South Africa’s factory rebound and Cairo’s market relief; what could tip it is a wider war in the Horn of Africa.

For a foreigner living or working in Africa, the practical read is simple: watch fuel prices and union calendars as closely as the headlines. Friday’s strike in Nigeria is the next test.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened between Ethiopia and Eritrea on 1 October 2026?

Ethiopia said it would close its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats with 48 hours to leave. Eritrea then said it would sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia.

Why are Nigerian public servants going on strike?

The JNPSNC says President Tinubu’s Independence Day speech ignored its demands on petrol prices, a wage award and new minimum-wage talks. The warning strike runs from Friday 2 to Sunday 4 October. See our Nigeria coverage.

How much did fuel prices rise in Zambia?

Petrol rose from K25.29 to K31.46 a litre and diesel from K26.86 to K33.27, about 24%, after a six-month tax relief ended.

Is Algeria bringing back the death penalty?

The lower house voted on 1 October to allow executions again for deliberate arson, certain acts of sabotage and child abduction. The upper house must still approve the reform, and Algeria has carried out no execution since 1993.

01 The session in one read

The MASI, short for Moroccan All Shares Index, tracks every share listed on the Casablanca Stock Exchange. It fell 0.87% to 17,579.17 points on Thursday, a loss of 153.89 points.

The day started well. The index rose 0.06% at the open and reached a high of 17,780.94. It closed at its low of the day.

The MASI 20, which follows the 20 most liquid stocks, fell harder at 1.08% to 1,270.22 points. The MASI ESG index lost 0.98% to 1,301.98, and the MASI Mid and Small Cap index slipped 0.64% to 1,717.34.

Turnover on the central market was 152.47 million dirhams (US$15.5 million). TGCC alone accounted for 50.68 million dirhams (US$5.2 million), about a third of the total. Market capitalisation ended the day at 1,034.25 billion dirhams (US$105.4 billion).

Assessment: A broad but orderly decline MEDIUM The large stocks fell more than the small ones, as the steeper loss in the MASI 20 shows. That points to selling in the most liquid names rather than panic in thin shares. The move was orderly: no single stock carried the index lower, and turnover was concentrated in one name. The weak point is the close at the session low, which leaves little cushion going into Friday. A second losing day would confirm the downtrend that has left the MASI 6.72% lower this year.

02 The day’s numbers

Measure Level Change Read MASI 17,579.17 −0.87% Closed at the session low; −6.72% year to date MASI 20 1,270.22 −1.08% Most liquid stocks fell hardest MASI ESG 1,301.98 −0.98% Best-rated ESG companies also lower MASI Mid and Small Cap 1,717.34 −0.64% Smaller companies held up better USD/MAD 9.8083 +0.96% Late quote; dirham weaker against the dollar Turnover MAD 152.47m — About US$15.5 million on the central market

The MASI’s high of 17,780.94 came early, and the close at 17,579.17 was the low of the day. The full range was about 1.1%, a normal swing for Casablanca.

The dirham does not float freely. Bank Al-Maghrib, the central bank, sets a central rate from a basket made up of 60% euro and 40% US dollar. The dirham may move up to 5% either side of that rate. When the dollar firms against the euro, the dirham usually loses ground against the dollar.

The late quote put the dollar at 9.8083 dirhams, against 9.7148 on Wednesday. That is a 0.96% rise for the dollar. The figure is an intraday reading, not a final close.

03 Why it moved: sectors and big names

The selling was spread across the market. Agri-food stocks were the weakest sector, down 4.2%. Electricity fell 3.53%, and engineering and industrial equipment lost 3.18%.

Taqa Morocco, the listed power producer, fell 3.53% to 1,640 dirhams (US$167.20), in line with the electricity sector.

A few corners rose against the trend. Real-estate investment companies gained 2.21%, and Aradei Capital rose 2.78%. Forestry and paper rose 1.65%, and insurers added 1.01%.

The big names drifted lower. Maroc Telecom lost 2.15% and Banque Centrale Populaire 1.20%. Attijariwafa bank slipped only 0.29%, and TGCC fell 0.76% despite its heavy volume.

04 Thursday’s session, step by step

Here is how the day unfolded on the Casablanca Stock Exchange.

Opening. The MASI began the session 0.06% higher at 17,744.12 points. Early buyers briefly pushed it to 17,780.94.

Afternoon. The index gave up its gain and kept falling into the close.

Close. The MASI ended at 17,579.17, its low for the day. The MASI 20 fell 1.08%, more than the broad index.

Turnover. Trading reached 152.47 million dirhams (US$15.5 million). TGCC, Attijariwafa bank and Résidences Dar Saada were the three most traded stocks.

05 The day’s movers

Driver Close Change Note TGCC MAD 655.00 (US$66.78) −0.76% Most-traded stock: MAD 50.68m (US$5.2m) Attijariwafa bank MAD 678.00 (US$69.13) −0.29% MAD 14.06m (US$1.4m) traded; largest bank Résidences Dar Saada MAD 160.00 (US$16.31) −6.43% Third most traded: MAD 8.99m (US$0.9m) Stokvis Nord Afrique MAD 51.31 (US$5.23) −9.98% Biggest loser of the session Maroc Telecom MAD 93.45 (US$9.53) −2.15% Telecom heavyweight lower Aradei Capital MAD 440.00 (US$44.86) +2.78% Property investor among top gainers

TGCC set the tone for trading. Its volume of 50.68 million dirhams (US$5.2 million) was more than three times that of Attijariwafa bank. Yet the stock moved only 0.76%, which suggests large orders were matched without much pressure on the price.

Résidences Dar Saada was the clearest loser among the actively traded names. The developer fell 6.43% to 160 dirhams on turnover of 8.99 million dirhams (US$0.9 million).
