World.title: Islamabad hints at cautious shift on US sanctions against Iran
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan on Thursday signalled a cautious shift in its approach to the newly imposed US sanctions on Iran, saying it would adhere to “all applicable sanctions regimes” under international and domestic law, a formulation that goes beyond Islamabad’s earlier emphasis on international law and bilateral trade commitments with Tehran.

“Pakistan is a responsible member of the international community and adheres, and shall continue to adhere, to all applicable sanctions regimes in accordance with international and domestic laws,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing.

The spokesperson did not explain what Islamabad considers “applicable” even though there is a fine difference between restrictions being legally applicable or practically applicable.

The shift is nevertheless significant because when the US announced its latest sanctions against Iran, the then FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi had said: “About trade with Iran, Pakistan is following international law and our bilateral trade agreements with Iran.”

FO reiterates commitment to strategic ties with Washington, rules-based international system

Technically, the earlier formulation placed the emphasis on Pakistan’s international legal obligations and its bilateral commitments to Iran while the new one is broader, bringing “all applicable sanctions regimes” and “domestic law” into the framework.

That does not mean US unilateral sanctions automatically become binding international law for Pakistan, but it’s an acknowledgement that their practical reach can extend to Pakistani banks and companies because they operate within the international financial system and depend on access to dollar clearing, correspondent banking and financial messaging networks.

SWIFT, the international financial network, neither works as a sanctions authority nor does it decide whether transactions are lawful, but it says responsibility for compliance rests with the financial institutions handling transactions and the relevant national and international authorities.

SWIFT, which is incorporated under Belgian law, has previously disconnected Iranian banks to comply with European sanctions. This showed how sanctions adopted by a jurisdiction to which SWIFT is legally subject can affect a bank’s access to the international financial messaging network.

For Pakistan, the issue is therefore less about complying with US sanctions and more about the financial consequences of dealing with Iranian entities because US secondary sanctions can expose foreign financial institutions to restrictions on their access to the US financial system, including correspondent or payable through acc­ounts. Washington has specifically warned of such exposure as part of its expanded Iran sanctions campaign.

Therefore, the new Foreign Office formulation appears to leave Islamabad room to take those risks into account without explicitly accepting the US unilateral sanction as legally binding.

Here the assertion about compliance with domestic laws comes into play as this potentially gives Islamabad regulatory space to restrict or limit Iran-related transactions on the basis of Pakistani banking, foreign exchange and AML requirements.

For instance, State Bank’s Pakistan-Iran trade mechanism expressly requires clarity that transactions with Iran do not involve entities subject to international sanctions. Due to this clause, the businesses have been generally cautious about transacting with Iran, even before the latest sanctions. However, the government has per se not announced a suspension of trade with Iran or any decision to join the US sanctions campaign.

The Foreign Office spokesman also sought to underline Pakistan’s relationship with Washington.

“Pakistan highly values its enduring and multifaceted strategic partnership with the United States and remains fully committed to further strengthening its long-standing diplomatic, economic and security ties with Washington,” Mr Khan said.

At the same time, Islamabad reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and international law.

“Pakistan reaffirms its commitment to a rule-based international system rooted in multilateralism and international law,” Mr Khan said, adding that Islamabad remained in “constant and constructive communication with all relevant stakeholders”.

The balancing act comes at a time when Pakistan is trying to preserve its role as an intermediary between the US and Iran. Mr Khan said Pakistan would continue urging US and Iran to exercise restraint and settle their differences through diplomacy.

“Pakistan, being a mediator in communication between Iran and the United States, believes that it is important to continue urging both sides to exercise restraint, resolve outstanding issues through dialogue and diplomacy, and honour their respective commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding,” he said.

Pakistan believes this remains the “only viable pathway” to resolving the conflict peacefully, he added.

Published in Dawn, October 2nd, 2026

World.title: IMF praises oil crisis handling, urges gas sector reforms
World.content:
• Seeks faster work on targeted gas subsidies, Rs3.6tr circular debt

• Acknowledges power sector’s improvement in recoveries, loss reduction

• Govt, lender to discuss direct cash support for deserving power consumers next week

ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has appreciated Pakistan’s handling of the oil crisis without supply disruptions or an additional budgetary burden despite regional challenges during six months of the US-Iran conflict, but it asked the authorities to expedite groundwork for managing the rising gas sector circular debt and providing targeted subsidies to consumers below the poverty line.

Informed sources told Dawn that initial discussions on a proposed plan to shift gas-sector subsidies from consumer tariffs to BISP-based direct transfers had concluded that the “gas sector is far from ready given data and ownership-related challenges”.

As a result, the application of a uniform tariff linked to the average prescribed gas price of around Rs1,700 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), worked out by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra), appeared premature.

The Petroleum Division, led by Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, has been advocating uniform gas rates, as advised by Ogra, to cover the actual cost of supply, which is around Rs1,700-1,750 per mmBtu for the two gas utilities, reduce cross-subsidies from the industrial sector and curtail gas-sector debt.

The debt has now risen to around Rs3.6 trillion, including principal payables of about Rs1.8tr and an almost equivalent amount in accrued interest and late payment surcharges.

Another Petroleum Division proposal to increase the petroleum levy by a couple of rupees to finance part of the gas-sector circular debt has not found favour at relevant government forums and therefore has not been taken up with the IMF.

The introduction of a protected category for domestic consumers, involving gas prices of Rs200-350 per mmBtu, had widened the pricing gap and resultantly added to circular debt, the division suggested.

Only four of the 12 consumer slabs covered the cost of gas supply during winter, while rates remained below breakeven levels for around eight months of the year even after the imposition of substantial fixed charges.

Sources said discussions with the visiting IMF staff mission showed that documentation of gas-meter ownership and premises remained a serious problem in a large number of cases.

Consumers often avoid reporting changes in names or property ownership for decades to avoid fresh security charges and other formalities, making it difficult to identify households below the poverty line on the basis of meter data.

The problem was even more prono­unced in the commercial sector, where titles often remained unchanged while premises changed hands on “pagri”.

In contrast, documentation in the power sector was considerably more advanced despite its substantially larger consumer base.

Therefore, the IMF staff is not yet convinced by the workability of the groundwork done so far, although the Fund has consistently been insisting on targeted gas subsidies and has advised further deliberations with consultants to develop a more workable mechanism over the longer term.

The Fund also acknowledged Pakistan’s management of petroleum prices without creating an additional burden on the budget or facing product shortages.

Sources said it noted that some other regional countries had faced supply shortages, additional burdens on national budgets or state-owned corporations, or both higher fiscal costs and supply disruptions.

The IMF had initially raised questions over an increase of Rs65-70bn in power-sector circular debt, which stood at Rs1.675tr at the end of June 2026.

However, it recognised that the power sector had actually “overperformed” on efficiency targets, including bill recoveries and loss reduction, while the overall increase in debt was caused by around Rs95bn in lower disbursements by the Ministry of Finance on account of tariff differential subsidy, based on the ministry’s own subsidy calculations.

The Ministry of Finance also endorsed these figures but reported that the budgeted subsidy was higher than the actual requirement calculated on the basis of units supplied.

It was also noted that power-sector circular debt could have declined further had K-Electric paid around Rs200bn on time instead of holding up disbursement through litigation.

It was reported that the high court and appellate tribunal had upheld Nepra’s decision envisaging around Rs200bn in savings to power companies, although KE could still pursue further legal remedies.

The IMF staff was reportedly convinced, at least as far as the comparable numbers were concerned.

The two sides are expected to finalise practical plans during policy-level discussions next week for providing subsidies directly in cash to poor power consumers through the Benazir Income Support Programme, instead of through subsidised tariffs.
