World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.title: The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019065/The Enduring Appeal of China’s Eight Immortals
World.content:
This summer, “All Wishes Come True!” took in more than 1.8 billion yuan ($268 million) at the Chinese box office, becoming the latest in a string of hit animated films inspired by traditional Chinese myths and legends. The movie reimagines the Eight Immortals, a group of legendary figures in Chinese mythology and Taoism, as ordinary mortals who pose as immortals and venture into the celestial realm of Penglai. There, the mismatched group finds itself caught up in a conflict involving powerful gods, including the warrior deity Erlang Shen.

Despite the film’s widespread acclaim, some Taoist friends of mine were far from impressed. They believe it trivializes important figures in Taoist tradition, completely reimagining their stories while simply borrowing the names of Chinese immortals as a gimmick. But how fixed are the stories of the Eight Immortals in the first place?

Firstly, what makes the Eight Immortals — one of the best-known groups of immortals in Chinese culture — so special? And how exactly are they understood within Taoism?

Let’s start with why there are eight. In traditional Chinese culture, the number eight has long been associated with completeness and balance. The “Zhou Yi” (or “Book of Changes”), for example, describes the eight trigrams; traditional cosmology divides space into eight directions; and ancient people worshipped eight agricultural deities collectively associated with the harvest.

Then there are the “immortals” themselves. The Chinese word xian, or “immortal,” has long been associated with hermits who withdraw into the mountains in pursuit of spiritual cultivation. In Taoism, immortals are distinct from shen, or deities, in that ordinary humans can attain immortality through cultivation. Immortals thus occupy a space between the human and sacred worlds, embodying the Tao in the human realm.

Before the Eight Immortals became established as a group, several individual members had already appeared in historical writings and paintings from the Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) dynasties, each associated with their own supernatural feats.

Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin practiced neidan, a Taoist tradition of spiritual cultivation sometimes called “internal alchemy,” and frequently interacted with the influential Taoist priest Chen Tuan. Zhang Guolao once demonstrated various miraculous Taoist arts before Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Han Xiangzi could make flowers bloom instantly. Lan Caihe was a beggar who wore a shoe on one foot while leaving the other bare, often singing and dancing while intoxicated and carrying a large clapper.

Once they had formed into a group, however, the Eight Immortals did not simply retreat into the mountains or ascend to heaven. Instead, they remained closely connected to the human world. The most representative figure in this respect is Lü Dongbin, who chooses to remain among mortals and save them. He assumes various guises, including those of a fisherman, an ink and paper peddler, a sick beggar, and even a pregnant nun. Stories and images of Lü spread across China, with saving and enlightening ordinary people becoming a central theme in legends surrounding him.

The Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) mural “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” at Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, in northern China’s Shanxi province, shows that the Eight Immortals had by then become an established subject in Taoist art. But closer inspection reveals that the only female member of today’s group, He Xiangu, is missing. In her place is Xu Shenweng, a Taoist figure associated with the Northern Song period (960–1127) who once ranked among the Eight Immortals. In other words, the Eight Immortals were originally an all-male group.

So, when did He Xiangu become one of the Eight Immortals? One early appearance of her as part of the group comes in the Yuan dynasty drama “Chen Jiqing Mistakenly Boards a Bamboo Leaf Boat” by Fan Kang. By the time Wu Yuantai wrote the mythological novel “Journey to the East” during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), she had become a permanent member of the group.

This change came amid the flourishing of women’s literary and religious activity during the mid-to-late Ming. Like male scholars, educated women participated in religious and intellectual life and produced literary works of their own. In “Journey to the East,” He Xiangu’s defining supernatural ability is her power to foresee good and bad fortune. Born into a family that ran an herbal medicine shop, she possesses medical knowledge and uses encounters with people seeking treatment as opportunities to encourage them to do good.

With the addition of He Xiangu, the lineup familiar today became fixed and increasingly popular. The Eight Immortals eventually became influential enough to attract the attention of European missionaries studying Chinese religion and folklore. French Jesuit Henri Doré (1859–1931), for example, compiled stories about them in “Researches into Chinese Superstitions,” his multivolume study of Chinese popular religion, folklore, and customs.

The Chinese Jesuit priest Pierre Hoang (1830–1909), also known as Huang Bolu, meanwhile, described the Eight Immortals as representing a cross-section of society: the old and young, men and women, the rich and poor, the noble and lowly. In another interpretation, Zhang Guolao represents old age; Lan Caihe and Han Xiangzi, youth; Zhongli Quan, the military; Lü Dongbin, the scholar; Cao Guojiu, the nobility; Li Tieguai, the sick; and He Xiangu, women.

The Eight Immortals thus came to encompass a broad range of social identities and experiences. They had, collectively, seen many sides of the human world, allowing people from different backgrounds to recognize something of themselves in the group. Their differences also created a kind of balance, recalling a passage in Chapter 2 of the “Tao Te Ching,” which states: “Thus existence and non-existence produce each other; the difficult and the easy bring about each other; the long and the short impart form to each other; the high and the low comply [or change places] with each other; sounds and voices harmonize with each other; priority and sequence alternate with each other.”

From the mid-to-late Ming dynasty onward, the Eight Immortals also became a popular decorative motif on ceramics produced in both imperial and private kilns. They often appeared more subtly on everyday objects, including furniture, utensils, clothing, and architectural decorations. Rather than depicting the immortals themselves, artisans represented them through eight objects associated with the group: Li Tieguai’s gourd, Zhongli Quan’s fan, Zhang Guolao’s fish drum, Lan Caihe’s flower basket, Cao Guojiu’s jade tablet, Han Xiangzi’s flute, He Xiangu’s lotus, and Lü Dongbin’s sword. Craftsmen combined these symbols with scrollwork, bats, clouds, and waves to create decorative compositions that also conveyed wishes for longevity, good fortune, and wealth.

Stories about the Eight Immortals were similarly adaptable. Among commoners, plays such as “The Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea” and “The Eight Immortals Assembly Celebrate Longevity” were widely performed. By the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns (1736–1820) of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), such stories were increasingly associated with birthday celebrations, with gatherings of the Eight Immortals symbolizing longevity, joy, and good fortune.

Among intellectuals, meanwhile, the Eight Immortals served as a source of creative inspiration. One example is “The Record of Handan,” the last of the “Four Dreams of Linchuan” by the great Ming playwright Tang Xianzu. Rather than focusing on reunion, the play uses Lü Dongbin to explore the illusory nature of worldly ambition.

In the play, Lü meets a poor scholar obsessed with achieving fame and gives him a porcelain pillow. After putting on a pot of rice to boil, the scholar falls asleep and dreams that he marries, places first in the imperial examinations, and spends decades navigating political machinations before becoming a powerful and honored official, only to eventually die from overindulgence. Waking to find his pot of rice still cooking, the scholar realizes his entire lifetime of ambition was merely a brief dream. Lü then begins the process of enlightening him, introducing him to the other immortals, who appear one by one to admonish him until he finally awakens to the emptiness of his desires.

All this shows just how adaptable the stories of the Eight Immortals have always been. Taoist traditions and popular folklore have continually shaped and reshaped one another, producing new versions of the group for different audiences and eras.

In that sense, what is happening to the Eight Immortals today is nothing new.

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: An Eight Immortals room screen at a museum in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.title: She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019071/She Sold 192 Porsches in a Year. Then Came an AI-Fueled Smear Campaign.
World.content:
Editor’s note: After Mu Qianwen hit the headlines in 2024 as one of Porsche’s top sales consultants worldwide, she became the target of toxic online abuse, including sexually explicit AI-generated videos. For this 35-year-old mother in Qingdao, in the eastern Shandong province, the harassment got so bad that she even contemplated suicide. Rather than give in, she decided to fight back through the courts. Here, Mu shares her ordeal in her own words.

I first started attracting attention online in early 2024. I’d already been “sales champion of the month” at my dealership more than 20 times, but on the last day of 2023, our sales manager presented me with a crystal trophy. I had sold 170 cars that year.

When I posted about the achievement on Xiaohongshu (the lifestyle platform known globally as RedNote), it soon became a trending topic, and more than a dozen media outlets asked me for interviews.

But there was also a huge backlash, with some questioning how I could have sold so many cars and suggesting that the dealership must have inflated my sales figures. Our general manager issued a statement to refute any talk of deception, but the allegations kept coming.

A woman selling luxury cars seems like an easy formula for a viral story. Some people claimed I was making 3 million yuan ($447,000) a year. Porsche pays its salespeople about 2,000 to 3,000 yuan in commission for every car sold. We can earn several hundred thousand yuan a year, but exceeding 1 million is extremely difficult. I make enough to give my family a comfortable life, and I do own an entry-level Porsche, but I’ve never made anything close to that amount.

Rumors also began circulating that I treat my customers to lavish dinners, which is pure innuendo. In reality, I work such long hours that I barely have time to eat, let alone entertain. I’ve never dated a customer or had any kind of inappropriate relationship. More than 60% of my buyers are women.

After people claimed that the dealership had exaggerated my sales figures, I set myself a goal: In 2024, I would sell another 170 cars, no matter what. On Dec. 31, I was still one car short of the target. But then a female customer walked in. I told her about my goal and offered her an attractive price on a model. It was win-win. A little after 3 p.m., she placed an order.

In 2025, I sold even more cars — 192. At this point, I felt I’d answered all my critics. But the online abuse had only gotten worse. Early that year, I discovered that someone had spread a sexually explicit rumor about me using an overseas social media platform. They claimed that I slept with customers, and posted as “proof” a fabricated video and audio recording using a different woman, whose face was concealed throughout.

I tried to brush it off and told myself not to take it too seriously, that this was just the price of publicity. But my friends urged me to report it to the police, so I ultimately filed a report.

At first, the explicit material mainly circulated on overseas websites and social media, so the impact was limited. But last October, things escalated. Someone shared a misleading video via (the instant-messaging platform) WeChat that combined one of my sales-promotion posters with footage of a woman with a completely different body shape to me undressing in a hotel room. There were also some demeaning AI-generated videos.

This time, the content spread incredibly fast among my circle. Friends, colleagues, and customers all started asking me what was going on. I felt like my world was collapsing. I again reported the videos to the police.

My phone number was also leaked, and I began receiving harassing calls, sometimes at one or two in the morning. A man in Qingdao called out of the blue to ask me to “come over and spend the night with him.” I recorded the conversation and sent it to the police, who issued the man a warning.

My WeChat was blowing up, too. I didn’t know whether a new friend request was from someone looking to buy a car or for something else. Some people would start by talking about cars and then steer the conversation toward asking me out. Others were more covert, asking me to record a video showing the “backseat legroom.” I knew what they really wanted. One person messaged, “I know it’s not you in those videos, but I fantasize that it is. Can you provide me with services?”

Social media is an important source of customers for me, so I couldn’t just ignore it. I still had to livestream. But when I was on camera introducing cars, I’d always see inappropriate comments pop up, like “I saw that video” or “You’re so hot.”

I even overheard some customers in the showroom talking about me. That hit me hard. I could no longer pretend that this online smear campaign wasn’t affecting me.

By now, the enthusiasm and confidence I used to have with customers was gone. I feared talking with people, paranoid that they must be gossiping about me.

At my lowest point, I briefly considered jumping from a building. I felt there was no point in being alive, that the world had become dark. It seemed everyone looked at me differently.

I told my supervisor that I had reached breaking point and needed time off. I was given three days, so I took my son back to my hometown, Yantai (about a three-hour drive from Qingdao), where we stayed at a beautiful guesthouse. I told myself that I had to keep living for my child and be responsible for my family. I had to clear my name.

When I returned to work, I was so anxious I couldn’t walk straight; my muscles were so tense I unconsciously leaned to one side. I wore a neck brace because even the slightest jolt during a test drive would send sharp pains up my back. I developed insomnia and tinnitus. At one point, I even struggled to speak.

Zero to hero

I started in auto sales in 2013, initially selling Audi and Lincoln cars in Beijing. I joined the Porsche dealership in downtown Qingdao in 2018. At first, my performance was so poor that I nearly lost my job.

Most of the salespeople had years of experience, and I was the youngest. Social media wasn’t the powerful tool it is today; business depended largely on walk-ins and referrals. For the first six months, I barely sold anything. At our 2019 New Year’s meeting, the sales manager asked everyone to share their goals for the year ahead. I said, “I want to survive at Porsche.”

I didn’t know the different models or specifications well enough. If a knowledgeable customer asked me a question, I felt intimidated and out of my depth. I started getting up at 6 a.m. to memorize technical information. I’d stand near colleagues and listen as they explained different cars. I studied the way they talked.

One colleague said I needed to dress better, so I started wearing tailored shirts and paying more attention to the cut and quality of everything I wore. In sales, it’s appearance, not skill, that makes the first impression. When I applied makeup, I felt more confident. Even though I had only four days off a month, I scheduled manicures and eyelash extensions, and sometimes skin booster injections.

I was a core consultant by my second year, became one of the dealership’s top performers in 2020, and was closing 17 deals a month in 2021.

Demand for foreign luxury cars has declined in the past two years, but my sales have continued to increase, largely because of social media. Of my 170 customers in 2023, 15% found me through social media. In 2025, it was 41%.

I also run a Porsche owners’ WeChat group with several hundred members. I organize monthly group events, such as camping trips, yacht outings, and nature walks. If I stop talking to someone as soon as a deal is done, they’ll always be just a customer. But if we spend time together, we can become friends. Referrals are an important part of my sales.

My typical workday runs from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. I’ve hardly taken any annual leave in all these years. If I go on vacation, customers disappear. I’m competitive by nature. I crave deals, performance figures, the feeling of being number one. I’m currently leading Porsche’s global sales rankings for September 2026, but someone could still overtake me.

The hardest word

When selling cars, effort usually pays off. But clearing a damaged reputation? That’s different.

Someone can casually share something about me online, and suddenly I have to spend money, time, and energy to respond. I have to pay lawyers and gather evidence. I filed 31 complaints to Douyin (China’s version of TikTok) alone between October 2025 and April this year about abusive messages, videos that used my image without permission, and people cloning my voice to promote get-rich-quick books.

I hand the most egregious messages directly to the police. One man I reported was initially very cocky. He seemed to think I was bluffing and wouldn’t be able to track him down. The authorities eventually found him, and he sent me an apology.

A 20-something Porsche owner in Qingdao forwarded some offensive material about me in a group chat and was given five days of administrative detention. I later accepted his apology, too, but then his family called my dealership’s customer service line to complain — they couldn’t understand why he still needed to be detained. I had no say in his punishment, but they obviously never stopped to think about how his actions might have affected me.

Even the outcomes of such cases haven’t halted the spread of false allegations; I still encounter vitriol during livestreams and on social media.

In July this year, the police gave me details of a 30-something man in the eastern Fujian province who’d been behind one of the AI-generated videos. I’d never met him. He was given 10 days of administrative detention in last October, but he never contacted me to apologize.

I think receiving punishment is not the same as saying sorry. This man was punished for spreading rumors, but what about the harm he caused? So I decided to file a civil lawsuit against him. All I want is for him to apologize and say explicitly that the woman in that video is not me.

Some friends urged me to press criminal charges, but I don’t want him to bear the consequences for the rest of his life. As a mother, I think about what would happen to his child if he were prosecuted. My lawyer says that if the civil case goes to trial, it could take up to two years. No matter how long it takes, I need to see it through.

Now I’m facing claims that the lawsuit is a publicity stunt, that I’m dredging things up again. In reality, just because the story is no longer in the headlines, it doesn’t mean those negative voices have disappeared from my life.

My son is in kindergarten. He doesn’t have a phone, and he knows nothing about what’s going on. All he knows is that his mom is the top salesperson at Porsche Qingdao. When I asked him what he wanted to do when he grew up, he said he wanted to sell cars. He’s proud of his mom.

What happens when he grows up, gets a phone, and sees what people have said about his mother? What if his classmates use the rumors against him? Who takes responsibility for that? The same goes for my parents. I want to clear my name for my family’s sake.

I still like being number one, but after everything that’s happened, my ambition has waned. I want to focus more on family and my health.

My life used to be a straight line between work and home, but over the past two years, I’ve started leaving more time for myself — meals with colleagues and friends, live music bars, taking my son to the mountains or the beach.

I wonder whether the rumors will disappear once the lawsuit is over. If people keep talking, there might be nothing more I can do. I’ve done everything within my power. If I win the case, that will be the end of it for me.

Women have sent me long messages of support, telling me how brave I am. Many professional women have shared that they have been the targets of similar smear campaigns and felt completely helpless. They ask me what they should do. I don’t know what to tell them.

As told to reporter Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Mu Qianwen at her workplace in Qingdao, Shandong province, August 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.title: Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019076/Chinese Village to Spend Millions on NPCs to Boost Tourism
World.content:
A northern Chinese village has announced it will spend 30 million yuan ($4.5 million) to recruit 100 character performers — known in China as NPCs, or non-playable characters — to interact with tourists. Successful hires will receive a range of salaries, with the highest reportedly reaching 10 million yuan a year.

Situ Town, a scenic spot located in Situ Village in the northern Shanxi province, will finance the recruitment partly through its publicity budget and partly from startup funds, Zhou Xiaoming, the village Party secretary, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper on Sunday.

Once a coal town, Situ Village’s coal was gradually depleted by the end of the 20th century. To address its lack of resources, in 2009, the village built an agricultural ecological park — an area that combines farming with ecological protection and tourism — on a slag heap, which later grew into a highly rated national attraction. The village is known for its “iron flower” performances — a folk art in which local blacksmiths hurl molten iron into the air.

Zhou announced the NPC recruitment on Sept. 19 in a video posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. “No matter what your talent is, as long as you can make the tourists on stage have fun, and the audience below enjoy themselves, we’ll give you a platform — and 1 million, even 10 million (yuan),” he said in the video.

The plan quickly drew suspicion online, with some arguing that the money would be better spent investing in the scenic area itself, such as by adding amusement parks, building affordable guesthouses, improving green spaces, upgrading the “iron flower” show, or supporting local artists.

Previously, the scenic spot had announced a short video contest — also led by Zhou — in August in which 5 million yuan was offered to participants based on likes and views. Winning the top prize of 1 million yuan required 10 million likes and 300 million views.

Official data showed that in 2025, Situ Town received 2.2 million tourist visits, double the year prior, generating a total revenue of 350 million yuan. Meanwhile, tourism-related jobs grew from 500 to more than 1,000, the latter accounting for roughly a third of the village’s labor force.

Zhou noted, however, that the scenic spot has faced steep losses in recent years. “In 2023 we lost 500,000 yuan, in 2024 we lost 500,000 yuan, and in 2025 we lost money, but not much,” he said.

More than 7,000 people have applied for the NPC positions so far, with video interviews planned for over 50, Zhou said, adding that they have not yet set an application deadline. Zhou added that NPC salaries will range from 500,000 to 10 million yuan depending on the traffic they generate, the emotional value they bring to tourists, and tourists’ degree of satisfaction.

Recruiting NPCs is reportedly the scenic spot’s first step, with the goal of eventually cultivating its own homegrown talent. Its employees, Zhou said, are actually the biggest NPCs, but they need a good environment and role models to imitate — and those recruited with the 30 million yuan are meant to set an example.

Zeng Bowei, a professor at the Tourism College of Beijing Union University, told The Paper that the most important value of NPCs is transforming culture into something tourists can see and participate in.

“Although NPCs have been called ‘non-playable characters,’ their true value to scenic areas is precisely making each tourist into a player,” Zeng said, adding that with the right roles, stories, and cultural backing, NPCs can increase traffic in the long term.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019070/Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.title: Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019070/Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.content:
The hair business in Xuchang, in China’s central Henan province, has been growing since the 16th century. Starting from opera props, the city is now the “Wig Capital of the World.”

Roughly 60% of wigs on the global market come from Xuchang. According to the local commerce bureau, the industry’s total import-export value hit 11.56 billion yuan ($1.72 billion) in the first half of 2026, up by nearly 11% year on year.

The core of this pillar industry, Jian’an District, is home to 311 foreign trade enterprises shipping hair products — and business is booming. Yet life behind the sales figures isn’t so rosy.

Although cross-border e-commerce platforms have helped companies reach new markets, including North America and Europe, businesses here say the commissions they charge are making it difficult to turn a profit.

The industry is also facing a potential serious labor crisis, with high-than-average salaries failing to attract more talent, especially younger workers.

Long and short of it

According to local historical archives, people in Xuchang began collecting human hair as early as the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), using it to make theatrical props and fake beards.

It wasn’t until 1900, when Bai Xihe from the city’s Quandian Village collaborated with a German merchant to establish a hair trading depot, that a wider industry began to emerge. Soon, villagers were fanning out nationwide to find supplies, with the raw materials pooled in Jian’an.

By the 1930s, Xuchang had dozens of workshops making processed hair, or dangfa, which was shipped through ports in Qingdao in the eastern Shandong province and Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, to overseas markets including Japan and the Philippines.

Dangfa is a semi-finished product made from human hair that has been washed, straightened, sorted, and tied into bundles. It’s a key upstream raw material for wigs.

Many rural families opened small home-based operations, forming the embryo of a cottage industry. The men would travel around the nation collecting hair, while the women stayed home to sort and knot wigs strand by strand, an essential craft that takes at least six months to master.

“An industrial ecosystem doesn’t come together overnight,” says Tian Liangjun, vice president of the Xuchang Hair Products Association, established in 2004. “Our industry has more than a century of accumulated history. The raw materials, the talent, the technology, the market intelligence are all here — and so are the supporting accessories, equipment, printing, and packaging.”

By the time China began to open its economy in the late 1970s and early ’80s, Xuchang possessed the raw materials and manufacturing capacity, but companies from South Korea had control of the network channels to overseas markets. They purchased hair and semi-finished goods from Xuchang and sold finished products to beauty supply stores in the United States. Chinese enterprises were consigned to contract processing, with limited profits and little market leverage.

“In the past, more than 80% of the U.S. hair-product market was controlled by South Korean companies. They had us by the throat,” Tian says. “We depended on them, so when South Korean agents came to Xuchang to inspect the goods, they acted like they were above us. Some of us even had to bring them bowls of water to wash their hands at the end of their inspection.”

However, things changed in 1990, when entrepreneur Zheng Youquan founded the Xuchang Hair Products General Factory, which saw local businesses advance to producing finished wigs.

Zheng was born in 1954 in the city’s Xiaogong Village and learned wig-making as a child before entering the hair processing trade in the ’80s.

When he opened his own factory, he faced a major challenge: the three-head sewing machine, a core piece of equipment, wasn’t made in China and no foreign manufacturers would sell him one. So he enlisted the help of a retired factory worker from Qingdao who could draw the machine’s inner workings from memory, which a team of local engineers then used to build it.

Using this technology, Zheng’s plant produced Xuchang’s first wigs for foreign buyers, branded Qicai Xiufa, meaning “colorful tresses.” Three years later, he established Rebecca Hair, a Sino-U.S. joint venture with Sina International Corp., and entered the North American market. In 2003, Rebecca became the first hair-product enterprise listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

Tian believes Zheng helped catapult the local industry to a new level, transforming the city from a trading hub for raw materials into a major production base for finished goods.

Cutting out the middleman

The emergence of cross-border e-commerce in the mid-2010s was another game changer. Global platforms such as AliExpress and Amazon enabled Xuchang manufacturers to bypass the middleman and deal directly with overseas consumers, as well as create their own brands.

UNice, which specializes in hair products for Black and Latino women, began trading on multiple platforms in 2014 and set up its own sales website about four years later. “We decided to create our own brand and registered trademarks in China, the European Union, and the United States,” says Wang Qi, who works for the brand. “With third-party platforms, you need to play by their rules, and there are all sorts of uncertainties. Building our own site reduced our dependence on platforms and put operations in our own hands. More importantly, we have full control over product quality.”

Some Xuchang companies have also opened warehouses overseas to gain a better understanding of the destination market and to cut costs with cheaper bulk freight.

“In 2025, the cumulative additional tariffs the U.S. imposed on Chinese hair products reached 145% at one point, and the tariff costs on small parcels below the $800 tax-free threshold rose sharply,” recalls Bo Luwen, who runs a wig business in Jian’an. “Surrounding factories shut down because they couldn’t ship anything.” His company had a stockpile in U.S. warehouses, so it was shielded from the market shock.

He adds that warehouses do more than provide cover in emergencies; they also improve the customer experience. A consignment shipped from China to North America can bob on the ocean for weeks before reaching the buyer, whereas goods sent from within the continent can arrive the next day.

OQ Hair, an online brand offering 100% human hair products, released a glueless wig in 2023 that promises to cut application time from 30 minutes to a few seconds. Thanks in part to a short promotional video that garnered 3 million views, the company recorded sales of more than 10 million yuan within six months.

“The rise of cross-border e-commerce completely broke the South Korean monopoly over distribution channels,” Tian says. “We went from contract manufacturing to making our own brands — from passive to active. This was when our industry truly came into its own.”

Split ends

Yet the hard work is far from over. Although cross-border e-commerce platforms led to a breakthrough in distribution, “they bred new problems, too, including relatively high commissions and ever-shifting rules,” Tian explains. “Sellers also can’t autonomously decide what to sell or how to price it.”

The commissions charged by Amazon, AliExpress, and Temu run from 5% to 20%, he says. “This is squeezing our companies’ already-thin margins. It’s hard for sellers on those platforms to make money.”

Another concern is the worsening talent shortage. Many steps in industrial wig-making still require manual labor, and anecdotal evidence suggests that fewer people are willing to work in Xuchang’s factories, especially younger generations. Some businesses are even offering to pay front-line employees 8,000 yuan a month, well above average, yet still struggle to fill vacancies.

A hand-sewn wig takes a skilled worker about a week to complete, and machines cannot fully replace hand-knotting. As older craftspeople are aging out, some skill-intensive tasks are now being outsourced overseas.

Against this backdrop, many companies see only one way forward: abandon the low-end price war in favor of premium, branded products. Leading enterprises are also investing in research and development, hoping to move toward fully automated production.

On the retail side, there’s also Xuchang Hair Expo City, a specialized wig trading and commercial market near the city’s railway station and long-distance bus terminal.

“Xuchang may be the wig capital, but for years, visitors couldn’t find a single place to actually buy one here,” says Tian, who has run the market since it was founded in 2022. ‘There were plenty of manufacturers, but none of them served walk-in customers. The industry had no storefront you could see and touch.”

Inside, shelves are stacked with everything from synthetic wigs selling for a few dozen yuan to hand-knotted wig caps made from 100% real human hair priced at more than 10,000 yuan.

“We want buyers worldwide to know that when it comes to buying a wig, Xuchang is all they need,” Tian says. The market’s annual sales volume, including via e-commerce channels, is now about 200 million yuan, with most customers coming from other regions of China. However, he adds that the number of foreign buyers is increasing.

Whatever happens, Tian believes that genuine quality is the ultimate trump card. “If your goods aren’t good, no one will want them, even if you beg.”

(Due to privacy reasons, Wang Qi and Bo Luwen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Cheng Ting, Kang Jiaxin, Yang Yuan, and Fang Yuejia.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Eunice Ouyang; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Workers style wigs at a factory in Xuchang, Henan province, 2019. VCG)

World.title: A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019051/A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.content:
By 8 p.m. on Aug. 26, the great banyan tree at the center of Boshi Village is already surrounded by offerings. Bowls filled with fresh fruit, roasted meat, and other snacks are stacked rows deep among the tree’s gnarled roots. The air hangs thick with candle and incense smoke.

Locals have laid out the smorgasbord of treats as part of the Shigu festival, a series of rituals predominantly held in southern China each year that is often likened to Mexico’s Day of the Dead.

While it’s far from well-known overseas, Shigu has long been one of China’s most important and vibrant festivals. Like the Day of the Dead, it’s a centuries-old tradition to honor the deceased and draws on a rich mix of religious and folk practices.

But Shigu is also a distinctly local celebration that embodies many unique aspects of Chinese culture — and especially the culture of Chaoshan, the southern coastal region where Boshi Village is located.

Shigu — which literally translates as “feeding the lonely ghosts” — sees communities come together to care for the spirits of the departed: making offerings, chanting Buddhist scripture, and even communicating with the deceased.

It’s unclear when the festival first emerged, but references date back to at least the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279). For a long time, the Shigu festivities in Chaoshan drew bigger crowds than any other event apart from Chinese New Year.

To grasp Shigu’s significance, it’s necessary to understand how it fits into China’s traditional cosmology. According to Confucian and Taoist practices, families have a responsibility to care for the spirits of their departed loved ones, leaving offerings of food, paper money, and even alcohol to ensure they are comfortable in the afterlife.

But many people die with no children to care for their souls, while seafarers and soldiers often perish far from home and their bodies are never returned to their hometowns. If neglected, these spirits become “lonely ghosts” that wander the Earth, spreading woe and harassing the living.

The Shigu festival is designed to prevent this. Taking place in the seventh lunar month of the traditional Chinese calendar — when Yanwang, the king of hell, is said to open the gates of the underworld — communities lay out offerings for these lonely souls, giving the hungry ghosts temporary relief.

In this, Shigu differs from the Day of the Dead, which is more about families honoring their ancestors. China’s Qingming Festival in early April is perhaps a closer equivalent in that sense, though its traditions of tomb-sweeping and quiet family ceremonies are quite different.

Over the centuries, the Shigu festival has become more elaborate. Offerings are now often accompanied by communal rituals that blend Buddhist and local folk traditions. (In many places, the festival is also called “Pudu,” a name that derives from the Buddhist concept of “universal salvation” — or delivering all souls from suffering.)

In Chaoshan, many groups organize “spirit-writing” ceremonies — a practice akin to using a Ouija board to communicate with ghosts, except characters are written in sand. Others organize processions between local temples and offering grounds, led by officials chanting Buddhist scripture.

Local charities, meanwhile, donate everything from medicine to coffins to people in need in mass “merit-making ceremonies.” Most famously, the impoverished are allowed to grab the food laid out for the spirits during a ritual known as the “scramble for the offerings” — though these days the contests tend to be infiltrated by a fair number of tourists.

Today, Shigu is still marked across the Chinese-speaking world, but the celebrations are particularly central to life in Chaoshan — a reflection of the region’s turbulent history.

Chaoshan has long had a large population of hungry ghosts. For centuries, wars and uprisings across the region left countless people without a proper burial. More recently, millions set sail from Chaoshan to seek work overseas, forming large diasporas across Southeast Asia and even further afield.

To care for all these wandering souls, towns and villages across Chaoshan still mark Shigu at the end of every summer. Though the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, known as the Zhongyuan Festival, is widely regarded as the height of the Shigu festival, communities hold their ceremonies on different days throughout the month. No one is sure how and when the dates were selected.

In Nansha, a village near the city of Shantou, the Zhongyuan Festival celebrations are in full swing when Sixth Tone visits in late August. Shopkeepers unable to join the collective village ceremony set up tables outside their businesses to lay out offerings. Other villagers gather at the local temple and ancestral hall to organize the main events.

Elderly residents take charge. Some use loudspeakers to blare out appeals in Chaoshan dialect, calling on villagers to donate money and rice for the Pudu. Others fold triangular paper offerings or prepare baskets of “guye fish rice,” a staple offering used in local rituals.

Inside the temple, a group of women performs a ceremony to honor the wandering spirits — known affectionately as guye, or lonely elders. Donated flour, rice, cooking oil, and fruit are piled in front of the temple for needy villagers to collect.

At the ancestral hall, neat stacks of rice cakes, bread, snacks, and baskets of “guye fish rice” are arranged in a courtyard in front of the main entrance. Lin Qiwei, a local village elder, begins a ceremony to make the offerings at 3 p.m., kneeling and chanting a sacrificial text.

“Orphaned souls with no one to claim you, come here and eat,” Lin calls. “Once you have eaten your fill, return each to your place; do not disturb the living; do not frighten the children.”

After the ceremony comes the much-anticipated “scramble for the offerings,” where locals compete to grab the delicacies. Local beliefs hold that consuming food blessed by the spirits brings good fortune. The ritual also serves as a form of charity, to help villagers who have fallen on hard times.

But the “scramble for the offerings” has become controversial in recent years. As the ritual’s fame has grown — with influencers posting videos of the spectacle on Chinese social media — it has begun to attract large groups of outsiders, who often crowd out those who are truly in need.

Yet, despite its viral popularity, the reality is that today’s Shigu festival is a shadow of its former self. In the early 20th century, practically every household in Chaoshan took part in the festivities and incense burned all month long, according to folk-custom researcher Lin Xuejin.

After 1949, the festivals were suspended for decades, as traditional practices and beliefs were discouraged as “feudal superstitions.” They slowly revived after “reform and opening-up” began in the late 1970s, but mass internal migration and breakneck economic development have also taken their toll.

Today, while villages across Chaoshan still hold Shigu, the monthlong community-wide celebrations have dwindled to one-off collective events on selected days, run almost entirely by older residents. Young people are noticeably scarce in Nansha — except for the gaggle of influencers and creators filming and livestreaming the events.

The Chinese internet’s sudden embrace of Shigu can feel jarring. As Lin chants his appeal to the lonely ghosts before an audience mostly made up of retirees, several drones whir overhead, waiting to capture the excitement of the coming “scramble for the offerings.”

But locals hope the trend can help revive the festival. Several villagers say the influx of content creators has encouraged younger generations to value their local culture more — and pushed older residents to keep organizing the ceremonies despite falling attendance.

Fu Xingcong, a Ph.D. candidate at Beijing’s Minzu University of China studying Shigu practices in Chaoshan, tells Sixth Tone that these external forces have strengthened local cultural identity and given the declining tradition a much-needed boost.

Back in Boshi Village, locals are doing their best to preserve the festival in their own way. Chen, a woman in her 40s, drives up from the nearby city of Chaozhou to pay her respects shortly after 8 p.m.

Watched by her teenage daughter, she carefully inserts incense sticks into her specially prepared bowls of braised goose, cured pork, and soft white rice cakes, arranges them on the ground, and then kowtows while murmuring her wishes.

Chen, who gave only her surname, says she returns to her ancestral village for the Shigu festival every summer. Though she moved to the city many years ago, she still feels it’s important to maintain this link to her old home and pass it on to the next generation.

“This was something I absorbed from childhood,” Chen tells Sixth Tone. “Once you grow up and get married, it becomes your responsibility to perform these rituals.”

Cunxin Charity Hall, Downtown Shantou

Nansha Village, Shantou

This article is co-authored by Wu Huiyuan.

(Header image: At the “scramble for the offerings” in Shantou’s Nansha Village, Guangdong province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: GCash prices Philippines’ biggest-ever IPO at P6.60 per share
World.content:
The IPO now moves to its October 6 to 12 public offer period, when retail investors will be able to subscribe to shares at the P6.60 price

MANILA, Philippines – GCash parent Mynt has set its final initial public offering (IPO) price at P6.60 per share, putting a price tag of roughly P442 billion on the fintech company ahead of its stock market debut.

The final price – set on Thursday, October 1 but disclosed on the Philippine Stock Exchange on Friday, October 2 – is below the maximum P10-per-share price Mynt initially indicated in its prospectus. The roughly P442-billion valuation is based on Mynt’s approximately 66.9 billion shares outstanding after the offer, multiplied at the final offer price. At the earlier P10 ceiling, the company would have been valued at about P669 billion.

At P6.60, Mynt’s base offering of up to 8.03 billion shares would be worth around P53 billion. If its 1.20-billion share overallotment option is fully exercised, the IPO could raise as much as P60.9 billion, still putting it on track to become the largest IPO in Philippine history, ahead of the previous record held by Monde Nissin, whose 2021 listing raised about P55.89 billion including primary and secondary shares.

The P6.60 price also matches the level previously indicated by several of Mynt’s cornerstone investors. More than 20 local and international institutions, including funds managed by BlackRock, Capital Research and Management Company, T. Rowe Price, and the World Bank Group’s International Finance Corporation, have committed around P36.5 billion to the offering.

Mynt’s base offer consists of up to 1.61 billion newly issued shares and another 6.42 billion shares being sold by existing shareholders, alongside an overallotment option covering as many as 1.20 billion more shares. (READ: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday)

In other words, roughly 80% of the base shares on offer are being sold by existing shareholders, meaning most of the proceeds from the share sale will not go to GCash as fresh capital that it can use to fund its business, but instead to investors cashing out part of their stakes.

The IPO now moves to its October 6 to 12 public offer period, when retail investors will be able to subscribe to shares at the P6.60 price. Mynt is targeting an October 20 listing on the Philippine Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol GCASH. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Mind The Gap] Buyer’s remorse on Trump? Vote your pocketbook!
World.content:
Sitting on the sidelines is no longer an option because our families here and back home are paying the price. Every vote counts.

When I gas up now, it’s past $6 a gallon for regular gasoline, and if you’re a big rig trucker, diesel is over $9 a gallon in California. When I do my groceries at the Island Pacific supermarket, a pound of bok choy for my pork neck bone sinigang, the same bunch that cost 99 cents before, is $2.99 now, even with my 12% senior citizen discount on Tuesdays.

And it’s not just our wallet being emptied here. The oil shock from the Iran war is also wreaking havoc on our loved ones in the Philippines, even as they continue to wade through stagnant flood water from the Habagat, worsened by crumbling flood control infrastructure, some of them with retaining walls built without rebar. And with diesel nearly P100 a liter, or about $6.50 a gallon, jeepney drivers are on the streets demanding higher fares.

At a time when they need remittances the most, we’re the ones cutting back as we try squeezing our own budget to put food on the table first. Those who count on $400 a month now get $200, if we can spare it.

With the US accounting for about $15 billion or 40% of all cash remittances to the Philippines every year, the whole country feels it when we pull back, with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas already forecasting remittance growth to slow to 2.7% in 2026, down from 3.3% in 2025.

‘It’s the economy, stupid!’

People say voters vote with their pocketbook. “It’s the economy, stupid!” — the line from Democratic strategist James Carville that helped win Clinton the presidency in ’92 — feels almost quaint now. But it’s happening again. Millions of Americans are struggling with the high cost of living, and just like the Iran war, there seems no end in sight to rising prices.

If you voted for Trump, that’s okay, nobody’s perfect. But you didn’t vote for higher prices, never asked for endless international conflicts even with our close allies, and never wanted Republicans in Congress to introduce a bill curtailing our immigration right to petition our own elderly parents.

Nor we imagined that our US citizenship can be revoked when audited for trivial mistakes, like a misstatement at the time of our application.

Because Filipinos have one of the highest naturalization rates — roughly 1.6 million, or 76% of our population — we are mathematically more likely to be caught in this arbitrary audit, with the United States Customs and Immigration Services (USCIS) setting a quota of 100 to 200 cases a month to strip citizenship from naturalized Americans in 2026.

MAGA flag in tatters

Besides, Trump’s core support is showing deep fractures even among his MAGA faithful, especially those in Red States affected by the cost of tariffs and diesel fuel.

“Donald Trump is dragging down Republicans, even in some of the most Trump-y states,” according to New York Times contributing writer E.J. Dionne Jr. after reporting in Indiana and Kansas, where Trump’s approval is down in the 40s in both states.

While it’s impossible to argue with the rabid, Charlie Kirk-quoting Pinoy MAGAs, we have a potent voting bloc of the undecided and the disillusioned that can swing battleground states like Nevada where presidential and Senate races are routinely decided by thin margins.

Furthermore, while California is reliably blue, there are highly competitive US House districts across the Central Valley, Orange County, and parts of Los Angeles and San Diego. Since 41% of FilIpino eligible voters live in California, a surging turnout could help flip or hold the seats that can determine control of Congress.

Add to this the nearly 50 million Gen Zers ages 18 to 29 who will be eligible to vote this November, with more of them were registered as of July than at this point before the last midterm. Though more than 21 million eligible Gen Zers didn’t vote in 2024, their top concern now is the economy, which gives them a reason to show up.

Fence-sitters

Though there are more than four million Filipinos in the US, second only to the Chinese, we’ve been fence-sitters for so long in American politics that we’ve allowed those who came here after us, like the Indians and the Vietnamese, to gain a political clout we can now only dream of.

It could be apathy, why we are underrepresented in American politics. Our reluctance to take risks while sitting pretty on relative affluence from good-paying jobs made us lazy and indifferent to sort of flex our political power in terms of our large numbers.

We have often voted as individuals rather than organizing as a collective force, like in donating to candidates, which Indians generously do, or in walking the precincts or manning phone banks for our own kababayan running for office, or join protest rallies to support our rights as immigrants.

This midterm election, sitting on the sidelines is no longer an option because our families here and back home are paying the price. Every vote counts. As the Emperor in “Mulan” says, “a single grain can tip the scale.”

Let’s vote our pocketbook in November. – Rappler.com



Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

World.title: [OPINYON] Para sa iyo, estudyanteng Inglesero
World.content:
Kailangan natin ang mas maraming magtataguyod ng Filipino hindi lámang sa malikhaing pagsulat at sining. Kailangan natin ng mahuhusay na engineer, mathematician, philosopher, chemist, physicist, at iba pang mga propesyonal na gagamitin ang ating wikang pambansa.

Sorry, dude, pare, chong, bro.

Hindi ako sorry na magfi-Filipino sa pagkausap sa iyo ngayon.

Nabalitaan ko na di na raw ganoong nagfi-Filipino sa maraming pribadong paaralan natin. Kompara noong panahon ko circa early 2000s. Oo, may pinagkatandaan na rin pala ako.

Kailangan ko sigurong mag-under-cover sa mga sumunod na araw para malaman kung totoo talaga itong penomenon na ito na naghari na ang English-Only Policy.

Pero kung totoo talaga ito, una ko nang sasabihin na isang malaking kawalan sa sinumang estudyante kung hindi ka magiging mahusay sa Filipino. Isang bentaha o advantage ang pagiging bilingual. Minimum ang pagiging bilingual. Kayâ magbabahagi lang din ako ng kaunting danas tungkol sa sariling pagtataguyod ng ating wika.

Tulad ninyo, sabi nila, trademark daw ng ilang mga paaralan ang Ingles nila. Narinig ko na ito sa isang kaibigang babae noong undergrad pa ako sa isang paaralan sa España. Siyempre, kapag una mong narinig, ipagmamalaki mo. Wow, may sariling paraan pala kami ng pag-i-Ingles na mahusay.

Pero saan ba táyo nadala ng husay na iyon? Para sa ating tagumpay sa mas mataas na edukasyon? Para makakuha ng magandang trabaho? Para kapag nag-alumni homecoming ay magyayabangan tayo sa isa’t isa at mag-i-Inglesan? Naisip ko ulit na hindi rin naman pala mga konyo ang ka-batch ko. Wagas nga ang pagfi-Filipino namin. Sagad sa buto ang mga mura, biruan, at pangangatwiran.

Sana matanong ninyo rin sa hinaharap para masagot ito: Ingles lámang ba ang makatutulong para maging mabuting mga Filipino táyo ngayon at sa hinaharap?

Samantalang may wika táyo na itinaguyod ng mga nauna sa atin para tugunan iyon: ang maging mas mabuti at mahusay na Filipino.

Bakit? Dahil mas maiintindihan táyo ng mga kapuwa natin kapag ginamit natin ito. Sa trabaho ko bilang mananaliksik ng wika at kultura, nalibot ko na rin ang Filipinas at masasabi ko sa inyo na nagkakaunawaan kami ng kausap ko na Lambangian gáling Magindanaw o Itnëg mulang Abra kapag ginamit namin ang Filipino sa harap ng mga pagkakaiba namin sa wika. At, siyempre, nagtatangka rin akong matutuhan ang mga wika nila kahit kakaunti lámang ang ibinigay na panahon.

Haharapin mo rin ito kapag lumabas ka na rito sa iyong pugad ng pribilehiyo. Malamang magtutungo ka sa unibersidad na default ang wikang Ingles. Tandaan mo, default lang, at puwedeng-puwede mong gamitin pa rin ang wikang pambansa natin. At paglabas sa mga unibersidad patungo sa mga alternatibong unibersidad ng mga pamayanan nating dapat paglingkuran, makikita mo na hindi naman umiikot sa Ingles ang bayan natin.

Kayâ habang bata ka pa, kailangan mong malaman na kailangan natin ang mas maraming magtataguyod ng Filipino hindi lámang sa malikhaing pagsulat at sining. Higit pa rito, kailangan natin ng mahuhusay na engineer, mathematician, philosopher, chemist, physicist, at iba pang mga propesyonal na gagamitin ang ating wikang pambansa.

Pangarap natin kasi iyon sa wika natin, ang maging isang intelektuwalisadong wika tulad ng Ingles, Japanese, Spanish, German, atbpa. Intellectualized kasi ginagamit sa iba’t ibang field para lumikha ng karunungan. Intellectualized kasi araw-araw ginagamit ng mga user nito at hindi lámang tuwing Buwan ng Wika.

Hámon ko po sa iyo ito, estudyanteng Inglesero: magpakahusay ka sa Filipino. At sakâ, kilalanin at aralin mo ang mga wika ng iyong magulang at lolo’t lola na nagsasalita ng Ilokano, Sebwano, Hiligaynon, Ivatan, atbpa. Kayamanan at angat ang pag-iisip ng isang táong hindi lámang isa ang nalalamang wika.

Bakit? Kapag higit sa isang wika, higit sa isang paraan ng pag-iisip at kultura ang nabubuksan sa isip mo. Matututuhan mong hindi lámang pag-iisip ng mga Amerikano o Britong nag-i-Ingles ang umiiral. Mayroon din táyong sarili sa Filipino, meron din táyong maraming magkakaugnay at magkakaibang sarili sa ating 137 katutubong wika.

Kayâ sa pagtatapos, gusto ko lang ding magpugay sa mga naging guro ko sa Filipino sa aking munting paaralan sa Shaw Boulevard na sina Ginang Lumanog at Binibining Rarang. Kasama na rin sina Sir Jepoy at Sir VJ, na nagturo sa akin ng kasaysayan sa sariling wika. Kung babalikan ko nga, dapat mas pinagbuti ko pa sa kanilang klase. Kasi, tulad mo, feel na feel ko rin na sa Ingles lang ako dapat maging magaling dati. – Rappler.com

Sumusulat si Roy Rene S. Cagalingan ng mga tula at sanaysay. Kasapi siya ng Linangan sa Imahen, Retorika, at Anyo (LIRA) at Unyon ng mga Manunulat sa Pilipinas (UMPIL). Naglilingkod siya sa Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (KWF).

World.title: Have P5,000? You can invest in RTB 32 and earn 6.8% per year
World.content:
When the common public purchases these bonds, they are not merely performing a civic duty; they are securing a reliable, wealth-building vehicle to shield their savings from inflation and market volatility.

Last Tuesday, September 29, the Bureau of Treasury (BTr) launched the public offering of its latest retail bond issue, the Retail Treasury Bonds Tranche 32 (RTB-32).

RTB-32 has a term of 2.5 years and features an attractive coupon rate of 6.875% per annum, with interest paid quarterly and subject to a 20% final withholding tax. The auction’s first day had an overwhelming oversubscription, raising P84.9 billion against an initial target of P30 billion.

To allow the high participation of the common public to become investors in the issue, the minimum investment requirement is P5,000 only.

Investors can subscribe over-the-counter through authorized selling banks or digitally via the BTr Online Ordering Facility, the LANDBANK Mobile Banking App, OFBank App, RCBC Pulz, ATRAM apps, PDAX, and GCash via its GBonds platform.

Additionally, investors holding specific older government securities can choose to swap them directly for RTB 32 before the final settlement of this new issue on October 12, 2026.

RTBs are considered powerful and stable, non-inflationary instrument used to fund national budgets, build infrastructure, and manage fiscal deficits. It is also one of the ideal instruments that could help promote financial inclusion and literacy to the general public, many of whom still remain with limited access to mainstream investment services.

In this regard, RTBs were actually the subject of discussion at the Monday Circle’s latest forum. Like always, the subject was given a critical eye on what it has been doing in financing the government and on its role in promoting savings and financial literacy.

Invited as guest speaker for the occasion was Director Robert Dominick “Doms” Mariano, head of the research department of the Bureau of Treasury (BTr). Mariano has more than 15 years of work experience on debt management, government finance, and fiscal programming. He also has an extensive background on national government treasury management, financial market surveillance, risk management, and macroeconomic and fiscal planning.

Historical context

RTBs have gone a long way from a tradeable small-denominated bonds under the “Small Investors Program” in late 1998 into what it is now as a pillar of the country’s national debt management strategy.

Over the last 25 years, RTBs have transitioned from a niche financial inclusion project into a strategic financing instrument for the government. They have become the cornerstone for sovereign fund mobilization or the process by which the government gathers, pools, and deploys its financial resources at the same time serving as a practical, real-world classroom that elevates the financial literacy of the general public.

Today, RTBs are no longer a minor funding source. They consistently make up to roughly 35% of the government’s outstanding domestic debt securities. The government has been intentionally utilizing RTBs to protect the national budget from extreme foreign exchange shocks and global market volatility.

RTBs became a critical crisis-management tool during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government leaned heavily on its RTB-25 and RTB-26 bond issues to strategically raise billions for pandemic response programs and health infrastructure.

Public financial literacy

The regular distribution model of RTBs teaches the mechanics of passive income and cash flow management because RTBs pay out interest on a fixed, quarterly basis. When an ordinary saver receives a direct credit to their account every three months, the concept of “money working for you” transitions from a textbook phrase into a tangible reality.

Moreover, this predictable structure teaches individuals how to budget around recurring income streams, encouraging long-term financial planning over impulsive short-term spending. Thus, RTBs are the perfect beginner tool for financial literacy for the common public.

Again, when the government launches an educational roadshow or a financial literacy webinar to explain how an RTB works, it is not doing it as a formality only. It is actively promoting these bonds to raise the money the country needs.

Conversely, when the common public purchases these bonds, they are not merely performing a civic duty; they are securing a reliable, wealth-building vehicle to shield their savings from inflation and market volatility.

This process creates a chain reaction where one good thing leads to another. As government outreach increases public awareness, the general saving public becomes more financially literate. A more financially literate population, in turn, demands a higher volume of secure, transparent investment products, driving deeper demand for subsequent government bond issuances.

Over time, this collaborative mechanism fosters a robust domestic capital market, reduces the national dependency on foreign debt, and builds a financially resilient society capable of weathering macroeconomic shocks.

Economic bridge

As summarized by Mariano, the RTB program illustrates that sound fiscal policy and public financial empowerment are not competing priorities, but mutually reinforcing pillars of long-term economic development. They are a powerful economic bridge that balances the government’s financial needs with the public’s wealth goals.

By offering a safe, high-yielding alternative to standard savings, RTBs gather scattered public money to fund critical infrastructure. At the same time, they open up the financial world to everyone, transforming the common public into disciplined, smart, and tech-savvy investors. – Rappler.com
