World.title: ANZ drops KPMG as auditor after almost 60 years
World.content:
ANZ has dropped KPMG after almost 60 years of the firm holding the $29.3 million contract to audit the bank’s accounts, in a fresh blow to the consulting firm that continues to contend with the fallout from a damaging whistleblower scandal.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but was given short shrift until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

ANZ has ditched KPMG as its auditors after they worked together since 1969. Bloomberg

That has led to companies including Macquarie Bank ditching KPMG as their auditors in a series of repercussions that escalated on Friday when ANZ announced its board had also decided to open up its contract for tender.

“ANZ’s external audit service has been provided by KPMG since 1969,” a spokesman said. He attributed the bank’s decision to the length of time KPMG had worked with the bank, and did not mention the whistleblower scandal that has led to numerous senior staff leaving and mass layoffs.

World.title: Revealed: Compo for Greene as Cats snare the Giants’ greatest player in free agency coup
World.content:
It’s official. The Giants’ captain and best player is out the door to Geelong.

GWS confirmed on Friday they would receive a second round draft pick as compensation for the 33-year-old, who is an unrestricted free agent.

Toby Greene has played his final game for GWS. Getty Images

“Toby has been an incredible part of this football club for 15 years and we’ll never lose sight of what he’s given to the Giants,” GWS list boss Jason McCartney said.

“While we’re disappointed that his journey with us has come to an end, we’re also incredibly proud of what he achieved and the role he played in helping build this club.

“An inaugural player at the club, Toby arrived at the Giants as a teenager and grew into a remarkable leader who not only performed at the highest level but just as importantly, he helped shape the club into what it is today.

“While again it’s difficult to see him go, we respect Toby’s decision to return home to Victoria and we thank him for the enormous contribution he made to the club.”

World.title: Minister grilled on call to play popular 2032 Olympics matches out of state
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Minister grilled on call to play popular 2032 Olympics matches out of state Dominique Tassell October 2, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Sport Minister Tim Mander has defended the decision to host soccer preliminaries outside Queensland for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games. He confirmed on Friday Sydney and Melbourne would host matches if the sport was locked in for 2032. Queensland Sport Minister Tim Mander, pictured with a piece of the Brisbane 2032 emblems at Wild Horse Mountain Lookout on the Sunshine Coast. Dominique Tassell “As I keep saying all the time, we’ll confirm all those things once the sport’s confirmed, but they’ve always been slated to have football games, yes,” he said. “It’s important we take advantage of the most popular sports, and obviously football is one of the most popular sports and will be the ones that draw the biggest crowds,” he said.



“It’s our commitment to Queenslanders these Games are cost-neutral – to do that we have to make sure we maximise ticket sales on the sports that are the most popular with the public.” Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics How a regional river became the centre of a political storm and international intrigue Mander said venue allocation would be confirmed once the sports program has been approved by the International Olympic Committee, which was expected by the end of the year. He said once approved, the government aimed to finalise the venue plan in the first quarter of 2027. When asked why the matches would not be played at venues in regional Queensland, Mander said the regions would get their share of events and noted Townsville and Sunshine Coast had been earmarked to host matches as well. “I don’t need to run through all the other sports that have already been slated for the regional areas,” he said.



“Our regions will be well and truly serviced by great sports.” Mander then shot down the suggestion that tennis preliminaries would be in Melbourne. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece Olympic soccer has traditionally been spread across an Olympic host nation. For Los Angeles 2028, matches will be in New York, Columbus, San Diego, San Jose, St Louis and Nashville, along with the host city.



The Gabba was redeveloped in the late 1990s so it could host Olympic soccer during the Sydney 2000 Games. Other host cities in 2000 were Melbourne, Adelaide, Canberra and, of course, Sydney. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Fireworks and floating stages: Missy Higgins lights up Sydney Harbour with emotional show
World.content:
Mrs Macquaries Point, October 1

On a balmy night there was a palpable buzz in the air as a legion of loyal fans flocked to see Missy Higgins perform for “the first time” on a floating stage.

Most of us were caught unawares as fireworks boomed over Sydney Harbour from the moment Higgins began her hour-and-a-half-long set, as if to ignite Sydney’s coming calendar of outdoor performances.

Missy Higgins’ unfiltered performance has allowed her to forge a strong bond with her fans. Ben Symons

Twenty-five years into her illustrious career, the pyrotechnics seemed fitting for her performance for the series of concerts dubbed The Point, and her only Sydney show of the year. The display complemented the enchanting openers: the haunting Don’t Ever and an unflinching ballad Edge of Something.

Both laid the groundwork for a nostalgia-laced evening traversing her diverse catalogue, from pop to indie, acoustic folk and dashes of rock and country that have become Higgins’ cross-genre signature sound (along with her endearing Aussie twang).

Higgins crisscrosses genres in a manner that has become her signature sound. Ben Symons

Her defiance of categorisation, and her confidence, even in unguarded moments, are what make Higgins special. A conversational delivery that places raw storytelling and vulnerability at the forefront, both in song and conversation, offers insight into her world.

Throughout the evening, alongside almost unfaltering vocal delivery, this unfiltered style of performance has earned the ARIA Hall of Famer powerful ties with her audience. It’s on full display throughout older tracks, including a still-affecting Everyone’s Waiting and the stirring delivery of The In-Between, the buoyant Craters and the forthright, hymn-like When 4 Became 3 from post-divorce album The Second Act. A crowd-pleasing acoustic rendition of Sabrina Carpenter’s Coincidence had everyone dancing, too.

Higgins performs with emotion. Ben Symons

“A soundtrack to cry to was my service to the world,” quipped Higgins, as she balanced her tear-inducing ballads with self-deprecating wit.

Meanwhile, classics from the gritty The Special Two to the uplifting Scar and also Steer had everyone singing in unison. There was also a big response to the newer Blue Velvet Dress and NYE, a quirky cover she also sang for the ABC’s New Year’s Eve concert in 2021 – the day her marriage effectively ended. It was a full-circle moment for a happier Higgins as fireworks burst once more.

The pyrotechnics were fitting for a set that celebrated the many ways she has made it through tumultuous times, both professionally and personally. And the evening was a testament to the legacy she is still writing – endearingly, unapologetically and authentically.

The Point series of concerts includes The Teskey Brothers on October 2, Hot Dub on the Harbour on November 20 and Harbourlife on November 21.

World.title: The Greens want to catch the Mamdani wave. But can the minor party really become ‘unashamedly populist’?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the first day of this year, at New York’s City Hall, socialist senator Bernie Sanders declared it was time for wealthy corporations to pay their fair share of tax as left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani was sworn in. Mamdani, the charismatic 34-year-old, had come out of nowhere to excite a million New Yorkers into voting for his platform of free childcare, free transport and higher taxes for the rich to foot the bill. The Greens elected hard-left senator David Shoebridge as leader in a rare contested ballot on Wednesday, hoping he will bring fresh energy. Nine A month later, in the United Kingdom, Greens leader Zack Polanski said UK Labour could no longer take progressive voters for granted as his party for the first time seized a seat from the government in a byelection, promising to tax the super rich. The Australian Greens have been saying much the same thing, for most of this year. But in the polls, they’ve gone nowhere. “There’s eternal frustration that we haven’t cracked through more,” says one Greens insider. It’s been a source of head-scratching outside the party, too, as Labor’s vote sinks in the polls while the Greens fail to take a slice. How come the Greens have stalled while One Nation surges? Why, by contrast, have Mamdani and Polanski succeeded? Will the Greens ever crack the ceiling of a 12 per cent share of the federal vote?



These questions were ventilated in the mainstream this week, when Larissa Waters, a well-liked consensus-builder, tendered a shock resignation over her health issues. The party room of 11 MPs elected hard-left senator David Shoebridge in a rare contested ballot. Greens supporters hope that new leadership holds at least some of the answers. The political mood has shifted since last year’s election returned a lousy result for the Greens, who lost three lower house MPs, including party leader Adam Bandt. Inflation and interest rates are again on the rise, Labor is on the nose, and voters are ditching the establishment across the Anglosphere. Waters has kept the party’s vote intact despite turbulence elsewhere, and most people in the Greens emphasise their respect and affection for her. But they believe her leadership has been lacking bite and energy. Outgoing Greens leader Larissa Waters (left) with the new leadership team of Steph Hodgins-May and David Shoebridge on Wednesday. Sam Mooy “Larissa was great in trying to get the best out of others, but that doesn’t lend itself to being a firebrand in the public eyes. She was a good internal leader, but I’m not sure she cut across,” a member close to the NSW Greens says. The party is spying opportunity in this week’s change. Leadership contender senator Sarah Hanson-Young said as much in her pitch to colleagues this week, according to people in the room.



“The Greens have to be able to work with the government to get things done that our voters and supporters want,” says another source in the federal party. “But you have to be able to do that while calling bullshit when you see it. The challenge for David is whether he can do both.” Shoebridge clearly thinks a breakthrough is possible. He wants the Greens vote to be higher, and its influence in parliament to multiply – although he’s not yet set targets. “This is an extraordinary moment in politics, not just in Australia, but across the world,” he says in an interview. “The challenge for the Greens has been connecting with that anger, letting people understand that we see it and we feel it. And directing the political focus, not on migrants or your neighbour from the Philippines is working in the local emergency department, but on the 1 per cent who are driving [inequality].” Shoebridge says the party’s competitive election is evidence of a party “bursting with talent”. Sam Mooy This is already the Greens’ message, though. Pressed again on what’s been missing, Shoebridge says: “I have been hearing people want a party that is going to be out there overtly fighting for them. Going into parliament and rejecting [the status quo and incremental change] loudly, clearly, and directly. “The feedback I’ve been getting about the team that we put together, Steph Hodgins-May and myself, is there is this powerful sense that we have the leadership team connected to a party room that is up for this fight. Look at my political history.”



That was the combative approach of Max Chandler-Mather, the one-term MP and firebrand who is now leading the party’s think-tank, the Green Institute. Both he and Shoebridge have emphasised another missing factor: a grassroots mass movement of everyday Australians. Related Article Political leadership Max Chandler-Mather is back to lead a Greens think-tank. Can he fire up a left-wing movement? “People often ask how to recreate the political success and energy of UK Greens leader, Zack Polanski or New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani,” Chandler-Mather wrote in an open letter to the Greens’ MPs on Tuesday, before the leadership vote. “The recipe for their success doesn’t just lie in their policies, rhetoric or even organising strategy. It lies in the process by which they won their elections.” One way to do that, he argued, was giving all Greens’ members a say in choosing their leader. “We say we want to build a movement ... But if we’re serious about that it means putting real power and trust in the hands of ordinary people – and trusting they will make the right choice,” he says. It didn’t happen this week, but the debate has gained fresh energy. Meanwhile, Chandler-Mather’s Green Institute has been working on the broader project, pulling together research and focus groups to help map the electorate and guide the Greens’ targeting strategy. Core to the vision is a version of the Greens that sets itself apart from Labor and positions itself as an alternative party of government – not a crossbench party that helps the government pass progressive legislation. Shoebridge has indicated this could see a return to a more obstructionist approach to parliament than the past 18 months under Waters.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, a notorious Greens detractor, has rubbished Shoebridge’s vow to replace Labor. “It was somewhat concerning ... at a time when we see a rise of a far right-wing party,” he said this week. “It sounded a lot like some of the people who didn’t win their seats at the House of Representatives election last year.” But the Greens took a different message out of their election result. The party’s 2025 election review, which was not made public, said the party did not do enough to differentiate itself from Labor. Its core campaign message – Keep Dutton out and get Labor to act – failed to make a compelling case for the Greens. Some within the federal party say they railed against the message at the time, but their complaints fell on deaf ears. Expect that to change. The Greens are harnessing the populist language and promises that Mamdani and Polanski have used. “When we say that we want to tax these blood-soaked war profits of our export gas industry ... When we say that we want to put in guardrails and clear laws to stop US billionaire tech bros covering the country with AI data centres like mushrooms, it turns out that’s really popular,” Shoebridge says. “I’m unashamedly populist because our agenda is unashamedly for the 99 per cent.” Not everyone think the Greens should be following in Mamdani or Polanski’s footsteps. Australia’s political environment has typically rewarded centrism – at least until Hanson’s rise, which has not yet been tested at a federal election – and progressive issues are not under attack in the way they have been in the United States.

World.title: Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft Marc McGowan October 2, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A strong group of prospects have separated themselves at the top of next month’s AFL draft. Port Adelaide list boss Jason Cripps revealed this week that Essendon will bid on the Power’s next-generation academy prospect Dougie Cochrane at No.1, but there is plenty of other intrigue in how the top 10 might shake out. Top draft prospects (left to right) Ethan Drever, Cody Walker and Harry Van Hattum. Getty/Michael Howard This is our latest top 30 – but it is not a mock draft – based on performance, potential, injury risk and intangibles, based on discussions with recruiting staff at AFL clubs, junior coaches, and this masthead’s own views. Among those considered but missed out were Ethan Herbert, Billy Wigmore, Xavier Ladbrook, Wil Antrobus, Blake Justice, bolter Jake Soutar and fellow mature-ager Brady Wright, Keenan Boi and Zac Antonellos.



1. Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide NGA) Patella tendonitis, which required surgery, delayed the No.1 pick-elect’s season until August, meaning Cochrane missed the under-18 championships. But he remains the standout prospect. Cochrane can play almost anywhere, is a great athlete, reads the play well, and has sticky hands and sublime skills. After returning in the SANFL as a forward – and being starved of the ball in a 70-point loss to Norwood – he was swung into defence for his last three games with great effect. Cochrane’s penetrating kick was put to use for kick-in duties. 2. Ethan Drever



The do-it-all midfielder, who carried a heavy load at the Rebels, is firming to be Essendon’s first live selection once they place a bid on Port Adelaide’s NGA sensation Cochrane. If so, the chatter about the Bombers’ once-small onball brigade will be no more. Drever would join Sullivan Robey and Dyson Sharp. Drever is big and powerful, puts his body on the line to win the Sherrin, and bursts away from stoppages before driving long kicks inside 50. There are questions about his ball drop, but Drever is universally liked as a prospect. 3. Arki Butler Arki Butler at this week’s draft combine. via Getty Images Butler is believed to be in the mix at Richmond’s selection. He is exquisitely talented, executes kicks others would not dare, has huge upside, and is as footy smart as anyone in the draft class. Butler needs to improve his running to realise his potential, while there are behavioural concerns – but they are not expected to impact his standing. He will mostly make his AFL living as a forward, but could at least pinch-hit at centre bounces. Butler missed time with a collarbone injury, but returned early to captain Brighton Grammar’s premiership.



4. Gus Teixeira Teixeira isn’t the big personality that his Sandy teammate Butler is, but his football speaks loudly. He rocketed into top-five contention with some eye-catching performances at the under-18 championships. Some recruiters think Teixeira has more upside than any player other than Cochrane. He has power and speed, which he puts to use to escape from stoppages, while his creativity and vision make him dangerous with his kicking. Teixeira hasn’t put up numbers as big as others, but there are few doubts he can make it as a midfielder. 5. Heath Mellody



Mellody is one of the year’s big risers. He won the Larke Medal at the under-18 championships before seamlessly transitioning to playing against the WAFL’s best. Mellody was once viewed as a half-back or wing, but proving his onball wares has heightened his reputation. Mellody is a beautiful kick who creates scoring opportunities, is clean at ground level and accelerates out of stoppages. The Tigers could consider him, and most think West Coast would be mad not to snap the local boy up, particularly after he starred against their reserves. 6. Cody Walker (Carlton father-son) Some scouts still rate him as the second-best prospect – raving about his ball-winning ability, toughness and power – whereas others have him further down, largely based on his at-times scratchy kicking and decision-making. Either way, Carlton won’t hesitate to bring Andrew Walker’s son in, and will have the chance to prove people right or wrong. The new draft rules could work in the Blues’ favour, given the bottom-five clubs will all score a start-of-second-round pick if Essendon bid on Dougie Cochrane. In that scenario, Walker could slide a bit. Cody Walker at draft testing. via Getty Images



7. Harry Van Hattum Van Hattum has fans as a top-three prospect, and fits a need for both Essendon and Richmond, but where he is selected is one of this draft’s mysteries. He is a giant of a man, and very athletic and agile for his size, which he makes good use of on the field. Van Hattum won a few scouts over late in the year with his aggression and competitiveness, while his kicking skills are exceptional for a big man. He can impact the game aerially, but could do more of that. Not many ruckmen are taken in the top 10, so it will be interesting to see who pulls the trigger. Harry Van Hattum with AFLW draft prospect Maddison Meagher. Wayne Taylor 8. Ethan Matthews (GWS academy)



Matthews’ limited exposure this year due to a stress reaction in one of his feet is probably the only reason he is this low. There are recruiters who rate him a better prospect than Drever, and rival clubs will want to get a bid in before the Giants’ first pick (currently No.7) to prevent them double-dipping. Matthews has not played since the injury cut his under-18 championships short, but his dazzling form before that has not been forgotten. He wins his own ball – and lots of it – finds space, is a relentless runner, and is creative with his trusty left boot. 9. Mitch Harris Every recruiter who spoke to this masthead ranks Harris as the best key defender in this draft. The jungle drums suggest North Melbourne are considering him at their first selection, while Melbourne could also consider him. Harris reads the ball superbly in the air and his marking in general is a strength, on top of being a strong one-on-one defender who knows when to spoil instead. He performed well in the SANFL seniors late in the season to enhance his draft stock. Harris needs to develop physically, but looks a great prospect with big scope to improve.



10. Caylen Murray (Brisbane Lions academy) Brisbane Lions Academy/Allies

Defender/midfielder, 181cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 16/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 24 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 5.5 contested possessions There is enough love for Murray that he looks a surefire top-10 selection, with some recruiters believing he could attract a bid just outside the top five, which would be a disaster for the Lions. New draft rules make it much harder for a high-performing club such as Brisbane, who must pay a 20 per cent loading after making the grand final and use no more than two selections to match a bid. Murray will likely start as an attacking half-back flanker in the AFL, but can fill various roles with his speed, endurance, evasiveness, neat skills and smarts. 11. Sam Gayfer Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Key forward, 194cm

DOB: 21/5/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 12.4 disposals, 2.3 goals, 7.1 score involvements



Gayfer has established himself as the top key forward available, with both St Kilda and Collingwood believed to be interested. He is physical, tough, aggressive and athletic, uses his body well to take contested grabs, and kicked loads of goals in the Talent League, under-18 championships and for Parade College. Gayfer can be inconsistent, doesn’t always run to the right spots, and his set-shot kicking is a query, but there is lots to like here. His biggest fans see him as a forward, whereas others think he will be more effective as a defender. Sam Gayfer and Lewis Houndsome run the two-kilometre time trial at this week’s draft combine. via Getty Images 12. Wil Malady Malady’s highlights package is as good as anyone’s, and his aerial prowess, speed and general athleticism make him an enticing prospect. The consensus is he sits somewhere just outside the top 10. Malady had some outstanding performances throughout the year, including five goals in the Power’s Talent League grand final win, but recruiters would love to see him win more of the ball. Malady projects primarily as a third-tall forward, but has occasionally been used on a wing and there are scouts who think he could slot in at half-back as well.



13. Clancy Snell Snell was all the rage early in the season and is still a highly touted prospect, but he didn’t finish the year quite as well as he started it. In his favour was a mature VFL performance for Collingwood that was another tick for his draft resume. Snell is an excellent interceptor, his athleticism and height are ideal for a key defender in the AFL, he is cool in a crisis, and he kicks well. Snell was a major reason Gippsland made the Talent League grand final and is one of three tall backmen who could be selected in the first 15 picks. 14. Tyson Bradley Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Key defender, 196cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 12.6 disposals, 3.4 intercept marks, 3.1 rebound 50s



Tyson Bradley at the draft combine. via Getty Images Bradley’s draft stock is only going up. Vic Metro’s MVP award-winner had to win over critics who pointed to his lack of speed, agility and athleticism, but they can’t argue with his track record. Significant for Bradley was the job he did in the Talent League finals on fellow first-round prospect Sam Gayfer, who was viewed as a test of his limitations. He is highly intelligent, already physically strong, and makes up for his athletic shortcomings with outstanding footwork and positioning. Melbourne are one club monitoring him around this area of the draft. 15. Lochie Burrows Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Utility, 181cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 15 disposals, 3.6 inside 50s, 1.2 goals Burrows is rising fast, with St Kilda believed to be among the clubs tracking him closely. His numbers might not leap off the page, but it is easy to see him succeeding in the AFL with his athletic traits, work ethic and versatility. Burrows had not played down back until this year’s under-18 championships, but his performances opened a few eyes and even saw him used in the same role for the Dragons in the finals. He can leap for marks up forward, run through the midfield or even do a job in defence, so expect him to be snapped up pretty early.



Lochie Burrows competes in the time trial. via Getty Images 16. Leo Steed Swan Districts/Western Australia

Midfielder, 177cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 7/3/2008

WAFL League stats (averages): 14.3 disposals, 5.8 contested possessions, 3.7 tackles Steed is as reliable as they come, and a safe pick in this section of the draft. He might even go earlier, and it will be interesting to see if West Coast or Fremantle trade up for him. Steed is a busy player around stoppages, unafraid to burrow into traffic, loves to tackle, and makes quick and good decisions, particularly by hand. Clubs are increasingly turning to bigger-bodied midfielders, so Steed does not fit that mould, but needs only to look at the likes of Lachie Neale, Touk Miller, Dion Prestia and Zach Merrett for inspiration. 17. Toby Krasna



Related Article Explainer

Draft Talent is just the start. What do footy recruiters look for in young players? Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Wingman, 181cm

DOB: 28/2/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 21.3 disposals, 4.2 inside 50s, 5.1 score involvements Another interesting name to follow. A hamstring injury sidelined Krasna at the end of a breakout under-18 championships, but he was an impressive performer in more of an inside midfield role once he did return, including 13 clearances across his last two matches. Krasna is on track to be a top-20 selection, and could end up closer to 10 than 20. He might be slight, but is willing to get his hands dirty, difficult to tackle, quick, a good decision-maker and regular goalkicker, so don’t be surprised if he keeps pushing up. 18. Gabe Patterson Glenelg/South Australia

Forward, 185cm

DOB: 26/3/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 18 disposals, 1.8 goals, 6.8 score involvements



There was lots of hype about Patterson entering the season – and even top-10 draft projections – but much of this year did not materialise how he hoped. A key reason was a shoulder injury that derailed the first half of his campaign. Patterson showed glimpses of his upside as a dynamic forward at the national championships, but it was afterwards in the SANFL that he reminded everyone of his ability, including 23 disposals and two goals in the under-18s grand final. He is quick, slippery in traffic, has a nice leap, neat skills and kicks some brilliant goals. 19. Jake Eime Central District/South Australia

Defender, 183cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 29/7/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 22.3 disposals, 3.6 rebound 50s, 4.2 intercept possessions Eime is a prototypical running defender who might also spend time on a wing in the AFL. He accelerates quickly, is shifty with the ball, takes opponents on and his kicking has improved. Eime made his case as a potential first-round selection with an impressive national championships, but probably didn’t finish the season quite as strongly as he started it. Like some others in this section of the draft, his range is somewhere between 15 and 25. Fremantle are one club believed to be considering him. 20. Jack Pickett



Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Key forward, 193cm

DOB: 6/3/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 5 disposals, 3 marks, 2 goals What might have been. A season-ending knee injury in April at a Falcons training session changed the course of Pickett’s draft year – and any hope of him being a top-10 selection. Recruiters are now torn on what to do with him, weighing up the risk versus reward he presents. Pickett is often likened to Jack Gunston and Logan Morris as a forward of similar height with good football IQ and craft, and an ability to create separation who is an accurate set-shot kick. He can play a one-out role closer to goal or roam further afield. 21. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) Western Jets/Vic Metro

Forward, 176cm

DOB: 4/7/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 17.9 disposals, 2.9 goals, 3.1 tackles The Bulldogs can theoretically match any bid on El Souki, but so much depends on what happens with incoming superstar Zak Butters and whether they will still have the necessary draft collateral. El Souki missed most of the under-18 championships recovering from a broken ankle, but rebounded to lead the Talent League in goals during the home-and-away season. He is richly talented, powerful, plays with aggression – look out if he tackles you – and has a wonderful goal sense, but does need to improve his running.



22. George Dimer Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Forward, 173cm

DOB: 21/6/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 14.7 disposals, 1.4 goals, 3 tackles Does Dimer’s lack of height even matter anymore? Not everyone can be Nick Watson – and no one suggests Dimer is at his level or a replica of his style – but the Hawks star has paved the way for pint-sized forwards. The Sandringham product has fast feet, is clean at ground level, a creative handballer and seems well suited to the demands of playing the high half-forward role in the AFL. He was also Haileybury College’s school and football captain, and would add leadership and high-end character to whichever club he ends up at. 23. Jackson Phillips Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

Midfielder, 184cm

DOB: 30/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 19.4 disposals, 3.5 inside 50s, 2.8 clearances



Phillips’ good is really good, and he is one of the most skilful players – with both feet – in the draft pool, but recruiters often report wanting to see more from him. He can play on the inside and outside as a midfielder, although he spent the under-18 championships on a wing, in part because of perceived deficiencies in the contest. Some scouts envision him as a midfielder-forward and want to see him put his kicking to better use in the forward half in creating scoring opportunities. 24. Noah Williams Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Midfielder/defender, 176cm

DOB: 22/1/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 21 disposals, 5 clearances, 7.8 tackles Williams is no longer in top-10 contention, and may not even be a first-round pick, after an injury-interrupted season, but he is versatile enough to play in the midfield, across half-back or possibly as a pressure forward. He is small in stature, but quick, tough, competitive, loves to tackle and mostly uses the ball well on his left boot. Williams co-captained Vic Country with Cody Walker and has a reputation as a hard-working and popular teammate. 25. Harvie Cooke



Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Midfielder/forward, 176cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 14/4/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 24.7 disposals, 5.4 inside 50s, 5.9 clearances Not every club rates Cooke in the top 30, but he won most recruiters over with his consistently strong performance, athletic profile, work ethic and forward craft, including being a good mark overhead, particularly for his size. He played a lot through the midfield as a junior, but the expectation is most of his AFL minutes will be in attack while pinch-hitting in the centre. Cooke’s critics query how effective he will be at the top level and whether there is a role for him. 26. Koby LeCras Koby LeCras. via Getty Images West Perth/Western Australia

Forward, 193cm

DOB: 26/4/2008

U18 WAFL stats (averages): 19 disposals, 6 marks, 1 goal



LeCras was viewed as a likely first-round selection entering the season, but similar to fellow tall forward Jack Pickett, a knee injury ruined his plans. He suffered a partially torn ACL while making his WAFL senior debut in April and was not sighted again, but his early season form was strong, including a three-goal effort for the AFL Academy against Richmond’s VFL team. LeCras also recorded a good result in the two-kilometre time trial at this week’s draft combine, but recruiters are keen to see his medical report before making a call on him. 27. Kodah Edwards South Adelaide/South Australia

Midfielder/forward, 184cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 25/7/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 23.5 disposals, 5.5 clearances, 5.2 tackles Another polarising prospect who some scouts wouldn’t draft at all, while others like him more than this ranking. Edwards captained South Australia at the under-18 championships, where he was a consistent performer, and he rounded out his season by playing and acquitting himself well at senior SANFL level. He is not a great athlete or runner, and the suspicion is he will need to make it as a forward to be a successful AFL footballer. Edwards has shown he can be an impact forward who values defence. 28. George Gale



Related Article Draft How Essendon’s plan for pick No.1 is going to help bitter rivals Carlton Claremont/Western Australia

Midfielder, 190cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 6/9/2008

He graduated to WAFL seniors late in the season and handled the step-up in standard. The general belief is Gale will find a role for himself at the next level and maximise his talents, given his running ability, professionalism and work ethic. 29. Under-18 All-Australian

World.title: ‘Women home alone’: Sydney home invasion gang stopped en route to alleged third attack
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime ‘Women home alone’: Sydney home invasion gang stopped en route to alleged third attack Amber Schultz and Riley Walter Updated October 2, 2026 — 12:51pm ,first published 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A trio of men who allegedly violently physically and sexually assaulted two women in separate home invasions in Sydney’s south-west were captured while on their way to attack a third, police allege. The three men, aged 18, 19 and 20, have been charged with offences ranging from breaking and entering, depriving a person of liberty, choking and rape after allegedly breaking into two women’s homes and attacking them. Sex Crime Squad Detective Superintendent Virginia Gorman said on Friday police believed the men had “specifically targeted” the women after conducting research. Gorman labelled the alleged attacks as “planned” and “excessively violent”. The men were allegedly armed with a knife and duct taped the women’s mouths before punching and assaulting the first woman, and sexually assaulting the second. “The violence was over the top … against vulnerable women home alone,” Gorman said.



As local detectives and officers from the sex crimes squad investigated the two alleged assaults, which occurred four weeks apart in Bankstown and Arncliffe, they became aware of a potential third attack, Gorman said, and intervened. ‘“The violence was over the top … against vulnerable women home alone’ Detective Virginia Gorman “We believe that they were on their way to target another person potentially last night, and we’ll be further investigating that matter,” she said. “We were very concerned about the level of violence, and we had to take the [alleged] offenders out as soon as possible.” Detectives believe the trio targeted the women, who are sex workers, because they believed they would have cash at their homes, and may be hesitant to report the alleged assault to police.



The men allegedly forced their way into a unit on Jacobs Street, Bankstown, just after midnight on September 1, 2026, where they allegedly assaulted a 32-year-old woman and stole money. A month later, on Tuesday, the three men allegedly forced their way into a second woman’s home on Marinea Street in Arncliffe, allegedly threatening a 31-year-old with a knife and stealing money. The 19-year-old allegedly twice sexually assaulted her as the other two allegedly robbed her. Both women were taken to hospital for treatment of minor injuries. On Thursday, strike force detectives, alongside Public Order and Riot Squad, Southwest Metropolitan Operations Support Group, and local police, executed three search warrants in Belmore, Punchbowl, and Greenacre. Chawkat Ibrahim El Cheikh, 20, was arrested in Belmore and taken to Burwood Police Station, where he was charged with aggravated break and enter and deprivation of liberty, aggravated robbery and deprivation of liberty, two counts of choke person intent to commit an indictable offence, common assault and use of an offensive weapon in company with intent to commit an indictable offence.



He was refused bail to appear at Burwood Local Court on Friday. Arman Nangyal,19, was arrested in Punchbowl and taken to Campsie Police Station, where he was charged with aggravated break and enter and deprivation of liberty, two counts of choking a person with intent to commit an indictable offence, two counts of aggravated sex assault-deprivation of liberty, aggravated robbery and deprivation of liberty, common assault, use of an offensive weapon in company with intent to commit an indictable offence and fail to comply with a digital evidence access order direction. Adam Fakhouri,18, was arrested in Greenacre and taken to Bankstown Police Station, where he was charged with aggravated break and deprivation of liberty, aggravated robbery and deprivation of liberty, two counts of choking a person with intent to commit an indictable offence, common assault and use of an offensive weapon in company with intent to commit an indictable offence. Fakhouri and Nangyal were refused bail to appear at Bankstown Local Court on Friday. Nangyal was on conditional release at the time of the alleged offences. In June, he had been found guilty of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in the company of others and destroying or damaging property, but no conviction was recorded. He was issued an 18-month conditional release order.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491

World.title: Lamarre-Condon’s holiday video with Jesse Baird revealed
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon’s holiday video with Jesse Baird revealed Michaela Whitbourn Updated October 2, 2026 — 12:45pm ,first published October 2, 2026 — 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beau Lamarre-Condon made a seemingly romantic video of him with Jesse Baird and texted two different versions of it to a friend about a year before he allegedly murdered the former Network Ten producer and presenter, a court has heard. The video was released by the NSW Supreme Court after it was shown to the jury in former police officer Lamarre-Condon’s trial over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, and Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies, 29. Loading Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering the couple in Baird’s Paddington share house on the morning of February 19, 2024. The court heard that the accused, then a NSW police officer, texted his colleague Alexandra Scobie two versions of the video of him and Baird in March 2023.



Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial The 1600-word text accused killer allegedly sent to fake a cancer diagnosis “I’m sending you these two videos because we need to discuss them tomorrow haha,” he texted at 7.32pm on March 26, 2023. “Below, two very different edits.” Crown prosecutor Caitlin Diggins asked Scobie if she understood Lamarre-Condon “wanted your feedback on which edit he should post online, and to the world at large, about Jesse?” “That’s how it read, yes,” Scobie said. Scobie agreed that in part of the video the accused appeared to be filming Baird while he was asleep.



“Did the accused tell you whether or not Jesse had any input in this video?” Diggins asked. “Not that I can recall,” Scobie said. The video was tendered in evidence by the defence and played to the 15-person jury on Thursday. A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW Supreme Court. Rocco Fazzari Scobie, a plain clothes senior constable working in criminal investigations, said under cross-examination by Lamarre-Condon’s barrister, John Stratton, SC, that she did not specifically remember the accused sending her a clip of a holiday he had with Baird in the country.



After the video was played in court, Scobie said the only thing she recognised from it was the bed. During re-examination by the Crown, Diggins took Scobie to the texts Lamarre-Condon had sent along with two versions of the clip. “Do you recall these videos actually had a soundtrack playing over the top of them?” Diggins asked. “I believe there would have been a soundtrack he would have sent,” Scobie said, adding that it was common for the accused to post videos with songs. “The accused clipped together a lot of little videos and stitched them all together?” Diggins said.



“That’s my understanding from that video, yes,” Scobie said. Loading She did not remember discussing the videos, or whether he posted them online. The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird with his police-issued pistol after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023. Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, was killed to eliminate a witness to the crime, the Crown alleges.



There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon was at the terrace when Baird and Davies died, that they died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol, and that he was disguised as a delivery rider. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Housemate’s startling discovery at alleged Lamarre-Condon crime scene However, the defence case is that Lamarre-Condon was there to pick up some of his belongings and did not expect anybody to be home. A struggle ensued in which his gun accidentally went off twice, killing Baird, and Davies accidentally shot himself in a second struggle after grabbing the gun, the defence says. Scobie gave evidence on Thursday that the accused was angry with Baird in early 2024 “because he was sleeping with Luke”. She said he asked her later if hire cars could be tracked, before adding something like: “Don’t freak out, I’m just asking.” He called her that evening and assured her he was “not going to do anything illegal”, she told the court.



The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon sent a series of text messages to Baird’s housemates’ group chat on February 20, the day after his death, to give the false impression he was still alive. On Friday, former NSW police officer Ben Higginson gave evidence that he discussed the 2023 murder of Sydneysider Lilie James with Lamarre-Condon, including that police believed James’ killer, her ex-boyfriend Paul Thijssen, used her phone to text her father after her death. Higginson said Lamarre-Condon seemed “pretty blase” in the conversation on February 18, 2024, the day before the alleged murders, and had said Thijssen was “stupid for doing this on CCTV”. Lamarre-Condon also asked him if Thijssen “would ... have got away with it” if he had not died by suicide, Higginson said.



The court has heard Baird’s housemates, dubbed Belinda Smith and Sarah King in the proceedings, had asked Baird to move out earlier that year so that a female friend could move in. He was slated to move out on February 20. “Hi both!! I’ve hired an air tasker to come and collect my things … I might be doing a road trip to Perth with mates on Thursday night so should be flying back Sunday and will 100% have it out by then,” read a message from Baird’s phone at 12.28pm on February 20. Smith replied: “Hey Jesse, sorry I’m a bit confused. I thought you said you were moving out today 20th Feb. Your final rent payment ends tomorrow and [the new housemate] starts paying from Thursday.” Smith texted King on February 20: “I’m genuinely scared this dude isn’t moving out today.” At 5.56pm on February 19, hours after the alleged murders, Smith texted King a photo of what she believed to be “rusted water” near surfboard bags and a tarpaulin in the courtyard of the home to another housemate.



Related Article Graphic content

Lamarre-Condon trial The bullet hole and the cartridge case: Images of alleged Lamarre-Condon crime scene revealed The second housemate, known as Sarah King in the case, replied: “What the actual f---?” King told the court on Friday she had poked either the surfboard bag or the tarp, and “it just sounded like a tarp”. Smith told the court on Thursday that she inspected the backyard again the following day and “saw that the surfboards had been cleared, and the liquid was gone”. The prosecution has told the jury that Lamarre-Condon cleaned the scene while the housemates were out, including throwing items from Baird’s bedroom into a skip bin in Cronulla.



The court has heard that police visited the home for the first time on February 21, after items were found in the skip bin by groundskeepers. Three cleaners were at the home at the time because they had been booked by King ahead of the arrival of the new housemate. The trial continues.
