World.title: ANZ drops KPMG as auditor after almost 60 years
World.content:
ANZ has dropped KPMG after almost 60 years of the firm holding the $29.3 million contract to audit the bank’s accounts, in a fresh blow to the consulting firm that continues to contend with the fallout from a damaging whistleblower scandal.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but was given short shrift until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

ANZ has ditched KPMG as its auditors after they worked together since 1969. Bloomberg

That has led to companies including Macquarie Bank ditching KPMG as their auditors in a series of repercussions that escalated on Friday when ANZ announced its board had also decided to open up its contract for tender.

“ANZ’s external audit service has been provided by KPMG since 1969,” a spokesman said. He attributed the bank’s decision to the length of time KPMG had worked with the bank, and did not mention the whistleblower scandal that has led to numerous senior staff leaving and mass layoffs.

World.title: Revealed: Compo for Greene as Cats snare the Giants’ greatest player in free agency coup
World.content:
It’s official. The Giants’ captain and best player is out the door to Geelong.

GWS confirmed on Friday they would receive a second round draft pick as compensation for the 33-year-old, who is an unrestricted free agent.

Toby Greene has played his final game for GWS. Getty Images

“Toby has been an incredible part of this football club for 15 years and we’ll never lose sight of what he’s given to the Giants,” GWS list boss Jason McCartney said.

“While we’re disappointed that his journey with us has come to an end, we’re also incredibly proud of what he achieved and the role he played in helping build this club.

“An inaugural player at the club, Toby arrived at the Giants as a teenager and grew into a remarkable leader who not only performed at the highest level but just as importantly, he helped shape the club into what it is today.

“While again it’s difficult to see him go, we respect Toby’s decision to return home to Victoria and we thank him for the enormous contribution he made to the club.”

World.title: Minister grilled on call to play popular 2032 Olympics matches out of state
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Minister grilled on call to play popular 2032 Olympics matches out of state Dominique Tassell October 2, 2026 — 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Sport Minister Tim Mander has defended the decision to host soccer preliminaries outside Queensland for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games. He confirmed on Friday Sydney and Melbourne would host matches if the sport was locked in for 2032. Queensland Sport Minister Tim Mander, pictured with a piece of the Brisbane 2032 emblems at Wild Horse Mountain Lookout on the Sunshine Coast. Dominique Tassell “As I keep saying all the time, we’ll confirm all those things once the sport’s confirmed, but they’ve always been slated to have football games, yes,” he said. “It’s important we take advantage of the most popular sports, and obviously football is one of the most popular sports and will be the ones that draw the biggest crowds,” he said.



“It’s our commitment to Queenslanders these Games are cost-neutral – to do that we have to make sure we maximise ticket sales on the sports that are the most popular with the public.” Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics How a regional river became the centre of a political storm and international intrigue Mander said venue allocation would be confirmed once the sports program has been approved by the International Olympic Committee, which was expected by the end of the year. He said once approved, the government aimed to finalise the venue plan in the first quarter of 2027. When asked why the matches would not be played at venues in regional Queensland, Mander said the regions would get their share of events and noted Townsville and Sunshine Coast had been earmarked to host matches as well. “I don’t need to run through all the other sports that have already been slated for the regional areas,” he said.



“Our regions will be well and truly serviced by great sports.” Mander then shot down the suggestion that tennis preliminaries would be in Melbourne. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘A toothpick?’ Brisbane 2032 emblems design riddle deepens with new piece Olympic soccer has traditionally been spread across an Olympic host nation. For Los Angeles 2028, matches will be in New York, Columbus, San Diego, San Jose, St Louis and Nashville, along with the host city.



The Gabba was redeveloped in the late 1990s so it could host Olympic soccer during the Sydney 2000 Games. Other host cities in 2000 were Melbourne, Adelaide, Canberra and, of course, Sydney. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Fireworks and floating stages: Missy Higgins lights up Sydney Harbour with emotional show
World.content:
Mrs Macquaries Point, October 1

On a balmy night there was a palpable buzz in the air as a legion of loyal fans flocked to see Missy Higgins perform for “the first time” on a floating stage.

Most of us were caught unawares as fireworks boomed over Sydney Harbour from the moment Higgins began her hour-and-a-half-long set, as if to ignite Sydney’s coming calendar of outdoor performances.

Missy Higgins’ unfiltered performance has allowed her to forge a strong bond with her fans. Ben Symons

Twenty-five years into her illustrious career, the pyrotechnics seemed fitting for her performance for the series of concerts dubbed The Point, and her only Sydney show of the year. The display complemented the enchanting openers: the haunting Don’t Ever and an unflinching ballad Edge of Something.

Both laid the groundwork for a nostalgia-laced evening traversing her diverse catalogue, from pop to indie, acoustic folk and dashes of rock and country that have become Higgins’ cross-genre signature sound (along with her endearing Aussie twang).

Higgins crisscrosses genres in a manner that has become her signature sound. Ben Symons

Her defiance of categorisation, and her confidence, even in unguarded moments, are what make Higgins special. A conversational delivery that places raw storytelling and vulnerability at the forefront, both in song and conversation, offers insight into her world.

Throughout the evening, alongside almost unfaltering vocal delivery, this unfiltered style of performance has earned the ARIA Hall of Famer powerful ties with her audience. It’s on full display throughout older tracks, including a still-affecting Everyone’s Waiting and the stirring delivery of The In-Between, the buoyant Craters and the forthright, hymn-like When 4 Became 3 from post-divorce album The Second Act. A crowd-pleasing acoustic rendition of Sabrina Carpenter’s Coincidence had everyone dancing, too.

Higgins performs with emotion. Ben Symons

“A soundtrack to cry to was my service to the world,” quipped Higgins, as she balanced her tear-inducing ballads with self-deprecating wit.

Meanwhile, classics from the gritty The Special Two to the uplifting Scar and also Steer had everyone singing in unison. There was also a big response to the newer Blue Velvet Dress and NYE, a quirky cover she also sang for the ABC’s New Year’s Eve concert in 2021 – the day her marriage effectively ended. It was a full-circle moment for a happier Higgins as fireworks burst once more.

The pyrotechnics were fitting for a set that celebrated the many ways she has made it through tumultuous times, both professionally and personally. And the evening was a testament to the legacy she is still writing – endearingly, unapologetically and authentically.

The Point series of concerts includes The Teskey Brothers on October 2, Hot Dub on the Harbour on November 20 and Harbourlife on November 21.

World.title: The Greens want to catch the Mamdani wave. But can the minor party really become ‘unashamedly populist’?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the first day of this year, at New York’s City Hall, socialist senator Bernie Sanders declared it was time for wealthy corporations to pay their fair share of tax as left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani was sworn in. Mamdani, the charismatic 34-year-old, had come out of nowhere to excite a million New Yorkers into voting for his platform of free childcare, free transport and higher taxes for the rich to foot the bill. The Greens elected hard-left senator David Shoebridge as leader in a rare contested ballot on Wednesday, hoping he will bring fresh energy. Nine A month later, in the United Kingdom, Greens leader Zack Polanski said UK Labour could no longer take progressive voters for granted as his party for the first time seized a seat from the government in a byelection, promising to tax the super rich. The Australian Greens have been saying much the same thing, for most of this year. But in the polls, they’ve gone nowhere. “There’s eternal frustration that we haven’t cracked through more,” says one Greens insider. It’s been a source of head-scratching outside the party, too, as Labor’s vote sinks in the polls while the Greens fail to take a slice. How come the Greens have stalled while One Nation surges? Why, by contrast, have Mamdani and Polanski succeeded? Will the Greens ever crack the ceiling of a 12 per cent share of the federal vote?



These questions were ventilated in the mainstream this week, when Larissa Waters, a well-liked consensus-builder, tendered a shock resignation over her health issues. The party room of 11 MPs elected hard-left senator David Shoebridge in a rare contested ballot. Greens supporters hope that new leadership holds at least some of the answers. The political mood has shifted since last year’s election returned a lousy result for the Greens, who lost three lower house MPs, including party leader Adam Bandt. Inflation and interest rates are again on the rise, Labor is on the nose, and voters are ditching the establishment across the Anglosphere. Waters has kept the party’s vote intact despite turbulence elsewhere, and most people in the Greens emphasise their respect and affection for her. But they believe her leadership has been lacking bite and energy. Outgoing Greens leader Larissa Waters (left) with the new leadership team of Steph Hodgins-May and David Shoebridge on Wednesday. Sam Mooy “Larissa was great in trying to get the best out of others, but that doesn’t lend itself to being a firebrand in the public eyes. She was a good internal leader, but I’m not sure she cut across,” a member close to the NSW Greens says. The party is spying opportunity in this week’s change. Leadership contender senator Sarah Hanson-Young said as much in her pitch to colleagues this week, according to people in the room.



“The Greens have to be able to work with the government to get things done that our voters and supporters want,” says another source in the federal party. “But you have to be able to do that while calling bullshit when you see it. The challenge for David is whether he can do both.” Shoebridge clearly thinks a breakthrough is possible. He wants the Greens vote to be higher, and its influence in parliament to multiply – although he’s not yet set targets. “This is an extraordinary moment in politics, not just in Australia, but across the world,” he says in an interview. “The challenge for the Greens has been connecting with that anger, letting people understand that we see it and we feel it. And directing the political focus, not on migrants or your neighbour from the Philippines is working in the local emergency department, but on the 1 per cent who are driving [inequality].” Shoebridge says the party’s competitive election is evidence of a party “bursting with talent”. Sam Mooy This is already the Greens’ message, though. Pressed again on what’s been missing, Shoebridge says: “I have been hearing people want a party that is going to be out there overtly fighting for them. Going into parliament and rejecting [the status quo and incremental change] loudly, clearly, and directly. “The feedback I’ve been getting about the team that we put together, Steph Hodgins-May and myself, is there is this powerful sense that we have the leadership team connected to a party room that is up for this fight. Look at my political history.”



That was the combative approach of Max Chandler-Mather, the one-term MP and firebrand who is now leading the party’s think-tank, the Green Institute. Both he and Shoebridge have emphasised another missing factor: a grassroots mass movement of everyday Australians. Related Article Political leadership Max Chandler-Mather is back to lead a Greens think-tank. Can he fire up a left-wing movement? “People often ask how to recreate the political success and energy of UK Greens leader, Zack Polanski or New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani,” Chandler-Mather wrote in an open letter to the Greens’ MPs on Tuesday, before the leadership vote. “The recipe for their success doesn’t just lie in their policies, rhetoric or even organising strategy. It lies in the process by which they won their elections.” One way to do that, he argued, was giving all Greens’ members a say in choosing their leader. “We say we want to build a movement ... But if we’re serious about that it means putting real power and trust in the hands of ordinary people – and trusting they will make the right choice,” he says. It didn’t happen this week, but the debate has gained fresh energy. Meanwhile, Chandler-Mather’s Green Institute has been working on the broader project, pulling together research and focus groups to help map the electorate and guide the Greens’ targeting strategy. Core to the vision is a version of the Greens that sets itself apart from Labor and positions itself as an alternative party of government – not a crossbench party that helps the government pass progressive legislation. Shoebridge has indicated this could see a return to a more obstructionist approach to parliament than the past 18 months under Waters.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, a notorious Greens detractor, has rubbished Shoebridge’s vow to replace Labor. “It was somewhat concerning ... at a time when we see a rise of a far right-wing party,” he said this week. “It sounded a lot like some of the people who didn’t win their seats at the House of Representatives election last year.” But the Greens took a different message out of their election result. The party’s 2025 election review, which was not made public, said the party did not do enough to differentiate itself from Labor. Its core campaign message – Keep Dutton out and get Labor to act – failed to make a compelling case for the Greens. Some within the federal party say they railed against the message at the time, but their complaints fell on deaf ears. Expect that to change. The Greens are harnessing the populist language and promises that Mamdani and Polanski have used. “When we say that we want to tax these blood-soaked war profits of our export gas industry ... When we say that we want to put in guardrails and clear laws to stop US billionaire tech bros covering the country with AI data centres like mushrooms, it turns out that’s really popular,” Shoebridge says. “I’m unashamedly populist because our agenda is unashamedly for the 99 per cent.” Not everyone think the Greens should be following in Mamdani or Polanski’s footsteps. Australia’s political environment has typically rewarded centrism – at least until Hanson’s rise, which has not yet been tested at a federal election – and progressive issues are not under attack in the way they have been in the United States.

World.title: Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Exquisitely talented, daring, smart: This Brighton Grammar footy captain is shaking up the draft Marc McGowan October 2, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A strong group of prospects have separated themselves at the top of next month’s AFL draft. Port Adelaide list boss Jason Cripps revealed this week that Essendon will bid on the Power’s next-generation academy prospect Dougie Cochrane at No.1, but there is plenty of other intrigue in how the top 10 might shake out. Top draft prospects (left to right) Ethan Drever, Cody Walker and Harry Van Hattum. Getty/Michael Howard This is our latest top 30 – but it is not a mock draft – based on performance, potential, injury risk and intangibles, based on discussions with recruiting staff at AFL clubs, junior coaches, and this masthead’s own views. Among those considered but missed out were Ethan Herbert, Billy Wigmore, Xavier Ladbrook, Wil Antrobus, Blake Justice, bolter Jake Soutar and fellow mature-ager Brady Wright, Keenan Boi and Zac Antonellos.



1. Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide NGA) Patella tendonitis, which required surgery, delayed the No.1 pick-elect’s season until August, meaning Cochrane missed the under-18 championships. But he remains the standout prospect. Cochrane can play almost anywhere, is a great athlete, reads the play well, and has sticky hands and sublime skills. After returning in the SANFL as a forward – and being starved of the ball in a 70-point loss to Norwood – he was swung into defence for his last three games with great effect. Cochrane’s penetrating kick was put to use for kick-in duties. 2. Ethan Drever



The do-it-all midfielder, who carried a heavy load at the Rebels, is firming to be Essendon’s first live selection once they place a bid on Port Adelaide’s NGA sensation Cochrane. If so, the chatter about the Bombers’ once-small onball brigade will be no more. Drever would join Sullivan Robey and Dyson Sharp. Drever is big and powerful, puts his body on the line to win the Sherrin, and bursts away from stoppages before driving long kicks inside 50. There are questions about his ball drop, but Drever is universally liked as a prospect. 3. Arki Butler Arki Butler at this week’s draft combine. via Getty Images Butler is believed to be in the mix at Richmond’s selection. He is exquisitely talented, executes kicks others would not dare, has huge upside, and is as footy smart as anyone in the draft class. Butler needs to improve his running to realise his potential, while there are behavioural concerns – but they are not expected to impact his standing. He will mostly make his AFL living as a forward, but could at least pinch-hit at centre bounces. Butler missed time with a collarbone injury, but returned early to captain Brighton Grammar’s premiership.



4. Gus Teixeira Teixeira isn’t the big personality that his Sandy teammate Butler is, but his football speaks loudly. He rocketed into top-five contention with some eye-catching performances at the under-18 championships. Some recruiters think Teixeira has more upside than any player other than Cochrane. He has power and speed, which he puts to use to escape from stoppages, while his creativity and vision make him dangerous with his kicking. Teixeira hasn’t put up numbers as big as others, but there are few doubts he can make it as a midfielder. 5. Heath Mellody



Mellody is one of the year’s big risers. He won the Larke Medal at the under-18 championships before seamlessly transitioning to playing against the WAFL’s best. Mellody was once viewed as a half-back or wing, but proving his onball wares has heightened his reputation. Mellody is a beautiful kick who creates scoring opportunities, is clean at ground level and accelerates out of stoppages. The Tigers could consider him, and most think West Coast would be mad not to snap the local boy up, particularly after he starred against their reserves. 6. Cody Walker (Carlton father-son) Some scouts still rate him as the second-best prospect – raving about his ball-winning ability, toughness and power – whereas others have him further down, largely based on his at-times scratchy kicking and decision-making. Either way, Carlton won’t hesitate to bring Andrew Walker’s son in, and will have the chance to prove people right or wrong. The new draft rules could work in the Blues’ favour, given the bottom-five clubs will all score a start-of-second-round pick if Essendon bid on Dougie Cochrane. In that scenario, Walker could slide a bit. Cody Walker at draft testing. via Getty Images



7. Harry Van Hattum Van Hattum has fans as a top-three prospect, and fits a need for both Essendon and Richmond, but where he is selected is one of this draft’s mysteries. He is a giant of a man, and very athletic and agile for his size, which he makes good use of on the field. Van Hattum won a few scouts over late in the year with his aggression and competitiveness, while his kicking skills are exceptional for a big man. He can impact the game aerially, but could do more of that. Not many ruckmen are taken in the top 10, so it will be interesting to see who pulls the trigger. Harry Van Hattum with AFLW draft prospect Maddison Meagher. Wayne Taylor 8. Ethan Matthews (GWS academy)



Matthews’ limited exposure this year due to a stress reaction in one of his feet is probably the only reason he is this low. There are recruiters who rate him a better prospect than Drever, and rival clubs will want to get a bid in before the Giants’ first pick (currently No.7) to prevent them double-dipping. Matthews has not played since the injury cut his under-18 championships short, but his dazzling form before that has not been forgotten. He wins his own ball – and lots of it – finds space, is a relentless runner, and is creative with his trusty left boot. 9. Mitch Harris Every recruiter who spoke to this masthead ranks Harris as the best key defender in this draft. The jungle drums suggest North Melbourne are considering him at their first selection, while Melbourne could also consider him. Harris reads the ball superbly in the air and his marking in general is a strength, on top of being a strong one-on-one defender who knows when to spoil instead. He performed well in the SANFL seniors late in the season to enhance his draft stock. Harris needs to develop physically, but looks a great prospect with big scope to improve.



10. Caylen Murray (Brisbane Lions academy) Brisbane Lions Academy/Allies

Defender/midfielder, 181cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 16/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 24 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 5.5 contested possessions There is enough love for Murray that he looks a surefire top-10 selection, with some recruiters believing he could attract a bid just outside the top five, which would be a disaster for the Lions. New draft rules make it much harder for a high-performing club such as Brisbane, who must pay a 20 per cent loading after making the grand final and use no more than two selections to match a bid. Murray will likely start as an attacking half-back flanker in the AFL, but can fill various roles with his speed, endurance, evasiveness, neat skills and smarts. 11. Sam Gayfer Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Key forward, 194cm

DOB: 21/5/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 12.4 disposals, 2.3 goals, 7.1 score involvements



Gayfer has established himself as the top key forward available, with both St Kilda and Collingwood believed to be interested. He is physical, tough, aggressive and athletic, uses his body well to take contested grabs, and kicked loads of goals in the Talent League, under-18 championships and for Parade College. Gayfer can be inconsistent, doesn’t always run to the right spots, and his set-shot kicking is a query, but there is lots to like here. His biggest fans see him as a forward, whereas others think he will be more effective as a defender. Sam Gayfer and Lewis Houndsome run the two-kilometre time trial at this week’s draft combine. via Getty Images 12. Wil Malady Malady’s highlights package is as good as anyone’s, and his aerial prowess, speed and general athleticism make him an enticing prospect. The consensus is he sits somewhere just outside the top 10. Malady had some outstanding performances throughout the year, including five goals in the Power’s Talent League grand final win, but recruiters would love to see him win more of the ball. Malady projects primarily as a third-tall forward, but has occasionally been used on a wing and there are scouts who think he could slot in at half-back as well.



13. Clancy Snell Snell was all the rage early in the season and is still a highly touted prospect, but he didn’t finish the year quite as well as he started it. In his favour was a mature VFL performance for Collingwood that was another tick for his draft resume. Snell is an excellent interceptor, his athleticism and height are ideal for a key defender in the AFL, he is cool in a crisis, and he kicks well. Snell was a major reason Gippsland made the Talent League grand final and is one of three tall backmen who could be selected in the first 15 picks. 14. Tyson Bradley Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Key defender, 196cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 12.6 disposals, 3.4 intercept marks, 3.1 rebound 50s



Tyson Bradley at the draft combine. via Getty Images Bradley’s draft stock is only going up. Vic Metro’s MVP award-winner had to win over critics who pointed to his lack of speed, agility and athleticism, but they can’t argue with his track record. Significant for Bradley was the job he did in the Talent League finals on fellow first-round prospect Sam Gayfer, who was viewed as a test of his limitations. He is highly intelligent, already physically strong, and makes up for his athletic shortcomings with outstanding footwork and positioning. Melbourne are one club monitoring him around this area of the draft. 15. Lochie Burrows Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Utility, 181cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 15 disposals, 3.6 inside 50s, 1.2 goals Burrows is rising fast, with St Kilda believed to be among the clubs tracking him closely. His numbers might not leap off the page, but it is easy to see him succeeding in the AFL with his athletic traits, work ethic and versatility. Burrows had not played down back until this year’s under-18 championships, but his performances opened a few eyes and even saw him used in the same role for the Dragons in the finals. He can leap for marks up forward, run through the midfield or even do a job in defence, so expect him to be snapped up pretty early.



Lochie Burrows competes in the time trial. via Getty Images 16. Leo Steed Swan Districts/Western Australia

Midfielder, 177cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 7/3/2008

WAFL League stats (averages): 14.3 disposals, 5.8 contested possessions, 3.7 tackles Steed is as reliable as they come, and a safe pick in this section of the draft. He might even go earlier, and it will be interesting to see if West Coast or Fremantle trade up for him. Steed is a busy player around stoppages, unafraid to burrow into traffic, loves to tackle, and makes quick and good decisions, particularly by hand. Clubs are increasingly turning to bigger-bodied midfielders, so Steed does not fit that mould, but needs only to look at the likes of Lachie Neale, Touk Miller, Dion Prestia and Zach Merrett for inspiration. 17. Toby Krasna



Related Article Explainer

Draft Talent is just the start. What do footy recruiters look for in young players? Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Wingman, 181cm

DOB: 28/2/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 21.3 disposals, 4.2 inside 50s, 5.1 score involvements Another interesting name to follow. A hamstring injury sidelined Krasna at the end of a breakout under-18 championships, but he was an impressive performer in more of an inside midfield role once he did return, including 13 clearances across his last two matches. Krasna is on track to be a top-20 selection, and could end up closer to 10 than 20. He might be slight, but is willing to get his hands dirty, difficult to tackle, quick, a good decision-maker and regular goalkicker, so don’t be surprised if he keeps pushing up. 18. Gabe Patterson Glenelg/South Australia

Forward, 185cm

DOB: 26/3/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 18 disposals, 1.8 goals, 6.8 score involvements



There was lots of hype about Patterson entering the season – and even top-10 draft projections – but much of this year did not materialise how he hoped. A key reason was a shoulder injury that derailed the first half of his campaign. Patterson showed glimpses of his upside as a dynamic forward at the national championships, but it was afterwards in the SANFL that he reminded everyone of his ability, including 23 disposals and two goals in the under-18s grand final. He is quick, slippery in traffic, has a nice leap, neat skills and kicks some brilliant goals. 19. Jake Eime Central District/South Australia

Defender, 183cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 29/7/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 22.3 disposals, 3.6 rebound 50s, 4.2 intercept possessions Eime is a prototypical running defender who might also spend time on a wing in the AFL. He accelerates quickly, is shifty with the ball, takes opponents on and his kicking has improved. Eime made his case as a potential first-round selection with an impressive national championships, but probably didn’t finish the season quite as strongly as he started it. Like some others in this section of the draft, his range is somewhere between 15 and 25. Fremantle are one club believed to be considering him. 20. Jack Pickett



Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Key forward, 193cm

DOB: 6/3/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 5 disposals, 3 marks, 2 goals What might have been. A season-ending knee injury in April at a Falcons training session changed the course of Pickett’s draft year – and any hope of him being a top-10 selection. Recruiters are now torn on what to do with him, weighing up the risk versus reward he presents. Pickett is often likened to Jack Gunston and Logan Morris as a forward of similar height with good football IQ and craft, and an ability to create separation who is an accurate set-shot kick. He can play a one-out role closer to goal or roam further afield. 21. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) Western Jets/Vic Metro

Forward, 176cm

DOB: 4/7/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 17.9 disposals, 2.9 goals, 3.1 tackles The Bulldogs can theoretically match any bid on El Souki, but so much depends on what happens with incoming superstar Zak Butters and whether they will still have the necessary draft collateral. El Souki missed most of the under-18 championships recovering from a broken ankle, but rebounded to lead the Talent League in goals during the home-and-away season. He is richly talented, powerful, plays with aggression – look out if he tackles you – and has a wonderful goal sense, but does need to improve his running.



22. George Dimer Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Forward, 173cm

DOB: 21/6/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 14.7 disposals, 1.4 goals, 3 tackles Does Dimer’s lack of height even matter anymore? Not everyone can be Nick Watson – and no one suggests Dimer is at his level or a replica of his style – but the Hawks star has paved the way for pint-sized forwards. The Sandringham product has fast feet, is clean at ground level, a creative handballer and seems well suited to the demands of playing the high half-forward role in the AFL. He was also Haileybury College’s school and football captain, and would add leadership and high-end character to whichever club he ends up at. 23. Jackson Phillips Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

Midfielder, 184cm

DOB: 30/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 19.4 disposals, 3.5 inside 50s, 2.8 clearances



Phillips’ good is really good, and he is one of the most skilful players – with both feet – in the draft pool, but recruiters often report wanting to see more from him. He can play on the inside and outside as a midfielder, although he spent the under-18 championships on a wing, in part because of perceived deficiencies in the contest. Some scouts envision him as a midfielder-forward and want to see him put his kicking to better use in the forward half in creating scoring opportunities. 24. Noah Williams Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Midfielder/defender, 176cm

DOB: 22/1/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 21 disposals, 5 clearances, 7.8 tackles Williams is no longer in top-10 contention, and may not even be a first-round pick, after an injury-interrupted season, but he is versatile enough to play in the midfield, across half-back or possibly as a pressure forward. He is small in stature, but quick, tough, competitive, loves to tackle and mostly uses the ball well on his left boot. Williams co-captained Vic Country with Cody Walker and has a reputation as a hard-working and popular teammate. 25. Harvie Cooke



Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Midfielder/forward, 176cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 14/4/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 24.7 disposals, 5.4 inside 50s, 5.9 clearances Not every club rates Cooke in the top 30, but he won most recruiters over with his consistently strong performance, athletic profile, work ethic and forward craft, including being a good mark overhead, particularly for his size. He played a lot through the midfield as a junior, but the expectation is most of his AFL minutes will be in attack while pinch-hitting in the centre. Cooke’s critics query how effective he will be at the top level and whether there is a role for him. 26. Koby LeCras Koby LeCras. via Getty Images West Perth/Western Australia

Forward, 193cm

DOB: 26/4/2008

U18 WAFL stats (averages): 19 disposals, 6 marks, 1 goal



LeCras was viewed as a likely first-round selection entering the season, but similar to fellow tall forward Jack Pickett, a knee injury ruined his plans. He suffered a partially torn ACL while making his WAFL senior debut in April and was not sighted again, but his early season form was strong, including a three-goal effort for the AFL Academy against Richmond’s VFL team. LeCras also recorded a good result in the two-kilometre time trial at this week’s draft combine, but recruiters are keen to see his medical report before making a call on him. 27. Kodah Edwards South Adelaide/South Australia

Midfielder/forward, 184cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 25/7/2008

U18 SANFL stats (averages): 23.5 disposals, 5.5 clearances, 5.2 tackles Another polarising prospect who some scouts wouldn’t draft at all, while others like him more than this ranking. Edwards captained South Australia at the under-18 championships, where he was a consistent performer, and he rounded out his season by playing and acquitting himself well at senior SANFL level. He is not a great athlete or runner, and the suspicion is he will need to make it as a forward to be a successful AFL footballer. Edwards has shown he can be an impact forward who values defence. 28. George Gale



Related Article Draft How Essendon’s plan for pick No.1 is going to help bitter rivals Carlton Claremont/Western Australia

Midfielder, 190cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 6/9/2008

U18 WAFL stats (averages): 31 disposals, 13.7 contested possessions, 5.3 inside 50s Gale is a big midfielder who has a knack for finding the Sherrin and uses his size and strength well in the contest, but recruiters are mulling over how much his lack of speed will dull his influence in the AFL. He graduated to WAFL seniors late in the season and handled the step-up in standard. The general belief is Gale will find a role for himself at the next level and maximise his talents, given his running ability, professionalism and work ethic. 29. Albert MacGowan Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Midfielder/wingman, 187cm

Under-18 All-Australian

DOB: 27/7/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 27.9 disposals, 4.8 clearances, 6.7 score involvements



MacGowan might not be quick – the most common asterisk on his draft portfolio – but you can’t argue with his outstanding production, including claiming Sandringham’s best-and-fairest award. He capped a consistently excellent season by being the only prospective draftee to beat six minutes in the two-kilometre time trial, which again highlighted his running capacity. MacGowan might start his AFL career on a wing, but his ball-winning ability and smarts could see him move inside eventually. 30. Lachie Hicks Western Jets/Vic Metro

Midfielder/forward, 183cm

DOB: 19/1/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 28.5 disposals, 4.6 clearances, 8.3 score involvements Hicks sneaks into this top 30, but has a wide draft range. He is a great athlete – it runs in the family, with his brother Brodie representing Australia in the 4 x 400-metre relay at the world under-20 championships – and put up gaudy numbers all season, including a solid carnival for Vic Metro. The Jets rave about him. Hicks’ upside is tantalising, but a common concern among recruiters is that he is inconsistent with his effort within matches, which could lead to him sliding a little. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: 'Three family members' found dead in Auckland's Papatoetoe
World.content:
Auckland Police say the three people found dead in Papatoetoe are family members.

In a video posted to social media, Counties Manukau District Commander Superintendent Shanan Gray said their condolences were with the family of those who had died.

"I know the family at this time will be reeling at the loss of three family members," Gray said.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406082423112

Police were supporting the family, he said.

Gray reassured the community that it was an isolated incident, and there was no ongoing risk to the public.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier, a man told RNZ he saw a body lying on the front porch of his neighbour's home as police and ambulances arrived at the scene.

Police responded to the scene on Cambridge Terrace after receiving a call at 6.40pm on Thursday about a dead person at an address, Detective Inspector Karen Bright said.

On arrival, Bright said police located the person and two others who were found dead in the home.

"While our investigation is in the early stages, we are not currently looking for anyone else in connection to what has occurred."

Bright said police didn't believe there was any risk to the wider public.

RNZ / Felix Walton

"We are waiting for the completion of the scene examination, which will help us piece together the circumstances that led to this tragic event," Bright said.

"Police recognise events like this hit at the hearts of our communities, and we are doing everything we can to answer the many questions around this devastating incident."

Quentin Fenton told RNZ he saw ambulances and police start showing up before seeing a body lying on a front porch and "blood everywhere".

Ten minutes earlier, Fenton had sent his children up to the shops. They walked past the neighbour's house and waved to a man outside, who smiled back at them.

Fenton said those who live in the house are "good people" who have helped him jumpstart his car.

He said the incident was a "big shock" and "too close to home".

RNZ / Felix Walton

"I've got four kids myself, just a bit freaked out by this."

Fenton said it was "all a bit surreal" and "too much".

Manukau Ward councillor Alf Filipaina said he had spoken to a senior district police officer who reiterated that there was no concern for the wider community.

Filipaina, who was himself in the Police for over 38 years, is concerned by reports that members of the public saw a dead body at the property.

"My humble suggestion, being in the Police for quite a few years and seeing quite a few incidents that people should never see, is just to seek help for themselves as well, it's just so important to do that.

World.title: Media watchdog demands answers after Samoan PM's security reportedly deletes journalist's photos
World.content:
The Journalists Association of Samoa (JAWS) is demanding answers over the removal of a journalist's camera and the deletion of photographs taken while she was covering a public event.

According to the Samoa Observer, Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt's son reportedly deleted photographs taken by one of the newspaper's female reporters at a police event held at the Government Building in Apia on Tuesday morning.

According to the report, the journalist was told by one of the La'auli's security personnel that "there is a law that prevents the Samoa Observer from taking any pictures of the Prime Minister".

RNZ Pacific has contacted the Samoa government for comment and is yet to receive a response.

JAWS said it was "deeply disturbed" by the reported treatment of the Samoa Observer journalist by members of PM La'auli's security detail.

The Pacific Islands News Association (PINA) reported that the group has called for the circumstances surrounding the incident to be properly established.

JAWS said journalists attending public events have a professional right and responsibility to observe, record and report what took place.

This includes when senior public officials or people connected to them are present.

The Association said any legitimate security concern should have been dealt with through lawful and proportionate procedures.

"Security cannot become a pretext for obstructing legitimate journalism," it said.

The Association also said that issues or disagreements with media organisations should not be handled through physical interference with equipment or the deletion of material.

"If there are concerns about the conduct or reporting of a journalist, there are established avenues for complaint, correction and legal redress," it said.

World.title: At least 12 whales dead on Ninety Mile Beach as rescue continues
World.content:
DOC staff, iwi and volunteers are battling difficult conditions as they try to rescue a group of whales stranded on Ninety Mile Beach in the Far North.

Joel Lauterbach, northern North Island operations director for the Department of Conservation, said 12 to 15 pygmy killer whales had died so far, while an unknown number had been refloated.

The whales, which could grow up to 2.6 metres long, were scattered across several kilometres of beach.

They were roughly 10km north of Hukatere, a key access point on Ninety Mile Beach/Te Oneroa-a-Tōhe.

Lauterbach said DOC was first notified of the stranding about 7pm on Thursday.

Staff rushed to the site but conditions were challenging and hazardous, due to an incoming tide and fading light, and they withdrew when it was no longer safe to continue the response.

Conditions remained challenging today, he said.

DOC was working closely with Far North iwi Ngāti Kuri, Ngāi Takoto and Te Aupōuri.

The dead whales were being moved for burial and tikanga processes were underway.

Lauterbach said the department's immediate focus was working with iwi and gathering information to understand the full circumstances of the stranding.

It's not the first time pygmy killer whales have come to grief on Ninety Mile Beach.

A dozen of the rare whales stranded in 2018, also in difficult conditions, with eight survivors transported to the calmer waters of Rārawa Beach on the opposite coast.

World.title: Fijian PM Rabuka confident of numbers as parliament debates crucial constitution bill
World.content:
Lawmakers in Fiji are set to debate and vote on a government bill on Friday to amend the country's constitution, after a marathon parliamentary sitting that stretched late into Thursday night (NZ time).

Fiji's government tabled its 150-page [https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Bill-No.-32-Constitution-Amendment-Bill-2026.pdf Constitution (Amendment) Bill for the first time on Wednesday evening.

MPs were given less than 48 hours to read it ahead of the debate, which is scheduled for later this evening.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's coalition wants to replace the 2013 Constitution and needs the bill to be passed in parliament on its second and third readings to put it to a referendum.

Rabuka needs a two-thirds majority - 36 out of 53 MPs currently in parliament - vote in favour for the bill to progress to the next stage.

Rabuka told local reporters in a news briefing on Thursday that he was confident he had the numbers.

He said if the bill fails to pass, the country will go to the polls - though a date is yet to be confirmed.

Meanwhile, the Centre for Democracy & Dialogue (CDD), an independent civil society organisation, described the text of the Fijian government's draft constitution in the bill as "a significant downgrade" from the draft constitution proposed by a Constitution Review Commission released last month.

The Commission's recommendations included repealing coup immunity provisions of the 2013 Constitution, giving the Great Council of Chiefs constitutional recognition, replacing the electoral and parliamentary system, and reducing the military's role in national politics.

"Some of the most laudable elements of the [Constitution Review Commission] Draft Constitution, which would have provided significant democratic and accountability safeguards, have all been removed," CDD chief executive Nilesh Lal said.

World.title: Fire destroys Apparelmaster warehouse in Petone
World.content:
The Professional Firefighters Union says crews were "on the back foot" responding to a devastating blaze in Lower Hutt overnight.

The fire that engulfed a commercial building in Petone shortly after midnight on Friday escalated to third alarm, the union said, drawing in crews from across the Wellington region.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said the fire had been brought under control by early morning, but crews were still on the scene on Friday and the damage was extensive.

Apparelmaster, the business operating from the site, has been contacted for comment.

Police told RNZ there were no injuries and no ongoing road closures.

Do you know more? Contact RNZ at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hayden Overton, who works at a business nearby, said the fire did not spread far and his business was not affected.

"The road was all blocked off and there were fire engines everywhere, no smoke or anything, and then a whole load of police turned up," he said.

He said the area had a strong smell but the situation appeared to be under control.

NZPFU Wellington secretary and station officer Kurt Walsh told RNZ the warehouse on Petone Ave had been "destroyed" and crews would have been scrambling to get to the blaze.

He said the nearest station to the fire - Hutt City - had been shut down in 2021 due to toxic black mould.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Crews had been relocated to stations 10 minutes away, Walsh said, but it meant firefighters couldn't respond as quickly to emergencies in and around the Petone area.

"This morning... they would have been tipped out to a building fire and they'd be going, 'shit'. Y'know, you're already on the back foot because it's taking longer for you to get there and it really does weigh heavy on them.

"It's been like this for five years and it does impact the staff severely."

RNZ has contacted FENZ for comment.

Walsh said an operational Hutt City station may not have changed the outcome of the building blaze in Petone, but said its ongoing closure put the community at risk.

Bureaucracy within FENZ was hindering progress on reinstating it, he said.

Walsh said the area was busy with thousands of residents and also industrial complexes, and FENZ needed to "pull trigger" on a Hutt City station.

"Someone's just got to make a decision and go, we're doing this, and that's it - y'know, they need to put the community first."

FENZ told RNZ in August that Lower Hutt had the same number of firefighters responding to emergencies as it always had.

"We moved our people to Avalon because their previous building wasn't safe," the organisation said.

"Operational requirements for Hutt City will be approved by the end of September, and a business case is underway. That work tells us what's needed, where, and what it costs."

World.title: Man charged in relation to Rotorua triple homicide granted bail
World.content:
A man charged with assault in relation to a triple homicide in Rotorua has been granted bail.

Emergency services arrived at the home on High St in Glenholme shortly before 10.30pm on 7 September.

They found the bodies of two young children, aged 3 years and 11 months old, along with a critically injured woman who died at the scene.

Police began a homicide investigation and a man in his early 20s appeared in the Rotorua District Court the following day, charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship.

He reappeared in court today and was granted electronically monitored bail.

World.title: Auditor-General won't investigate LNG yet but 'remains interested' in Govt plans
World.content:
The Auditor-General will not launch an inquiry into the Government's plans to build an LNG terminal, but says his office "remains interested" in the project.

His letter declining the inquiry reveals officials were still working on the case for LNG, including who would pay for it.

Consumer and climate groups requested an inquiry in August over what they said were concerns about transparency and value for money.

The signatories - including Consumer NZ, Lawyers for Climate Action and the Sustainable Business Network - said the process was being "rushed towards an artificial deadline" without properly considering the alternatives.

The Government confirmed in June it was proceeding with plans for a $1 billion-plus facility in Taranaki, saying importing liquefied natural gas was the best option to see off a "dry year" risk while more renewable energy was developed.

The proposal has been widely questioned, including by some gentailers.

As late as last month, Energy Minister Simeon Brown said a contract could still be signed during the election campaign, so the terminal could be up and running in time for winter 2028.

However, following a Cabinet committee meeting on 23 September, the Government said it would no longer try to sign a contract before the election.

Energy Minister Simeon Brown has said a contract could still be signed during the election campaign. Calvin Samuel/RNZ

In his letter declining an inquiry, Auditor-General Grant Taylor said his office had met with Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) officials.

"From those discussions, we understand that work is still underway to update and review the financial, economic, and strategic case for an LNG fuel solution and to identify a preferred model or provider," he wrote.

That included "understanding who would bear the costs and how any cost-recovery arrangements would work".

The Government originally said the costs of the terminal - which will be built by a third-party provider and leased back - would be covered by a levy on all electricity users.

However, it scrapped that plan in June and said details on alternative funding would be revealed "in due course".

Officials were also still working on the implications for electricity prices, security of energy supply, investment incentives, and other sources of energy, Taylor said.

"We will remain interested in this process as it progresses but, as the Government is yet to decide the approach it will take and select a provider, we do not propose carrying out inquiry work now," he wrote.

"Our specific interests, once a model has been decided and/or a provider selected, will be related to demonstrating value for money."

That included whether the "expected costs, benefits, risks, and beneficiaries were clearly understood, including who would bear the costs and how any cost-recovery arrangements were justified".

MBIE also needed to show that alternatives to LNG had been identified and assessed on a comparable basis, that its preferred approach was supported by robust analysis, and that the scale of public resources being used was proportionate to the problem.

World.title: South Island's new weather radar gets a home
World.content:
The Government has announced the site has been chosen for a new radar for the top of the South Island, to address a black spot in the country's weather forecasting coverage.

The project has been fast-tracked by the Government with funding of up to $5 million, following the severe storms and flooding last July.

South Island Minister James Meager said the Nelson Tasman region had limited radar coverage as it relied largely on the Wellington radar, which could not adequately monitor parts of northwest Tasman.

"The region has experienced several high-impact flooding events in recent years, including five states of emergency since 2011. The new radar will make a huge difference in better preparing communities for future disasters."

The radar will be located near Horoirangi Peak, about 15km northeast of Nelson City at 630m above sea level. It is expected to be operational by mid-2027.

MetService will install and operate the radar, with ongoing annual operating costs expected to be around $260,000. It will feature modern Doppler dual-polarisation technology, which provides more accurate rainfall estimates and enhanced weather monitoring capability.

MetService general manager of observing systems Kevin Alder. Samantha Gee / RNZ

MetService general manager of observing systems Kevin Alder said the Prime Minister's announcement last July that the Government would fund a radar for the region (came as "a bit of a surprise"), and a lot of work had gone on since then to make it happen.

He said MetService had evaluated around 10 sites on the eastern hills around Nelson and the central hills around Moutere and over towards Motueka and the Kahurangi National Park, and the Horoirangi site was chosen because it was at the right altitude and had landowners willing to host the infrastructure.

Alder said the key challenges were finding a location that was not too high, as the radar would miss the weather and not too low where it would be blocked by mountains and ranges.

He said the new radar would provide hydrologists, Civil Defence and the community with real-time information they could trust. The radar would provide information about precipitation, wind fields, thunderstorms and hail.

"At the moment the coverage from the Wellington radar doesn't have the level of detail that is required, so we're going to see an increase in confidence in their ability to make decisions for the regions.

"It's about making sure communities are well informed and able to respond in a timely manner because we're all here to protect life and property."

Minister for the South Island James Meager, centre, at an announcement about the location of the weather radar for Nelson Tasman. Samantha Gee / RNZ

Andrew Stephens of Ngāti Tama ki Te Waipounamu said the Horoirangi maunga and surrounding area was very dear to iwi.

His great-grandmother Hūria Mātenga, her husband and several other Māori had helped to rescue people off the American-built brigantine Delaware, when it was caught in a storm and wrecked on the rocks off the coast of nearby Whakapuaka in 1863.

"It's quite apt that the knowledge we will gather prior to an event will be available from this maunga," he said.

"It's going to save lives. It's going to help industry and it's going to help the community."

Tasman Mayor Tim King said things had moved relatively quickly, since the Government announced it would fund the radar after last year's floods and it would be another "very valuable tool" when it came to preparing for floods.

"We already invest significantly, between Nelson and Tasman, in both the rain-gauging network and the river monitoring network. All of that carries a significant risk because as we found during the June-July events, they can be damaged, destroyed and become inoperable," he said.

"This provides a real degree of resilience because it's separated from the actual weather event itself."

King said while it would provide more data, people were still needed on the ground to interpret the information that came in from different sources, in order to provide advice to incident controllers and decision makers.

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith said it was a relief to know the radar would soon be up and running, as the region had dealt with "too many emergency events" over the last decade.

"It's a really difficult call as to whether you're going to evacuate people, not wanting to put people out and declare a state of emergency and not having adequate information to be able to make those big calls was one of the reasons that both myself, Tim King and others were such strong advocates for getting the additional technology."

But Smith said there was no "single magic bullet" to manage the risks associated with storm events and climate change.

"There will always be a level of risk, but what we can do with hand-on-heart is say that this new equipment will enable us to better manage those risks in the future, it will save lives and it will make our community more resilient."

The location of the new weather radar for the top of the South Island. Supplied

Retired Tasman District Council hydrologist Martin Doyle said he had campaigned for a weather radar to be installed in the region since 2010 (when there was a massive flood in the Aorere River) and hydrology staff were left without knowledge of where the rainfall had come from.

He said there were many small river catchments across the region and it was impossible to have a rain gauge in each one.

Retired Tasman District Council hydrologist Martin Doyle. Samantha Gee / RNZ

"Having the ability to see where rain is falling in a very confined area is going to be very beneficial for hydrologists but also the community members out there can do their own analysis and make their own decisions by having that radar."

World.title: Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad
World.content:
Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Selectors confirmed on Thursday night that Maddinson had been called into the Test squad after not featuring in Australia's red-ball side for almost 10 years.

Sam Harper has also been drafted in as a back-up wicketkeeper, with a finger fracture now officially ruling Josh Inglis out of the first Test in Durban starting next Friday.

Inglis was hurt while playing in the series-opening ODI against South Africa last week, with further scans back home in Perth revealing a fracture.

Cameron Green is in doubt for the first Test after being injured in the Potchefstroom ODI against South Africa. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

There are now similar concerns around Green following the third ODI in Potchefstroom on Wednesday after he hurt his abdomen trying to pull a ball while batting in Australia's dead-rubber win.

Australian medical staff will now keep close watch on the allrounder, who will be "assessed further" in the coming week.

Regardless, the latest abdominal injury will raise question marks over Green's ability to bowl, after having not done so yet in a game on this tour.

The one bit of good news for Australia is opener Matt Renshaw has been cleared of a wrist injury after being hurt while fielding in the final ODI.

But the injuries do leave Australia's line-up for the first Test largely up in the air with up to two spots in the top-six unclear if Green is not fit.

Inglis had stood a chance of coming into the side for Marnus Labuschagne if selectors had opted to drop the Queenslander for the series opener.

Australia Test batter Nic Maddinson reveals testicular cancer diagnosis Former Australia batter Nic Maddinson has revealed he underwent chemotherapy for testicular cancer.

Maddinson could now fill one of those roles, with Cooper Connolly the other reserve batter in the Test squad.

Maddinson last played a Test on Boxing Day in 2016, and has since overcome a battle with testicular cancer to restart his cricket career.

The 34-year-old did not play a first-class match last summer, but struck 126 for NSW in a one-day match against Victoria last week.

Harper looms as another option, after being called into his first Australian squad at age 29.

The Victorian was the second-leading run-scorer in last summer's Sheffield Shield with 677 at 35.63 and is fresh off hitting a century for Australia A against India A in Pudcherry.

"Sam gives us wicketkeeping cover as Josh continues his recovery, while Nic provides flexibility throughout the batting order," chief selector George Bailey said.

Australia will play an intra-squad warm-up match in Potchefstroom this weekend, before moving to Durban on Monday to commence preparations for the first of three Tests.

AAP

World.title: Pallister and Short continue winning form at short course title
World.content:
Lani Pallister and Sam Short, Australia's stars of the pool in 2026, have continued their terrific year with more success at the national short course championships in Sydney.

The pair, who had already scooped a hatful of Commonwealth and Pan Pacific titles, made it five Australian titles between them in a week at Olympic Park Aquatic Centre.

They are intent on ending their year with more gold at the world short course championships in Beijing in December.

Pallister, having already lifted the 200 metre and 1,500m freestyle titles, powered to victory over 400m on the penultimate night of racing on Thursday, as did Short, who had already won the 800m.

Forrester breaks 17yo record Jenna Forrester has never competed at the short course world championships, but winning a silver and a gold in the same evening, also beating a 17-year-old a national record, has put her in pole position to do so.

Short was in an imperious mood as he took the 16-lap title in 3 minutes and 35.16 seconds, easily inside the Beijing qualifying time of 3:39.14, which convinced him the world record of 3:32.25 was sure to fall at the famed Water Cube venue that hosted the 2008 Olympic swimming program.

"I think that's gone in a couple of months at [the] world short course," Brisbane star Short said.

"I haven't swum much short course … in some ways it keeps you hungry."

Former short course 400m world champion Elijah Winnington, though, was just outside the time needed, as he clocked 3:39.24 to finish runner-up.

Pallister was in a class of her own as she prevailed in 3:54.55, the fastest women's time ever recorded in Australia, shaving 0.03 seconds off the old mark set by Ariarne Titmus six years ago.

Runner-up Jenna Forrester, who won 400m individual medley gold in a national record, was 0.65 seconds outside of qualifying time.

In the women's 50m, Iona Anderson continued her breakthrough year by completing her sweep of the backstroke events, clocking 25.88 seconds as she got closer to Kaylee McKeown's Australian record of 25.35 seconds.

AAP

World.title: A town, a team and a dream come together as Newcastle rises as one
World.content:
All week the scribes have been falling over themselves to come up with the best way to describe what the Knights mean to Newcastle ahead of Sunday's grand final against the Roosters.

The love between the team and the town is easy to valorise and even easier to fetishise as you lose yourself in coalfield cliches and well-worn stories about 1997.

The truth is it's something that's easier to feel than it is to describe. In a league of franchises, they are a club in the truest sense of the word because they are a vessel for the community, for its hopes, dreams and fears, for its joy, sorrow and pride.

From tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle has gone Knights crazy From fresh tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle goes all out ahead of the NRL grand final.

They are the prism through which Newcastle feels it's feelings and at their best they become avatars of every quality the Hunter likes about itself — that they are hard-working and loyal to their mates, that they're courageous and daring, that they can walk as tall as anyone and fear nothing.

The Knights make it easier to cry, to dream of better times, to roar with triumph if they arrive and despair if they don't, to tell someone you love them or show them just how much.

The Knights are a way of life. The Knights are home. The Knights will make you believe the words of the club song, that this game is their game as surely as this town is their town.

The Knights are Newcastle and Newcastle is the Knights, and both mean more to the other than they could ever really say.

That meaning was in the tears that dried on the faces of current players, former legends and fans alike as Sandon Smith went on his run to paradise last Sunday.

Cody Hopwood, who will be the youngest prop to start a grand final since Josh Perry did for the Knights in their 2001 premiership at just 20 years of age, is 196cm and 105kg of Maitland iron with a grip like a pitbull's bite and a firm belief that the best way through any rugby league problem is to run directly through it.

Through this semi-final run he's forgotten what fear feels like, if he ever knew at all, and while he's a great chat for a young fella he doesn't even know what to call the thing that rose inside him upon realising Newcastle were through to the grand final.

"I was on the 30-metre line in tears. I just wanted to get down to him and give him a cuddle, even if I wasn't moving the fastest," Hopwood said of Smith.

"I just started crying, I don't know what came over me, all these emotions. I can't really describe the feeling."

The meaning is in the red and blue lights that have shot into the night sky all week from Newcastle City Hall in the middle of town and the paint that adorns houses throughout the region.

Old newspaper article shows Knights blueprint Writing in 1987, Newcastle's inaugural coach spelled out the player that would lead to club success.

It's in the ink that fans are putting on their bodies, which the tattooists can't do fast enough.

It's in the red and blue sausages that aren't quite as hard to find as grand final tickets but are flying off the shelves as quickly as they come in.

A trip to five different butchers earlier this week in an effort to bring some back to Sydney as proof of the terminal case of grand final fever that had broken out ended fruitlessly.

Butchers are normally as good at chewing the fat as they are cutting the meat, but the demand had them harried. On Tuesday morning alone, one had sold 50kg in half an hour.

Selling out Hunter Stadium for a grand final watch party didn't take nearly that long — on Thursday, Knights fans snapped up all 22,500 tickets in four minutes.

That shouldn't be a surprise. Newcastle shows up for their Knights, shining armour or not. This is the team which once went a whole season with only one win to show for it but had its average attendance rise from the year before.

Aside from the COVID years, where crowds were restricted, the Knights have played 449 games in Newcastle since 1988 and only ten of them attracted fewer than 10,000 people.

The Newcastle fans have never abandoned the Knights. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

That's through five wooden spoon seasons and, before this year, just four finals wins since that last premiership in 2001.

In darker days, the club took that support for granted. Their people loved them so much they didn't need their team to love them back.

But they never stopped coming, like they always knew it would work out right and they could start anew.

It's in those crowds that Tyson Frizell, once of the Illawarra but now an adopted son of another steel city, first felt it.

"I got a sense of it when I was out and about but it's not until we got everyone back at our home games that I understood how much of rugby league is in people's DNA," Frizell said.

"It's what they look forward to every week, it can make their week better or worse.

"It felt like home straight away. It's easy for it to feel like home because people are so welcoming.

"It's a country town on a big scale, people know who you are and are willing to do anything for you — they reach out, there's a community feel.

The Knights are on the verge of their first premiership since 2001. (Getty Images via All Sport: Nick Laham)

"There's great people everywhere, but there's nothing like Newcastle people."

If you don't have a ticket to the grand final or the watch party there's still other options.

If you want to go Hollywood style, Tower Cinemas will be showing the game on at least three big screens, like they did for the finals wins over New Zealand and Penrith.

Or, if you're after a wilder crowd, every pub in the area will be heaving, like they have been all week as they've filled with talk about last weekend's heroics and confident assertions that someone like Mat Croker is a dark horse for the Clive Churchill Medal.

The region is a fertile ground for public houses, bowls clubs and various other watering holes and it does them better than some places do cathedrals.

When Fletcher Sharpe, Cessnock's greatest export since the Johns brothers, gets asked what the home of the Goannas will be like on game day he just shakes his head.

"It'll go off, I can tell you that. The Leagues Club will be packed with people who couldn't get tickets to go down," Sharpe said.

"I know it'll be wild."

The Newcastle fans have been going wild all week. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The sense of anticipation hangs in the air like smoke. "Up the Knights" has replaced hello, goodbye and thank you.

It is a conversation starter and ender, and it can fill the gaps in the middle. If you say it in Newcastle, even if it's to someone you've just met, it is proof you're not a stranger.

Plenty of Novocastrians who have gone far and wide are planning to head home for the weekend, just to be there if this becomes a dream from which they never have to awaken.

They have been waiting so long for this. Before last week, Dane Gagai was the only player in the NRL that had played in a preliminary final for Newcastle.

The last man standing from their most recent premiership was Timana Tahu and he's been retired for 12 years. Tony Butterfield, who started up front for them in 1997, is 60 years old and both Johns brothers are past 50.

Some fans were there during those old days and crave a win to make them feel young again as they don faded jerseys with long-vanished sponsors.

Newcastle's past triumphs have been at the forefront all week. (Getty Images via All Sport: Nick Laham)

Some remember it from childhood and only now, a generation later and after going to hell and back, have a true appreciation for what it means.

But for plenty, this is their first time. They have heard all the old stories so many times, they have seen the photos of Joey on the skateboard or heard Matty exhorting that it was better than Lego or watched the tape of the ambush of Parramatta in 2001 until it replaced their own dim memories, until it was more real than their own lives.

This is their first chance to be part of it for true, to live a new version of legends they were raised on, to roll back the nostalgic fog and realise that history isn't always about the past.

To do so, they'll have to beat the Roosters and taking on a team like that is to defy an empire, even if Newcastle have found a way to weaponise attacking miracles.

The odds are against them but given they have been each of the past three weeks it feels like that doesn't matter.

Newcastle out for salvation ten years after horror season In 2016, Newcastle hit rock bottom in a season where they won just one game. Ten years later, one more win can deliver them a premiership.

The team will leave for Sydney on Saturday morning. The bus route has been detailed in the Newcastle Herald and on all the club's socials. There are no secrets left.

The people will line the road for miles, and they will wave their flags and lift their signs and go wild for one last look before their heroes try to bring back a little piece of heaven and for one last chance to prove they've loved them all along.

The Knights will leave for their date with destiny and on Sunday they'll meet their fate armed with everything their people have got, which is all they've ever really needed.

Their fans will dominate the day and they will chant that three-syllable symphony that fills stadiums and hearts as, far from home and at the edge of a dream a quarter-century in the making, team and town will prove once more that they are one.

World.title: Carlton continues push for AFLW top four in win over Hawks
World.content:
Carlton have weathered wet and wild conditions to leap into the AFLW's top four with a 12-point win over Hawthorn.

On a day when profiting from key moments defined the Princes Park clash, four minutes of first-quarter magic set the Blues up for a 5.6 (36) to 3.6 (24) victory on Thursday.

Carlton fired three scintillating goals in unrelenting rain while keeping the Hawks scoreless until midway through the second term.

But the visitors suddenly found themselves firmly in the contest when forward Poppy Stockwell and midfielder Kaitlyn Ashmore kicked back-to-back third-quarter majors to level the scores.

Carlton slotted two goals either side of three-quarter time to put themselves in the box seat for victory.

Midfielder Abbie McKay (33 disposals, six clearances) was typically inspirational for Carlton while Irish star Erone Fitzpatrick posted 26 disposals and two goals to help last season's preliminary finalists (6-2) go third on the ladder.

"[It was] great Irish weather, so the Irish are used to this," Fitzpatrick told Channel 7.

"It was just the kind of game that you just need to keep getting the ball forward, whether it's a handball, a kick on the ground, or just a surge kick."

For the Hawks (4-4), the loss keeps them out of the congested top eight with four games remaining as they struggled to capitalise on their 52 inside 50s.

Regardless, star ruck Lucy Wales shone with 20 disposals and nine hitouts, while midfielder Eliza West registered 22 disposals.

Hawthorn had the first seven inside-50s of the match, but it was Carlton who drew first blood when Sophie McKay scooped up a loose ball and kicked a goal.

Moments later, Blues midfielder Dayna Finn capitalised on a rogue handball from defender Lavinia Cox before Fitzpatrick added another major.

Trailing 19-0 at the first break, the Hawks were finally rewarded when Stockwell kicked a goal to close the deficit to 12 points at halftime.

Hawthorn upped the ante again, giving the Blues barely any attacking ball as they scored two majors before Fitzpatrick grabbed her second of the evening to re-establish the home team's advantage.

With the game in the balance, Carlton's Keeley Sherar poked the ball through the centre sticks and the home team emerged victorious.

AAP

World.title: Australia and India to kick off next year's Cricket World Cup
World.content:
Australia will launch its defence of the men's Cricket World Cup in South Africa next year with a blockbuster opener against India, the powerhouse it defeated to win the crown in 2023.

As the fixtures for the 2027 event in southern Africa were unveiled on Thursday, Pat Cummins's side learned it would take on the title favourite and world number one side on October 7 in its first match in Cape Town.

Australia 2027 men's Cricket World Cup draw India — Thursday October 7, Cape Town, South Africa Qualifier — Tuesday, October 12, Paarl, South Africa Zimbabwe — Friday, October 15, Harare, Zimbabwe Afghanistan — Monday, October 18 KuGompo City, South Africa Pakistan — Friday, October 22 Paarl, South Africa

Both teams will also feature in a potentially explosive group A with Pakistan.

The India-Pakistan clash will take place at Johannesburg ‌in the famed "Bullring" atmosphere of the Wanderers' ground just three days after the Australia match, and that venue will also stage the final on November 21.

Also in Australia's group will be co-hosts Zimbabwe, which it has just beaten 3-0 in an one-day international series at the same Harare venue, as well as Afghanistan and one of two qualifiers yet to be decided.

Its last group fixture will be against Pakistan at Paarl, where Australia will also play the qualifying side.

The other group looks potentially even more challenging, with co-host South Africa, desperately seeking its first men's World Cup, facing England, New Zealand, Sri Lanka and another qualifier.

The best four sides will then go on to the semifinals, which will both be played in South Africa.

Men's 2027 Cricket World Cup draw. (ICC)
